<meta>This page serves as the introduction to Gustav Theodor Fechner’s foundational 1860 work, which established the field of psychophysics. Fechner introduces his ambition to bridge the gap between the physical and the mental through mathematical measurement.</meta>

## PREFACE.

<margin>II.</margin>
By psychophysics—following the explanation provided in more detail in Chapter 2—I mean a doctrine that, although ancient in its objective, is presented here in such a new way regarding its framing and treatment that the new name should be found neither unfitting nor unnecessary. In short, it is an exact science of the functional relationships between the body and the soul <note>German: *Leib und Seele*. This refers to the classical philosophical "mind-body problem," which Fechner sought to solve through mathematical means.</note>.

As an exact science, psychophysics—much like physics—must be grounded in experience and the mathematical connection of empirical facts. This requires a means of measurement <term>measure (German: *Mass*): a standardized scale used to quantify observations</term> for what experience provides and, where such a measure is not yet available, seeking it out. Since the measurement of physical quantities already exists, the primary task of this work will be to establish a measurement for mental <note>German: *psychischen*. In this historical scientific context, "psychic" refers to sensory and mental phenomena rather than the supernatural.</note> quantities, which has been lacking until now. The second task will be to explore the practical applications and developments arising from this.

It will be shown that establishing a mental measurement is not merely a matter for the scholar’s desk or philosophical insight <note>original: *Aperçus*. This refers to a brief summary or an intuitive grasp of a subject.</note>, but requires a broad foundation in experience. Based on both my own investigations and those of others, I believe I have provided sufficient evidence here to secure the principle of this measurement, and enough examples of its application that its utility will be recognized. However—

<summary>Gustav Fechner introduces "psychophysics" as a new exact science dedicated to the mathematical relationship between the physical body and the mental soul. He identifies the primary goal of this book as establishing a method for measuring mental quantities, similar to how physics measures physical ones.</summary>
<keywords>psychophysics, body and soul, physics, physical quantities, mental quantities, measurement, experience, scientific principle</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Gustav Theodor Fechner’s "Elements of Psychophysics" (1860). It follows from the previous page where Fechner argued that establishing a mental measurement requires a broad empirical foundation. VI

...the empirical basis for the development of psychophysical **measurement** <term>measurement (German: *Masslehre*): the formal theory and system of quantifying psychological sensations</term> still requires great expansion, and what has been provided in terms of applications only demonstrates that incomparably more will need to be provided in the future.

In short, psychophysics, in the form in which it appears here, is a doctrine still in its first state of becoming; therefore, one should not misunderstand the title of this work, ***Elements***, as if it were a presentation of the essentials of an already established and formalized doctrine—an elementary textbook—but rather the presentation of the beginnings of a doctrine that is still in its elemental <note>German: *Elementarzustande*. Fechner uses a wordplay here: his book is titled "Elements" not because it is a simple "Elementary" guide for students, but because it deals with the "Elemental" or embryonic state of a brand-new science.</note> state. One should not, therefore, place demands on this work that would be placed on an elementary textbook. It frequently offers investigations, detailed explanations, and compilations that would be quite inappropriate in such a textbook, but which may contribute to making such a textbook possible one day. I believe that what was required—maintaining a focus on specific points of investigation and summarizing the results in specific directions—will not be found lacking.

However, just as little as an elementary textbook, one should not look here for a collection of the entire material of psychophysics, but rather primarily for that which belongs to the foundation of psychophysical measurement and enters into its applications. Countless things that form a subject of psychophysics could find no place here, because they have not yet progressed far enough to be included in such a system.

While some things in this work may already be too much and others too little, there is certainly reason to be lenient in this regard, since formally almost nothing and materially only scattered fragments existed upon which I could stand and to which I could refer; but a house cannot be built without hauling stones to it; and where the plan must be drafted even before the house is built, one can

<summary>Fechner clarifies that his work is not a basic textbook for an established field, but rather the foundational "elements" of a new science still in its infancy. He asks for the reader's patience as he gathers the "stones" (data and theory) to build the house of psychophysics.</summary>
<keywords>psychophysics, theory of measurement, Elements of Psychophysics, scientific foundations, empirical research, methodology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Gustav Theodor Fechner’s "Elements of Psychophysics" (1860). Fechner is concluding his introductory remarks on the "elemental" state of his new science, admitting that this first attempt at a formal system of psychological measurement will naturally contain imperfections and require future refinement.</meta>

VII

...in the first attempt at this, not everything is positioned correctly and does not yet have the right measure. Every subsequent attempt of this kind will be able to be more complete from one perspective, and shorter and more precise from the other.

No less than for formal deficiencies, I must surely ask for indulgence regarding factual errors that may have remained in this writing, especially in the treatment of so many subtle, difficult, and new questions, such as will present themselves even more in the following parts than in this one. In the long course of these investigations, while holding to general principles that have become increasingly firm, I have traversed so many wrong paths and obscurities in detail—for the entire field lay previously buried in obscurity—that I do not dare to hope I have left them all behind in the current revision <term>revision (German: *Redaction*): the process of editing and preparing a manuscript for publication</term>. But I would not be able to offer these investigations at all if I wanted to wait for complete certainty in this regard; and yet I hold the confidence that, since so much in this doctrine has gradually corrected and clarified itself, it will also be capable of further progress in this direction.

Ultimately, the only question is whether what is offered here, and how it is offered, provides a sustainable and fruitful beginning. Should this be found to be the case, one should not take the omissions and errors too seriously; it will at least be their merit to have provoked something better <note>Fechner is humbly suggesting that even his mistakes will be useful if they inspire other scientists to find the correct answers.</note>.

In this, I am far from saying that what is presented in this writing is something absolutely new, and it would likely be a poor recommendation if it were. Rather, in order to do justice to rightful claims of priority <note>German: *Prioritätsansprüchen*. Fechner is acknowledging that others may have had similar ideas before him and wants to ensure they receive proper credit.</note> from the outset, and at the same time to show that something more than a subjective whim underlies this work, I will briefly touch upon a few historical points right here in the preface, which I will go into more detail in their proper place and finally in a special historical chapter.

<margin>
Preliminary remarks, methodology, historical points, priority claims, revision, errors, principles
</margin>

<summary>Fechner acknowledges that his work is a first attempt filled with potential errors and formal flaws, but argues that a "fruitful beginning" is more important than waiting for perfection. He also signals his intent to address the historical origins and previous scientific claims related to his theories.</summary>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of Gustav Theodor Fechner’s "Elements of Psychophysics" (1860). Fechner is transitioning from a humble defense of his work's "elemental" nature to establishing its scientific lineage. He identifies the "father" of his field and argues that his new "measurement principle" is actually a rigorous synthesis of established mathematical and physical laws discovered by his predecessors.</meta>

->VIII<-

The empirical law, which forms the main foundation of the <term>science of mental measurement</term> <note>German: *psychische Masslehre*; the study of quantifying internal experiences</note>, has long since been established by various researchers in different fields. It has been expressed and experimentally proven with a relative degree of generality, notably by <term>E. H. Weber</term> <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878) was a German physician whose research into the "just noticeable difference" in touch and weight perception became the foundation for Fechner's work</note>, whom I would broadly call the father of <term>psychophysics</term>. On the other hand, the mathematical function—which represents the most general and important case of applying our <term>measurement principle</term>—was also established long ago on this law for specific cases belonging to psychophysics. This was done by various mathematicians, physicists, and philosophers, such as <term>Bernoulli</term> (<term>Laplace</term>, <term>Poisson</term>), <term>Euler</term> (<term>Herbart</term>, <term>Drobisch</term>), and <term>Steinheil</term> (<term>Pogson</term>), and has been reproduced or accepted by other researchers. Although all of this did not occur from the perspective of a <term>mental measure</term> <note>German: *psychisches Mass*</note>, and without attracting much attention until now, it will easily become clear—once the principle of this measurement is explained later in Chapter 7—that it was already contained in the function established by those researchers.

Accordingly, our mental measurement is indeed a generalization from one side and, from another side, the clear statement of the significance of what already existed as a mental measure. Referring to this history should help reduce the mistrust that the announcement of such a measurement might initially provoke. The problem of this measurement is indeed not the problem of the <term>squaring of the circle</term> <note>A classic geometric problem that was proven impossible to solve; Fechner uses it as a metaphor for a "fool's errand"</note> or a *<term>perpetual motion machine</term>* <note>original: "Perpetuum mobile"; a hypothetical machine that works forever without an energy source, which violates the laws of physics</note>; rather, it has effectively been solved by researchers whose names are a guarantee of the validity of the solution.

After having reflected upon these merits of earlier researchers regarding the main subject of this writing, I would neglect a primary duty if I did not also acknowledge the equally essential support and promotion that I myself received from my...

<summary>Fechner argues that his science of psychophysics is not a new or impossible invention, but a synthesis of established laws and mathematical functions previously identified by giants of science like E. H. Weber and Bernoulli. He positions his work as a formalization of these existing principles into a unified system of mental measurement.</summary>

<keywords>psychophysics, mental measurement, E. H. Weber, measurement principle, historical precedent, mathematical psychology, Weber's Law</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page concludes the opening acknowledgments of the preface. Fechner is transitioning from crediting his predecessors (like Weber and Bernoulli) to acknowledging his contemporary collaborator, Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann, and arguing for the necessity of psychophysics as an independent experimental science.</meta>

->IX<-

...investigation by **Volkmann** <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877) was a German physiologist and a close friend and brother-in-law of Fechner. His empirical data on vision and touch were crucial for Fechner’s mathematical formulations</note>. The willing participation of this sharp and refined researcher in the interests of this study—which, incidentally, led him onto his own paths far beyond the requirements initially set—and the growth of the empirical foundations of this work that resulted from it, truly place me under the greatest obligation of thanks.

At the same time, I venture to claim it as a favorable sign for the **principle** and character of the doctrine of this work that it can not only point to support in the exact investigations of the most excellent researchers, but is also able to provide points of connection for such studies. Indeed, apart from those theoretical and experimental investigations upon which it is based, and which have already attached themselves to it, the course of this writing has frequently offered occasion to point toward investigations to be undertaken or continued in the future. These are partly necessary for the further development of the <term>science of psychophysical measurement</term> <note>German: *psychophysische Masslehre*; the systematic study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations</note>, and partly enter into its applications. Despite the great interest these investigations hold, they would not have presented themselves without the perspective of this doctrine. The **psychophysical experiment**, which has until now only found an occasional place in either the physics or physiology laboratory, now claims its own room, its own apparatus, and its own methods. It is also certain that the field of these investigations will expand more and more the more it is cultivated. Thus, I seek the main fruit of our investigation thus far less in what it has yielded until now, than in what it once promises to yield. What lies before us is a scant beginning of a beginning.

Regarding the way in which **mathematics** is introduced in this writing, and notably how it will take its place in the following part, I wish that mathematicians might [consider] these elements...

<summary>Fechner acknowledges the vital experimental contributions of A.W. Volkmann and argues that psychophysics is maturing into an independent scientific discipline with its own specialized laboratories and methods.</summary>
<keywords>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann, psychophysical measurement, experimental psychology, scientific methodology, empirical foundations</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s preface to his foundational work on psychophysics. He is discussing the intended audience of the book, specifically the tension between writing for mathematicians, physiologists, and philosophers. He then moves to acknowledge Johann Friedrich Herbart’s pioneering role in mathematical psychology while distancing his own approach from Herbart’s specific system.</meta>

->X<-

...considered written for non-mathematicians, and for mathematicians on behalf of non-mathematicians, in that my endeavor was directed toward being understandable to the former and satisfying the latter—an effort that did not proceed entirely without conflict. May the mathematicians, in particular, excuse many somewhat broad and popular explanations provided in the interest of the non-mathematicians; I kept in mind that this work might primarily interest **physiologists**, while it also desires to interest **philosophers**. To expect to find mathematicians among both groups, however, is not yet as permissible today as it really should be required. <note>In the mid-19th century, the fields of physiology and philosophy were becoming increasingly specialized, and Fechner is lamenting the lack of mathematical training among these scholars.</note>

On the other hand, may the non-mathematicians accept derivations they cannot follow—even though only those with very low demands on mathematical understanding occur—as **mathematical facts**, and here and there skip a chapter, an insertion, or an elaboration that delves a bit too deep. If I am not mistaken, everyone will find the course and content of this work generally graspable if they only know what a **mathematical equation** is and are familiar with the properties of **logarithms**, or are willing to follow the brief <term>recapitulation</term> <note>A summary or review of previous principles</note> of them given at the beginning of the following part. Of others, I would not wish that they concern themselves with this work, and least of all that they pass judgment upon it, which in no case could be an insightful one.

I intentionally refrain in this work from entering in any way into the contrast that the mathematical conception of psychological relations presented here will offer against that of **Herbart**. <note>Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was a German philosopher and psychologist who was the first to attempt to apply mathematics to the study of the mind, though his approach was purely theoretical rather than experimental.</note> To Herbart will always remain the merit of having not only first voiced the possibility of a mathematical conception of these relations but also of having made the first ingenious attempt at carrying out such a conception; and everyone after him will, in this regard, remain only a second. In fact, however, the following...

<summary>Fechner explains his attempt to balance the book's accessibility for non-mathematicians (physiologists and philosophers) with the rigor required by mathematicians, while also acknowledging Herbart as the pioneer of mathematical psychology.</summary>

<keywords>audience, mathematics, physiology, philosophy, logarithms, Johann Friedrich Herbart, psychological relations, mathematical conception</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Fechner’s preface, moving from his technical considerations for different audiences to the philosophical positioning of his work. Having just mentioned Johann Friedrich Herbart, he now clarifies that his own "attempts" start from such different premises that a direct comparison or debate would be unproductive and potentially distracting.</meta>

XI

...attempts <note>original: "Versuche"; continuing from the previous page's sentence regarding his efforts or investigations</note> under fundamental points of view so essentially different from his own that there is as little need for a special emphasis on the difference between the two as it would be idle and inappropriate to attempt a reconciliation between the two here; especially since such a task could not take place without a dispute over fundamental philosophical questions, which is to be avoided here at any price. The decision between the two, which will at the same time be a decision regarding these fundamental questions, I must leave to the future.

Perhaps one also expects here a preliminary explanation of the position that this writing will take regarding **materialism** and **idealism** and the fundamental religious questions, with which every investigation into the relationship between **body and soul** must necessarily come into contact. Now, as far as the first point is concerned, this writing does not enter into the dispute over the basic relationship between body and soul that divides materialists and idealists at all; its explanations and consequences will lie neither one-sidedly in one sense nor the other, in that it represents the experiential relationships between both sides of existence through a <term>functional relationship</term> <note>Fechner’s "functional relationship" (Functionsverhältniss) is the core of psychophysics: the idea that mental and physical events change in a mathematically predictable correspondence without one necessarily "causing" the other in a traditional sense.</note>, which of its own accord excludes this one-sidedness.

As far as the second point is concerned, all conclusions that we would hereby be forced to accept the consequences of materialism regarding fundamental religious questions would be premature. It is obvious that the basic view—briefly expressed on page 4, which forms the background rather than the starting point for the developments of this writing—can experience a one-sided materialistic interpretation and application, and regarding the **question of immortality** seems initially to lead to the same conclusion. However, I wish to offer no further objection against this here than that this entire writing has grown upon the foundation and in the context of a completely opposite conception and interpretation of that view,

<summary>Fechner distances his work from the heated philosophical debates of his time, arguing that psychophysics uses a neutral "functional relationship" to bridge the gap between materialism and idealism. He also warns readers not to assume his scientific approach automatically supports materialistic views on religion or immortality.</summary>

<keywords>materialism, idealism, body and soul, functional relationship, immortality, philosophy of science, psychophysics</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the preface of Fechner’s seminal work, "Elements of Psychophysics." It transitions from the justification of his philosophical stance to a roadmap of the two-volume work, distinguishing between the empirical foundations provided here and the theoretical/mathematical developments to follow in the second volume.</meta>

XII

...which I have expressed in earlier works, and I must point the reader toward those if they wish to pursue those concerns, as this is not the right occasion for a more detailed discussion.

The present volume of this work contains the foundations of <term>mental measurement</term> <note>original: "psychisches Mass"; the core concept of psychophysics, which proposes that the intensity of a mental sensation can be measured relative to a physical stimulus</note>—that is, the establishment of its principle and the presentation of the methods, laws, and facts that belong to its empirical foundation. The following volume will develop the <term>mental measurement function</term> <note>original: "psychische Massfunction"; the mathematical formula—now known as Fechner's Law—that relates stimulus to sensation</note> itself, along with its consequences that bridge from the external to the internal world. Consequently, the current volume claims more of an empirical interest, while the following claims more of a mathematical and philosophical interest. It holds a mathematical interest insofar as the field of new applications opened for mathematics in this present part will be explored to certain limits in the next; and a philosophical interest insofar as these applications yield significant viewpoints for the understanding of the relationship between **body and soul**.

->Leipzig, December 7, 1859.<-

<summary>In the conclusion of his preface, Fechner outlines the structure of his work, distinguishing the first volume's empirical and methodological focus from the second volume's mathematical and philosophical exploration of the mind-body relationship.</summary>

# Introduction.

## I. General Considerations on the Relationship Between Body and Soul.

While the doctrine of the material world has flourished through various branches of <term>natural science</term> <note>In the 19th century, "Naturwissenschaft" encompassed physics, chemistry, and biology, which were rapidly becoming more rigorous and mathematical.</note> to a great level of development, and enjoys sharp principles and methods that ensure its successful progress; and while the doctrine of the spirit in psychology and logic has gained firm foundations, at least to certain limits; the doctrine of the relationships between body and spirit, or **body and soul**, has remained until now almost merely a field of philosophical dispute. It lacks a firm foundation and lacks secure principles and methods for the progress of investigation.

The most immediate reason for this unfavorable situation is, in my opinion, to be found in the following factual circumstance—though this circumstance itself prompts us to ask for its own deeper, underlying cause. We can track the relationships of the physical world on their own, directly and in context, through experience; we can do the same for the relationships of the inner or spiritual world. We can track the former as far as our senses and their magnifying aids <note>Such as microscopes or telescopes.</note> reach, and the latter as far as each individual's own soul extends. In this way, we are able to obtain fundamental facts, basic laws, and essential relationships in each of these two areas, which can serve us as secure foundations and starting points for deduction and further progress. This is not the case with the connection between the physical and spiritual worlds; for of the two factors belonging directly together in this connection, only one ever enters into immediate experience at a time, while the other [remains] under the cover... <note>The text cuts off here at "unter der Decke," implying the "other" factor (either the soul or the physical process) is hidden from direct observation when the first is being experienced.</note>

<summary>Fechner introduces "Psychophysics" by arguing that while physics and psychology have matured as separate sciences, the study of how they interact—the mind-body problem—has remained stuck in philosophical debate. He suggests this is because we can never observe both a physical process and a mental experience at the same moment from the same perspective.</summary>

<keywords>psychophysics, body and soul, natural science, psychology, philosophy, empirical experience, dualism, Gustav Theodor Fechner</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction where Fechner describes the divide between the internal experience of the soul and the external observation of the body. He begins to introduce his famous "identity" analogy using the geometry of a circle.</meta>

...remains. For while we are immediately conscious of our sensations and thoughts, we can perceive nothing of the movements in the brain which are linked to them and to which they, in turn, are linked; the physical here remains under a <term>mental cover</term> <note>original: "geistigen Decke." This suggests a veil or shroud that hides the physical mechanisms of the brain from our internal self-awareness.</note>. On the other hand, while we can subject the bodies of other people, animals, and all of nature directly to anatomical, physiological, physical, and chemical investigation, we are unable to experience anything directly of the souls belonging to the former, or of the God belonging to the latter; here, the mental remains under a <term>physical cover</term>. Thus, there remains a great deal of room for hypotheses and denial. Is there anything at all under one cover or the other, and what is to be found there?

The uncertainty, the wavering, and the arguing over these questions of fact have so far allowed for no firm starting point or point of attack for a theory concerning the relationships of something whose very existence is still largely being debated.

And what could be the reason for this peculiar relationship—that we can observe body and mind each on its own, and yet never both together as they directly belong together, even though we usually observe things that are directly connected most easily together? Given the unyielding nature of this relationship between the mental and physical realms, we might suspect that it is a fundamental one, rooted in their very basic relationship. But is there nothing similar that could at least illustrate this fact for us, if not lead us to its underlying cause?

Indeed, one can point to this or that. For example, if someone stands inside a circle, its <term>convex</term> <note>The outer curve of a circle or sphere.</note> side lies completely hidden from them under the <term>concave</term> <note>The inner curve of a circle or sphere.</note> surface; if they stand outside, conversely, the concave side lies under the convex surface. Both sides belong together just as inseparably as the mental and physical sides of a human being, and these can, by comparison, also be understood as an inner and an outer side; however, it is just as impossible to view both sides of the circle at once from a single standpoint in the plane of the circle as it is to view these two sides of a human from a single standpoint within the realm of human existence. Only when we

<summary>Fechner explains that the body and soul are two sides of the same reality, hidden from each other by our perspective, and introduces the analogy of a circle's concave and convex sides.</summary>
<keywords>dual-aspect monism, brain-mind relationship, circle analogy, internal vs external perspective, consciousness, anatomical investigation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction where Fechner describes the divide between the internal experience of the soul and the external observation of the body. He begins to introduce his famous "identity" analogy using the geometry of a circle.</meta>

...change the standpoint, the side of the circle that we perceive changes, and the other hides behind the one we see. But the circle is only an image <note>metaphor</note>, and the question now concerns the actual matter at hand.

It is not the task or intention of this writing to enter into deep or somehow definitive discussions regarding the fundamental question of the relationship between **body and soul** <note>original: "Leib und Seele." In German philosophy of this era, "Leib" often refers to the lived, organic body, while "Körper" refers to a physical object; Fechner uses "Leib" here to emphasize the living connection to the soul.</note>. Let each person seek to solve the riddle in their own way, insofar as it appears as such to them. It will therefore be of no binding consequence for what follows if I briefly address this view here with a few words—containing nothing essentially decisive for the further pursuit of this work—simply to avoid leaving the question of the general view which formed the starting point of this writing (and still forms its background for me) entirely unanswered. Simultaneously, I wish to offer a point of reference in this field of wavering ideas to those who are still searching for such a point, rather than believing they have already found it. Despite the great temptation at the beginning of a work such as this to lose oneself in extensive and far-reaching discussions in this regard, and the significant difficulty in avoiding them altogether, the reader will at least excuse the brief exposition of the view to which I shall henceforth limit myself.

First, a second explanatory example to accompany the first. Seen from the sun, the solar system presents a completely different view than it does from the earth. From the sun, it is the <term>Copernican world</term>; from the earth, the <term>Ptolemaic world</term> <note>The Copernican system places the sun at the center, while the Ptolemaic system (the older view) places the earth at the center. Fechner uses this to show how the same reality looks different depending on the observer's location.</note>. It will always remain impossible for the same observer to perceive both <term>world systems</term> simultaneously, despite the fact that both belong inseparably together; just as the concave and convex sides of the circle are, at their root, merely two different <term>modes of appearance</term> <note>original: "Erscheinungsweisen." This is a philosophical term referring to how things present themselves to our senses or consciousness.</note> of the same thing from different standpoints. Again, it is sufficient simply to change the standpoint, and the one world replaces the other in our perception.

The whole world consists of such examples which prove to us that what is a single entity in reality appears as two different things from two different standpoints, and that one cannot possess the same thing from one standpoint as from another. Who would not admit that it is always thus and cannot be otherwise? Only in

<summary>Fechner explains that the "body-soul" divide is a matter of perspective, using the astronomical shift between Copernican and Ptolemaic systems as an analogy for how the same reality appears differently from different standpoints.</summary>
<keywords>body and soul, standpoint, Copernican system, Ptolemaic system, dual-aspect monism, modes of appearance, world systems</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues Fechner’s foundational argument regarding the "identity view." He transitions from the astronomical analogy of the sun and planets used on the previous page to the central focus of his work: the relationship between the mental (mind/spirit) and the physical (body).</meta>

Regarding the greatest and most decisive example, people either do not admit it or have not thought of it. But this is exactly what the relationship between the spiritual and bodily worlds offers us.

What appears to you from an internal standpoint as your **mind** <term>Geist: A central term in German philosophy meaning mind, spirit, or intellect; here Fechner uses it to describe the internal "I" of consciousness</term>—you who are this mind yourself—appears from an external standpoint, by contrast, as the bodily foundation of this mind. There is a difference between whether one thinks with the brain, or looks into the brain of the person thinking.*) There, completely different things appear; but the standpoint is also completely different—an internal one there, an external one here; even unspeakably more different than in the previous examples, and therefore the difference between the modes of appearance is unspeakably greater. For the double mode of appearance of the circle, or the planetary system, is basically only obtained from two different *external* standpoints; in the middle of the circle, or on the sun, the observer remains outside the path of the circle, outside the planets. But the **self-appearance of the mind** is obtained from a true internal standpoint of the underlying being toward itself—the standpoint of **coincidence** <note>original: "Coincidenz"; the state of being identical with oneself or occupying the same "space" of experience</note> with itself—whereas the appearance of the corresponding corporeality is obtained from a truly external standpoint, that of non-coincidence.

From this it now becomes immediately self-evident why we first sought the reason why no one can perceive mind and body—despite how directly they belong together—simultaneously. Quite simply, no one can stand externally and internally toward the same thing at the same time.

For this reason, too, no mind perceives another mind directly *as* a mind, even though one might think it would most easily perceive a being of its own kind; because as another being, it does not coincide with it, and therefore only has the bodily mode of appearance of that mind. Therefore, no mind can perceive another at all except with the help of its corporeality; for what shines outward from the mind is precisely its bodily mode of appearance.

*) Equivalent <note>original: "Aequivalent"</note> to "looking into" is the act of forming an adequate conception based on conclusions drawn from what is seen externally—representing how the internal state would appear if the obstacles to looking inside were removed.

He explains that we cannot see both at once because it is impossible to be inside and outside a thing simultaneously.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that the difference between mind and body is a matter of perspective (standpoint). Having established the astronomical analogy on the previous page, he now addresses the classic "problem of soul and body" by critiquing and expanding upon the famous clock analogy used by the philosopher Leibniz.</meta>

Therefore, the mode of appearance of the **mind** is always, at any one time, only one, because there is only one internal standpoint; meanwhile, every **body**, by contrast, appears in many different ways according to the multiplicity of external standpoints and the diversity of those standing upon them.

Thus, the previous way of thinking covers the most fundamental relationships between body and soul, which every basic view on the matter should seek to cover.

One more thing: body and soul go together; a change in the one corresponds to a change in the other. Why? **Leibniz** <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a prominent German philosopher who explored how two different substances—mind and matter—could act in unison.</note> says: one can have various views on this. Two clocks fastened to the same board adjust their movement to each other through the mediation of this common fastening (provided, that is, they do not deviate too much from one another); this is the common **dualistic** <term>Dualism: The belief that the mind and body are two distinct and separate substances that somehow interact.</term> view of the relationship between body and soul. Someone could also move the hands of both clocks so that they always move harmoniously; that is the **occasionalist** <term>Occasionalism: A theory suggesting that mind and body do not affect each other directly, but that God intervenes at every moment to make them correspond.</term> view, according to which God produces the mental changes to match the physical ones and vice versa in constant harmony. They could also be set up so perfectly from the very beginning that they always go exactly with one another on their own, without needing assistance; that is the view of their **pre-established harmony** <term>Pre-established Harmony: Leibniz’s own theory that God synchronized the soul and body like two perfect clocks at the moment of creation.</term>. Leibniz forgot one view, and indeed the simplest possible one. They can also go harmoniously with one another—indeed, never diverge at all—because they are not two different clocks at all. With this, the "common board," the constant assistance, and the artificiality of the initial setup are spared. What appears to the external observer as the organic clock with a mechanism and movement of organic wheels and levers—or as its most important and essential part—appears to itself internally quite differently: as its own mind with the flow of sensations, drives, and thoughts. It should not be offensive that man is called a clock here. If he is called so in one respect, he should not be called so in every respect.

The difference in an appearance, however, does not depend solely on the difference of the standpoint, but also on the difference of those standing upon it. A blind person, at just as favorable an external standpoint as a see-ing—

<summary>Fechner proposes a "unity" view of the mind-body problem, arguing that they are not two separate synchronized clocks (as Leibniz thought), but a single "clock" viewed from two different perspectives. He explains that the internal experience of thought is the same event as the external observation of brain activity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Fechner’s critique of the clock analogy. ...sees nothing from the outside; and thus a dead clock—despite having a standpoint of coincidence with itself just as favorable as that of a brain—sees nothing from the inside; it exists only for external appearance.

Natural science consistently positions itself at the external standpoint of observing things, while the science of the mind <note>original: *Wissenschaft vom Geiste*. In Fechner’s time, this referred to the humanities or the study of human consciousness and culture.</note> positions itself at the internal one; views of life are based on the alternation of standpoints, and the **philosophy of nature** <term>Naturphilosophie: A movement in German philosophy that sought to understand the organic unity between the natural world and the human spirit.</term> on the identity of that which appears twice from two different standpoints; a doctrine concerning the relations between mind and body will have to track the relations between both modes of appearance of the **One** <note>Fechner refers here to the single underlying reality that manifests as both matter and mind.</note>.

These are the fundamental points of a view through which I seek not so much to clarify the ultimate underlying essence of body and mind, as to link their most general factual relations under a unified point of view.

Yet, as stated, everyone remains free to choose through which other view they wish to attempt the same, or whether they wish to attempt it at all. What each person finds most suitable in this regard will depend on the connection to their other views; and indeed, this will retroactively establish the possibility or impossibility of finding a suitable general connection between them. Here, however, it will not matter from the outset whether one conceives of **body** and **soul** merely as two different modes of appearance of the same being, or as two beings brought together externally, or the soul as a point within a network <note>original: *Nexus*</note> of other points of essentially similar or dissimilar nature, or wishes to renounce a unified basic view altogether—provided only that everyone recognizes the empirical relations between body and soul and allows for an empirical investigation of them, however forced their representation of them may be. For in what follows, we shall base ourselves only on the empirical relations between body and soul; and in doing so, we shall moreover use the most common expressions to describe the facts—expressions which lean more toward a **dualistic** sense than our **monistic** <term>Monism: The philosophical view that mind and matter are not two separate things, but two ways of perceiving the same underlying reality.</term> view, even if they allow for an easy translation into it.

<summary>Fechner argues that while natural science looks outward and mental science looks inward, his new approach focuses on the factual relationship between these two perspectives. He invites readers of all philosophical backgrounds (dualist or monist) to join his empirical study of how the body and soul interact.</summary>

<keywords>standpoint, natural science, philosophy of nature, body and soul, monism, dualism, empirical relations, psychophysics</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page transitions from Fechner's philosophical justification of the "dual standpoint" to his methodology. He emphasizes that his new science, psychophysics, does not rely on metaphysical assumptions but on empirical observation, comparing the search for "elementary laws" of the mind-body connection to the laws of physics like gravitation.</meta>

This is not to say that the theory that will be developed here is indifferent to the way we perceive the fundamental relationship between body and mind, or that it will have no influence upon it. On the contrary. However, one should not confuse the consequences that may one day flow from this theory—and which are already beginning to take shape—with the foundation of the theory itself. This foundation is, in fact, purely **empirical** <term>Empirical: Knowledge derived from observation, internal experience, or scientific experiment rather than from abstract theory or logic.</term>, and every preconceived assumption must be rejected from the outset.

One might ask: Does the possibility of such a foundation not stand in direct contradiction to the fact we started with—that the relationships between body and soul are hidden from observation? In truth, they are not hidden from observation entirely; rather, it is only the **immediate** relationships that are withdrawn from **immediate** observability <note>Fechner is distinguishing between what we can feel directly (the "immediate") and what we can measure or infer through experiments (the "mediate").</note>. Even our understanding of the general relationship between body and soul was based on experiences of a very general kind regarding their connection—even if this doesn't seem like a necessary conclusion to everyone who approaches this text with fixed preconceptions. What follows will show that we have no fewer "special" or specific experiences at our disposal. These can serve partly to orient us in the realm of "mediate" or indirect relationships, and partly to establish conclusions about the immediate ones.

In fact, a general perspective alone, even if it were accepted, would not be enough. The reliability, productivity, and depth of any general view does not depend on the "general" at all, but on the "elementary." The law of gravitation and molecular laws (which arguably include the former) are elementary laws; if they were thoroughly known and their full scope exhausted in their logical consequences, then the theory of the physical world would be complete in its greatest generality. Accordingly, it will be necessary to obtain **elementary laws** for the relationship between the physical world and the mental world <note>original: *Geisteswelt*. This refers to the realm of consciousness, thoughts, and feelings.</note> in order to gain a durable and developed doctrine instead of a mere general opinion. These laws, in this field as in any other, can only be founded upon elementary facts.

Psychophysics is a science <note>original: *Lehre*. While often translated as "doctrine" or "theory," in this context Fechner is proposing a rigorous scientific discipline.</note> that must be grounded upon these perspectives. More on this in the following chapter.

## II. Concept and Task of Psychophysics.

By **psychophysics**, we should here understand an exact theory of the functional or dependency relationships between the body and the soul, or more generally, between the physical and the psychological, the material and the mental worlds.

To the realm of the mental, the psychological, or the soul, we generally assign everything that can be grasped through **inner perception** <term>Inner perception: The ability to observe one's own conscious thoughts, feelings, and sensations (often called introspection).</term> or can be abstracted from it. To the realm of the physical, the corporeal, or the material, we assign that which is graspable through **outer perception** or can be abstracted from it. These terms are intended merely to designate the spheres of the "world of appearance" <note>original: "Erscheinungswelt". Fechner uses this term in a Kantian sense, referring to the world as we experience it through our senses, rather than the "ultimate reality" that might exist behind it.</note> with whose relationship psychophysics will concern itself. It is assumed that one understands "inner" and "outer" perception in the sense of common usage, referring to those activities through which existence in general becomes manifest as an appearance.

All discussions and investigations in psychophysics relate solely to the side of appearance of the physical and mental worlds—to that which appears directly through inner or outer perception, or is inferable from what appears, or is graspable as a relationship, category, connection, sequence, or law of what appears. In short, it deals with the physical in the sense of physics and chemistry, and with the psychological in the sense of empirical psychology <note>original: "Erfahrungsseelenlehre". Literally "experience-soul-teaching," referring to psychology based on observation rather than philosophical deduction.</note>, without regressing in any way to the "essence" of the body or the soul behind the world of appearance in the sense of metaphysics <term>Metaphysics: The branch of philosophy that deals with abstract concepts like "being" and "essence" that cannot be directly measured or observed.</term>.

Generally, we call the mental a **function** of the physical, or dependent upon it, and vice-versa, insofar as such a constant or lawful relationship exists between the two that the existence and changes of one can be inferred from those of the other.

<margin>Handwritten mark (similar to 'd')</margin> The fact of functional relationships between body and soul is generally undisputed; however, an undecided conflict remains regarding the reasons, the interpretation, and the extent of this fact.

Without regard for the metaphysical viewpoints of this conflict—which relate more to the so-called "essence" than to the appearance—psychophysics attempts to [capture] the act-

<summary>Fechner defines psychophysics as the scientific study of the functional relationship between the mind (inner perception) and the body (outer perception). He emphasizes that this field focuses on observable phenomena and laws rather than metaphysical speculation about the nature of the soul.</summary>
<keywords>psychophysics, body and soul, inner perception, outer perception, world of appearance, functional relationship, empirical psychology, metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the methodology of psychophysics, specifically focusing on the functional relationship between the physical and the mental. The previous page established that psychophysics deals with the "world of appearance."</meta>

...factual functional relationships between the appearance-realms of body and soul as precisely as possible.

What belongs together, quantitatively and qualitatively, distantly or closely, in the world of the body and the world of the mind? According to what laws do their changes follow one another or proceed together? Generally speaking, psychophysics asks these questions and seeks to answer them exactly.

Put another way, though saying the same thing: what belongs together in the inner and outer modes of appearance of things, and what laws exist for their respective changes?

Insofar as a functional relationship exists between body and soul, nothing in itself would prevent us from examining and tracking it in one direction just as much as the other. This can be aptly illustrated by the mathematical **functional relationship** <term>Functional relationship: A mathematical concept where one variable (like *y*) changes in a predictable way based on another variable (like *x*).</term> that exists between the variables ***x*** and ***y*** of an equation, where each variable can be viewed as a function of the other, and has the other dependent on it for its changes. However, there is a reason for psychophysics to prefer tracking the dependence of the soul upon the body rather than the reverse: it lies in the fact that only the physical is directly accessible to measurement. Meanwhile, the measurement of the mental can only be obtained through its dependence on the physical, as will be shown later. This reason is decisive and determines the direction of our progress in the following pages.

The materialistic reasons for such a preference are neither discussed nor given any weight in psychophysics. The dispute between **materialism** <term>Materialism: The philosophical belief that everything, including thought and consciousness, results from material interactions.</term> and **idealism** <term>Idealism: The philosophical belief that reality is fundamentally mental or immaterial.</term>—as it concerns which of the two is the "essence" or cause of the other—remains foreign and indifferent to this field, which relates merely to the world of appearance.

One can distinguish between **immediate and mediate** <note>In modern terms, we might say "direct and indirect."</note> dependency relationships, or direct and mediated functional connections between body and soul. Sensory sensations stand in immediate dependence on certain activities in our brains, insofar as when one is present, the other is also established, or follows immediately; however, they have only a **mediate** dependence on those external stimuli which...

The <term>question of the nature of psychophysical activities</term>, that is, regarding their <term>substrate</term> and <term>form</term>, is set aside from the beginning, and no <term>assumption</term> is made about it. Indeed, this can initially be set aside for two reasons: first, because in establishing the general <term>foundations of psychophysics</term>, we will be dealing with <term>quantitative relationships</term> just as in <term>physics</term>, where <term>qualitative relationships</term> are first made dependent on <term>quantitative</term> ones; and second, because according to the following <term>division</term> of our <term>teaching</term>, we will not yet need to take any <term>special consideration</term> of <term>psychophysical activities</term> in the first <term>part</term> of it.

By the <term>nature of the matter</term>, <term>psychophysics</term> is divided into an *outer* and an *inner* branch, depending on whether the <term>relationship of the mental</term> to the <term>bodily external world</term> or the <term>bodily internal world</term>—with which the <term>mental is in the closest relationship</term>—is considered; or, in other words, into a <term>theory of...</term>

Thus, we will everywhere have to mentally insert the unknown "middle link" which is necessary to complete the chain of effects.

Related to psychology and physics already by its name, psychophysics must, on the one hand, be based upon psychology and, on the other hand, promises to provide it with mathematical foundations. From physics, outer psychophysics borrows its tools and methods; inner psychophysics leans more on <term>physiology</term> and anatomy, specifically of the <term>nervous system</term>, and presupposes a certain acquaintance with them. The point of view from which we will approach our doctrine here is this:

## III. A Preliminary Question.

Even though all the obscure and disputed questions of **inner psychophysics** <note>The study of the direct, internal relationship between physiological processes (like brain activity) and mental experiences.</note>—and currently, almost all of inner psychophysics consists of such questions—must be set aside until the path of experience provides the means to decide them, one of these questions, which concerns the prospects of psychophysics as a whole, must be briefly addressed in advance. This is so that it can be answered as far as a general viewpoint allows, while referring the rest to future findings.

If we designate thinking, willing, and the finer aesthetic feelings as **higher mental** functions, and sensory sensations and drives as **lower** ones, then in this life at least—leaving the question of the <note>original: "Jenseits"</note> afterlife entirely open—the higher mental activities can no more take place than the lower ones without accompanying physical activities, or without being bound to **psychophysical activities**. No human being can think with a frozen brain. It is equally beyond doubt that a specific sensation of sight or hearing can only occur to the extent that specific activities of our **nervous system** take place. This, too, is not doubted; indeed, the very concept of the sensory side of the **soul** <note>original: "Seele"; here the author refers to the sensory and emotional life of an individual.</note> is based on the fact that it stands and falls in precise connection with corporeality. 

However, it is doubted all the more whether every *specific* thought is also bound to an equally *specific* movement in the brain, or whether instead an active brain *in general* is sufficient for thinking and the higher mental activities altogether, without such activities needing a particular type and direction of physical brain activity in order to proceed in a specific way. Indeed, the essential difference between the higher and lower mental realms (distinguished by some as **spirit** <note>original: "Geist"; used here to denote the higher intellect or rational mind as distinct from sensory "soul."</note> and **soul** in a narrower sense) is sought precisely here.

Suppose now that higher mental activities were truly exempt from a **specific relationship** <term>Specialbeziehung</term> <note>The idea that a specific mental state (like thinking of a horse) corresponds to a specific physical pattern in the brain.</note> to physical activities; even so, the general relationship between them, which must be recognized as a matter of fact, would still be subject to consideration and investigation by inner psychophysics. For

Everything seems to agree with this indication, which could easily be further developed and expanded. But neither the execution nor even the mere assertion of this is our business here in the introduction.

## IV. Concepts Regarding Sensation and Stimulus.

Given the current state of incompleteness in psychophysical investigations, providing a full list, definition, and classification of every possible mental state would be of little use. For now, we will primarily concern ourselves with sensory sensations in the common sense of the word "sensation," for which I will use the following system of names.

<margin>y</margin>
I will distinguish between <term>intensive sensations</term> and <term>extensive sensations</term> <note>Intensive refers to the "strength" of a feeling, like how bright a light is; extensive refers to "how much space" it takes up, like the size of a shape.</note>, depending on whether the sensory perception involves something whose magnitude is graspable as intensive or extensive. For example, I would categorize the sensation of brightness as an intensive sensation, while the perception of spatial extension through sight or touch would be an extensive sensation. Accordingly, I will also distinguish between the intensive and extensive magnitude of a sensation. If one object appears brighter than another, the sensation it provides is called intensively greater; if it appears larger than another, it is extensively greater. This is merely a matter of definition and, when understood in this general way, does not yet require a specific way to measure sensation.

In all sensations generally, whether intensive or extensive, we can distinguish between <term>magnitude</term> and <term>form</term>; however, in intensive sensations, magnitude is more frequently called <term>strength</term> and form is called <term>quality</term>. In the case of musical tones, <term>pitch</term>, although graspable as a quality of the tone, also has a quantitative side, insofar as we can distinguish between a greater and lesser height <note>The author uses the word "height" (Höhe) to refer to what we call pitch.</note>.

Should the **soul** be moved by external and internal excitations only to the extent that their effects have reached a certain point in the **body**, then all sensations—insofar as their dependence on the body is admitted—would merely be the **consequential effects** of bodily movements. Accordingly, even the most internal physical conditions of sensation would fall under the concept of **stimuli**. Conversely, if sensations were bound to physical movements that accompany them essentially and stand in a functional relationship to them, it would not be permissible to include these **simultaneous conditions** of sensation—with which the sensation is immediately established—among the stimuli. Rather, one should only include those things that serve to call forth those movements in the first place, if one does not wish to confuse different concepts. 

However, we do not yet need to decide between these two views here. The resulting differences in how we conceive of "internal stimuli" have no influence on our **practical observations**, as long as we assume and account for the existence and **magnitude** of internal stimuli based solely on their **equivalent effect** compared to external stimuli. For us, they are initially an "x" that is unknown in terms of its location and quality; however, it enters the realm of phenomena with a specific quantitative effect comparable to that of external stimuli, and it receives its name and value according to this effect.

We will have no hesitation in including many things under the name of **stimulus** that one might hesitate to include in everyday life—for example, **weights**, insofar as they cause the sensation of pressure when pressing down, or the sensation of **heaviness** when lifted. # **External Psychophysics.**

## **The Theory of Psychophysical Measurement.**

### **V. Measurement of Bodily Activity. Living Force.**

No <term>stimulus</term> [Reiz] <note>In Fechner's work, a stimulus is any physical energy that triggers a sensory response.</note> acts as something inert; rather, some stimuli, such as light and sound, are immediately graspable as motions. And even if this does not hold true for others, such as weights or stimuli of smell and taste, we may nonetheless assume that they only produce or modify <term>sensation</term> [Empfindung] by evoking or altering some form of activity within our body. Thus, according to their magnitude, they are representatives of the magnitude of those bodily activities related to sensation, which stand in some relationship of dependency to them.

Without occupying ourselves here with the specific measurements of various stimuli and the bodily activities they excite—assuming instead that such measurements from physics and chemistry are already known—we wish to enter into several discussions regarding the general measurement of bodily activity that are significant for what follows.

Even in everyday life, we apply a certain standard to the magnitude or strength of a bodily activity, seeking it partly in the speed of the movements performed and partly in the size of the mass moved, yet without having more definite ideas about it. At first, it seems most natural to take the product of the size of the moved mass and the speed with which it moves—that is, the <term>quantity of motion</term> [Quantität der Bewegung] <note>Today known as momentum (mass × velocity).</note>—as the measure of the magnitude of an activity. Indeed, in collisions and in the communication of motion in general, the speed which...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous page's discussion on "quantity of motion" (momentum) to a more precise definition of physical activity. Fechner is arguing that the proper measure of bodily activity in physics and physiology is "living force" (kinetic energy) rather than momentum.</meta>

...that the impacted body assumes, or the size of the mass to which a given speed can be communicated, is proportional to the <term>quantity of motion</term> [Quantität der Bewegung] <note>Now known in modern physics as momentum ($p = mv$).</note> of the impacting body. If one were to regard this effect as the standard for the magnitude of activity, one would indeed find its measure in the quantity of motion. This undeniably depends on the definition of bodily activity. However, if one wishes to grasp it in the sense used in exact physics, mechanics, physiology, and even in daily life, then not the quantity of motion, but only the **living force** can serve as the measure of bodily activity.

The living force discussed here is by no means to be confused with the "life force" <note>Fechner is distinguishing his mechanical concept from "Lebenskraft," a popular 19th-century philosophical idea that a non-physical "vital spark" animated living things.</note> of the philosophers, but is a precise measurement concept with the following meaning.

The living force of a material particle, whether conceived atomistically or *not* atomistically, is obtained by multiplying its mass *m* by the square of its velocity *v*, so that the expression of the living force for that particle is *mv*²\*). The living force of a whole system is then the sum of the living forces of its particles; thus, in a system of three or more particles with masses *m*, *m'*, *m''*.... and velocities *v*, *v'*, *v''*....

->$= mv^2 + m'v'^2 + m''v''^2 \dots$<-

which is usually expressed briefly for any number of particles by

->$\Sigma mv^2$<-

where one must only take care that the summation sign $\Sigma$ does not mean a summation of several identical products $mv^2$, but of as many different products as there are particles with different masses and velocities.

Without wishing to delve here into the deeper reasons for introducing this measurement concept, a few more immediate reasons can be cited.

---

\*) Strictly speaking, in mechanics only half of the product **mv²** is understood as the living force of the particle; <note>Modern physics defines kinetic energy as $1/2 mv^2$. In Fechner's time, the term "living force" (*vis viva*) was often used for the full $mv^2$.</note> however, some also apply the name to the entire product, which I also do here for the sake of convenience, as this different usage obviously has no influence on the ratios that depend on the living force, but merely changes the unit of measurement.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument for why "living force" (kinetic energy) is a superior measure of physical activity compared to "quantity of motion" (momentum). He moves from the mathematical necessity of using squares of velocity to avoid zero-sum totals in vibrating systems to the practical application of these concepts in mechanical work and daily life.</meta>

Following the entire spirit of the <term>mathematical theory of motion</term> <note>Now known as kinematics and dynamics, the study of how and why objects move.</note>, one must designate velocities directed in opposite directions with opposite algebraic signs (plus or minus). From this, it is clear that if one were to ask what total sum of activity has been developed within a given time in a system whose particles are in vigorous vibration, this sum of activity would be found to be effectively zero if one attempted to use the <term>quantity of motion</term> <note>In modern physics, this is called momentum ($p = mv$).</note> as the standard for activity. This is because the velocities of the back-and-forth movements, due to their opposite signs, produce products with the (always positive) mass that cancel each other out during summation. Such a result would be by no means appropriate, given that just as much force is required for the outgoing movements as for the returning ones. By contrast, when applying **living force** <note>Living force, or *vis viva* ($mv^2$), was the 19th-century term for kinetic energy. Fechner argues it is better for measuring activity because squaring a negative velocity makes it positive, ensuring back-and-forth motions add up rather than canceling out.</note> as the measure, both the outgoing and returning movements contribute to the increase of the total sum of activity, since the square of a negative quantity is just as positive as that of a positive quantity.

Secondly, by measuring physical activity through living force, one is doing nothing other than measuring it by the physical performance or **work** that can be achieved thereby. This brings us into connection and relationship with the concepts of daily life and practical mechanics. According to the common concepts of work, a person or a machine has worked twice or three times as much if they have lifted a given weight to twice or three times the height. If they perform another kind of work besides lifting weights, one can always reduce it to this type of work in order to have a comparable measure for it.

Now, according to known laws, the height reached by a stone thrown vertically upwards—disregarding air resistance—does not increase in proportion to the simple velocity given to it at the moment of the throw, but rather in proportion to the square of that velocity; consequently, it increases in proportion to the living force imparted to it at the moment of the throw. Yet, the same velocity that is imparted to it all at once during a throw (or rather, in very rapid increments) is imparted to it in gradual increments during slow lifting. Thus, the <term>lifting height</term> <note>The vertical distance an object is raised against gravity.</note>, just like the <term>throwing height</term>, depends on the magnitude—

...the **living force** <note>In the 19th century, *lebendige Kraft* (living force) or *vis viva* was the term used for what we now call kinetic energy ($1/2 mv^2$).</note> which is implanted in a stone—or more generally a load or weight—in the direction against gravity, or which resides within it by its own nature.

In order to climb a mountain, a person must—disregarding secondary circumstances—generate as much living force in their upward movement as would be necessary to throw their own weight to that height.

And so, quite generally, the living force possessed by a body of a given mass at a given moment—regardless of the direction of its velocity—represents a certain height that this mass (or an equal mass) would reach above a given point by virtue of that same velocity, if one imagined this velocity were applied to it at that point in the direction opposite to gravity. At any point during the body's ascent, one can represent the living force existing at that point by the height reachable above it; this does not contradict the initial definition, as the reachable height above a given point decreases along with the steadily diminishing living force.

Ultimately, however, as far as we are able to trace it, not only all creation, but also the transfer, propagation, and modification of living force has its basis in the interaction of parts. The whole of nature is a single, interconnected system of interacting parts, in which, however, various subsystems produce, utilize, and transfer **living force** <note>As established, *lebendige Kraft* is the historical term for kinetic energy ($1/2 mv^2$).</note> to one another under different forms, while observing general laws through which the connection is governed and maintained. A system can appear to be at rest and yet develop a very great **living force** <note>original: *lebendige Kraft*. This is the historical term for kinetic energy ($1/2 mv^2$). Just as the living force of a blow can seemingly disappear into the invisible tremors of a bell, the living force of imperceptibly small tremors can, conversely, break out into powerful visible motions through appropriate mediation.

Thus, the entire living force of a rolling **steam carriage** <note>original: *Dampfwagen*. A 19th-century term for a locomotive or steam-powered vehicle.</note> is merely a transformation of the living force of the imperceptibly small tremors produced by the **combustion process** in the fuel (including the ether that permeates it). From there, it is transferred to the parts of the machine, and from there to the carriage itself. And what emerges here as living force in visible motions disappears in the realm of the invisible motions of the fuel, whereby the ongoing maintenance and stoking of the heating process through new material and a steady draft becomes necessary if the process itself is to stay in motion. Even without the addition of the machine and the carriage, this [input of fuel] would be necessary for that purpose.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the conversion of work into heat, specifically focusing on the fluctuations of "living force" (kinetic energy) within mechanical systems. It builds on the previous page's explanation of the mechanical equivalent of heat to explain why energy appears to "disappear" in certain physical processes.</meta>

...[of the] pendulum increases during its descent and decreases during its ascent. However, if the **living force** <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; a 19th-century term for kinetic energy, calculated as $mv^2$.</note> does not remain the same in these cases, it nevertheless restores itself to the same magnitude whenever the bodies of the system—formed in the first case by the sun and a planet, and in the second by the sun and the earth—return to the same position relative to one another under the influence of the system's internal forces. Now, in many other systems, under the influence of their own inherent forces, a circular or **oscillating motion** <term>oscillating motion</term> takes place in such a way that the parts always return to a given position after an interval of time; and for this case, the law generally known as the **Law of the Conservation of Living Force** <note>This is an early formulation of the Law of Conservation of Energy, specifically regarding mechanical systems.</note> applies. According to this law, the living force in a system that has been left to its internal forces after some prior impulse always restores itself to its original magnitude when the parts of the system return to their original position, regardless of the internal mediations or the paths by which the return may have occurred—which in complicated systems indeed cannot always happen as simply as in the simplest systems mentioned above.

If we strike a piece of steel, the living force implanted into the steel particles during the act of impact, together with the heat generated, will perfectly represent the living force lost by the striking body. If the body is perfectly elastic, the particles—swinging back and forth from the moment of impact under the influence of their own forces—will always regain the same living force when passing through their original **position of equilibrium** <term>position of equilibrium</term>, but they will not retain it for the duration of the oscillation as they leave the original position. If, instead of steel, we have a piece of lead with little elasticity, it will remain permanently compressed; the living force with which the particles moved away from their equilibrium position during the act of impact will not be able to restore itself. Rather, under these circumstances, living force truly disappears, which, as it is expressed, is used to produce a permanent change in the position of the particles.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Law of the Conservation of Living Force" (kinetic energy). The previous page established that while energy seems to fluctuate, it restores itself when a system returns to its original configuration. This page clarifies that such a return to a "starting state" is rare in the real world, leading toward the broader Law of Conservation of Energy.</meta>

The Law of the Conservation of **Living Force** <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; this is the historical term for kinetic energy ($mv^2$).</note> therefore does not prevent the living force of a system, or a part of the infinite world-system, from temporarily changing, increasing, or decreasing, nor does it prevent it from changing permanently. It merely establishes that this force restores itself when the parts of the system—after any number of prior impulses—return to their original positions under the influence of internal forces. However, the law cannot generally guarantee this return itself, and in many cases, it simply does not occur. It does not even occur in a simple system of three bodies attracting one another according to the law of gravitation, except under very specific conditions. Furthermore, as is well known, the planets of our solar system never return to exactly the same positions relative to one another and the Sun due to the **incommensurability** <term>incommensurability</term> <note>This refers to the fact that the orbital periods of planets do not share a common divisor; they are irrational ratios, meaning the planets will almost never perfectly align in the exact same way twice.</note> of their orbital periods. They only return approximately over vast periods of time, which means the living force of our planetary system also restores itself only approximately, not exactly.

Undisputedly, within the infinity of the universe, a decrease in living force experienced by one part of this infinite system could be more or less compensated by an increase experienced by another part at the same time. However, there is no principle that links the decrease in one part to the increase in another in such a way that we could rely on an exact and permanent compensation. There is even less reason to assume such a thing because another principle exists—one that establishes a different constant relationship for living force, but not one that requires it to remain at the same level.

It is not the magnitude of the living force currently present, but rather the magnitude of the current living force combined with the magnitude of the living force that can still be generated by existing causes of motion—which we shall briefly call **potential force** <term>potential force</term> (the more common term is **tension force** <term>tension force</term> <note>original: "Spannkraft"; here the author is describing what we now call potential energy.</note>)—that is a constant value for every system removed from external influences, and thus undoubtedly for the world.

To illustrate this, let us imagine a string vibrating in empty space without resistance, transferring none of its motion to the
