The **living force** <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; this is the historical term for kinetic energy ($mv^2$).</note> of this string is variable. It is zero at the limits of its excursion <note>The furthest points of the string's vibration before it swings back.</note>; but at those same points, its **potential force** <term>potential force</term> <note>original: "potenzielle Kraft"; historical term for potential energy.</note> is at its greatest. For at every point the string passes through from that limit toward its position of equilibrium, it generates a new quantity of living force that adds to what came before, until it reaches the maximum living force while passing through the position of equilibrium.

When the string was at the limit of its excursion, this—now actual—living force existed as its potential force; that is, the living force that had not yet been generated, but which could still be generated by virtue of the existing causes of motion. In the movement from the limit of excursion to the central position, this entire potential force was converted into living force. However, as much living force as was created, just as much potential force was lost; for what had already been generated as living force could no longer be generated, until, upon reaching the central position, the entire potential force was exhausted. At this point, no further increase in living force at the expense of potential force is possible. From that point on, however, the process reverses: following a corresponding course, the potential force grows at the expense of the living force, and so on, alternating indefinitely. Thus, the sum of the living and potential forces of the string always remains the same, though now one, then the other, increases at the expense of its counterpart.

What holds true here for the string holds true for the world. Living force can only grow at the expense of potential force, and vice versa. The only difference is that not all parts of the world complete this alternation between rising and falling living and potential force in a synchronized, parallel fashion like the parts of a string. Rather, the most diverse parts of the world can be found in entirely different states in this regard. Furthermore, they contribute only collectively <note>original: "solidarisch"; meaning the parts of the universe work together as a single system to maintain the total balance of energy.</note> to the fulfillment of this law. Consequently, the living force that one body loses by transferring it to another does not result in an increase in its own potential force; conversely, what it receives through such a transfer is not gained at the expense of its own potential force. This is the great principle of the so-called *conservation of force* <note>original: "Erhaltung der Kraft." While "Kraft" is the German word for force, in this context it refers to what we now call "Energy."</note>, connected with the aforementioned conservation of living force, yet of even more general significance than that; a principle which, although grounded in long-known general principles of mechanics, was first developed with clarity by *Helmholtz* <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a polymath who published "On the Conservation of Force" in 1847, formalizing the law of conservation of energy.</note>, highlighted in its full significance, and explained in its most important applications. Since then, it has found the most extensive consideration and application in the fields of inorganic and organic physics. It is generally valid only for **central forces** <term>central forces</term> <note>Forces that act along the line connecting the centers of two objects, like gravity.</note> that are not functions of time or velocity; however, until now, no reason has been found to doubt its universal validity in the fields of the organic and inorganic.

This may at first appear striking. In the field of electricity and magnetism, insofar as the latter is reducible to electricity, there are forces that, according to *W. Weber's* <note>Wilhelm Eduard Weber (1804–1891), a physicist who developed sensitive instruments to measure magnetic and electrical phenomena.</note> investigations, depend on velocity and acceleration. But it has every appearance that these elementary forces combine in such a way that the law maintains its validity in all natural effects. For magnetic and the substitutable effects of electric currents, this is self-evident, insofar as they can indeed be represented as effects of central forces that are independent of velocity and acceleration. Furthermore, Prof. *W. Weber* informed me orally upon my inquiry that he has generally found the law to be in force in all cases to which his investigation led, even beyond the limits of those effects, even though its full universal validity for the domain of these forces still requires rigorous proof.

According to this law, in a system left to its own internal effects, the living force generated by previous external impulses or previous internal force effects can only continue to grow at the expense of its potential force, and the capacity for this growth is accordingly exhausted as the potential force, through the continuing growth—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the Law of Conservation of Energy (referred to here as "force"). It moves from the specific example of a vibrating string and air to the broader "world system," explaining that while energy shifts between kinetic and potential forms and between different parts of a system, the total sum remains constant, preventing the universe from either accelerating infinitely or grinding to a permanent halt.</meta>

[...the store] <note>The text begins mid-word; likely "Reichthum" (abundance/store) or "Wachsthum" (growth).</note> of **living force** <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; a historical term for kinetic energy.</note> is exhausted and, conversely, rises with the decrease of living force, so that while there is an exchange of living force between increase and decrease—and a transfer from one part of the system to another—neither a continuous growth to an unlimited height, nor a decrease to permanent extinction, can take place in a system left to its own internal effects. This undeniably applies to the **world system** <note>The universe or the solar system as a closed mechanical system.</note>, whereby the preservation of the world's activity within certain **oscillation limits** <term>oscillation limits</term> <note>original: "Oscillations-gränzen"; the boundaries within which a system fluctuates without reaching an extreme state of total rest or infinite speed.</note> is secured from the most general point of view.

Conversely, the living force in one part of a system can grow without a decrease in **potential force** <term>potential force</term> <note>original: "potenzielle Kraft"; a historical term for potential energy.</note> and decrease without an increase in the same, provided that it simultaneously decreases or increases respectively in another part of the system by virtue of the transfer of living force from one part to another. Insofar as every finite body is a part of the general world system, the law is applicable to each only under this consideration; that is, the constant balance between potential and living force holds for an individual body specifically only in regard to its internal effects. In regard to external effects, however, it holds only in connection with the larger system to which it belongs—and in the final instance, the entire world.

Note well that the **principle or law of the conservation of force** <note>original: "Erhaltung der Kraft." While the author uses the word "force," in this context he is describing what we now call the Conservation of Energy.</note> tells us nothing about the course or the manner of the reciprocal conversion between living and potential force, nor does it tell us what state a system must be in regarding this at any given time. Rather, that depends on the specific conditions and circumstances of each system, which are not determinable by any general principle but can only be derived from experience. The principle of the conservation of force tells us merely that, however the conversion between living and potential force occurs in a system left to its internal effects, it can only occur such that the constant sum of both is preserved as a whole. Within this rule, the freedom remains for the conversion to occur in infinitely different ways. It therefore constrains the system only from a certain very general perspective; the complete determination of the course of phenomena is not to be sought within it.

<meta>This page transitions from the mechanical laws governing the "world system" discussed on the previous page to the application of these laws to human biology and psychology. It argues that human free will does not exist outside of natural laws like the conservation of energy, but rather operates through them.</meta>

However free a human being may be, there are factual limits for his will and **spirit** <note>The German "Geist" can mean mind, spirit, or intellect; in this context, it refers to the seat of consciousness and will.</note>—not only in the mastery of external natural forces, but also internal ones—which are drawn by the general laws of nature.

A person can walk wherever they wish on the Earth, shifting their **center of gravity** <term>center of gravity</term> <note>original: "Schwerpunct"; the point at which the weight of a body is concentrated.</note> in any direction they please; no known law of nature binds or hinders them in this. Yet, they can only do so as long as the law of the preservation of the center of gravity is maintained, which is itself a consequence of the **principle of the equality of action and reaction** <note>Newton's Third Law: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note>. When falling or jumping from a height, a person—despite all freedom of will—is not in a position to shift their center of gravity a hair's breadth from the vertical line of gravity's pull, except perhaps in cases where air resistance provides a slight possibility. For, according to that general principle, no physical system can shift its center of gravity through its own internal activity alone. It requires external help or an external resistance. Free will, therefore, is able to express the freedom of movement not *against* that law, but only *on the basis* of it.

It will be no different with **living force** <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; a historical term for what we now call kinetic energy.</note>. Let the will, the thought, the entire spirit be as free as it likes; it will not be able to express its freedom *against* the general laws of living force, but only *on the basis* of them. Insofar as the spirit's path is bound to the path of **psychophysical activity** <term>psychophysical activity</term> <note>original: "psychophysische Thätigkeit"; the physiological processes in the brain and nervous system that accompany mental states.</note>, and the latter is bound to the **law of the conservation of force** <term>conservation of force</term> <note>original: "Erhaltung der Kraft"; today known as the Law of Conservation of Energy.</note>, the spirit itself will be bound by it.

This is no misfortune; for the law of the conservation of force is a law for the preservation of the world; and it is no misfortune that the spirit is bound to feel, think, and will in the sense of this preservation.

A general and definitive proof for the extension of this law’s validity to psychophysical activity has not yet been established; however, it can be asserted that all experiences, so far as we can make them, point in this direction and can be interpreted without force only by means of this law. We shall, therefore, have to adhere to it so long as no counter-proof is provided.

### VI. Principle of Measurement for Sensitivity.

Even with the same method of application, one and the same stimulus <term>stimulus</term> <note>original: "Reiz"; in this context, any external physical energy that triggers a sensory response.</note> can be perceived more strongly or weakly by one subject or organ than by another, or more strongly or weakly by the same subject or organ at one time than at another; conversely, stimuli of different magnitudes may, depending on circumstances, be perceived as being of equal strength. Accordingly, we attribute a greater or lesser sensitivity <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"; the capacity of an organism to respond to stimulation.</note> to the subject or organ at one time or another respectively.

Where the sensory organs are paralyzed, even the strongest stimuli are no longer felt; the sensitivity to them is zero; in certain excited states of the eye or ear, however, even the weakest light or sound stimulus evokes a vivid, perhaps even troublesome sensation; the sensitivity to it is enormously increased. In between, there are all intermediate degrees of sensitivity. There is therefore sufficient reason to distinguish and compare degrees of it; but the question remains how this can be done in a precise manner—how it can truly be measured.

The following must be considered here. Generally, the measurement of a magnitude <term>magnitude</term> <note>original: "Grösse"; a quantifiable extent or size.</note> consists in determining how many times a magnitude of the same kind, taken as a base unit, is contained within it. In this sense, sensitivity as an abstract capacity has as little a measure as abstract force. But instead of measuring sensitivity itself, one can measure something related to it and dependent upon it, which, according to its definition, increases and decreases as sensitivity does—and with which sensitivity conversely increases and decreases. In this way, one gains an indirect measure of it, in the same sense as is also the case with force. Instead of measuring force <term>force</term> <note>original: "Kraft"; here referring to the physical concept of power or energy used in Newtonian physics.</note> itself, we measure the related, dependent velocities which are imparted to equal masses, or the masses...

<margin><unclear>scribble</unclear></margin>
Upon superficial consideration, one might be inclined to consider the measure of sensitivity for stimuli and that for stimulus differences to be reducible to one another. If two tones of different physical intensities are given, one can imagine a third tone whose intensity is equal to the difference in intensity between those two; and one might then believe, for example, that the weakest possible tone that can still be heard on its own, and the weakest possible difference that can still be recognized between two tones, generally have the same magnitude. But this is factually invalid. Rather, even casual experiences teach—and it will be proven more precisely later—that the difference between two physical tones, lights, and so on, must be greater in order to still be recognizable the greater their absolute intensity is, while the absolute intensity that one can just barely perceive remains the same.

This indeed makes it necessary to distinguish between sensitivity (and the measure of sensitivity) for stimuli and for <term>stimulus differences</term> <note>original: *Reizunterschiede*; the physical gap between two distinct stimuli.</note>.

Insofar as the same stimulus difference is recognized more or less easily depending on whether it exists between small or large stimuli—and since, according to later investigations, the magnitude of the <term>sensation difference</term> <note>original: *Empfindungsunterschied*; our internal, mental perception of how different two things feel.</note> produced by a stimulus difference depends essentially on its relationship to the stimuli, or the ratio of the stimuli to one another established thereby—the <term>difference sensitivity</term> <note>original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*; our ability to detect that two stimuli are not the same.</note> is not only variable according to the state of the individual, but also according to the magnitude of the stimuli; in general, it is lower for large stimuli than for small ones. Determining the law according to which difference sensitivity depends on the magnitude of the stimuli—that is, how the magnitude of the difference between stimuli must change with the magnitude of the stimuli themselves in order to still strike the sensation with equal clarity—is one of the most important and consequential tasks of <term>outer psychophysics</term> <note>The branch of science dealing with the relationship between external physical stimuli and the resulting internal sensations.</note>.

<meta>This page continues from page 48, where Fechner established the distinction between sensitivity to a single stimulus (like a single light) and sensitivity to the difference between two stimuli (like comparing two lights). Here, he begins to mathematically define "relative difference," which is the core of what we now call Weber’s Law.</meta>

In more detail, the following investigations into various <term>sensory domains</term> <note>original: *Sinnesgebieten*; refers to the different senses such as sight, hearing, and touch.</note> will show that—at least within certain limits—a difference between given stimuli always remains equally noticeable to our sensation if it increases or decreases in the same proportion as its <term>components</term> <note>original: *Componenten*; the two individual stimuli being compared, such as two weights or two lights.</note>. Consequently, the sensation of the difference remains the same if the relative stimulus difference and (what is connected to it) the ratio of the stimuli remains constant, regardless of how the absolute size of the stimulus difference and the stimuli themselves might change.

By "relative stimulus difference," we generally mean the difference between the stimuli in relation to their sum, their average, or to one of the individual stimuli. The specific choice is irrelevant here, because if one of these ratios remains constant, the others will necessarily remain constant as well. Similarly, the stability of the relative stimulus difference and the stimulus ratio are always linked, so it does not matter which one we refer to.

For example, if the components 5 and 3 both double <note>becoming 10 and 6</note>, the ratio between them remains $\frac{5}{3}$ and their relative difference remains unchanged. This holds true whether we define the relative difference as $\frac{5-3}{5+3} = \frac{2}{8}$, or as $\frac{5-3}{5} = \frac{2}{5}$, or as $\frac{5-3}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$. After doubling, these values become respectively $\frac{4}{16}, \frac{4}{10},$ and $\frac{4}{6}$, all of which are fractions that equal the previous ones.

Conversely, if the stimulus ratio changes, the relative stimulus difference always changes in the same direction and vice versa, but not in direct proportion. For instance, if the ratio of $\frac{5}{3}$ between components 5 and 3 changes to $\frac{6}{3}$ (because component 5 changes while component 3 stays the same), then the relative stimulus difference of $\frac{5-3}{5+3} = \frac{2}{8}$ changes to $\frac{6-3}{6+3} = \frac{3}{9}$ (or from $\frac{1}{4}$ to $\frac{1}{3}$). This is a change in the ratio of 3 : 4 rather than 5 : 6.

Now, as long as the law holds—that a difference remains equally noticeable if it increases or decreases in the same proportion as its components (and thus the relative stimulus difference and the stimulus ratio remain the same)—one would have to say that the sensitivity to differences [varies] with the magnitude of the... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

It may, however, appear practical to treat sensitivity to differences as a proportional value. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 50, where Fechner began defining the different types of sensitivity (absolute versus differential). These distinctions might still appear to be minute and idle classifications. However, it will be shown later that they are by no means so; rather, the clarity in our conception of the most important factual relationships depends on this distinction. Furthermore, the confusion that has prevailed in the theory of irritability until now is partly due to the previous lack of a clear distinction between them.

In general, the term "sensitivity" means nothing other than what is otherwise designated by the names **irritability**, **excitability**, or **sensibility**; the only difference is that these latter names are used more generally—not merely regarding the elicitation of sensations, but also regarding movements caused by external or internal stimuli. However, since ultimately all sensations depend on internal movements, one could also relate the concept of sensitivity to the underlying <term>psychophysical movement</term> <note>Fechner uses "psychophysical movement" to refer to the physical activity in the brain or nervous system that directly corresponds to a conscious sensation.</note> instead of to the sensation itself. Thus, one could say of **absolute** sensitivity, for example, that it is equal, double, or triple in magnitude depending on whether an equal, half, or double external or internal stimulus is required to evoke the same psychophysical movement. The only issue is that this conceptual framing is not practical, because psychophysical movement is not accessible to direct observation.

Those names—**irritability** and **excitability**—are otherwise used sometimes as synonyms and sometimes distinguished arbitrarily, without such distinctions ever having been based on clarified factual relationships. However, once the concept of the various types of sensitivity has been clarified, it will be convenient to introduce a distinguishing usage. Accordingly, in the future I shall use **irritability** exclusively for **absolute sensitivity**, and **excitability** for **differential sensitivity** <note>original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*; the ability to detect a change or difference between two stimuli.</note>—the former regarding sensations themselves, and the latter regarding sensed differences.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of sensitivity, moving from general definitions of irritability and "psychophysical movement" to the specific distinction between how we perceive the intensity of a stimulus versus its physical size or extension in space.</meta>

As is well known, according to the experiments of E. H. Weber <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878) was a pioneer of experimental psychology who studied the "two-point threshold"—the minimum distance at which two points touching the skin are felt as two rather than one.</note>, a certain span of a compass placed with its points on the skin is required for the distance to appear just barely noticeable. Furthermore, nothing prevents us—following a modification of his procedure that I shall speak of in the future—from determining distances on different parts of the skin that appear to be of equal size. In doing so, it becomes clear that the actual physical size of the distances that appear "just noticeable," or more generally "equal in size," varies greatly across different areas of the skin. It can also be demonstrated by methods to be specified later that the differences in distance that can still be recognized on different skin areas vary in size. Analogous differences in the perception of spatial magnitudes and differences in magnitude—similar to those between different skin areas—can be found between different parts of the retina, specifically between the more central and peripheral areas. Thus, one can speak of a varying sensitivity in the perception of <term>extensive magnitudes</term> <note>Extensive magnitude refers to spatial dimensions—length, area, or volume—as opposed to "intensive" magnitude, which refers to the strength or vividness of a sensation.</note> just as well as in the perception of intensive magnitudes, and briefly contrast the two as **extensive and intensive sensitivity**.

The absolute measure and the difference measure of the extensive sensitivity of various skin or retinal locations will then be found in the reciprocal value <note>In this context, the "reciprocal value" means that sensitivity is the inverse of the threshold: the smaller the distance required to feel a sensation, the higher the sensitivity.</note> of the extensions, differences in extension, or ratios of extensions that appear equal on them. This is the same as finding the measure of intensive sensitivity in the intensive magnitudes, differences in magnitude, or ratios of magnitude of the stimuli that appear equal. Therefore, for example, one skin area would be considered to have twice the absolute extensive sensitivity of another if a compass distance half as large appears just as large upon it.

Regardless of the fact that the extensive sensitivity of given parts undoubtedly stands in some relationship of dependence to the number of so-called <term>circles of sensation</term> <note>German: *Empfindungskreise*. Now, measured data regarding both extensive and intensive sensitivity—based on the principles established here—certainly only have the value of **observational data**. From the outset, one might harbor the concern that, given the great variability of sensitivity according to differences in individuals, time, and countless internal and external circumstances, it might be entirely fruitless to strive for a measurement of it. This is argued, first, because something constantly changing is not accessible to precise measurement, and second, because the results lack constancy and therefore value, insofar as results observed in certain individuals at a certain time and under certain circumstances would not be found elsewhere or at another time.

In fact, it cannot be denied that in this respect, measurements in our <term>psychophysical</term> <note>Psychophysics is the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the mental sensations they produce.</note> field face difficulties that do not exist for measurements in purely physical or astronomical fields. But rather than measurement or the possibility of achieving fruitful results being abolished by this, the scope of the investigation is actually expanded, and considerations are introduced that do not exist for those other fields.

## VII. Principle of Measuring Sensation.

The measure of sensitivity discussed in the previous chapter is a measure of the mere capacity for sensation. It should neither be confused with a measure of the sensation itself, nor does it presuppose one (in the sense stated); rather, it only requires the observation of cases where sensations are equal, partly under the same and partly under changed <term>stimulus conditions</term> <note>original: "Reizverhältnisse"; the physical intensity or ratio of the external triggers affecting the senses.</note>. In doing so, we are actually measuring not the sensation, but only the stimuli or the difference between stimuli that produce an equal sensation or an equal difference in sensation. The question therefore remains whether and to what extent a measurement of the sensation itself, and of the mental realm in general, is possible.

In fact, no such measurement currently exists or, to speak more cautiously, has been recognized as such until now; rather, until very recently, it has been doubted or denied that such a thing could even be found. Even <insert>Johann Friedrich</insert> Herbart's <note>Herbart (1776–1841) was a pioneering German philosopher and psychologist who argued that mental activities could be modeled mathematically, though he lacked a way to physically measure them.</note> attempt at a **mathematical psychology** was unable to rest upon such a foundation; this has always been the most significant objection raised against him, despite the fact that Herbart placed the measure, so to speak, in the...

From the outset and in general, it cannot be denied that the mental domain <note>original: "das Geistige"; this refers to the realm of the mind, spirit, or psychological experience.</note> as a whole is subject to quantitative relationships. For not only can one speak of a greater or lesser strength of sensations, there is also a varying strength of drives; there are greater and lesser degrees of attention, of the vividness of memory and fantasy images, and of the brightness of consciousness as a whole, as well as the intensity of individual thoughts. In a sleeping person, consciousness is entirely extinguished; in someone in deep reflection, it is heightened to its highest intensity; and within that general brightness, individual ideas and thoughts rise and fall. Thus, higher mental functions are no less subject to quantitative determination than sensory ones, and the activity of the mind as a whole no less than in its individual parts.

Initially and immediately, however, we only have a judgment regarding a "more," a "less," or an "equal" in all these relationships, but not regarding a "how many times"—which is required for a true measurement and which we aim to achieve. Without yet having a real measure of sensation—and let it suffice from here on to pursue the subject in relation to sensation—we are able to say: this pain is stronger than that one, or this sensation of light is stronger than that; but for a measure of sensation, it would be necessary that we could say this sensation is twice, three times, or in general so-and-so many times as strong as that one, and who has been able to say this until now? We are certainly able to judge equality in the field of sensation; our entire measurement methods for sensitivity, which we will discuss in detail later, and our <term>photometric measurement methods</term> <note>original: "photometrischen Massmethoden"; scientific techniques used to measure the intensity of light as perceived by the human eye.</note> are based on this; but with all that, we still do not have a measure of the sensation itself.

In fact, it will be shown that our **psychic measurement** <note>original: "psychisches Mass"; the quantitative measurement of mental events, a core concept in Fechner's psychophysics.</note> fundamentally comes down to nothing other than physical measurement: the summation of a certain number of equal units.

Of course, we would attempt in vain to perform such a summation directly. Sensation does not divide itself on its own into equal inches or degrees that we could count and sum. But let us remember that it is no different with physical quantities. Do we count time intervals directly from time itself when we measure time? Do we count space intervals directly from space when we measure space? Rather, we apply an external scale—specifically, for time, a scale that does not consist of mere time; for space, a scale that does not consist of mere space; for matter, a scale that does not consist of mere matter. The measurement of each of these three requires the other two. Why should it not be the same in the spiritual and psychic realm? The fact that people have always sought the measurement of the psychic purely within the psychic realm may be a primary reason why it could not be found until now.

It seems that in this regard, things have often been confused. Every quantity can only be compared to a unit of its own kind; and to that extent, one can certainly say that space can only be measured by space, time only by time, and weight only by weight. However, it is a different matter with the **means of measurement** <note>original: "Massmittel"; the tools or instruments used to measure.</note> and the **procedure of measurement** <note>original: "Massverfahren"; the method used to obtain a measurement.</note>. Insofar as the quantities to be measured do not exist abstractly in the nature of things, and cannot be abstracted or handled separately from one another, one also cannot find the abstract unit of measurement or a procedure for it in the nature of things. It is simply a matter of arranging the practical measurement procedure with the concrete measurements of reality so that the relationship between what is being measured and the unit of measurement is clearly revealed.

The more precise investigation using the relevant methods leads to a general lawful relationship—already stated <margin>x</margin> in Chapter 6—between the **variable stimulus increments**, which change according to the magnitude of the stimulus but always yield the same sensation increment, and the **constant sensation increments**. From this, in a manner to be specified later, one can derive the functional relationship between the total stimulus (summed from the variable stimulus increments) and the total sensation (summed from the constant sensation increments).

...bringing <term>sensitivity to differences</term> <note>The ability of an observer to distinguish between two slightly different stimuli</note> to a high level of precision. From this, we derive the functional relationship between the sums of these increments, which allows us to determine the total measure of sensation based on the measured stimulus.

In principle, our measure of sensation amounts to dividing every sensation into equal sections—that is, the equal increments through which a sensation grows, starting from the <term>zero-state</term> <note>The threshold of perception, or the point at which a stimulus is first felt</note>. We then conceive of the number of these equal sections as being determined by the number of corresponding variable stimulus increments required to produce them, much like the markings on a ruler. It is like measuring a piece of fabric: we determine the number of equal sections within it by the number of ells <note>A traditional unit of length, roughly the length of a man's arm</note> required to cover it; the only difference here is that instead of "covering" the distance, the stimulus is "producing" the sensation. In short, we determine the magnitude of the sensation—which we cannot measure directly—by how many equal parts it contains, which we *can* determine. However, we do not read this number from the sensation itself, but from the stimulus that carries the sensation along and makes it easier to read. Finally, we replace the counting of an infinite quantity of infinitely small increments—which is only established in principle and would be impossible to carry out in reality—with an <term>infinitesimal summation</term> <note>In modern terms, this refers to "integration" in calculus: adding up an infinite number of tiny changes to find a total value</note> of those increments. This provides the result of the count without needing to perform it piece by piece.

According to the general **principle of continuity**, no sensation arises abruptly and suddenly at its full height beyond which it cannot grow. Instead, it passes through all intermediate degrees from a state of being unnoticeable <note>German: *Unmerklichkeit*; this refers to the "threshold," the point where a stimulus is too weak to be felt</note>, often, of course, in such a short time that the full height of the sensation seems to appear to us all at once. Referring to this growth is, at the same time, the ingenious method <note>German: *Kunstgriff*, literally a "clever trick" or "artful handle"</note> that alone makes measuring sensation possible. No measure can be applied to a sensation once it has already matured, since no quantitative plurality can be distinguished within it. However, in a growing sensation, the increments from which it arises do present a plurality that is particularly graspable according to the methods we shall present in the future.

In a certain sense, this method provides the same advantages for the treatment of mental magnitudes as the corresponding technique does for the treatment of spatial magnitudes. A curve or a surface is presented as given; but **calculus** <term>infinitesimalrechnung</term> <note>The mathematical study of continuous change</note>, instead of grasping it as a whole, lets it grow from its increments. In a corresponding way, we will provide the most precise insight into the relative path of stimulus and sensation by giving a general expression for how the variable increment of the stimulus relates to the continuously constant increment of sensation, and from this, establishing a function between stimulus and sensation. The **mental measure** <note>German: *psychisches Mass*</note> will always remain less easy and simple in its construction and application than the **physical measure**; specifically for the reason that, with physical measures, equal divisions of the measuring scale generally correspond to equal divisions of the object being measured. In contrast, experience reveals a general circumstance: as the magnitude of the <term>stimulus</term> <note>German: *Reiz*; the physical energy or trigger, such as light or sound</note> and the <term>sensation</term> <note>German: *Empfindung*; the internal mental experience</note> increases, ever-larger **stimulus increments** are required to produce the same increment in sensation. This is somewhat comparable to a case where unequal divisions of a scale correspond to equal divisions of the object being measured. As previously stated, this does not prevent us from concluding the sum of one from the other if the relationship between them is known—which is the essential point. However, the magnitude of the stimulus and the sensation are no longer proportional as a whole. The simplest possible relationship imaginable between scale and object—which actually occurs with physical measurements of space, time, and weight—does not exist between the mental object and its physical measuring scale. This is a second reason why the discovery of a mental measure has been delayed.

Meanwhile, experimental investigation shows that the next simplest relationship imaginable exists here. It is found that, while the *absolute* magnitude of the stimulus increments needed for equal sensory increments grows ever larger as the sensation itself increases, the *proportional* magnitude of these increments remains constant for equal increments of sensation (assuming constant sensitivity and normal or average circumstances). Thus, equal *relative* stimulus increments always correspond to equal increments in sensation—provided that, as before, we understand "relative increment" to mean the size of the absolute increment in proportion to the magnitude of the stimulus (or divided by the magnitude of the stimulus) to which it is added.

From this follows the circumstance that as sensation grows, the absolute magnitude of the stimulus increments required for equal increments of sensation increases more and more. This is simply a logical consequence: as the stimulus grows alongside the sensation, the same proportional part of the stimulus must result in an absolutely larger amount, because the base value of which it is a fraction has become larger.

Insofar as we wish to follow the analogy of the scales of the *physical* and demand for the concept of a scale of the *psychical* <note>German: *Psychischen*; referring to the mental or internal experience</note> that equal divisions of the scale correspond to equal divisions of the object being measured, we will also be able to satisfy this demand. We do this by regarding the *relative stimulus increments*—rather than the *absolute* ones—as the actual "inches" <note>German: *Zolle*; used here metaphorically to mean the standard units or "tick marks" on a ruler</note> or divisions of the *psychical scale*. The determination and *summation* of continuously equal relative stimulus increments as the stimulus and sensation rise represents a summation of just as many corresponding equal sensation increments. We need only relate their sum to a unit of their kind to have a *measure of the whole sensation*.

Strictly speaking, this summation must be performed with *infinitely small increments*, because the associated relative stimulus increments have a precisely determinable value only for infinitely small sensation increments. If we were to consider the *relative stimulus increment* for a finite sensation increment all at once, we would have to consider that the stimulus itself passes through various magnitudes during the increase, each of which could claim to act as the divisor for the increment to produce the relative value. The difficulty that seems to arise from this is resolved in the manner already frequently mentioned: a simple mathematical function can be established. This function includes the result of such a determination and counting without requiring the calculation of an infinite number of *infinitely small stimulus increments* in detail. The derivation of this function belongs to the simplest applications of <term>infinitesimal calculus</term> <note>The mathematical study of continuous change, pioneered by Newton and Leibniz</note>, while its understanding and application require only elementary knowledge.

And so the final link of the *psychical measure* finally rests in a function which, being of a mental nature itself

<summary>Fechner explains that while absolute stimulus increments grow, relative increments remain constant in relation to sensation, allowing for a "psychical scale." He introduces the necessity of using calculus to sum these infinitely small increments into a functional measure of sensation.</summary>

---

The law that larger stimulus increments <note>German: *Reizzuwüchse*; the amount of additional physical energy (like light or sound) added to a baseline</note> are required in the higher parts of the stimulus scale than in the lower ones to produce an equal increase in sensation has long been known, as it is a matter of daily experience.

One hears the word of a neighbor very clearly in the silence or during faint daytime noise; on the other hand, as the saying goes, one no longer hears one’s own word—finding the increment caused by it to be unnoticeable—when a great deal of noise is present.

The same difference in weight that is felt very strongly with small weights becomes unnoticeable with large weights.

Strong light intensities, which differ very significantly when measured photometrically <note>referring to the objective measurement of light energy</note>, nevertheless appear nearly equally bright to the eye. Thus, a light seen in a mirror appears almost as bright as the light outside, despite the fact that a significant loss of light occurs during reflection.

Analogous examples can easily be found in the realm of all sensory perceptions.

But this general fact was not sufficient as a foundation for a psychical measure <note>German: *psychische Mass*; a mathematical way to quantify internal experience</note>. The more precise statement—that the size of the stimulus increment must continue to grow in exact proportion to the size of the stimulus already present to achieve the same growth in sensation—was first made and supported by experiments in some generality by E. H. Weber <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878), a German physician whose work on the sense of touch laid the foundations for experimental psychology</note>. For this reason, I have named it **Weber’s Law**.

In individual cases where it is relevant, however, it has been stated and proven even earlier, as can be seen in more detail in the 9th Chapter, where this law is specifically addressed.

<summary>Fechner explains that while everyone knows from experience that louder or brighter stimuli require larger changes to be noticed, E. H. Weber was the first to prove the mathematical proportion of this relationship. Fechner officially dubs this principle "Weber's Law" and frames it as the foundation for measuring the human mind.</summary>

### Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics. 5

On the other hand, the mathematical function that links the magnitude of the stimulus with the magnitude of the sensation was established from particular points of view more than a hundred years ago. It was proposed by Euler, and later repeatedly by Herbart and Drobisch, regarding the dependence of the sensation of musical intervals on the ratios of vibration frequencies <note>Leonhard Euler (1707–1783) was one of the first to use logarithms to describe the relationship between musical pitch and physical frequency</note>. Slightly before Euler, it was proposed by Daniel Bernoulli, and later by Laplace and Poisson, regarding the dependence of moral wealth <note>original: *fortune morale*; this refers to the subjective utility or value of money</note> on physical wealth <note>original: *fortune physique*; the actual quantity of money or assets</note>. Finally, it was proposed by Steinheil and by Pogson regarding the dependence of differences in star magnitudes—which are nothing other than differences in the magnitude of sensations—on the photometric intensity of the stars. I shall return to these matters partly in Chapter 8 and partly in a later historical chapter.

If the universality and the significance of that law and this function had been recognized earlier, then psychical measurement would have been discovered much sooner.

Weber’s Law—which states that equal relative stimulus increments <note>meaning that it is the *percentage* of increase in energy that matters, not the absolute amount added</note> correspond to equal increments in sensation—is to be regarded as fundamental to the science of psychical measurement <term>psychische Masslehre: the study of how to quantify internal mental experiences</term> because of its great universality and the wide range within which it is strictly or approximately valid. However, its validity has boundaries and is subject to complications, which must be carefully discussed later. Yet even where this law ceases to be valid or pure, the principle of psychical measurement discussed here retains its pure and full validity. This is because any other relationship between constant sensation increments and variable stimulus increments—even if only empirically determined and expressible through an empirical formula—can serve just as well as the foundation for psychical measurement. Indeed, it must serve this purpose in those parts of the stimulus scale where that law loses its validity. In fact, such a relationship will provide a differential formula <note>a mathematical tool used to calculate instantaneous rates of change</note> just as well as Weber’s Law does, leading to an integral formula that contains the expression of the measurement.

This is a fundamental point of view; for according to this, Weber’s Law, with the limits of its validity, is not to be seen as setting a limit for psychical measurement itself, but only as limit...

Accordingly, in the interest of making the <term>psychical measure</term> <note>The quantitative value assigned to a sensation.</note> as universal as possible, research should not essentially focus on generalizing <term>Weber’s Law</term> as much as possible. Such an effort might easily bring with it a questionable tendency to generalize the law beyond its naturally set limits, or it might provoke concerns that it has been over-generalized just to serve that interest. Therefore, the development of these methods to ever greater precision and perfection is what matters above all in the <term>theory of psychical measurement</term>.

Despite all this, great advantages would be lost if the so simple <term>Weber’s Law</term> could not actually be used as a basis in <term>psychophysics</term> <note>The scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</note> within wide limits, either exactly or with a satisfactory approximation. It would be a loss of advantages similar to those we would face in astronomy if we could not use <term>Kepler’s Laws</term> as a basis, or in the study of <term>dioptric instruments</term> <note>Optical devices, like telescopes or microscopes, that use lenses to refract light.</note> if we could not use the laws of simple <term>lens refraction</term>. Now, however, the situation with Weber’s law is quite analogous to these laws. In <term>Kepler’s Laws</term>, perturbations <note>The small gravitational influences of other planets that cause a planet to deviate from a perfect elliptical orbit.</note> are ignored; in the laws of simple <term>lens refraction</term>, optical aberrations are disregarded. Indeed, they can become completely invalid if the simple conditions for which they hold no longer exist. Yet they always remain valid for the primary relationships around which...

The quantitative dependencies of sensation on the stimulus are thus ultimately translated into a dependency on those bodily activities which immediately underlie the sensation—briefly, the <term>psychophysical activities</term>—and the measurement of sensation through the magnitude of the stimulus is translated into a measurement through the strength of these internal movements. For this translation, it is necessary to know the dependency of these internal movements on the stimulus; however, insofar as this is not an object of direct experience, it must be inferred in an exact manner. Indeed, this entire investigation can proceed in an exact way and cannot fail—should one find that the goal has not yet been reached—to eventually yield the success of exact investigation.

## 1) Measurement Methods of Difference Sensitivity.

### a) General Description.

To date, three measurement methods for **difference sensitivity** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit</term> <note>The psychological ability to detect the smallest possible difference between two physical stimuli.</note> are at our disposal, which for the sake of brevity I shall designate as:
1) Method of **just noticeable differences** <term>eben merkliche Unterschiede</term>
2) Method of **right and wrong cases** <term>richtige und falsche Fälle</term>
3) Method of **average errors** <term>mittlere Fehler</term>

To provide an initial, general insight into the nature and the mutual relationship of these three methods, let them first be briefly explained using one and the same task—namely, investigating the degree of precision with which differences in weight are recognized, although only the first two of these methods have actually been applied to this purpose thus far.

To apply the method of **just noticeable differences** to our task, one should lift two vessels, *A* and *B*, which have been brought to slightly different total weights by loading them with a given weight, for comparison. If the difference between the weights is large enough, one will feel it; otherwise, it will not be found to be noticeable. The method of just noticeable differences now consists of determining the magnitude of the weight difference required to be recognized as just noticeable. The level of sensitivity...

--- Page 86 ---
<meta>This page continues the detailed explanation of the three psychophysical methods introduced on page 71. Having already touched upon "just noticeable differences," Fechner here elaborates on the mathematical relationship between sensitivity and stimulus difference, specifically detailing the "method of right and wrong cases" and the "method of average errors."</meta>

<page-num>72</page-num>

for weight differences, sensitivity is the <term>reciprocal</term> <note>original: reciprok; in this context, it means that as the measured difference decreases, the sensitivity is calculated as being proportionately higher (1/x).</note> of the size of the difference thus found.

Generally, with this method, it is practical to bring the difference down from a noticeable level to the degree of being just noticeable just as often as one brings it up from an unnoticeable level to that point, and then to take the average result.

If one chooses a very small weight difference, then upon frequent repetition of the experiment, one will sometimes be deceived regarding the direction of the difference, taking the vessel that is actually too light for the heavier one and vice versa; however, the greater the excess weight or the sensitivity, the greater the number of right cases will be compared to the number of false cases or to the total number of instances of judgment. The **method of right and wrong cases** <note>original: Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle</note> consists of determining the magnitude of the excess weight required under the various conditions—under which sensitivity is to be compared—to produce the same ratio of right and wrong cases, or of right cases to the total number of cases. The magnitude of sensitivity under these different conditions is set as the reciprocal of the magnitude of this excess weight.

Cases where one remains doubtful are not to be set aside, but are to be counted half as right cases and half as false cases.

If one has only the weight of one vessel given as a <term>standard weight</term> <note>original: Normalgewicht</note> by means of a scale, one can attempt to make the other—the test weight—equal to it based solely on the judgment of sensation. In doing so, one will generally commit a certain inaccuracy or error, which is found when one re-weighs the second vessel after it has been <term>estimated</term> <note>original: taxirt; evaluated or judged by the senses.</note> as equal to the first. If the experiment is repeated often, one will obtain many errors, from which an average error can be obtained by <term>taking the mean</term> <note>original: Mittelziehung</note>. Sensitivity for weight differences will be set as the reciprocal of the magnitude of the average error obtained in this way. This is the **method of average errors**.

Since positive and negative errors depend in the same way on a lack of correct perception, they are also to be used in the same way for measurement; thus, they are not to be subtracted from one another according to their absolute value, but are to be added.

one can apply these same methods in the fields of light sensations, sound sensations, and so forth, as well as to sensations of extension <note>The term "extension" here refers to the perception of physical space, such as the distance between two points on the skin.</note>. In the latter case, for example, one might use the **method of just noticeable differences** to investigate how large the difference between the spans of two compasses <note>original: Zirkel; referring to dividers or calipers used in early psychology to measure spatial sensitivity.</note> held before the eyes or placed upon the skin must be in order to appear just noticeable. According to the **method of right and wrong cases**, one would observe how often a correct or incorrect judgment is made when trying to estimate which of two slightly different compass distances is the larger one. According to the **method of average error**, one measures the magnitude of the average mistake <note>original: Durchschnittsfehler</note> committed when one attempts to set one compass distance to be equal in size to another.

These three methods lead to the same goal via different, complementary paths. In the first, the boundary between differences above the threshold of noticeability <note>original: übermerklichen</note> and those below it <note>original: untermerklichen</note> is observed as the "just noticeable difference." In the second, differences above the threshold are counted (which, due to chance, result sometimes in a correct and sometimes in a false sense). In the third, differences below the threshold of noticeability are measured.

All three methods use relatively very small—in some cases vanishingly small—differences as a <term>scale of sensitivity</term>. It will be shown later that this is precisely what is most advantageous when one seeks to find a foundation for the measurement of sensation in the measurement of sensitivity.

As far as can be seen, each of these methods is applicable to all sensory domains, yet much is still lacking in the implementation of even one of these methods across all senses; likewise, not all three have been fully carried out within any single sensory domain.

The **method of just noticeable differences** has likely been applied in individual cases before; for instance, by *Delezenne* to test sensitivity to deviations in the purity of musical intervals. However, it was applied with particularly great extent and the most successful results by *E. H. Hegelmayer* <note>original: stud. med.; a medical student</note> in Tübingen in the field of visual estimation, and by *Renz* and *Wolf* in the field of sound measurement; both were conducted by young men under *Vierordt's* auspices <note>original: Auspicien; meaning under his supervision or direction</note>, so one may well assume that *Vierordt* suggested the method, although this is not expressly noted. The **method of average error** is, in a certain sense, as old as the practice of making observations itself, where precision is determined by the size of the errors committed; however, to my knowledge, until now it has been viewed and used only from the perspective of the objective determination of accuracy in physical and astronomical observations, or to identify the magnitude of occurring **sources of error**, but not as a psychophysical measurement method for investigating the sharpness of the senses. It seems to me, however, to be one of the most excellent for this purpose, and I have used it in conjunction with *Volkmann* to investigate the sharpness of **visual** and **tactile estimation** <note>original: Tastmass; the ability to perceive and compare distances through the sense of touch, such as the space between two points on the skin</note>.

In practical terms, the **method of just noticeable differences** is the simplest and most direct among the three measurement methods; it leads to the goal relatively quickly and requires the least amount of calculation. However, for more in-depth investigations, it seems less suitable and capable of no such great definitive precision as the other two methods, toward which one might therefore find oneself driven in the course of an investigation.

Specifically, it is hampered by the fact that the degree of **being just noticeable** <note>original: Ebenmerklichseins</note> allows more room for subjective judgment than is the case with the other methods. It is nothing absolute; neither the first point where a difference in sensation becomes just noticeable, nor where it disappears, can be determined with total exactness; one passes through an interval of doubt as to whether it is noticeable or not. If one does not wish to set the degree of being just noticeable somewhat high—that is, to count only such a difference as "just noticeable" which appears as such without exception and with certainty during repetitions of the experiment—where a slightly smaller difference must then necessarily often still appear noticeable, the method shifts of its own accord into the **method of right and wrong cases**. In that instance, cases will always occur in which one is mistaken about the direction of the difference or remains in doubt—cases that demand to be taken into account in proportion to their greater number.

Nevertheless, experience teaches that one can, so to speak, come to an understanding with oneself regarding the feeling of a small yet still reliably enough perceived difference, and can reproduce this, if not absolutely then nearly exactly, across various experiments and obtain a good result by multiplying the trials. Nor are the previous remarks intended in any way to diminish the value of this method, but only to place its advantages and disadvantages in the proper light compared to the other methods. Without it, <term>psychophysics</term> <note>the scientific study of the quantitative relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they evoke</note> would lose, so to speak, its most convenient tool. fundamental data <note>original: "fundamentalen Data"; Latin plural for basic information points</note> obtained by means of the same have proven well-founded, and others, as well as I myself, have had sufficient opportunity to convince ourselves of their usefulness.

The **method of right and wrong cases** <note>original: "Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle"; now commonly known in psychology as the "Method of Constant Stimuli"</note> is probably the most tedious, and it is better, if one does not have a great deal of time and patience, not to get involved with it, since with only a few right and wrong cases almost nothing is accomplished; meanwhile, from many cases, one can obtain very good results—that is, results that agree well with one another—and can investigate and establish legal relationships <note>original: "gesetzliche Verhältnisse"; referring to the discovery of mathematical laws, such as Weber’s Law</note> in the realms of sensation. This requires the assistance of calculation, which can, however, be reduced to easily executable operations. While in the method of just noticeable differences one is fundamentally restricted to a single difference—the "just noticeable" one—as a scale for **differential sensitivity** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit: the ability to detect the smallest possible change in a stimulus</term>, in the method of right and wrong cases one can introduce somewhat larger or smaller differences into the experiment as one pleases, and specialize the comparison through the various numbers of right and wrong cases obtained thereby.

The **method of average error** <note>original: "Methode der mittleren Fehler"; also known as the "Method of Adjustment," where a subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard</note> also requires a large number of trials and a simple calculation aid. Both of these latter methods have the great advantage of being able to lean upon the proven principles of the **calculus of probabilities** <note>original: "Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung"; Fechner was a pioneer in applying the mathematics of chance and error to human perception</note> and can even contribute something to the validation of those principles. In fact, the interest I have found in the long-term practice of these methods has been greatly sustained and increased by this **point of view**.

### b) General Considerations and Precautions.

As simple as the methods briefly discussed above seem at first glance, and indeed are in principle, their execution and implementation nevertheless require many considerations and precautions—partly regarding observation and partly regarding calculation—which are specialized in part according to the method and the field of experiment. However, the following apply more or less generally.

In all three methods, irregular chance occurrences play a role, which are partly inherent in the manipulations and partly grounded in the subjective conditions of the perception of the compared magnitudes

<meta>This page continues the technical evaluation of psychophysical methods, specifically focusing on how random fluctuations or experimental "noise" affect the results of the Method of Just Noticeable Differences, the Method of Right and Wrong Cases, and the Method of Average Error.</meta>

[...rage error] <note>completing "average error" from the previous page</note> play a major role. If the margin of **random fluctuations** <term>Zufälligkeiten: unpredictable factors or "noise"—such as a lapse in attention or a slight muscle tremor—that can influence measurement results</term> is considerable, then in the **method of just noticeable differences**, the difference to be perceived will appear at times greatly increased and at times greatly decreased. Consequently, to declare it with certainty as "noticeable," the difference must have a more substantial magnitude than it would otherwise; the value one records as the just noticeable difference will thus increase due to large random fluctuations.

If, in the **method of right and wrong cases** <note>Also known today as the Method of Constant Stimuli</note>, random influences cause one weight to appear much heavier or much lighter than the other—so much so that the influence of the actual extra weight hardly matters compared to these chance influences—then, considering that irregular fluctuations act on average just as often to increase as to decrease the perception in either direction, the number of right and wrong cases will become noticeably equal. In any case, the number of right cases will be reduced compared to a situation where no or fewer random fluctuations were present.

Finally, in the **method of average error**, one can immediately see that the errors must turn out larger on average the more random fluctuations cause the compared magnitudes to appear now larger, now smaller, relative to one another.

In short, the stronger the irregular random fluctuations are, the smaller the resulting value which provides the **measure of sensitivity** <term>Empfindlichkeit: in psychophysics, the inverse of the threshold; a "smaller" value here means the subject is less sensitive to stimuli</term> across all three methods. There is no way at all to obtain a measure free from these random fluctuations; their average magnitude is always included as a factor in the measurement. This does not prevent us from obtaining comparable measures of sensitivity, provided this factor remains constant—that is, as long as the random fluctuations maintain the same average magnitude. Indeed, without these random fluctuations, the measurement methods of right and wrong cases and average error would not exist at all.

However, the previous observation leads to the important consideration that we should only regard those measures of sensitivity as comparable where one can assume an identical "play of chance." This demands exact comparability of both external and internal experimental circumstances. If the procedure <note>original: "Manipulation"; referring to the experimental setup or the way the stimuli are handled</note> changes in any way during the experiments, a different play of chance immediately occurs, and the measures cease to be comparable; likewise, because of possible...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how random fluctuations—such as shifts in attention or physiological changes—impact the reliability of psychophysical measurements. It emphasizes that these "random" factors vary between individuals and even within the same person over time.</meta>

...provides, one must consider that the variation of internal conditions in different individuals, and at different times within the same individual, does not assume the same margin for random occurrences. Therefore, wherever deviations appear between **measures of sensitivity** <term>Empfindlichkeitsmassen: quantitative values used to express how sensitive a person’s senses are to a stimulus</term>, one must always first ask whether they result from actual differences in sensitivity or from a lack of comparability in the circumstances under which they were tested.

In general, experiments must be greatly multiplied and, as already noted, a very large number of trials is especially necessary for the **method of right and wrong cases** <note>Now commonly called the Method of Constant Stimuli</note> and the **method of average error** <term>mittleren Fehler: a procedure where a participant adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard, and the researcher measures the average deviation from that standard</term> in order to obtain reliable results. A large number of observations here actually has a significantly different meaning than in physical and astronomical measurements. A physical or astronomical magnitude can be determined very precisely through an average of just a few accurate measurements using standard procedures. In contrast, in the method of average error and the method of right and wrong cases, the large number of trials is itself an essential condition for accuracy. 

A single observation here has almost no significance at all, and a small number of observations—no matter how precise—leads to no real accuracy. Individual right and wrong cases, or individual errors, fall in a truly irregular fashion; small groups of trials, despite being conducted under seemingly comparable external circumstances, can still yield wildly divergent results. Conversely, one is often astonished to see the most consistent results emerge from these irregularities once they are grouped into larger sets of trials. Here, the law known in the **calculus of probability** <note>original: Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung</note> as the **Law of Large Numbers** <term>Gesetz der grossen Zahlen: the principle that as a sample size grows, its mean gets closer to the average of the whole population; it suggests that "noise" cancels out over time</term> applies absolutely—the law that governs chance, provided that chance events are allowed to accumulate.

In this regard, one can hardly compare our methods with anything more fitting than a **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea god capable of changing his shape to avoid being captured. He would only reveal the truth if held fast through all his transformations.</note> who, instead of answering the questions posed simply and willingly, seems to evade every answer through the most varied forms he assumes; but it is enough to remain undeterred and hold him steadily at the same point, and he is forced to yield a reliable answer. In the past, I have lost much time, particularly with the method of right and wrong cases, by trying to draw conclusions from just a few trials...

...trying to draw results from hours or days of investigation without being able to reach anything solid; until I decided to repeat the experiments regarding the same point for entire months, daily with about 1 hour of **trial time** <term>Versuchszeit: the specific duration spent conducting experiments each day</term>, where I received results with which I have reason to be satisfied.

Aside from the influence—which cannot be eliminated—that the extent of the margin for irregular **random occurrences** <term>Zufälligkeiten: unpredictable factors like shifts in attention, fatigue, or mood that can skew results</term> has on the magnitude of the **measured values** <term>Masswerthe: the numerical data points derived from the experiments</term> (according to page 76), these random occurrences must compensate for one another through frequent repetition of the trials. In this way, as long as that margin and the sensitivity remain the same, one finds consistent measured values in experiments conducted at different times. Thus, individual chance loses its influence, and the definitive results become, in this sense, independent of chance. To be certain that this is the case, one will have to continue each series of trials for so long, or repeat it so often, until the larger **fractions** <note>original: "Fractionen"; here referring to subgroups or subsets of a larger data set used to check for consistency</note> or the repetitions thereof agree in the relevant result—allowing, of course, for deviations of such a small order as one must also permit as **observational errors** <term>Beobachtungsfehler: the small, unavoidable inaccuracies found in any scientific measurement</term> in physical observations; for the random occurrences that cannot be absolutely balanced represent the observational errors in our methods. 

One should not rest easy with an agreement between small fractions, as this agreement itself could be based on chance. Furthermore, the **calculus of probability** <term>Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung: the mathematical study of likelihood, used here to determine how many trials are needed to reach a certain level of statistical confidence</term> provides the means to determine in advance the degree of accuracy one can expect to achieve with a given probability through a given number of observations; on the other hand, it allows one to calculate the degree of accuracy actually achieved based on the number of observations and the degree of consistency shown by the individual observations or fractions of a series of observations.

The experiments should, from the outset, be set up as systematically as possible in relation to a specific purpose; however, a preliminary **trial and error** <term>Tatonnement: a French term for "groping" or "feeling one's way," describing exploratory testing before a formal study begins</term> can often be of great use in identifying the conditions most favorable for measurement and the incidental circumstances to be taken into account, in order to then establish the plan of the trials accordingly. ...to allow <note>The sentence fragment likely refers to allowing the effects of practice to stabilize</note> and thereby eliminate a portion of the changes dependent on it during the **main investigation** <term>Hauptuntersuchung: the primary phase of the scientific study conducted after preliminary trials have established a baseline</term>. In the meantime, the influence of **practice** <term>Uebung: the improvement in performance or change in sensitivity that occurs as a subject becomes more familiar with the experimental task</term> remains an element that must always be considered; it is therefore useful, right from the first preliminary trials, to take care to recognize and track it. To avoid obtaining one-sided results valid only for particular circumstances, the most extensive methodical variation of circumstances possible must be applied. I have so often experienced that what appeared quite regular under certain conditions turned out quite differently under others \*), that I have become very cautious about declaring results as general which have not proven themselves under very different circumstances. Now, however, a conflict arises. The more various circumstances one subjects to the experiment in combination, the fewer trials can be devoted to each individual one; consequently, the less accuracy one can establish for the measurement as a whole regarding those circumstances. One must therefore be just as careful not to try to investigate "everything at once," so to speak—by which one achieves nothing properly—as to avoid restricting the procedure too one-sidedly to certain fixed circumstances.

To illustrate this with the example of **weight trials** <term>Gewichtsversuche: experiments where a subject lifts two weights to determine the smallest difference in mass they can detect</term>, one can investigate how the **sensitivity** <term>Empfindlichkeit: the capacity of the senses to perceive or distinguish between stimuli</term> for weight differences changes depending on the magnitude of the main weights. But suppose one has determined the relationships in this regard by lifting the weights with one hand; will one also find the same results if the weights are lifted with the other hand? Or if, instead of lifting both with one and the same hand, one lifts one with one hand and the other with the other hand? Or if one changes the grip, the way the vessels are handled, or the position of the weights in the vessels? ...carry differences in the **lifting**? <note>original: "Hebung." Where it is necessary to compare the influence of different circumstances, the trials must be conducted alternately and in an alternating ascending and descending order with the larger and smaller values, whether on the same days or by alternating days. This is done to partly recognize, partly compensate for, and partly account for the influence that the sequence of trials has on the result—whether through changes in sensitivity or other reasons. In the example of weight trials, this applies to the series of different primary weights, different additional weights, different time intervals of lifting, etc., to which one subjects the experiment.

If, for example, trials are to be conducted with a series of different primary weights, one can proceed by going through the series first ascending and then descending on the same day; on the next day, one goes through it first descending and then ascending. Or, one might go through them only ascending on one day and only descending on the following day; such alternations are to be continued methodically throughout the entire series of days required for the experimental series.

In some experimental series, instead of always beginning and ending with the smallest or largest value, I have also begun and ended with each of the values to be tested in turn, moving through the series backwards and forwards as if it were arranged in a circle, where any starting point for traversing the circle can be chosen arbitrarily.
