In general, when considering the influence of the **time sequence** of trials, various circumstances—some of which counteract one another—come into consideration, partially in conflict, and can prevail now in one sense and now in another. On the one hand, especially when there is a lack of **practice**, the attention and the activity of the **sense organs** <term>Sinnesorgane: the biological structures, like eyes or ears, that receive stimuli</term> only get, so to speak, "into the swing of things" <note>original: "in Zug." Fechner uses this idiom to describe the period of warming up or reaching a state of focused readiness.</note> after a certain duration of trials, and begin to operate with a certain **uniformity**. On the other hand, they become exhausted, **fatigued** <term>Ermüdung: a decrease in sensory or mental performance resulting from prolonged activity</term>, or, depending on the circumstances, over-stimulated by a longer continuation of the work. Finally, from the very beginning and often through a long sequence of trials, the influence of increasing **practice** <term>Uebung: the gradual improvement in accuracy or sensitivity through repetition</term> makes itself felt up to certain limits. All these influences can be made the subject of special investigation; however, insofar as they come into play by themselves in every investigation, particular attention must be paid to the following.

If these factors are not themselves the object of the investigation, one must as far as possible avoid strong variations dependent upon them; thus, one should not continue the trials to the point of severe fatigue or over-stimulation, and one should prefer trials where the progress of practice is slow or already completed over those where practice is progressing rapidly. But since a certain sustained continuation of trials—partly within each day, and partly in the sequence of days—is on the other hand advantageous for **uniformity** as well as for the feasibility of the work in a given time, one must seek a certain measure in this regard, determined by individuality and circumstances. This must be left to the researcher’s own tact. In any case, the calculation should be based not on the exclusion, but on the exact determination and **compensation** <note>In this context, compensation refers to mathematical or methodical ways to balance out errors, such as alternating the order of trials to cancel out the effects of fatigue.</note> of those influences, which cannot be completely excluded at all. This requires a corresponding methodical arrangement of the trials, further information on which is to be sought in the discussion of the individual methods.

As useful and necessary as a methodical change of circumstances is for investigating the influence of their diversity, the greatest possible **constancy** of the same is nonetheless understandable, or, insofar as such cannot be attained, the greatest possible compensation...

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner’s foundational work on psychophysics, specifically focusing on the methodology for handling experimental data. Having previously discussed how time and the sequence of trials can influence results through factors like practice and fatigue, he now argues for a specific statistical approach—dividing data into smaller groups—to manage these "internal" fluctuations.</meta>

...of their variations is necessary for all experiments which are intended to be combined into a common result for given circumstances. Even if one has the external circumstances under control in this regard, one does not have the internal ones; since sensitivity itself, as well as the degree of it, is subject to a significant variability due to causes that can neither be calculated nor eliminated—namely, secondary internal conditions. This makes two considerations necessary: first, that one does not simply take measurement determinations from different time periods as comparable, even if made under identical external circumstances, unless one has convinced oneself of their comparability through the fact itself; second, that one divides longer **experimental series** <term>Versuchsreihen: a sequence of trials or tests conducted under specific conditions</term> not only into **fractions** <term>Fractionen: subsets or segments of a larger data set, often grouped by time</term> according to the different experimental circumstances, but also according to time, in order to examine these specifically, and generally prefers to combine the calculation results of the fractions of longer experimental series, rather than drawing the result from the entire unfractionated series all at once.

In general, **fractionation** <term>Fractionirung: the process of breaking a large body of data into smaller, chronological parts</term> has the advantage of assuring us of the greater or lesser constancy of the results, allowing us to follow any progress of **practice** <term>Uebung: the improvement in sensory accuracy or physical performance through repetition</term> and—which is a main point—to be able to more safely eliminate through calculation the influence of internal disturbances, which often manifest in opposite directions during longer series of trials, than if one treats the observations as a whole; as is shown by the special discussion of the methods.

Admittedly, the calculation result of each individual fraction, because of the smaller number of observations that go into it, has less certainty than that of the totality. But the **calculus of probability** <term>Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung: the mathematical study of chance and the likelihood of specific outcomes</term> shows that by combining the results of the fractions, one regains the certainty lost through fractionation in the individuals; according to which the stated advantages of fractionation still hold.

On the other hand, however, the complexity of the treatment and presentation of the experiments increases with fractionation, and the number of trials that one combines into a fraction has, in the **method of right and wrong cases** <note>This refers to the "constant method" where a subject judges whether a stimulus is greater, less, or equal to a standard.</note> and **mean error** <note>The "method of adjustment," where the subject tries to match a stimulus to a standard.</note>, one [effect] that only disappears with a large number of trials...

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner’s discussion on experimental rigor. Following his recommendation for "fractionation" (breaking data into smaller chunks), he now addresses the necessity of strict temporal and procedural regularity to prevent internal fluctuations—like hunger or expectation—from tainting the measurement values.</meta>

...[the] influence on the size of the **measurement values** <term>Masswerthe: numerical data points derived from experiments, used to quantify physical or psychological responses</term> is small enough to be accounted for by a **correction** <term>Correction: a mathematical adjustment made to data to account for known errors or variables</term>, or rendered harmless by using a consistently equal **number of trials** <term>Versuchszahl: the total count of individual tests performed within a single session or series</term>, as can be theoretically shown and proven through experience.

Since every somewhat extensive **series of experiments** <term>Versuchsreihe: a sequence of trials or tests conducted under specific conditions</term> requires a continuation over several days or even weeks and months, the experiments are to be conducted in the most regular time intervals possible and in regularly divided sections containing an equal number of experiments, arranged as identically or symmetrically as possible. Strict adherence to a fixed order in these regards contributes significantly not only to making and keeping the experiments of different days comparable and relatable to one another, and to preventing mix-ups and oversights in the arrangement of experimental circumstances, but also to simplifying the calculations and facilitating any use of the observations in general. Conversely, if one conducts observations sometimes many, sometimes few, sometimes in this sequence, sometimes in that, under these or those circumstances without a fixed rule, the usefulness of the observations suffers in every respect. The general **advantage** <term>Vortheil: the benefit or utility gained through structured methodology</term> that order has everywhere makes itself felt all the more tangibly in our method, the more details there are in general to arrange and keep in order.

In general, I always conduct the experiments of the same **observation series** <term>Beobachtungsreihe: a specific set of trials focused on a single phenomenon over time</term>, which run through a series of days, at the same time of day; since potentially the distance from the time of sleep and food intake can have an influence on the **sensitivity ratios** <term>Empfindlichkeitsverhältnisse: the relationship between stimulus intensity and the subject's ability to perceive it</term> to be investigated. Perhaps such an influence can often be neglected, all the more so if it affects the compared circumstances always in the same proportion; however, this will first have to be specifically investigated, and before such an investigation, this precaution will always be advisable, which, moreover, simply fits into the general rule of maintaining a fixed order in the timing of the experiments.

Insofar as the **judgment** <term>Urtheil: the participant's subjective decision or report regarding a sensation</term> in our methods is to be based on the pure statement of sensation, great care must be taken that it is not co-determined by an influence of the imagination, the expectation of the results to be obtained—in short, by what is usually called the influence of the **imagination** <term>Einbildungskraft: the mental faculty of forming images or concepts, which Fechner warns can bias scientific observation</term>...

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner's discussion on experimental rigor. ...on the other hand, in order to avoid an imagined influence of the **imagination** <term>Einbildungskraft: here referring to the subject’s mental expectation or preconceived notion, which can subconsciously bias their perception of a stimulus</term>, one must not make the procedure "blind," so to speak. In our methods, there are opportunities for both.

The arrangement of the **experimental circumstances** <term>Versuchsumstände: the specific environmental and procedural conditions, such as lighting or weight increments, under which a test is conducted</term>, the recording of the **observed values** <term>Werthe: the numerical data points collected during the experiment</term>, the summation of errors or correct and false cases, as well as all calculations to be based on them, must be organized and controlled—through repetition or other means—in such a way that the otherwise unavoidable oversights occurring amidst the mass of data to be recorded, summed, and calculated are avoided as much as possible; and in the recording and application itself, one must observe *unwavering fidelity*.

The adherence to these latter rules is more important and more difficult than one might think at first glance. According to the experiences I have had with myself and my fellow observers, I do not trust any summation or calculation that has not been controlled through repetition or some other means. Even during a repeated count or calculation, especially if it is done in the same form shortly after the first, one overlooks committed errors as easily as one misses typos when proofreading a text. *Care* and *caution* in this regard cannot be recommended enough; and as burdensome as the repetition or other control of such inherently tedious operations can be, it is necessary so as not to jeopardize the benefit of careful observation through oversights in its application.

Even before the recording, however, oversights can easily be committed given the generally necessary methodical variation of circumstances; one might confuse one circumstance with another in the arrangement, or continue through several experimental sections without the required change. Therefore, one must make it a rule to perform a controlling review in this regard.

As far as *fidelity* in recording is concerned, one feels only too often tempted—even without wishing to falsify the results—to exclude individual, unusual observation values; for example, in the **method of average errors** <term>Methode der mittleren Fehler: a fundamental psychophysical method where a subject attempts to adjust a variable stimulus to match a constant standard; the "average error" measures their precision</term>, one might want to exclude unusually large errors, perhaps blaming them on a lapse in attention. ### c) **Considerations regarding the temporal and spatial conditions of experiments; constant errors.**

Insofar as our methods involve comparing two magnitudes, **successive** perception is preferable to **simultaneous** perception; the latter is essentially impossible, as attention naturally shifts back and forth between one magnitude and the other. The experiment must therefore be arranged to observe the magnitudes to be compared in quick succession, yet each as undisturbed as possible by the interference of the other, performing their **superposition** <note>In this context, "superposition" refers to the mental act of laying one perceived image or sensation over another in the mind's eye or memory to compare them.</note> only within the memory. This ability to compare magnitudes in such a manner is quite remarkable, as **E. H. Weber** <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878) was a German physician whose work on the sense of touch and "just-noticeable differences" laid the foundation for experimental psychology.</note> has already pointed out, and its explanation can only be expected in the future from the progress of **inner psychophysics** <term>Innere Psychophysik: the study of the relationship between the mind/soul and the internal nervous system, rather than the external world.</term>. For now, we must simply rely on the fact of its existence.

However, the fact that the perception of the compared magnitudes does not **coincide** <note>original: "coincidirt"; meaning to happen at the exact same time or place</note> directly in time—just as they do not coincide directly in space and thus enter into a different relationship with the perceiving organs—produces effects that influence the measurement. I will briefly refer to such conditions as the temporal and spatial positioning of the compared magnitudes. The primary difficulties in establishing an accurate, comparable measure of sensitivity are based on this. Therefore, the refinement of our methods must focus on determining and eliminating these factors through experimental procedures and calculation. In this regard, we are capable of achieving more than might initially seem possible, though until now, this subject has received less attention than it deserves.

Generally, regarding temporal conditions, the following must be considered: 1) The duration during which a magnitude is perceived—for example, lifting a weight in **weight-lifting experiments** <term>Gewichtsversuche: experiments testing the perception of weight differences through physical sensation</term>, or observing a distance in **visual estimation experiments** <term>Augenmassversuche: tests measuring the accuracy of the eye in judging lengths or distances</term>, and so on. 2) The interval of time which one...

Incidentally, the existence of constant errors brings only a complication, not an inaccuracy, into the measurements made by our methods. Unfortunately, the constancy of "constant errors" does not exist in a strict sense. ### d) Specifics regarding the method of right and wrong cases, in application to weight experiments.

The experiments (begun in the year 1855), upon which the following explanations regarding the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle: a procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and identifies which is stronger; the precursor to the modern Method of Constant Stimuli</term> are based, were initially undertaken with the simple intention of a more precise testing of **Weber's law** <term>Weber'sches Gesetz: the principle that the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli is a constant proportion of the original stimulus</term>. Later, they were continued and further expanded in the interest of developing the method itself, after it became clear that the testing I had in mind first required a prior investigation into the conditions of the method's accuracy, and a development of its experimental and computational sides, which at the time did not yet exist. 

For several years, I regarded it as a kind of daily labor to conduct experiments in this interest for about one hour, and to continue these consistently for a greater number of days with regard to determining this or that specific ratio. Through this, a body of experimental material has grown that is by no means exhausted in this writing. Evidence of this is given by the large number of experiments appearing in some of the following chapters, and the multiple repetitions of experimental series to establish important points at different times and under altered circumstances; through this, a great deal of practice in the handling of the method has also arisen.

Insofar as our method depends on determining the ratio of the number of right cases to the number of false cases or to the total number of cases, I will—preferring the use of the latter ratio—designate the number of right cases with *r*, the false cases with *f*, and the total number of cases with *n*. Thus, the ratio with which we will mainly have to concern ourselves is $\frac{r}{n}$. However, when a total number of experiments regarding an observed value is divided into equal **fractions** <term>Fractionen: smaller subsets of data used to check for consistency or changes over time</term>, and these specifically in...

...be taken into account, where *r* and *n* refer to the number of correct and total cases for each *fraction* <term>Fraction: a specific set or subgroup of trials</term> specifically, while $\nu$ denotes the number of *fractions*, so that $\nu n$ is the total number of cases for the respective **observation value** <term>Beobachtungswerth: the specific magnitude or condition being tested, such as a specific weight difference</term>. If the entire series of observations, as is usually the case, relates to several observation values to be compared with each other, then naturally $\nu n$ must be multiplied by their number to obtain the total number of cases for the entire series.

Where the **judgment** <term>Urtheil: the subject’s decision on which weight feels heavier</term> remains doubtful, such a case is, as noted, to be counted half toward the correct and half toward the incorrect cases. To avoid the half-cases resulting from this, however, I count—since the formation of the ratio $\frac{r}{n}$ depends only on proportions—each correct judgment as two correct, each incorrect as two incorrect cases; and each where the judgment remains doubtful as one correct and one incorrect. <note>Fechner is mathematically doubling his data set to keep his tallies in whole numbers rather than dealing with 0.5 decimals.</note>

*P* will denote the **main weight** <term>Hauptgewicht: the base load used in both hands before any extra weight is added</term>, i.e., the weight of each of the vessels lifted for comparison including their load but without *D*; *D* will denote the **additional weight** <term>Zusatzgewicht: the small increment added to one weight to create a difference</term> (extra weight) used in the experiment. *h* denotes a value that is directly proportional to the **sensitivity to differences** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit: the ability of a person to detect small differences between stimuli</term>, and thus inversely proportional to the additional weight *D* that is capable of yielding an equal ratio of $\frac{r}{n}$; or, in short, the **measure of sensitivity to differences**, which is the objective of the study.

The method can be carried out in two ways: according to a first procedure, where one decides which is heavier or lighter only after repeated weighing back and forth of the loaded vessels; according to a second procedure, where one decides strictly after each individual comparative lifting of both vessels, or in case of doubt, places the judgment among the undecided, which are then counted half toward the correct and half toward the incorrect.

Previously, I always used the first procedure; but later I discarded all experiments performed with it and adhered exclusively to the second, after convincing myself of its far greater superiority. Not only can it be performed more uniformly than the first, but it also allows for a precise **elimination** <term>Elimination: the statistical removal of systematic biases, like being more sensitive with the right hand than the left</term> and determination of...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "method of right and wrong cases" (the method of constant stimuli). Fechner is explaining how to handle systematic biases (constant errors) and the practical differences between his two primary experimental procedures.</meta>

Co-influences depending on the position in time and space, which establish a **constant error** <term>Constant Error: a systematic bias in judgment, such as the tendency to perceive the second of two weights as heavier simply because it was lifted second</term>, can only be managed by using the second method. This is achieved through an appropriate counterpositioning of these influences against one another, as will be shown below.

Naturally, using the second method makes it easier to commit an **error** regarding the direction of the difference than in the first case. With the same difference *D* and an equal total number of cases, the number of undecided and false cases will be larger than in the first method. However, this does not make the method less accurate, provided that the method itself is based on the commission of errors; this can be compensated for by using a larger *D* to avoid obtaining ratios <gloss>r/n: the ratio of correct cases to the total number of trials</gloss> that are too small, which are just as disadvantageous for measurement as ratios that are too large. On the other hand, the second method provides many more cases in the same amount of time, and every single **double lift** <term>Doppelhebung: the act of lifting two weights in sequence to form one comparative judgment</term> can be made exactly the same as or comparable to the next.

In the first method, it is essential that the subject does not know the location of the **excess weight** <term>Mehrgewicht: the small additional weight added to one vessel to create a difference</term>. This requires an **assistant** to determine its position each time to exclude any influence of **imagination** <term>Einbildungskraft: the subject’s psychological expectations or bias</term> on the **judgment**. In the second method—according to the way it is carried out as described below—this is not only unnecessary but not even applicable. The reasons for this will be more clearly justified after a more detailed explanation of the method's entire situation.

In accordance with the remark on page 88, the lifting of the vessels must always be done successively. A double lift in the second method, which forms the basis for a judgment, thus arises from the sequential, single lifting of one vessel and then the other; it therefore includes two **simple lifts**. However, since every judgment is counted as two cases (in the manner specified on page 94 <note>Fechner doubled his tallying on the previous page to avoid using 0.5 for doubtful cases</note>), the **total number of cases** is determined by the number of simple lifts, not the number of double lifts.

If I lift both vessels with the same hand, I designate this as the **one-handed procedure**; if I lift one with one hand and the other with the other hand, I call it the **two-handed procedure**. The loading weights, which were checked by re-weighing, also had different sizes according to their various weights. Since the vessels had to be wide enough to accommodate even the largest weights, the small and even the medium-sized ones were not secured against shifting when the vessels were lifted. I assumed that the pressure would always fall with the full weight of the vessel upon the same points of the hand grasping the handles, and therefore no disadvantage could arise from any displacement of the weights within the vessels. However, given the multitude of other secondary circumstances that had to be investigated one after another—all of which might influence the procedure—I neglected to make this the subject of a specific investigation. 

This oversight resulted in a heavy penalty. <note>The German phrase "hat sich schwer gerächt" literally means "has revenged itself heavily," an idiom indicating that a past mistake caused significant later trouble.</note> For when I finally did direct my investigation toward this matter for the sake of certainty—by intentionally setting up comparative trials with loading weights fixed in the center versus at the very side of the vessel—it became clear that, due not to a change in the amount of weight but rather to a different **distribution of pressure**, the results in both cases turned out quite decisively different. Specifically, the vessel appears heaviest when the weight occupies the center of the vessel, and the difference is not even or insignificant when one compares extreme positions in this regard. 

Now, in my earlier experiments, only much smaller displacements could have occurred, which in all probability compensated for one another in the main due to the large number of trials. This has been confirmed partly by the consistency of the individual larger fractions in the numbers obtained, and partly by the fact that later experiments with the more perfect equipment led essentially to exactly the same results. Nevertheless, those earlier experiments no longer brought me any joy; their precision and binding force, if not as a whole then in their individual determinations, had become too precarious. I preferred the effort of resuming them with a new apparatus over the comfort of relying on the previous ones.

All experiments to which I shall refer in the following were carried out according to the second procedure (p. 94) under very uniform circumstances, which I describe here as **normal circumstances** or **standard conditions**, bypassing secondary points that I reserve for later addition in the *Methods of Measurement*. <term>Methods of Measurement (Massmethoden): Likely referring to Fechner's "Kollectivmasslehre" or a specific section of his psychophysical work where he details mathematical treatments of data.</term> These standard conditions were only deviated from insofar as the effect of such changes was itself to be made the subject of investigation.

weights of various thicknesses (made partly of lead and partly of zinc) were inserted so that they were held firmly in place and could not shift during the **lifts**. The vessel, containing the inserted weights and covered with a lid—on the center of which a small open box was soldered—collectively formed the **main weight *P***, which was carefully made identical for both vessels. The **additional weight *D*** <note>In Fechner's experiments, *P* represents the constant base weight, while *D* (from the German *Differenz*) is the small additional weight used to test the "just noticeable difference" in perception.</note> was then placed into the small box on the lid of one of the two vessels; in this way, it also maintained its fixed position in the center of the main weight. The handle of the vessels was a wooden roller, one Parisian inch <note>original: "par. Zoll." A Parisian inch was a pre-metric unit approximately equal to 2.7 centimeters.</note> in diameter, which could rotate around a horizontal axis and was grasped with the whole hand.

Each vessel, depending on whether a lighter or heavier lid was used, weighed 300 or 400 grams including the lid. Thus, 300 grams was the smallest **main weight *P*** that could be applied—namely, when no further loading weights were added while using the light lid. I used 3000 grams as the largest main weight; the apparatus might not have withstood a heavier load over the long term. When the goal was not to test the effects of using different main weights, I usually applied 1000 grams as the main weight.

The values 0.04 *P* and 0.08 *P* mostly served as additional weights.

Even though both vessels were constructed exactly alike, in every series of trials, the additional weight *D* was placed in one vessel just as often as the other under otherwise identical circumstances. This was done to compensate for the influence of any difference that might have gone unnoticed.

The **lift height** was limited by a horizontal board mounted at a certain height above the experimental table, so that it measured 2 inches and 9 Parisian lines <note>A "line" (*Linie*) was 1/12th of a Parisian inch. This total height is roughly 7.4 centimeters.</note>.

The lifts were performed with bare arms, in shirt sleeves.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of Gustav Fechner’s experimental protocols. On the previous page, he established the base weights (P) and the additional difference weights (D). ...which constitute just as many trials, I group together as an *experimental division*, during which *D* <note>The additional weight used to create a "just noticeable difference."</note> always remained in the same vessel. In the middle of each division, that is, after 32 simple lifts, the position of the vessels was swapped from left to right. The so-called *4 main cases* <term>4 Hauptfälle: These are the four possible combinations of spatial (left vs. right) and temporal (first vs. second lift) order used to cancel out position and sequence biases.</term> of the method—which will be discussed in more detail below—are based on the fourfold variation in the temporal and spatial position that the additional weight *D* thereby receives; each case was thus represented by 16 simple lifts or trials in every experimental division. Usually, 8 to 12 such divisions of 64 trials each were conducted in succession on every day of experimentation, varying the conditions to be investigated (*P*, *D*, etc.); in the larger series of experiments, this continued for mostly one month.

The time of each lift of a vessel, regulated by a *metronome* <note>original: "Zähler." While "Zähler" usually means "counter," in this context, it refers to a device used to mark the rhythm of the seconds.</note>, lasted 1 second; each setting down lasted 1 second; and the interval between setting down one vessel and lifting the other was also 1 second. Thus, the time for each **double-lift**, which constitutes one comparison or 2 trials, was exactly 5 seconds. I allowed an equal interval—that is, 5 seconds—between one double-lift and the next, during which the recording of the result took place. In the one-handed procedure, the recording was always done with the idle hand; in the two-handed procedure, it alternated between one hand or the other depending on the day of experimentation.

One soon becomes accustomed to performing these operations quite mechanically according to the *metronome*, and even the application of attention soon becomes quite mechanical and uniform. As I can demonstrate from my own experimental data, this attention shows no noticeable weakening by the end of the daily hour of testing. The judgments—right is heavier, left is heavier, or ambiguous—are jointly determined by the additional weight *D*, the constant influences of the temporal and spatial positions, and irregular coincidences. These judgments, which change irregularly in direction, are "delivered into the hand" (so to speak) with an objective character during the double-lifts, without the need for choice or deliberation, which was indeed required in the first method.

<meta>This page transitions from the physical setup of Fechner’s weight-lifting experiments to the mathematical logic behind them. He discusses how to calculate sensitivity based on the ratio of correct judgments to total trials.</meta>

How to easily count the individual cases separately is specified in more detail in the section on »Measurement Methods.«

So much for now regarding the external conditions of the experiments. I will now proceed to the more general conditions of the method.

The primary objective of the method is to investigate how **difference sensitivity** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit: The ability of a person to detect the smallest possible difference between two stimuli, such as weights.</term> for weights compares under various circumstances. For each set of conditions being compared, we must perform a sufficient number of trials to obtain a value for the ratio $r/n$ <note>Where *r* represents the number of "right" or correct identifications of the heavier weight, and *n* represents the total number of trials.</note>. Alternatively, by dividing the total number of trials into $\nu$ <note>The Greek letter "nu," representing a specific number of groups or fractions.</note> fractions, we can obtain $\nu$ values for $r/n$. From these, we derive the measure of difference sensitivity. Along with this, we can pursue the secondary task of determining the size and direction of the constant side-influences <note>Fechner is referring to "constant errors," such as a person’s natural tendency to always think the second weight lifted is heavier, regardless of the actual weight.</note> acting upon the experiments.

At this point, a fundamental difficulty seems to present itself from the very beginning.

We know that, under otherwise identical circumstances, the ratio $r/n$ increases along with the sensitivity to the weight difference. However, a value of $r/n$ that is twice as large does not correspond to a difference sensitivity that is twice as great, if we wish to remain faithful to the concept of measurement we have established. Rather, a **difference weight** <term>Zulagegewicht: The small additional weight (*D*) added to one of the two main weights (*P*) to create a perceptible difference.</term> *D* that is half as large, which yields an identical ratio $r/n$, corresponds to double the sensitivity. From a general perspective, we can observe the following:

Even if sensitivity is very low, one can always choose a difference weight *D* that is so large in proportion to the base weight *P* that almost all—or even all—cases are judged correctly. It is evident that even the most significant increase in sensitivity cannot then lead to an increase in the ratio $r/n$ <note>Because you cannot be "more correct" than 100%.</note>. Therefore, this ratio cannot serve as a suitable universal standard for sensitivity, as it can remain nearly or entirely constant even when sensitivity changes significantly. Conversely, with greatly increased sensitivity, a much smaller difference weight will suffice to bring the ratio $r/n$ to the same approximation of $n/n$ <note>Meaning a perfect score of 100% correct.</note>, and

<summary>Fechner explains the mathematical challenge of measuring sensitivity, noting that the ratio of correct answers (r/n) is not a direct linear scale for human perception. He argues that true sensitivity is better measured by how small a weight difference a person can detect with a specific level of accuracy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "method of right and wrong cases," moving from the raw data of trial ratios to the challenge of establishing a standardized mathematical measure for human sensitivity.</meta>

...based on this, one can judge the increase in sensitivity, such that the very nature of the matter points us toward the measurement scale we have established. But how should this find its place within our method?

Suppose, for example, I want to compare the sensitivity of the left and right hands for **weight differences**. Using the same **main weight** *P* <note>The standard weight used as a baseline in the experiment.</note> and the same **added weight** *D* <note>The small additional weight added to one of the containers to create a difference; from the German *Differenz*.</note>, I perform lifts of both vessels—once with the left hand (L.) and another time with the right (R.). Initially, I only obtain a different ratio of $r/n$ <note>The ratio of "right" or correct identifications (*r*) to the total number of trials (*n*).</note> for the left and right hands. While this allows me to conclude that one hand has greater or lesser sensitivity than the other, it does not yet provide a comparable *measure* of these sensitivities. The question then arises: how do I go about finding the different values for the added weight *D* that would yield the exact same ratio of $r/n$ for both the left and right hands?

Similarly, I may wish to investigate the sensitivity of a single hand, or the average of both hands, using different values for the main weight *P*. Experience shows that the same added weight *D* yields a larger ratio of $r/n$ when the main weight *P* is small than when it is large. However, the real task is to find the different values of *D* that produce the same ratio $r/n$ for different values of *P*. By taking the reciprocal value <note>In mathematics, the reciprocal is $1$ divided by the number ($1/D$). Fechner uses this because as sensitivity goes up, the weight difference needed to detect it goes down.</note> of these different *D* values, we obtain the measure of **difference sensitivity** for the various values of *P*.

The **method of right and wrong cases**, in the way it has been applied until now, was in fact only suited to indicate a "more" or a "less," but not to provide a comparable measure of sensitivity. However, the method can be further developed to provide such a measure.

First, the path of *trial and error* <term>original: *Tatonnement*. A method of searching for a value by making repeated adjustments until the desired result is reached.</term> presents itself. One could repeatedly alter the added weight under the compared circumstances until the same ratio $r/n$ is achieved. But since a reliable result for even a single value of *D* can only be drawn from a vast number of trials, this procedure—which requires a massive number of trials for every single *D* tested—is not only unspeakably tedious but also fails to achieve any real accuracy even after the most painstaking effort.

To be sure, one can interpolate between nearby values, and for a long time I sought to help myself in this way; however, the disadvantage of cumbersomeness and inaccuracy is only very incompletely remedied by this. Fortunately, however, there is a simple and complete solution.

According to a rule that is fundamentally precise and well-proven through my own experiments—founded on mathematical analysis yet easily translated into practice—one can determine from any ratio $r/n$ <note>The ratio of "right" or correct responses (*r*) to the total number of trials (*n*).</note> obtained at a certain added weight *D*, what value of *D* would have been required (with the same main weight *P* and all other circumstances kept equal) to yield any other arbitrary ratio $r/n$. This includes the ratio one might wish to use as a fixed baseline, provided that the $r/n$ from which one draws the conclusion was obtained from a sufficiently large total number of trials *n*. Indeed, one can find the measure of <term>differential sensitivity</term> <note>The ability of a person to detect a small difference between two stimuli, such as weights.</note> directly from a table without any calculation, using any $r/n$ based on a sufficiently large *n* \*) such that it corresponds to the concept of this measure we have established. It shall be shown immediately how this is to be achieved, after first offering a few words on the path that led to it.

During a study of the <term>calculus of probability</term> <note>The branch of mathematics dealing with the analysis of random phenomena.</note>, to which I found myself driven again and again by the interest in developing our methods, a two-fold observation presented itself to me: 1) that given the nature of our procedure, the measure of sensitivity for differences could be represented by the value usually designated as *h*, which according to <note>Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), the German mathematician whose "Gaussian distribution" is central to statistics.</note> **Gauss** provides the **measure of precision** of observations, insofar as—provided the modality of the procedure is kept comparable—the precision depends only on the sensitivity with which the difference is perceived; 2) that between the ratio $r/n$ provided by the experiments and the product of that measure *h* and the <term>added weight</term> *D* <note>The small weight added to the standard weight to test if the subject can feel the difference.</note> at which the $r/n$ was found—that is, between $r/n$ and $hD$—there exists a...

<meta>This page continues the technical justification for a mathematical formula that relates the ratio of correct responses to the degree of sensory sensitivity. The author is transitioning from the theoretical "why" to the practical "how" of his measurement system.</meta>

a mathematical relationship must exist that allows for the derivation of *$h D$* from $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The ratio of right answers (*r*) to the total number of trials (*n*).</note>, and subsequently, by dividing by *$D$* <note>The difference between two weights or stimuli.</note>, one can find the measure of <term>differential sensitivity</term> *$h$* <note>A mathematical value representing how precisely a person can distinguish between two stimuli; a higher *h* means higher precision.</note>.

My remaining task was first to establish this relationship theoretically, second to prove it through experimentation, and third to apply it practically to our <term>measurement method</term>. I believe I have solved these three tasks satisfactorily, which should finally grant the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>A procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records how often they correctly identify the difference.</note> the status of a true measurement method.

As for the <term>mathematical deduction</term> <note>The logical derivation of a formula based on existing axioms or principles.</note>, I will provide it in the following insertion, as it is not strictly necessary for the practical application of the method to understand it. The <term>experimental proof</term> essentially boils down to showing through testing that if one has obtained a certain value of $\frac{r}{n}$ at a certain value of *$D$* (while sensitivity remains constant), then the value of $\frac{r}{n}$ calculated for a different value of *$D$*—one that stands in a specific proportion to the first—according to our mathematical relationship will be confirmed by experiments. This allows, of course, for such small deviations as can be attributed to random chance. Or, to put it another way: the ratios of $\frac{r}{n}$ obtained experimentally at different values of *$D$* (but equal sensitivity) should, when using a table based on our mathematical relationship, yield values of *$h D$* that are proportional to *$D$*.\*) To support this, I have very extensive series of observations at my disposal, which I will share in "Measurement Methods." We will also naturally be led to some of these in the 9th and 12th chapters.

Following this, the subject can be presented so practically that anyone can use the method for measurement, even without understanding the reasoning behind the rules or possessing prior mathematical knowledge. One will also find this—

---

\*) Since the <term>differential sensitivity</term> discussed here varies with *$P$* <note>The "standard" or baseline weight used in the experiment.</note> (but not with *$D$*, as long as *$D$* remains small), a constant *$P$* is required for experiments intended to maintain consistent sensitivity.

### Mathematical Formulation and Derivation of the Calculation Rule for the Method of Right and Wrong Cases.

While there is currently no <term>a priori</term> <note>original: "aprioristisches Princip"; referring to knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation.</note> principle for how the ratio $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The number of correct cases (*r*) divided by the total number of cases (*n*).</note> must change relative to the size of the primary weight $P$ when the additional weight $D$ remains constant—rather, this must be viewed as a law to be established through experiment—it is, on the other hand, possible to state <term>a priori</term> according to the principles of the <term>calculus of probabilities</term> how the ratio $\frac{r}{n}$ must change (assuming a large $n$) if the additional weight $D$ changes while the primary weight $P$ and the overall <term>differential sensitivity</term> $h$ remain constant. This also applies if there is a change in whatever influence determines the apparent excess weight, which may be represented here once and for all by $D$. Indeed, the same principles are decisive here as those by which one can determine—assuming a constant precision of observation—the change in the relative number of observation errors according to changes in their magnitude. The relationship between $\frac{r}{n}$ and $Dh$ being discussed here cannot, however, be expressed by a simple equation, but only through an <term>integral expression</term> <note>A mathematical formula representing the area under a curve; in this case, the bell curve of probability.</note>. For practical use, this relationship must be represented in tabular form, as will be shown below.

The integral expression, to be designated hereafter as $\Theta$ <note>The Greek letter Theta.</note>, which comes into play here, is the same one used to determine the relative number or probability of errors within given magnitude limits. The only difference is that in place of the "error"—usually designated by $\Delta$—we use half of the additional weight $\frac{D}{2}$:

->$\Theta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{t} e^{-t^2} dt$<-

where $\pi$ is <term>Ludolf's number</term> <note>The mathematical constant pi (approximately 3.14159), named here after Ludolph van Ceulen.</note>, $e$ is the base of natural logarithms, $t = h\Delta = \frac{hD}{2}$, and $h$ is the <term>measure of precision</term> in the <term>Gaussian sense</term> <note>Referring to Carl Friedrich Gauss and the "Normal Distribution" or bell curve used to describe random errors.</note>. The value of $t$ that corresponds to a given value of $\Theta$ can be found in various tables, such as in the *Berlin Astronomical Yearbook* for 1834, p. 305 ff., up to $t = 2.0$, and in a separately published lithographed table (no longer available in bookstores) up to $t = 3.0$. Thus, if $\Theta$ is determined based on the ratio $\frac{r}{n}$, one can simultaneously determine $t$ or $\frac{hD}{2}$.

...integral.

Immediately below, the following equations, which are fundamental to our method, will be proven; by means of these, $\Theta$ <note>The Greek letter Theta, representing the value of the probability integral.</note> can be derived from $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The ratio of correct responses ($r$) to the total number of trials ($n$).</note>.

->$\frac{r}{n} = \frac{1 + \Theta}{2}; \frac{f}{n} = \frac{1 - \Theta}{2}; \frac{r}{f} = \frac{1 + \Theta}{1 - \Theta}$<-

and accordingly

->$\frac{2r}{n} - 1 = 1 - \frac{2f}{n} = \Theta$.<-

Of these relationships, it is sufficient to apply and consider the one between $\frac{r}{n}$ and $\Theta$ as follows. From the observed ratio $\frac{r}{n}$, one derives the value $\Theta$ according to the equation $\frac{2r}{n} - 1 = \Theta$, looks up the corresponding value $t = \frac{hD}{2}$ in a table of the integral $\Theta$, and divides it by $\frac{D}{2}$ to obtain $h$ <note>The precision of the observer's judgment.</note>, or divides by $D$ if one—as we shall do—takes the $h$ of the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> to be only half as large as that used in the <term>theory of errors</term>. However, in order to avoid having to manually calculate the value $\frac{2r}{n} - 1$ from the observed $\frac{r}{n}$ every time, I have converted the table of the integral $\Theta$ (where the relationship is given between $\Theta = \frac{2r}{n} - 1$ and $t$) into one where the relationship is given directly between $\frac{r}{n}$ and $t$. This provides the **Fundamental Table** found below.

The mathematical derivation of the above relationship between $\frac{r}{n}$ and $\Theta$ has passed the scrutiny of Professor **Möbius** <note>August Ferdinand Möbius (1790–1868), a famous German mathematician and astronomer.</note>, to whom I submitted it; therefore, from a mathematical standpoint, it may be regarded as beyond reproach. He was kind enough, however, to substitute my somewhat clumsy derivation with a shorter and more precise one that leads to the same result, which I therefore prefer to share in the following instead of my own.

The **Möbius** derivation uses the deviation of two parts of a straight line from equality as an example, rather than the deviation of two weights from equality. The principle, however, is the same in either case.

Let it be generally

->$\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{h \Delta} e^{-t^2} dt$<-

the probability that the error committed during the measurement of a magnitude falls within the limits of $-\Delta$ and $+\Delta$, in which expression $h$ is, as above, the <term>measure of precision</term> of the measurement, and $\pi$ is **Ludolf’s number** <note>The mathematical constant pi ($\approx$ 3.14159), named here after Ludolph van Ceulen.</note>.

Now, let there be for example:

->A C B<-

three points in a straight line; $C$ is situated very close to, but not exactly in, the middle between $A$ and $B$. In $n$ observations according to the method...

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of the "method of right and wrong cases" introduced on the previous page. It transitions from general formulas to a specific geometric example involving the estimation of a midpoint to illustrate how the ratio of correct to incorrect judgments relates to the probability integral.</meta>

of the <term>right and wrong cases</term><note>The author is using 'a' for right cases and 'b' for wrong cases, which correspond to 'r' and 'f' from the previous page.</note>, I judge *a* times that *C* lies closer to *A* than to *B*; therefore *CB* > *CA*; and I judge *n* — *a* = *b* times that *C* lies closer to *B* than to *A*, therefore *CB* < *CA*. According to this, the probabilities for *CA* < *CB* and for *CB* < *CA* relate to one another as *a* and *b*, and these two probabilities themselves are $\frac{a}{n}$ and $\frac{b}{n}$.

Now, in the line
<image-desc>A horizontal line segment with letters A, C, M, B positioned beneath it. A is at the left end, B at the right end. M is the midpoint, and C is located between A and M, placed very close to M.</image-desc>
-> ——————————————————— <-
-> A &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; C &nbsp; M &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; B <-

let *M* be the actual <term>midpoint</term> of *AB*, and let *C* lie a small distance from *M* toward *A*; thus, my judgment has been a correct one *a* times, and I have been mistaken *b* times. Specifically, I have believed the point *C* to lie between *M* and *B* a total of *b* times; in each of these *b* estimations, I have therefore mistakenly assumed the point to be further than the small line *CM*, specifically beyond *M* toward *B*, and have thus committed an error each time that is > *CM*, in the same direction.

-> The probability for this is, on one hand = $\frac{b}{n}$, and on the other hand = $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{h. CM}^{\infty} e^{-t^2} dt$ <-

where *CM* is to be regarded as a positive quantity. Now, since
-> $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{h. CM} \dots\dots + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{h. CM}^{\infty} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{2},$ <-
-> it follows that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{h. CM} \dots\dots + \frac{b}{n} = \frac{1}{2},$ and consequently <-
-> $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{h. CM} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{b}{n} = \frac{1}{2} - 1 + \frac{a}{n} = \frac{a}{n} - \frac{1}{2}.$ <-

Finally, therefore:
-> $\frac{a}{n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{h. CM} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{h. CM} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{-h. CM}^{\infty} \dots\dots$ <-
-> $\frac{b}{n} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{h. CM} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{h. CM}^{\infty} \dots\dots = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{-h. CM} \dots\dots$ <-

These two formulas for $\frac{a}{n}$ and $\frac{b}{n}$ could also be explained thus: In a sequence of *n* observations of the line *ACMB*, of which only the points *A* and *B* are visible, one believes in *a* cases that *M* lies somewhere between *C* and *B* (which is the truth); and in *b* cases (falsely), that *M* lies somewhere between *A* and *C*. However, the <term>limits of integration</term> also refer to these same two segments *CB* and *AC*, which for $\frac{a}{n}$ are $\dots\dots -h. CM$ and $\infty$, and for $\frac{b}{n}$ are $\dots\dots -\infty$ and $-h. CM$. For if the direction *ACMB* is taken as positive and *M* as the starting point, then the <term>abscissae</term><note>Horizontal coordinates on a graph.</note> of *C* and *B* = — *CM* and *MB*, and the abscissae of *A* and *C* = — *AM* and — *CM*; however, *AM* and *MB* are to be considered as infinite relative to *CM*<note>In error theory, the physical boundaries of an object are often treated as "infinite" if they are very large compared to the tiny errors being measured, allowing the use of standard calculus formulas.</note>.

So much for Möbius’s derivation <note>August Ferdinand Möbius (1790–1868) was a German mathematician; the author is likely referencing his work on the application of the law of errors.</note>.

To now reduce the example of the lines to the example of weights, one will have to compare one weight $P$ with line segment $AC$, the other weight $P + D$ with $BC$, and the length $AM = \frac{AC + BC}{2}$ with $P + \frac{D}{2}$ <note>$P$ represents a standard weight and $D$ represents the "difference" or the additional weight added to the second stimulus.</note>. Consequently, the segment $CM$ must be compared with $\frac{D}{2}$—therefore, $\frac{D}{2}$ must be substituted for $CM$ in the previous formulas. Furthermore, $\frac{a}{n}$ is equal to our $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>$r/n$ represents the ratio of "right" (richtige) cases to the total number of trials.</note> and $\frac{b}{n}$ is equal to our $\frac{f}{n}$ <note>$f/n$ represents the ratio of "false" (falsche) cases to the total number of trials.</note>, which yields the following formulas for the direct application of our method:

->$\frac{r}{n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{hD} e^{-t^2} dt$<-

->$\frac{f}{n} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{hD} e^{-t^2} dt$<-

or, if we denote the integral

->$\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{hD} e^{-t^2} dt$ briefly with $\Theta$<-

->$\frac{r}{n} = \frac{1 + \Theta}{2} ; \frac{f}{n} = \frac{1 - \Theta}{2} ; \Theta = \frac{2r}{n} - 1 = 1 - \frac{2f}{n}$<-

The fact that we, as noted above, set the <term>measure of precision</term> or <term>measure of sensitivity</term> ($h$) of our method to equal half the measure of precision used in the <term>theory of errors</term> <note>The "theory of errors" refers to Gaussian distribution; the author is adjusting the constant $h$ to fit the specific needs of psychophysical testing.</note> has no influence on the applications within our method, since here we are only concerned with the ratios of $t$ or $h$. It would, however, come into consideration if one wished to compare the results of the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> in absolute value with those obtained through the <term>method of average errors</term>. The integral $\Theta$ provides the means for this mediation, as it does for the a priori calculation of the probable error or the uncertainty of $\frac{r}{n}$ or $t$, though we shall not concern ourselves with those matters here.

Let us now turn to the practical application:

The rule in question simply comes down to this: using the fractional value $\frac{r}{n}$ obtained from the experiments, look up the corresponding value $t = hD$ in the following table—which I call the **Fundamentaltabelle** <note>Fundamental Table</note> of the method of right and wrong cases. This may require using <term>interpolation</term> <note>Estimating a value between two known values in a table.</note> if the exact value of $\frac{r}{n}$ is not found in the table. Then, by dividing this value by $D$, one determines the value $h$, which is the required measure of sensitivity—or else

...at a constant *D* <note>In psychophysics, $D$ usually represents the "Difference" or increment added to a standard stimulus (like a weight).</note>, to use the value *t = hD* found in this way directly as a measure, which is convenient in many cases.

This rule is sufficient if, besides the constant excess weight *D*, no other constant influences are present that could determine the judgment of where the heavier weight falls, or if such influences can be considered compensated for through the experimental design when obtaining the value $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The ratio of "right" (richtige) cases to the total number of trials ($n$).</note>. Where this is not the case, constant <term>co-influences</term> <note>These are "constant errors" or biases, such as a tendency to favor the stimulus presented on the left or the one presented second.</note> are included in the value *t*; it then no longer depends solely on *h* and *D*—if *D* is always understood merely as the additional weight—but also on these co-influences. In such cases, simple division of the value *t* by *D* can, of course, no longer correctly determine *h*, and the value *t* (even with a constant *D*) can no longer be used as a comparable measure instead of *h* unless the co-influences remain constant alongside *D*. However, a properly arranged procedure with the appropriate application of the Fundamental Table offers a simple remedy here, which will be discussed in detail below.

**Remarks.** 1) Insofar as it only depends on the ratios of $t$ or $h$, I usually use the digits in the values of $t$ from the table as whole numbers instead of decimal fractions. This will always be the case in future citations of values calculated according to the table. 2) It is only necessary to construct the table for values of $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The ratio of "right" (richtige) cases to the total number of trials ($n$).</note> above 0.5. If values of $\frac{r}{n}$ below 0.5 occur—as frequently happens under given experimental circumstances for this or that "main case" to be discussed below when $D$ <note>The difference between two stimuli, such as weights.</note> is not too large—one should instead look for $\frac{f}{n} = \frac{n-r}{n}$ <note>$f$ represents "false" (falsche) or incorrect cases.</note> in the $\frac{r}{n}$ column of the table. One then introduces the corresponding value $t$ with a negative sign into the equations to be presented later for determining $hD, hp, hq$. 3) For $\frac{r}{n} = 1$—that is, for the case where all responses turn out to be correct—the table gives an infinite value for $t$. Strictly speaking, however, this assumes an infinite number of observations. In general, one must choose a $D$ small enough and an $n$ large enough so that this case does not occur.

The previous table will be used most conveniently if one chooses $n = 100$ for one's observations once and for all; that is, determining $r$ for every 100 cases and dividing larger series of trials into fractions of 100. This allows one to later combine the individual $t$-values obtained therefrom into sums or <term>mean values</term> <note>The average of a set of numbers.</note>, since treatment in fractions is necessary or useful from other perspectives anyway. In effect, one then only has to strike out the zero and the decimal point at the front of the $\frac{r}{n}$ column to immediately find the numbers $r$ obtained through the experiment. One not only saves the division required to form the values of $\frac{r}{n}$ but also requires no <term>interpolation</term> <note>A mathematical method of estimating an unknown value that falls between two known values in a table.</note>, since all experimental numbers $r$ can then be found directly and exactly in the table.

Insofar as one chooses an $n$ other than 100, one will always encounter values of $\frac{r}{n}$ that are not found exactly in the previous table. Then, with the help of the differences in the "diff." column, one can easily determine the associated $t$-values through simple interpolation. In doing so, up to about $\frac{r}{n} = 0.85$, one can be off by at most 1 to 2 units of the last decimal in the $t$-value, which is irrelevant; using the 4th decimal place in observations of this kind can be regarded as a <insert>pointless</insert> luxury anyway. With higher values of $\frac{r}{n}$, however, one would [err] all the more...

In itself, the number $n = 100$ <note>The total number of trials in an experimental set.</note> has no special advantage; and I myself have always used $n = 64$ as a basis instead of $n = 100$. I divided all my larger experimental series into <term>fractions</term> <note>Fechner uses "fractions" to refer to smaller sub-sets or blocks of trials within a larger experiment.</note> where $n = 64$, subsequently added the $t$-values calculated specifically from those fractions, and then used these sum totals or the mean values derived from them. The reason for this was that 64, as a power of 2, allows for a greater <term>subdivision</term> <note>Mathematical splitting of a group into smaller, equal parts.</note> by 2 than 100 does, and I initially wanted to keep this option open for any arbitrary partitioning. Later, I stuck with this choice to keep all experimental series comparable in this regard, since—as will be noted later—the size of $n$ chosen as a basis has a certain influence on the magnitude of the <term>metrics</term> <note>German: *Masszahlen*. These are the calculated values used to measure sensitivity or the "measure of precision."</note>, which must be kept comparable throughout. The fundamental table I usually use is therefore set up directly for $r$ <note>The number of correct responses.</note> corresponding to $n = 64$, in order to avoid the conversion of the fraction $\frac{r}{n}$ into a decimal fraction and to save on <term>interpolation</term> <note>The process of estimating values between known points in a table.</note> in the same way as was described for the table above; and I include it here as well, in case others wish to use the same base number.

However, one is not easily led to these applications in practice by our method, since the above manner of determining *h*—or, depending on circumstances, merely *t*—remains that upon which everything ultimately depends.

One must not forget that the indicated simple use of the table occurs only under the specified condition: that the apparent <term>preponderance</term> <note>German: *Uebergewicht*. In this context, it refers to the statistical bias or the frequency with which one stimulus is judged "heavier" or "greater" than another.</note>, apart from chance occurrences, depends solely on *D*; in reality, however, it also depends on constant influences of time and space position. The value *t* to be derived from *r*/*n* according to the table is in this case not merely = *hD*, but = *h(D + M)*, where *M* is the algebraic sum of all constant <term>co-influences</term> <note>German: *Miteinflüsse*. In view of this, the practical task consists of combining the experiments and their calculation in such a way that *M* is compensated for, and one returns to the same value *hD* which, without the existence...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on using probability tables to calculate sensitivity (h) and stimulus differences (D). ...of the co-influences <note>Fechner uses this term to describe "constant errors" or systematic biases, such as a preference for the left hand or the first-lifted object, which can skew results.</note> would be obtained according to the simple use of the table described above.

As for the experimental method, our standard procedure, which was discussed previously, is specifically calculated for this purpose. Here, one alternates in a perfectly regular manner between four main cases of opposing temporal and spatial positions of the incremental weight <note>the "Mehrgewicht" or difference D added to the standard weight</note>: namely 1) where it is in the vessel on the left, and where this is lifted first; 2) where it is in the vessel on the left, and where this is lifted second; 3) and 4) correspondingly with the vessel on the right. Thus, to keep the four main cases clearly distinct according to where the weight lies:

1) in the left-hand vessel, lifted first,
2) — left-hand vessel, lifted second — —
3) — right-hand vessel, lifted first — —
4) — right-hand vessel, lifted second — —

For brevity, I designate these four main cases, in the aforementioned order, as

-> I >, II >, I <, II <. <-

The resulting number of correct responses obtained, summed specifically for each main case, are denoted as

-> $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ <-

and the values $t$ from the fundamental table <note>the mathematical values corresponding to the probability of a correct guess</note> associated with their quotients divided by $n$ (which can no longer be simply set as equal to $hD$) are denoted as

-> $t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4$ <-

where an equal $n$ <note>the total number of trials</note> is assumed for all main cases.

The method of complete compensation for $M$ <note>the total effect of the constant co-influences</note> then consists, as is easily shown, in adding the $t$ values thus obtained for the four main cases and dividing by four, such that one has

-> $hD = \frac{t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + t_4}{4}$ <-

after which division by $D$, as before, gives the pure value of $h$ <note>the measure of sensitivity</note>. Alternatively, one can use $hD$ or $4hD$ itself as a measure, provided $D$ is always kept constant.

This method of complete compensation for the co-influences $M$ is based on the following points. According to page 90, there is a co-influence on the determination of the apparent incremental weight that depends on the temporal sequence of the lifting and another on the spatial position of the vessels. The one depending on the temporal sequence—

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation for isolating systematic errors in perception experiments. Having established the four experimental cases (lifting order and spatial placement), the author now introduces variables p and q to represent these specific biases and shows how to calculate them alongside the primary sensitivity measure h.</meta>

...I will call the [time]-dependent influence <note>The text starts mid-word with "hängigen," referring to "zeitabhängigen" or time-dependent biases, such as the tendency to perceive the second weight as heavier simply because it was lifted second.</note> *p*, and the one depending on spatial position *q*. In opposing temporal and spatial positions, *p* and *q* have an opposite sign <note>meaning positive or negative mathematical values</note>. Which sign we choose to use for a given position is arbitrary, provided that we use the opposite sign for the inverse position. If we therefore assign a positive sign to *p* and *q* in the first main case, then *M* <note>the total "co-influence" or bias</note> takes the value + *p* + *q* in the first case, – *p* + *q* in the second, + *p* – *q* in the third, and – *p* – *q* in the fourth. We thus obtain the following values for the four main cases for *t* = *h* (*D* + *M*) <note>where *t* is the value from the probability table, *h* is the measure of sensitivity, and *D* is the actual difference in weight</note>:

-> *t*₁ = *h* (*D* + *p* + *q*) <-
-> *t*₂ = *h* (*D* — *p* + *q*) <-
-> *t*₃ = *h* (*D* + *p* — *q*) <-
-> *t*₄ = *h* (*D* — *p* — *q*) <-

Adding these four values and dividing by four gives *hD*; likewise, adding the first and fourth equations, or the second and third, and then dividing by two, is sufficient on its own to find *hD*.

These same equations are suitable for providing the values of *hp* and *hq*, and consequently of *p* and *q*, through additive and subtractive combinations. Specifically, one first obtains:

-> *hp* = (*t*₁ — *t*₂ + *t*₃ — *t*₄) / 4 <-
-> *hq* = (*t*₁ + *t*₂ — *t*₃ — *t*₄) / 4 <-

If one divides the values of *hp* and *hq* obtained in this way by the previously determined value *hD* = (*t*₁ + *t*₂ + *t*₃ + *t*₄) / 4, one arrives at the ratio of *p* and *q* to *D*. By multiplying this ratio by *D*, one finds the value of *p* and *q* in grams, provided that *D* itself is expressed in grams. Furthermore, just like *hD*, both *hp* and *hq* can be determined in two different ways using the *t*-values of only two main cases, and a cross-check <note>original: "Controle"</note> can be sought in the consistency of the values thus obtained.

Depending on the direction of the influences *p* and *q*, they can emerge from this method of determination with either a negative or positive sign. Thus, one determines both the magnitude and the direction of these influences simultaneously through this process; the sign is to be understood in relation to the way *p* and *q* were introduced into the fundamental equations <term>Grundgleichungen: the core mathematical formulas that define the relationship between physical stimuli and mental perception</term>.

->*h* = $\frac{t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + t_4}{4 D}$<-

A more complete and coherent account in this regard will be offered in the "<term>Measurement Methods</term>." <note>original: "Massmethoden"; likely referring to a specific section or future publication detailing these psychophysical protocols</note>

When I refer to this in the future, in accordance with the choice of signs made on page 114, I will treat the influence *p* (dependent on the <term>sequence of lifting</term> <note>original: "Zeitfolge der Hebung"</note>) as positive if, by virtue of it, the first-lifted vessel appears heavier, and as negative if the second-lifted vessel appears heavier, independent of the actual weight difference *D*. I will treat the influence *q* (dependent on the <term>spatial position</term> <note>original: "Raumlage"</note>) as positive if the vessel on the left appears heavier, and as negative if the vessel on the right appears heavier. If I say, for example, that the influence *p* weighed + 10 grams, this means that, regardless of any actual extra weight, the first-lifted vessel appeared 10 grams heavier than the second-lifted one. Chapter 12 will provide the opportunity to cite such determinations.

Even if the objective conditions of the vessels' temporal and spatial positions remain the same, *p* and *q* can still change due to internal reasons, since those objective conditions only matter according to how they are subjectively perceived—a process that is highly variable for unknown reasons.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mathematical elimination of systematic errors (p and q) when determining sensitivity (h). previous fatigue of the arms in both one-handed and two-handed procedures tends to change in a negative sense—that is, to take on smaller positive or larger negative values, or to switch from positive to negative values. Furthermore, *p* <note>the bias related to the sequence of lifting (time error)</note> and *q* <note>the bias related to the position of the weights (space error)</note> in one-handed procedures and under otherwise identical circumstances have larger positive or smaller negative values for the right hand than for the left; finally, the magnitude and direction of these influences do not depend significantly on the size of *D* <note>the weight difference being tested</note>. One might wish to effect the compensation of the co-influences *p* and *q* by combining the *r* <note>the number of "right" or correct judgments</note> of the 4 main cases before calculating the *t*-values, and deriving a common *t* from the resulting common $\frac{r}{n}$ according to the fundamental table, which one would then set as $= hD$. This procedure can be useful under certain circumstances, but I designate it as **incomplete** compensation, as it can be shown as follows that one does not truly return exactly to the value *hD* (and thus *h*) that would have been obtained without the existence of the co-influences.

For example, let the influence *p* be in favor of the second-lifted vessel, and let us assume, for the sake of exaggeration, that it is extraordinarily large—infinitely large. It follows self-evidently that the addition of a finite *D* to one of the two vessels would become entirely without influence in determining the judgment; the **second-lifted** vessel would always and every time appear as the heavier one. Therefore, if the vessel with *D* is lifted first just as often as it is lifted second (as occurs in our experiments), and if the cases of these two time-positions are taken together—which one might be tempted to consider sufficient for the elimination of *p*—the number of correct cases and false cases will turn out to be just as equal as if the sensitivity for the weight difference were zero, where one also obtains an equal number of correct and false cases. The sensitivity for *D* appears, so to speak, drowned out <note>original: "übertäubt"; literally "deafened," meaning the bias is so loud the signal cannot be heard</note> by the co-influence. Conversely, if the influence of the time sequence of the lifting were not present at all, *D* would assert its preponderance equally in both time-positions and establish a preponderance of correct cases for the vessel in which it lies, appropriate to its size and the existing sensitivity. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "incomplete compensation" method. The author is explaining why simply averaging results to eliminate biases (p and q) is mathematically flawed compared to calculating each case individually. He argues that strong biases can "drown out" the actual weight difference being measured.</meta>

...presupposed temporal sequences cannot be treated as equivalent to the case where no influence of temporal position existed at all. For, understandably, one approaches that presupposed extreme even more closely as the co-influence grows stronger. And what applies to *p* <note>the 'time error' or bias caused by the sequence of lifting</note> in this regard applies equally to *q* <note>the 'space error' or bias caused by the spatial arrangement of the weights</note> and to the simultaneous existence of both. In contrast, through our procedure of **complete compensation**—where the numbers *r* <note>the number of correct judgments</note> for the different main cases are used separately to derive *t*—one is truly led back to the same result regarding *hD* <note>the mathematical product of the precision of the senses (h) and the weight difference (D)</note> as if no co-influence of *p* and *q* were present; because those influences are thereby eliminated.

As is easy to see, just as the influence of *D* <note>the actual difference between the weights</note> can disappear relative to *p* or *q*, the reverse must also be possible. When *D* is very large, neither the influence of successive lifting nor the influence of hand position can remain perceptible; instead, the judgment is guided solely by the magnitude of *D*. Provided that *D* assumes opposite temporal and spatial positions with equal frequency—as is the case in our experimental method—the number of first and second cases, and of right-handed and left-handed cases, must become equal, or at least approach this equality as *D* increases.

Although all of this is easily derived in theory, I confess that I was only led to it through experience itself. With heavy <term>main weights<note>The standard or reference weights being compared.</note></term>, the influence *p* sometimes became so large that this kind of "drowning out" of the influence of *D* was noticeable during the experiments even without calculation. After the calculation, the legal dependencies of <term>differential sensitivity<note>The ability to detect the smallest possible difference between two stimuli, such as weights.</note></term> appeared significantly altered, because I had previously always grouped together the correct cases from different temporal and spatial positions before calculating the <term>t-values<note>Mathematical values used to determine the accuracy of sensory perception based on the ratio of correct answers.</note></term>.

As is easy to see, the procedure involving repeated back-and-forth weighing of the vessels (p. 94), which does not allow for a separation of the four main cases, can only ever provide this result of **incomplete compensation**.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical justification for the method of "complete compensation" in weight-lifting experiments.
