one does not have to presuppose any or any strong changes in the influences *p* and *q* <note>p represents the "time error" (bias from lifting sequence) and q represents the "space error" (bias from which hand is used)</note> during the course of the investigation. In that case, one could certainly not only combine the figures from all 4 <term>main cases</term> <note>the four permutations of experimental conditions: lifting the heavier weight first or second, with the left or right hand</note>, but also consider it unnecessary to first convert the correct figures into *t*-values <note>t-values are statistical measurements derived from probability tables to determine the precision of the senses</note>; for an equal, larger, or smaller number *r* <note>the number of correct judgments</note> for a given number of trials *n* and a given weight difference *D* would then demonstrate an equal, larger, or smaller <term>sensitivity to difference</term> <note>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit: the ability of the subject to perceive the small weight difference</note>. 

Yet one must not forget that this remains tied to the condition of the constancy of the influences *p* and *q*. However, according to what has been said, a significant magnitude of regularly alternating constant influences has the same effect as—according to page 77—a significant magnitude of irregularly alternating random variables: namely, to reduce the number of correct answers *r*. Thus, even with the same or even greater sensitivity to difference, the combined correct figures *r* of the 4 main cases can turn out lower if the constant side-influences are larger. Consequently, false proportions can arise in this manner, which only disappear through the method of **complete compensation**.

Insofar as one can never fully guarantee—due to the great <term>variability</term> of those influences from internal causes (cf. p. 115), even when external conditions are kept carefully comparable—that they enter into the compared values in a truly comparable way, the admittedly more cumbersome path of **complete compensation** (and thus the separation of the 4 main cases and the return to the *t*-values) will always provide greater certainty. Comparing the mere numbers *r* can only serve for more superficial and preliminary determinations.

The methodical maintenance of an equal number of observations and the regular rotation of the 4 main cases—without which the precise elimination and determination of the constant influences *p* and *q* cannot be achieved—presupposes a regular change in the position of the <term>additional weight</term> <note>the "D" or weight difference added to one of the vessels to see if the subject can detect it</note> and thus a constant knowledge of this position. ...since the outcome of every single <term>double lift</term> <note>original: "Doppelhebung"; a pair of lifts where two weights are compared</note> contributes to *r* <note>the total number of correct judgments</note>, the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Einbildungskraft"; here referring to the psychological bias or expectation of the observer</note> loses its influence. Consequently, in this second procedure, the use of an assistant—who is indispensable in the first procedure to change the position of the <term>additional weight</term> <note>original: "Mehrgewicht"</note> without our knowledge—becomes unnecessary. After spending several months conducting experiments using the first method—carefully maintaining ignorance of the additional weight's position—before transitioning to the second method where its position was known, I am well positioned to comparatively judge the conditions of both types of procedure. I would not have stuck with the second one had I not been sufficiently convinced that the necessary knowledge of the weight’s position in that method was also harmless.

When calculating, I usually divide the <term>series of trials</term> <note>original: "Versuchsreihen"</note> not just into the four main cases, but also—as previously noted—into <term>fractions</term> <note>original: "Fractionen"; smaller subsets of data used for statistical grouping</note> according to time and other circumstances. I then combine the *t*-values obtained from these fractions into sum or average values, instead of deriving the *t* of each main case from the total *n* <note>the total number of trials</note> provided by the series. I do this for reasons that have already been hinted at in general and will be discussed more closely in the "Measurement Methods" <note>likely referring to the section "Massmethoden" in his seminal work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*</note>.

Admittedly, the calculation becomes quite cumbersome in this way, especially with larger series of trials; however, variations in <term>constant influences</term> <note>factors that might bias the results consistently, such as the fatigue of the observer or the order of weights</note> become less detrimental as a result.

It must be taken into account that the value *hD* <note>a mathematical expression representing the product of sensory precision (*h*) and the weight difference (*D*)</note>, when derived from fractions, is on average slightly larger than when obtained from the totality—and the smaller the fractions are, the more this is the case. The theoretical reasons for this can be provided, but I will skip them for now. Consequently, to keep the values comparable, one must always derive them from fractions with the same *n*, and state the *n* upon which the fractioning was based. In the results I will present in the future, unless something else is expressly stated, this *n* has always been 64, referring to simple lifts.

There are still practically useful remarks to be made about the size of the *D* <note>the difference between the two weights being compared</note> to be used in the experiments—which should ideally be chosen to be neither too small nor too large—as well as about the reliability of the results and several secondary points. I will save the discussion of these for the "Measurement Methods."

I call the **normal distance** <term>Normaldistanz; the standard or reference distance</term> the distance that is constantly used as the basis for comparison in visual and tactile trials; I call the **error distance** <term>Fehldistanz</term> the distance—generally affected by an error—which was estimated to be equal to it. As noted on page 90, the mean error distance derived from many observations generally deviates from the normal distance by an often considerable amount, and the positive and negative sums of the raw errors are not equal in absolute value; instead, one usually outweighs the other considerably. ...error. I designate the **constant error** <term>constanter Fehler; a systematic bias caused by the experimental setup, such as a tendency to overestimate the first of two stimuli</term> with *c*, the **pure variable error** <term>reiner variabler Fehler; the remaining fluctuations in judgment once systematic bias is removed</term> with $\Delta$, and the sum of the pure errors obtained through a given series of observations or fraction with $\Sigma \Delta$. Only the pure errors are to be used for the **measure of sensitivity to differences** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit; the ability of a subject to detect small changes in stimulus intensity</term>, and only from them—not from the raw errors—should the **mean error** <term>mittlerer Fehler; a statistical average used to quantify the precision of observations</term> serving as this measure be derived. The constant error is based on constant influences of the **spatial and temporal positioning** <term>Raum- und Zeitlage; whether a stimulus is presented on the left or right, or first or second in time</term> of the compared magnitudes, and the way in which the judgment is affected by them, which is co-determined by subjective conditions.

The necessity of resolving the raw error into its components rests on mathematical as well as experimental grounds, which I discuss in the "Measurement Methods" <note>Fechner refers here to his "Massmethoden," the systematic procedures for psychological measurement later published in his *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860)</note>; there are also mathematical relationships between the raw error and its components that are useful to know when handling the method, which will likewise be a subject of special discussion in the "Measurement Methods," as I restrict myself here throughout to discussing the most essential aspects of the method.

Of fundamental importance for the method is the essential independence of the pure variable error from the constant one, which has been demonstrated through experiments; thus, when the spatial and temporal positioning of the compared distances is reversed—whereby the constant error changes in the opposite sense and the raw sum of errors often turns out very differently—one obtains noticeably the same pure sum of errors; unless the opposite constant spatial and temporal positioning simultaneously brings with it a play of irregular contingencies of a different average magnitude, which, however, according to experience, is not easily the case. According to this, it often appears unnecessary to repeat the experiments at opposite spatial and temporal positions of the compared distances to determine the ratios of the pure variable error; however, it is necessary when it comes to determining those of the constant error. By combining the values obtained at opposite spatial and temporal positions in an appropriate manner, one can separate it into various components according to its dependency relationships, as I show in more detail in the "Measurement Methods" and which the expert will recognize for themselves; a procedure which...

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner’s discussion on the mathematical treatment of errors. ...essentially corresponds with that which served in the **Method of Right and Wrong Cases** <term>Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle; a foundational psychophysical method where a subject determines if a comparison stimulus is greater, smaller, or equal to a standard</term> for the separate determination of the influences *p* and *q* <note>original: "Einflüsse p, q"; these variables represent constant biases or probabilities inherent in the experimental conditions</note>.

In **visual estimation experiments** <term>Augenmassversuche; trials where a subject judges distances or sizes by sight</term>, one must distinguish between right and left positions, or upper and lower positions, of the **standard distance** <term>Normaldistanz; the fixed reference stimulus</term> relative to the **comparison distance** <term>Fehldistanz; the variable stimulus being judged against the standard</term>, depending on whether the distances are horizontal or vertical. In **tactile experiments** <term>Tastversuche; trials testing the sense of touch, usually on the skin</term>, one must distinguish between holding the **standard compass** <term>Normalzirkel; a mathematical compass or caliper used to apply a fixed distance to the skin</term> with the right hand and the **comparison compass** <term>Fehlzirkel</term> with the left hand, and vice versa. Alternatively, if one conducts experiments with one hand upon the other, and therefore holds both compasses in the same hand, one must distinguish between holding one compass with the upper part of the hand and the other with the lower part, and vice versa. Furthermore, in the tactile experiments, I have also established a contrast based on time, depending on whether the standard compass or the comparison compass is applied first in each comparison.

When forming the **mean error** <term>mittlerer Fehler; a statistical average used to quantify the precision of observations</term> from the **pure variable error** <term>reiner variabler Fehler; the fluctuation in judgment that remains after systematic biases are removed</term>, one has the choice between two types of mean error. The first, which I call the "mean error" simply—or, to distinguish it from the following, the "simple mean error"—and denote with $\varepsilon$, is obtained through simple averaging of the sum of pure errors, according to the equation:

->$\varepsilon = \frac{\Sigma \Delta}{m}$<-

This is obtained when *m* represents the number of errors contributing to the sum of errors $\Sigma \Delta$. The other, which among astronomers bears the name "mean error" simply, but shall be called here the **quadratic mean error** <term>quadratischer mittlerer Fehler; known today in modern statistics as the standard deviation</term> and denoted with $\varepsilon_q$, is obtained by squaring the errors individually, dividing the sum of these squares $\Sigma (\Delta^2)$ by their number *m*, and taking the square root of the quotient, according to the equation:

->$\varepsilon_q = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma (\Delta^2)}{m}}$<-

In a word, it is the root of the mean squared error. Both mean errors, provided they are obtained from a large number of errors, have—theoretically speaking, according to the **calculus of probabilities** <term>Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung</term>—a constant ratio to one another, which is:

->$\frac{\varepsilon_q}{\varepsilon} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 1.2533 \dots$<-

...appears all the larger, the less one has carried out **fractionation** <term>Fractionirung; the practice of dividing a large data set into smaller subsets for separate analysis</term>; thus larger, for example, if one derives a pure **sum of errors** <term>Fehlersumme; the total of the deviations from the mean</term> from 100 raw errors all at once, than if one divides these 100 errors into 2 fractions of 50 each, derives the pure sum of errors from each of these fractions specifically, and combines these two sums of errors. The reason is twofold. The first lies in the fact that with a small **number of observations** <term>Beobachtungszahl</term>, the **mean error distance** <term>mittlere Fehldistanz; the average value used as a baseline to calculate deviations</term> and consequently the pure errors calculated against it are obtained deviating from the true values—which are to be regarded as those which one would obtain under the same observational conditions from an infinite number of observations. The other reason lies in the variations of the **constant error** <term>constanten Fehlers; a systematic bias or consistent leaning in one direction</term> which can never be completely excluded in longer series of trials. Through these, the pure error sums are contaminated and increased if one groups together observations that include such variations and uses them to derive the mean error distance and pure errors.

Because of the first of these causes, a **correction** <term>Correction</term> can be applied, which I call the correction for the finite $m$ <gloss>where $m$ represents the number of observations in a sample</gloss>. By this, the sum of errors or the mean error is reduced to the case where the true mean error distance is determined from an infinite number of observations and the pure errors are calculated against this. This correction has long been applied to the mean square error when it served to determine accuracy in physical and astronomical observations, and consists in taking $\varepsilon_q$ <gloss>the mean square error</gloss> as $= \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\Delta^2)}{m - 1}}$ rather than $= \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\Delta^2)}{m}}$. An expert mathematician has had the kindness to check the derivation of this correction, which is to be shared in the *Methods of Measurement*. The same correction factor must be applied to the correction of **sums of errors** <term>Fehlersummen; the total of all deviations added together</term> from a finite *m*, if one stops at the sums of errors without extracting the mean error ε from them. If one treats a **series of observations** <term>Beobachtungsreihe</term> in fractions—that is, determines the pure errors specifically according to the mean error distances of the respective fractions—then the correction for the finite *m* must also be applied to each fraction specifically according to the *m* of the fractions, not as a whole according to the total number of observations of all fractions. In this way, the reduction in the mean errors or sums of errors resulting from the finiteness of *m* affects them all in the same proportion.

For **sums of errors** <term>Fehlersummen; the total of all recorded deviations</term> that produce a very small mean error, it may become necessary to consider two other corrections, which I call the "correction for the size of intervals" and the "correction for the estimation of scale divisions." The first refers to the fact that we only ever record errors that are separated by certain finite intervals. These intervals are larger when the divisions of the **measuring scale** <term>Massstab; a ruler or reference scale</term> used to measure the errors are less precise, and when the estimation of decimal subdivisions is less rigorous; consequently, the infinite number of errors falling in between are reduced to the nearest points on this scale. This has an influence on the mean error. The second correction refers to the fact that, when measuring errors on the scale itself, one commits errors once again. Of greater importance are formulas and rules by which it is possible to determine the uncertainty of the **mean errors** <term>Mittelfehler; the average deviation of individual measurements from the mean</term> and **sums of errors** <term>Fehlersummen</term> according to the size of the number of observations, as well as rules by which the obtained individual results can be combined into the most probable result. Everything that is necessary to know in this regard can be drawn from **probability theory** <term>Wahrscheinlichkeitslehre; the mathematical study of random phenomena, which Fechner applied to human perception</term> and presented practically for use; however, to be done adequately, this would require many preliminary discussions that would lead too far here.

A discerning handling of the method of mean errors generally requires a knowledge of the main points of the mathematical theory of errors, which is a part of probability theory. I believe I can provide the essentials in this regard in the "Methods of Measurement" <note>original: "Massmethoden", likely referring to his systematic treatise on the subject.</note> even for those who do not wish to immerse themselves in this doctrine; yet, understandably, this cannot happen here.

### *f)* **Mathematical Relationship of the Three Methods.**

The question may be raised as to what relationship the measurement values obtained by means of the three methods <note>The three methods are: the Method of Just Noticeable Differences, the Method of Mean Errors, and the Method of Right and Wrong Cases.</note> have to one another. Suppose that for the same **sensitivity to differences** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit; the ability to detect a change in stimulus intensity</term> in a given sensory domain, the **just-noticeable difference** <term>eben merklicher Unterschied; the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected</term>, the mean error, and the ratio <sup>r</sup>/<sub>n</sub>—and herewith $t = hD$—have been determined. The question is: how will they relate to one another? The answer must be based on the following viewpoints:

Strictly speaking, one would have to say: the just-noticeable difference of a magnitude is that which, when applied as a difference between the magnitudes to be compared in the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle; a procedure where subjects judge if one stimulus is stronger or weaker than another</term>, yields no false cases at all, but may not be reduced without yielding them; for by the fact that it is still noticeable, its occurrence—and therefore any false case—is excluded, and by the fact that it...

<meta>This page continues the technical comparison between the three primary methods of psychophysical measurement. Fechner is specifically contrasting the "just noticeable difference" (the threshold of perception) with the statistical "mean error" derived from repeated trials.</meta>

...is only **just noticeable**, it is implied that it can no longer be felt with the slightest further reduction. But in reality, if one wishes to have no "false cases" <term>falsche Fälle; incorrect judgments in a sensory test</term> for a given difference, one must set the difference high enough so that random variations do not push it below the threshold of perceptibility. Exactly how high this must be, or how many false cases one is willing to permit among a predominant majority of correct ones while still classifying the difference as "just noticeable," depends partly on the average magnitude of the occurring **random variations** <term>Zufälligkeiten; chance factors or experimental noise</term> and partly on subjective judgment.

The **mean error** <term>mittlerer Fehler; the average amount by which a subject's adjustment misses a target stimulus</term>, on the other hand, is necessarily smaller than the **just noticeable difference** <term>eben merklich Unterschied; often abbreviated as JND, the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect</term>, provided that the latter is intended to allow for no (or only exceptional) false cases. For when using the **method of mean errors**, if a difference between, for example, two compass distances <note>original: "Zirkeldistanzen"; referring to the two-point threshold test where a subject identifies if they feel one or two points of a compass on their skin.</note> is still noticeable, the distance is changed until it becomes unnoticeable; and in general, all errors from zero upwards that are smaller than the just noticeable difference contribute to the determination of the mean error. However, for the reasons stated, it is also impossible to provide a fixed ratio between the just noticeable difference and the mean error.

In contrast, there exists a mathematical relationship—linked by the **principal integral of probability calculus** <note>This refers to the Gaussian distribution or "normal" error curve.</note>—between the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle; a method where a subject compares a constant stimulus to various comparison stimuli</term> and the **method of mean errors**. This relationship allows one to specify what ratio of right and wrong cases will result if one uses the magnitude of the simple or quadratic mean error as the **difference magnitude** *D* in the method of right and wrong cases, under otherwise comparable circumstances. And indeed, as I shall show in the "**Methods of Measurement**" <note>original: "Massmethoden", Fechner's detailed exposition of his experimental procedures.</note>, when using the simple mean error as the difference magnitude (the additional weight in the weight-lifting experiments), the ratio $\frac{r}{n}$ <note>The ratio of correct responses ($r$) to the total number of trials ($n$).</note> is noticeably $\frac{2}{3}$, or more precisely 0.655032.

This theoretical relationship, however, has yet to be proven through experiments. This may present some difficulty, insofar as it requires setting up the circumstances for the methods being compared in such a way that random variations exert an equal influence on both.

## 2) Measurement Methods of Absolute Sensitivity.

The field of these methods regarding intensive sensations <term>intensive Empfindungen; sensations of magnitude like brightness or loudness</term> has remained almost fallow until now. Apart from a determination by **Schafhäutl** regarding the just audible absolute intensity of sound, the determinations of **E. H. Weber**, and those of **Kammler** concerning just noticeable magnitudes of pressure—which will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 11—I do not know what else could be included here. In the field of light sensation, a pure determination of absolute sensitivity is not even possible, because one cannot eliminate an internal source of light sensation <note>original: "innere Quelle der Lichtempfindung"; Fechner refers to the "intrinsic light" of the eye, the faint gray or static one sees even in total darkness</note>, which I discuss in Chapter 9.

On the other hand, the measurement methods of absolute sensitivity have found a very extensive application in the field of extensive sensations <term>extensive Empfindungen; sensations involving spatial dimensions, such as area or distance</term>, insofar as much work has been done to determine just noticeable sizes or distances on the retina or the skin. In this latter regard, we have specifically the well-known and pioneering experiments of **E. H. Weber** concerning the just noticeable distances on the skin. These experiments represent one type of procedure that can be used for the measure of absolute sensitivity—a procedure analogous to the "method of just noticeable differences" used for measuring differential sensitivity <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit; the ability to detect a difference between two similar stimuli</term>. However, the other two methods of measurement also translate into an analogue for the measurement of absolute sensitivity.

**Volkmann** based his work on the easily confirmed observation that the width between compass points <note>original: "Zirkelspitzen"; referring to the points of a mathematical divider or caliper used to test the "two-point threshold" on the skin</note> that yields a just noticeable distance is not something absolutely fixed. Instead, it fluctuates within certain limits; the same width may be felt as a distance in one trial and not in another, as long as an upper limit has not been exceeded beyond which the width is always felt as a distance, or a lower limit below which it is never felt as such. These limits themselves are not capable of an absolutely precise determination. This does not prevent us, however—as experience itself has taught—from using the previous method to find a value that closely coincides with the upper limit, or lies between the upper and lower limits, by performing a majority of skin contacts with the compass points at varying widths

Now, one could use any arbitrary ratio of correct cases to the total number of cases as a comparative scale of sensitivity by seeking the compass width on different skin areas that yields that same ratio. However, the ratio preferred by **Volkmann** in this regard is perhaps most recommended: the point where perceptibility occurs just as often as non-perceptibility. Since it will not be possible to hit the corresponding compass widths with absolute precision, one can arrive at them accurately enough through interpolation of the neighboring widths used in the experiment. The experiments conducted by **Volkmann** according to this method regarding the progress of training tactile sensitivity are contained in the *Reports of the Saxon Society* <note>original: "Berichte der sächs. Societät"</note> 1858, p. 47 ff., and have well proven the applicability of the method through their interesting results.

Essentially, when applied to the tactile measure <term>Tastmass; a scale or unit used to quantify the skin's ability to distinguish spatial points</term>, it consists in the following: instead of using one compass <term>Zirkel; a two-pointed mathematical instrument used here to apply two simultaneous touches to the skin</term> on a single skin site, one uses two, designated *A* and *B*. While keeping the distance of compass *A* fixed on site *A*, one modifies the distance of compass *B* on site *B* until, according to the sensation of the skin, the distance on both sites appears to be equal. In reality, these distances may be exceptionally different depending on the varying sensitivity of the specific skin sites. In this way, one obtains equivalents <term>Aequivalente; different physical measurements that produce the same subjective sensation</term> of equally estimated distances for both skin sites. The reciprocal value of these distances, determined as an average from a large number of trials, can then serve as a measure of the spatial sensitivity.

One can easily be convinced that this method is very refined and precise. So long as the sensitivity of the skin sites maintains a constant ratio, it yields very consistent results with negligible uncertainty. The consistency is proven by comparing different segments of the experiment, while the precision is proven by the easily calculated "probable error" of the average result. Furthermore, whenever that ratio does vary, this method allows those subtle variations to be tracked in detail. Indeed, in experiments conducted over several months on the same body parts, I have seen the most constant ratio maintained when only a few trials were performed each day. However, just as clearly, I have several times observed gradual changes in the equivalent distance when many trials were performed daily. This created a significant influence of practice <term>Uebungseinfluss; the phenomenon where repeated testing improves a subject's sensory discrimination</term>. These changes generally consisted of the less sensitive part of the body becoming more similar to the more sensitive part, as the practice clearly benefited the former more than the latter.

In this case, the *A*-distance turns into the normal distance and the *B*-distance into the error distance. This is also shown by the fact that the relationships of the **constant error** and the **pure variable error** <note>In experimental psychology, a constant error is a systematic bias, while a variable error refers to random fluctuations in judgment</note> from the method of average errors reappear in a more general way in the method of equivalents. Just like the method of average errors, the method of equivalents therefore requires various considerations and precautions related to those of the former method.

The reversal of every comparison is especially essential. If one has, for example, determined the equivalent of *B*-lip against *A*-chin, one must determine the counter-equivalent of *B*-chin against *A*-lip through an equal number of trials, noting both results separately, but ultimately taking the average, in order not to have a one-sided result afflicted with a constant error...

## Fundamental Laws and Facts.

### IX. Weber’s Law.

The law which was first expressed only in general terms in Chapter 7 as a main foundation of psychic measurement <note>original: "psychisches Mass"</note>, and to which I give the name **Weber’s Law** <note>Named after Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878), whose experiments on weight and touch inspired Fechner's work</note>, shall now be discussed more closely in terms of its meaning, its foundation, and its limits, insofar as the investigations available thus far provide a basis for doing so.

One can express this law in various forms, which ultimately amount to the same thing in practice, but of which one or the other may be more appropriate for reference depending on the circumstances.

Primarily, one can say: a difference between two stimuli <term>Reize; physical inputs such as weight, light, or sound</term>, which can also be understood as a positive or negative increase to one stimulus or another, is always perceived as being of the same magnitude—or yields the same difference or increase in sensation <note>original: "Empfindungszuwuchs"</note>—if its ratio to the stimuli between which it exists remains the same, or, if it is grasped as an increase, if its ratio to the stimulus to which it is added remains the same, however much its absolute magnitude may change. So that, for example, an increase of 1 to a stimulus whose strength is expressed by 100 is felt just as strongly as an increase of 2 to a stimulus with a strength of 200, of 3 to a stimulus with a strength of 300, and so on.

Equivalent to the previous statement are the following shorter formulations: the difference or increase in sensation remains the same if the relative stimulus difference or relative stimulus increase remains the same; and: the difference or increase in sensation remains the same if the ratio of the stimuli remains the same. Here one must remember (cf. p. 49) that the constancy of the relative stimulus difference or increase automatically implies the constancy of the ratio of the stimuli, and vice versa, which allows...

...to replace the latter expression of the law with the former.

Finally, with regard to the conceptual discussions on differential sensitivity <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit; the ability to detect a difference between two stimuli</term> in Chapter 6, the law can also be stated as follows: simple differential sensitivity is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the components of the difference, while the relative sensitivity remains the same regardless of their magnitude.

One can consider the law in the domains of both intensive and extensive sensations <note>In 19th-century psychology, "intensive" refers to the strength or degree of a sensation (like loudness), while "extensive" refers to spatial qualities (like the length of a line)</note>. In the former, one looks at aspects of strength and pitch—insofar as a quantitative element of quality is present in the pitch of tones. One should not, however, feel entitled from the outset to view the law's validation in any one specific sensory domain as being simultaneously valid for another; rather, it requires a separate investigation in every field.

When asking whether the law is confirmed in the domain of extensive sensations, one must substitute the magnitude of extension and the difference in extension—perceived by the eye or the organs of touch—for "stimulus" and "stimulus difference" in the law's phrasing. One will find the law confirmed if, for example, for two lines that are twice as long, the difference must also be twice as great to remain just noticeable, or more generally, to appear equal in magnitude.

Regarding the pitch of tones, it is the number of vibrations <note>original: "Schwingungen"; what we now call frequency</note> which represents the magnitude of the stimulus.

If the law is correct, the correctness of many of its logical conclusions follows automatically. The proof that these conclusions are confirmed by experience is therefore to be regarded as part of the law's overall validation. Instead of entering into this in the abstract, however, I prefer to be led toward these points during the specific validations of the law in various fields, and in this regard, I refer specifically to the field of light sensation.

Regarding the historical context, I have already noted that E. H. Weber was not indeed the first to express and validate the law in general, but he was certainly the first to express and validate it with a certain degree of universality and to present it from a perspective of general interest. He

Regarding weight ratios, his experiments can be found in his *Programmata collecta* <note>original: "Programm. collect."; referring to Ernst Heinrich Weber’s "Annotationes Anatomicae et Physiologicae," published in 1834</note> on pages 81, 86, and following.

Weber distinguishes between two experimental methods: one where only the sensation of the skin is used through the pressure of heavier and lighter weights on the hand while it rests on a table, and the other where the sensation of the muscle force to be applied is simultaneously used by lifting the hand together with the weight. Whether 32 ounces or 32 <term>drachms; an old unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> were used as the larger weight, the just-noticeable relative difference to the smaller weight remained nearly the same in both experimental methods. For four participants and both sets of weights, this averaged 10.1 (ounces or drachms) for the first method, and 3.0 for the second.

The more detailed description of his experiments (from *Programmata collecta*, p. 86) is as follows:

> “In the hands of many people, while they rested on a table, I placed weights of two pounds and interposed a paper card. Afterward, without their knowledge, I decreased one of the weights and changed the hands carrying the weights, transferring the lighter weight now to the right, now to the left. Often I even replaced weights taken from the hands back onto the same hands, in such a way that the person could not suspect anything but could perceive only by touch <note>original: "tactu"</note> on which side the heavier weight was placed. Then, if the person correctly discerned the heavier weight from the lighter through repeated trials and frequent changing of hands, I noted it down.”

> “Afterward, the same experiments were repeated with the same people, but in this way: they would lift their hands, and the weights along with them, and balance the weights in their hands. When this was done, if I found at what weight difference the diversity between them was surely recognized, I noted it again and compared the numbers expressing the difference of the weights with each other.”

Although I had suspected that they might not feel the difference in weight of two bodies eight times smaller as clearly, yet it was proven by experiments that...

### 1) Light.

I have given a detailed presentation of the confirmations of our law in the field of intensive light sensation in the *Treatises of the Saxon Society of Sciences*, mathematical-physical class, Vol. IV, p. 457 ff., under the title: "On a Psychophysical Fundamental Law, and its Relation to the Estimation of Star Magnitudes," with a supplement to it in the reports of the same society from 1859, p. 58 ff., from which treatises I reproduce here the essentials with a few additions.

<meta>This page transitions from the physical experiments of E.H. Weber regarding weight perception to the author’s (Gustav Theodor Fechner’s) application of these principles to light. It establishes the historical context of the "Law of Sensation"—later known as Weber’s Law—by citing previous researchers in optics.</meta>

The law has already been confirmed in the field of light sensation through earlier experiments by **Bouguer**, **Arago**, **Masson**, and **Steinheil**, occasionally in connection with other investigations, and more recently by myself and **Volkmann**; however, it did not previously receive much attention.

All previous confirmations of the law rely on the <term>method of just noticeable differences; a psychophysical technique where a stimulus is changed until the participant can just barely detect the difference</term>, with the exception of the work by **Steinheil**, which is based on the principle of the <term>method of average error; a technique where a participant tries to match a stimulus to a standard, and the variations in their accuracy are measured</term>, and the indirect confirmation which the law has found in the way star magnitudes are estimated. <note>In astronomy, the logarithmic scale of star brightness (magnitudes) is a natural application of this law: as brightness increases geometrically, our perception of it increases only arithmetically.</note>

Since my own experiments offer the simplest, if not the most precise, confirmation of the law—and because my first empirical knowledge of the law was linked to them—I will begin with them here and use them to provide a general explanation of the law.

Under a half-overcast sky, one can usually easily find a few neighboring shades of clouds that present only a trace of difference to the eye, or a small cloud that is only just noticeably different from the background of the sky. After I had focused my eye on two such components of a <term>just noticeable difference; the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected</term> of light in the sky, I placed a pair of glasses before my eyes—of the kind now available at opticians for use by persons with light-sensitive eyes. According to a superficial <term>photometric; relating to the measurement of light intensity</term> test, each glass alone allowed slightly more than 1/4 of the light through, and both placed together allowed at most 1/16 of the light through. If we assume that with the single glasses the light of each component was reduced to 1/4, then the difference between them was simultaneously reduced to 1/4. It was natural to assume that this greatly weakened difference, since it was previously only just noticeable, would become unnoticeable through this weakening—or at least conspicuously less distinct. However, this was not the case. The difference remained at least as noticeable as before, and others whom I asked to perform the experiment expressed the same opinion.

The same experiment was repeated with the glasses doubled, using only one eye while closing the other, where the components along with their difference were reduced to at most 1/16...

...decreased, the difference remained at least as noticeable as before.

Finally, reducing the light intensity using colored glass—with which I achieved even significantly greater levels of darkness—yielded the same result. In doing this, one must not, of course, focus on clouds of different colors or a cloud against the blue sky, since colored glass exerts a different proportional <term>absorption; the process by which the glass soaks up certain wavelengths of light</term> on different colors.

If we now observe that while the absolute difference of the <term>components; the two individual light sources or surfaces being compared</term> was reduced in the previous experiments, the ratio of these components—and thus their relative difference—remained unchanged, we must see the persistent noticeability of that difference as a confirmation of our law. <note>Fechner is referring to the principle that our eyes detect the percentage of change in light, rather than the absolute physical amount of change.</note>

At first glance, it might certainly appear quite striking and in contradiction with everyday experience that a <term>photometric difference; a physical measurement of light intensity</term> reduced to 1/5, 1/7, or even much less should remain at least as noticeable to our sensation as it was without reduction; after all, we see light differences diminish and disappear through reduction every day. But one must not overlook the specific condition of the law, under which alone it demands this result, and under which alone it occurs: namely, that as the light difference is reduced, it maintains an unchanged ratio to its components, which are themselves reduced in the same proportion. Let us call the fulfillment of this condition the **first main case.**

However, the difference can be reduced in another way: by bringing the stronger component closer to the other through reduction alone, or the weaker closer to the stronger through increase alone. In this instance, which we shall call the **second main case**, the difference undergoes a reduction in its absolute value and its ratio to its components simultaneously. In this case, as can easily be proven through later experimental methods in agreement with general experience, the noticeability of the difference indeed decreases and vanishes entirely if the components are brought close enough together.

To these two main cases, a third can be added

...main case, which serves as an indirect confirmation of our law through the same logic as the first: namely, that instead of changing both <term>components; the two light sources being compared</term> in the same proportion, an equal "plus" (addition) is added to both, or an equal amount is subtracted from both. In this third case—in contrast to the first—the <term>absolute difference; the physical, measurable subtraction of one value from another</term> remains the same, while the <term>relative difference; the ratio or percentage of difference between two values</term> changes. It decreases when we add an equal amount to the components and increases when we subtract an equal amount.

Now, since the law links equal <term>noticeability; the ability of our senses to perceive a change</term> not to the equality of the absolute difference, but to the relative difference, we must expect—assuming the law is correct—that in our third main case, the noticeability of the difference will not remain the same, despite the fact that the difference remains equal when taken absolutely. Rather, we expect it to decrease or increase depending on whether an equal amount is added or subtracted.

To prove that this is indeed the case, there is no need for a specially devised experiment, even though confirmation through experiments is easily achieved. The same field of observation that has served us so far offers a sufficient confirmation in an everyday experience.

At night, everyone can see the stars; in full daylight, one cannot even see stars like <note>original: "Sirius und Jupiter"</note> Sirius or Jupiter. Yet the absolute difference in brightness between the points in the sky where the stars are located and the surrounding areas is just as great as it is at night. It is only that an equal "plus" of intensity has been added to both by the daylight. <note>Fechner explains that while the star is still technically "brighter" than the sky by the same physical amount, the massive addition of sunlight makes that difference a much smaller percentage of the total light, rendering it invisible to the human eye.</note>

It is possible that the success of our first experiments with <term>cloud nuances; the subtle variations in shading and light on a cloud's surface</term> could have been interpreted as follows: through the dark glasses, the difference between the nuances was indeed weakened in a very strong proportion, but it was still absolutely present; therefore, it still had to be perceived in regards to its absolute existence, without needing to make the continued perception dependent on the preservation of the same relative magnitude. But one sees from the aforementioned experience with the stars that the absolute existence of a light difference is by no means sufficient to make it perceivable. Indeed, even very considerable absolute differences completely vanish from the eye if they...

...show a very small relative magnitude. No one will consider the difference in brightness between the stars Sirius and Jupiter and the surrounding night sky to be small, yet no one, even with the keenest attention, will be able to discover these stars by day; so the claim may seem striking that the difference in brightness between them and their surroundings is just as great by day as at night. In fact, it is physically the same, while for sensation it is completely zero—indeed, in a sense, smaller than zero—insofar as it first requires a certain increase before it reaches the point from which it becomes <term>noticeable; the "threshold" or "limen" at which a stimulus is first perceived</term>.

One should not, however, think this phenomenon is limited only to points of light. The experiments with shadows to be cited later provide the most convenient opportunity to observe the same phenomenon on light surfaces of any extent with significant absolute differences; but experiences from daily life can also be cited in this regard.

As is well known, figures on varnished oil paintings, on <term>daguerreotypes; the first publicly available photographic process, using silver-coated copper plates</term>, painted plates, lacquered tables, and the like, become completely unrecognizable due to specular reflections <note>original: "spiegelnde Lichter" — the glare or highlights reflected off a shiny surface</note>. Now, as is known, the intensity of specularly reflected light does not depend on the color or darkness of the surface from which it is reflected, but—given the same material—only on its smoothness and the <term>angle of incidence; the angle at which light hits the surface</term>; it thus adds an equal "plus" <note>an identical amount of light</note> to the darker and lighter parts of the figures and the background, thereby making the differences between them unrecognizable.

The foregoing should already suffice as a confirmation of the law in general. But can it really be considered exact?

I have intentionally said that the difference in cloud nuances, when viewed through darkening glasses, appeared *at least* as noticeable as with the naked eye. For some of those whom I had repeat the experiment found it even somewhat sharper with glasses than without, and to me it often, though not always, appears so. One can certainly be sure from this that a difference in light does not—as one might most easily have expected—lose noticeability by a weakening of its absolute magnitude while its relative magnitude remains constant. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s investigation into the constancy of light perception. In this regard, there would still be a deviation from the law, which links a constant noticeability to the constancy of the relative difference.

Setting aside the fact that altered <term>irradiation conditions; the phenomenon where light spreads across the retina, making bright objects appear larger or blurred</term> might possibly come into play here, one could also think of a subjective illusion. Specifically, one might be inclined to consider an equally noticeable difference to be *more* noticeable, insofar as it is greater in relation to the weakened impression of the <term>components; the individual light intensities or surfaces being compared</term>. To achieve a result as independent of subjective illusions as possible, I combine the following counter-experiment with the previous experiment.

While holding glasses <note>likely darkened or smoked glass used to reduce light intensity</note> before my eyes, I seek out the weakest possible difference I can find in the sky—one rated as <term>just noticeable; the "threshold" or point at which a change in stimulus is first perceived</term>—and then I remove the glasses from my eyes. If the noticeability had been significantly increased by the glasses, then the difference that was only just noticeable *with* the glasses would have to disappear upon their removal. However, in multiple repetitions of the experiment—using both single and double-layered glasses—I have never been able to find even the slightest difference that I could not still recognize after removing the glasses, once the initial impression of momentary <term>glare; or "dazzling" (original: "Blendung")</term> had passed, by which the eye is struck upon removal of the glasses due to the suddenly incoming stronger light. And even when putting them on, I experience a momentary blurring of the difference due to the sudden change in light, though in both cases this passes quickly.

In all the experiments mentioned, it remains essential to use only very slight differences that possess the character of being just noticeable. For, although the law—as will be shown later—allows for an extension to larger differences, it is not easy to confirm it directly through them. The judgment as to whether such differences are equally distinct with and without glasses is very uncertain and fluctuating, and is indisputably co-determined by a multitude of circumstances. However, the main advantage of applying very slight differences is that combining the experiment with a counter-experiment allows one to remain entirely independent of judgments about equality or inequality. Instead, the conclusion is based solely on the existence of a difference for the <term>sensation; the internal perception resulting from an external stimulus</term>, a matter about which one is less easily deceived than about equality. If the weakest possible difference recognized without glasses is *still* recognized even with heavily darkened glasses, and if, conversely, the weakest possible difference recognized with heavily darkened glasses is still recognized *at all* <note>original: "überhaupt"</note>, then this provides a kind of objective proof. It shows that the difference cannot gain or lose <term>noticeability; "Merklichkeit," or the threshold at which a change is perceived</term> to any significant degree through the use of the glasses.

In any case, by combining the experiment and the counter-experiment, the possibility of a deviation from the validity of the law is restricted to very narrow bounds. This applies within the ranges of light intensity where verification has been held so far—ranges that reached neither near total darkness nor very <term>dazzling; "blendenden," referring to intense glare that overpowers the eye</term> lights. However, this is not to claim or demonstrate the unlimited validity of the law; rather, a deviation from it—both at the upper and lower limits—is certain, at least for the purposes of the experiment. And before we proceed to further proofs, it will be useful to speak of these limits of the law, since the proofs themselves can only occur and be understood in light of these limits.

Certainly, no one—even if the observation could be conducted without danger—would be able to recognize the spots on the sun (at least when the sun is high) with the naked eye, whereas everyone perceives them using darkened glasses. If the law were to hold up to the highest degrees of light, then the spots would have to be just as easily distinguishable from the surrounding background of light with the naked eye as they are with the help of dark glasses. It may therefore also be possible that, under very bright cloud illumination, a small gain in clarifying the nuances of cloud shading is achieved through the use of dark glasses. Regarding the lower <term>limit; "Gränze," referring to the threshold of perception</term>, it is obvious from the outset that if one were to go to the extreme in darkening the glasses, nothing at all could be seen, and thus no difference could be seen anymore, no matter how great it might appear or be without glasses. According to the <term>principle of continuity; "Continuitätsprincipe," the idea that natural processes and sensory perceptions change gradually rather than in sudden jumps</term>, one must already sense a diminished clarity when merely approaching this limit, as experience also confirms. Indeed, no matter how great a difference may be, one will always be able to find a degree of darkening of the glasses at which it appears less distinct than without glasses. The same <term>sunspots; "Sonnenflecke," dark patches on the sun's surface often viewed through protective filters</term> that become clear with moderately dark glasses will become indistinct again with very dark glasses and finally become completely unrecognizable.

Instead, therefore, of being able to claim an unlimited validity of the law, we can only claim, according to the testimony of the experiments, that it is confirmed within the—fairly wide—limits of intensity in which ordinary vision moves, to the extent that a deviation from the law is not detectable.

However, its validity within middle limits can even be inferred in a certain way from the opposite direction of the deviations at the upper and lower ends. With intensive light, clarity increases through attenuation; with very weak light, it increases through the strengthening of the components in the same proportion. Therefore, from a <term>mathematical perspective; "mathematischem Gesichtspuncte," looking at the data through the lens of ratios and proportions</term>, there must be a certain middle interval where it remains equally unchanged through strengthening and weakening. <meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how to test the law of sensation using light sources and shadows. The previous page ended while discussing "clouds," and this page picks up by comparing shadows or lights generated by a single object to measure the "just noticeable difference" in light intensity.</meta>

...shadows or lights produced by the same object, where the <term>photometric; relating to the measurement of light intensity</term> ratio of both shadows is not only easily adjustable but also—using light sources of equal brightness—easily measurable through the reciprocal ratio of the squares of the distances of both sources from their shadows. Meanwhile, the photometric equality of the sources can be easily verified by the equal brightness of the shadows at equal distances from them, and can be established by cleaning the lights or adjusting the <term>screws of the lamps; "Schrauben der Lampen," likely referring to the adjustment mechanism on oil or gas lamps to control flame height</term>. However, it is generally even more practical, instead of comparing two shadows, to focus the eye on a single shadow and the surrounding background as the components of the difference to verify the law. This is because the ratio of the shadow to the background completely surrounding it is even easier to judge. In the following experimental method, the following details come into consideration.

Let the two light sources be *L* and *L'*, and let *L'* be the one whose shadow we wish to observe. This shadow is still illuminated by the other light *L*, while the surrounding background is illuminated by both lights, *L* and *L'*. If one moves light *L'* further and further back from the board catching the shadows while *L* remains stationary, the background surrounding the shadow receives an ever-smaller addition of illumination from *L'*. Finally, this addition becomes so small that it becomes imperceptible to the eye; thus, the shadow disappears into the surrounding background. Once this point has been reached, a slight movement of one of the two lights, or a turn of the screw on one of the lamps in the correct direction, is sufficient to make it <term>just noticeable; "eben merklich," a central concept in Fechner's work referring to the smallest detectable change in a stimulus</term> again.

Now, one can first repeat the experiment and counter-experiment with <term>dark glasses; "dunkeln Gläsern," used here as neutral density filters to reduce light intensity</term>; in this way, one can confirm the law as well as the lower limit of the law.

Instead of weakening both components in the same proportion using dark glasses, one can achieve the same <term>attenuation; "Abschwächung," the reduction of intensity</term> by moving both light sources *L* and *L'* to increasingly greater distances from the shadow-catching board, while maintaining the same ratio between them. ...this was observed as a result of achieving the same degree of perceptibility <note>German: "Merklichkeit." This refers to the "just noticeable difference," a foundational concept in psychophysics where a stimulus is only just strong enough to be detected.</note>, as will become clearer in what follows. In this way, the new experimental method becomes a supplement and a control rather than a mere repetition of the previous one.

Since my own significantly weakened eyes <note>The author, Gustav Fechner, suffered a severe eye injury and partial blindness from staring at the sun during earlier experiments, which is why he required assistants for visual observations.</note> could not engage in such experiments—which require the most strenuous attention and the sharpest scrutiny to detect even traces of a shadow in the process of disappearing or reappearing—Volkmann <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a prominent physiologist and close collaborator of Fechner.</note>, with the help of several co-observers with good eyes, took over the execution of these tests. The following is the essence of the procedure and the results.

A rod placed vertically in front of a white board cast two shadows upon it under the influence of two light sources, *L* and *L'*. One light source, *L*, a burning stearin candle <note>Stearin candles were widely used in 19th-century laboratories because they produced a more consistent, smokeless flame than tallow candles.</note>, was kept at a given distance from the board, and the other—whose light intensity had been <term>photometrically; relating to the measurement of light intensity</term> confirmed to be equal to the first in two different ways—was moved back from the board by one of the co-observers until the shadow it cast, which was being closely watched by the observer, just ceased to be perceptible. For Volkmann’s eyes, the distance of candle *L'* from the shadow had to be 10 times as great as that of candle *L*; that is, the difference in illumination where the shadow just ceased to be perceptible 

<margin>1/100</margin>

amounted to 1/100th of the absolute illumination <note>original: "1/100 der absoluten Beleuchtung." This follows the inverse-square law: if the distance is 10 times greater, the light intensity is 1/100th ($10^2 = 100$).</note>. This same ratio of distances, and consequently of illumination levels at which this point occurred, was found even at entirely different absolute intensities of light. These varied intensities were obtained partly by changing the intensity of the flames themselves and partly by placing the flame *L* at a greater or lesser distance from the board. The distance of flame *L'* always had to be perceptibly 10 times as great to bring the shadow to the point of disappearance. Thus, the experiment varied the intensity of illumination *L* from 0.36 to intensities of 1, 2.25, 7.71, and up to 38.79—where 1 represents the illumination provided by a stearin candle at a distance of 3 decimeters <note>About 11.8 inches.</note> from the white board—without the ratio of the distance of the other light source to the board turning out to be perceptibly or significantly different. ...noteworthy small drop took place, meaning that the distance of the light source $L'$ had to be slightly less than 10 times the distance of light source $L$ (according to the table of results, 9.6 times) in order to make the shadow just disappear; undoubtedly, at this point, the lower limit of the law's experimental validity was beginning to be exceeded.

For the sake of brevity, I have only referred to the point of disappearance in this description. In reality, however, the light source $L'$ was moved back and forth around the point of disappearance, so that the point of <term>just-noticeability; the minimum level of stimulation or difference required for a person to detect a change</term> was determined as accurately as possible between the point of the shadow's disappearance and its reappearance. Since the light source $L'$ was moved by an assistant only at the command of the observer—whose eyes and attention were entirely focused on the <term>apperception; the conscious perception or recognition of a sensory stimulus</term> of the shadow—the final fixing of the distance occurred without the observer's knowledge. Thus, the result could not be influenced by such knowledge, making the outcome of these experiments all the more unambiguous.

These experiments were conducted by Volkmann <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann, a physiologist and Fechner's brother-in-law, who performed the visual observations Fechner's own failing eyesight prevented.</note> with the assistance of Prof. Knoblauch, Dr. Heidenhain in Halle, and Dr. Jung from Berlin, and were partly repeated in my own presence. Remarkably, for all the aforementioned observers, a value fluctuating only slightly around $\frac{1}{100}$ of the absolute illumination was consistently found to be the just-noticeable difference.

Admittedly, this procedure does not allow for great precision in individual trials, as one can move the light $L'$ within a certain range—which according to Volkmann may amount to about $\frac{1}{10}$ of the total distance—without knowing exactly where to fix the point of the shadow's just-noticeability; therefore, the average of several trials was generally regarded as the standard for each observer. Yet, the individual results often fluctuated only very little around the average, and the uncertainty remaining after calculating the averages is very small.

This method of experimentation with shadows corresponds to the first main case; understandably, however, the second case can also be easily satisfied by approaching or moving a single light toward or away from the board, making it brighter or darker;

<meta>This page continues the description of Antoine Masson's experiments with rotating disks. ...for which the ratio of the <term>angular size; the size of an angle as measured from the center of the disk</term> of the <term>sector; a portion of a circle similar to a slice of pie</term> to the total circular area was respectively 1/50, 1/60, 1/70, and so on up to 1/120. This enabled him to determine the boundaries within which the limit of sensitivity fell. A second method led to consistent results with the first; compared to the previous one, it is also interesting because it shows that <term>instantaneous light; light that flashes for a very brief moment, such as an electric spark</term> behaves the same as <term>continuous light; a steady light source like a lamp or the sun</term> regarding this law.

As is well known, if one rapidly rotates a circular disk divided into alternating white and black sectors and illuminated by daylight or a lamp, it appears as a uniform gray. If one illuminates it instead with an instantaneous electric spark, all the sectors are seen perfectly clearly <note>This occurs because the spark is so brief that the disk does not have time to move significantly during the flash, "freezing" the motion for the observer.</note>. If both types of lighting are used at the same time, it depends on the ratio of their intensities whether one sees a uniform gray or distinguishes the sectors; the former occurs when the electric light is too weak, and the latter when it is sufficiently strong. According to Masson, the ratio of these two lighting intensities at which the uniform gray appears is different for the eyes of different people, while it remains the same for the eye of the same observer.

The sectors disappear and the uniform gray appears when the instantaneous illumination of the white sectors by the electric light (the black ones reflect no significant light) no longer gives them a sufficient advantage over the uniform gray color—which would occur without the electric light—such that they can be distinguished by the eye. Depending on the relative width of the black and white sectors, which changes the gray, a different strength of electric illumination is required for this to happen under the same fixed lighting. If the eye is still able to distinguish a difference of 1/100 according to the previous experimental method, then if the white and black sectors are equal, the illumination of the white sectors by the electric light would have to be 1/200 of their illumination by the steady light. This is because the steady light is reduced to a gray of half the <term>photometric brightness; the perceived intensity of light as measured by a standard observer</term> by the rotation of the disk. The experiments using this method were conducted by Masson with significant variations for purposes other than proving our law,

> “By testing different eyesight, I found that for those considered weak, sensitivity varied from 1/50 to 1/70. The distance from the eye to the disk has no influence on sensitivity, provided one does not reach a certain limit determined by the angle subtended by the ring.”

> “The results were not modified when I changed the ratio between the diameter of the disk and the width of the ring. I used disks in which the surface covered by the black sector was one-third or one-fourth of the circle. I placed the black portion at the edge of the disk, at the center, and between the center and the circumference. Finally, I arranged several black portions on the same circle belonging to sectors with different ratios to the circle, and I used disk no. 5 \*\*). In all cases, the limit of sensitivity remained invariable.”

> “By illuminating the moving disk with colored lights, I was able to determine if the sensitivity of the eye varied with the nature of the light rays. Except for a few restrictions which I shall mention, I found that the limit of sensitivity is independent of color. Thus, I see the ring at 1/100 just as distinctly whether I illuminate the disk with natural light or use colored rays.”

> “I produced lights of various colors by passing the rays of the sun or those of a Carcel lamp through colored glass. I used the colors of a spectrum, and finally the photometric apparatus of Mr. **Arago** <note>François Arago (1786–1853), a physicist and politician who made significant contributions to optics</note>.”

<meta>This page continues the discussion of light intensity and visual perception, moving from Antoine Masson’s experiments to those of Karl August von Steinheil. <note>original: “Il résulte aussi des expériences...” (French)</note>
“It also follows from the experiments that I have conducted on several individuals, that while the sensitivity of their organ <note>The 'organ' refers to the eye or the visual system</note> remains the same for all colors, they experienced, when fixing the disk illuminated by red, a fatigue, a discomfort which indicated in them a kind of repugnance for this color. It would be curious to examine if this effect is not produced on some eyes by a color other than red.”

I finally come to Steinheil’s experiments. In his famous treatise on the prism-photometer*) <term>Prism-photometer; an instrument used to measure the intensity of light by comparing two light sources through a prism</term>, he found occasion to investigate whether the error made in estimating the equality of light intensities varies according to the magnitude of those intensities. On page 14 of his treatise, he briefly states the result of the observations made on this matter: “They show that one recognizes with great accuracy the point at which two surfaces are equally bright. The uncertainty of each individual estimate of this kind does not exceed ³/₄ <note>This fraction likely refers to the fractional difference in brightness that the eye can just barely detect</note> of the total brightness; this may be large or small.”

This statement includes the declaration of our law. For the uncertainty in estimating the equality of two light intensities understandably depends on the size of the still-perceptible difference; and if, at different intensities, one errs on average across a majority of trials by an equal proportional part, then the limit of noticeability of a difference must also lie at an equal proportional part of these intensities.

Steinheil himself views it this way when he says (p. 74) with reference to the same observation: “In Section B it will be shown... that in estimating equal brightness, one misses the mark every time by an aliquot part <note>An 'aliquot part' is a portion that is contained an exact number of times in the whole; here it refers to a constant percentage or fraction</note> of the total amount of light. From the latter it now follows that if one weakens the illuminated surfaces to the point of intensity where they can no longer be distinguished from the background of the sky, these then have an intensity which is proportional to that of the background of the sky.”

The absolute figure of ³/₅ <note>The OCR transcription lists ³/₅ and ³/₄; in the context of psychophysics, these represent the constant Weber fraction for light</note> may stand out compared to the earlier figures of ³/₄ to ¹/₂₀, and it remains questionable whether it depends on a difference in eyes or in method; but that does not affect the law, which is what is at stake here. At the same time, it should be noted—

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Karl August von Steinheil’s photometric experiments. ...notice that the fraction 1/33, which measures the uncertainty according to Steinheil, is indeed to be seen as proportional to the just noticeable differences—which the fractions 1/64 to 1/120 designate according to other observers—but it is not to be regarded as identical to them; although this remark does not explain the magnitude and direction of the difference between the results.

Steinheil’s experiments (p. 75 ff. of his treatise), insofar as they are considered for the confirmation of our law <note>The author is referring to Weber’s Law, which suggests that the ability to perceive a change in stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of that stimulus</note>, relate admittedly only to a scale of three intensities, which behave like 1.000, 1.672, and 2.887; they thus do not have a great range. Yet they are very valuable and important, not only because they stem from one of the most distinguished observers practiced in the application of photometric measuring tools <term>Photometry; the science of measuring the strength of light as perceived by the human eye</term>; but also because they rest on a different principle of confirmation than the previous ones, and thus testify all the more that the law withstands every kind of test.

Indeed, one easily overlooks the fact that in Steinheil’s confirmation, the principle of the **method of average error** <term>Method of average error; a psychological testing method where a subject tries to match a stimulus to a standard, and the researcher measures how much they miss on average</term> is used, whereas the earlier confirmations are based on the principle of the **method of just noticeable differences** <term>Method of just noticeable differences; a method determining the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect</term>.

Since the presentation and calculation of Steinheil’s experiments could not be done without some complexity, I refer for those details to the original or to my treatise p. 477, where, after a somewhat modified calculation and excluding one series of experiments that was not entirely comparable with the others, I find 1/45 instead of the fraction 1/33. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how Weber’s Law—which states that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity—applies to light. The author has just finished explaining Steinheil’s photometric experiments and is now expanding the law's application to sensations that are more than "just noticeable," specifically looking at historical astronomical data.</meta>

...combination of trial and counter-trial <note>original: *Versuch und Gegenversuch*</note> here does not allow us to infer equal noticeability from mere existence in the same way as with just noticeable differences. However, in my treatise on page 489, I cite the experience that when covering one eye, a light shadow settles over the field of vision <term>Field of vision; the entire area that a person can see when their eyes are fixed in one position</term>, which one is not inclined to consider lighter or darker, whether one looks at a fire or a wall. This is presented as an instance that, from a certain perspective, falls under our law <note>Referring to Weber’s Law</note> and can be interpreted as a confirmation of it for differences that are more than just noticeable. One may consult the discussion of this experience in the treatise itself.

However, from another side, there exists a—much more unambiguous—confirmation of the law for differences greater than just noticeable ones. This was, in fact, the very first confirmation to exist for the law, and it comes once again from that high field of observation from which the first cited confirmations were taken: namely, in the way stellar magnitudes <term>Stellar magnitude; a measure of the brightness of a star as seen by an observer on Earth. The lower the number, the brighter the star</term> are estimated. Here, one must assume that the practiced eye of astronomers has successfully overcome the difficulty of estimation in the sense of our law.

It has been known since ancient times (*Hipparchus*) that the estimation of stellar magnitudes does not happen according to their photometric <term>Photometry; the science of the measurement of light, in terms of its perceived brightness to the human eye</term> light value, but according to the impression they make on the eye. In this way, astronomers have sought to distinguish stars of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd magnitude, and so on, by equal differences in apparent brightness; in doing so, however, they let the numbers of the stellar magnitudes decrease while the apparent brightnesses increase. According to our law, the perceived difference in brightness between successive magnitude classes can only be equal if the photometric ratio between them is equal. Therefore, a geometric series <term>Geometric series; a sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number</term> of stellar intensities must correspond to the mathematical <note>i.e., arithmetic</note> series of stellar magnitudes—using "stellar intensity" to briefly designate the photometric value of a star.

However, there is a contradiction here: according to a statement in *Alexander von Humboldt’s Cosmos* based on *John Herschel’s* investigations, the series of stellar intensities belonging to successive stellar magnitudes is not a geometric series, but rather a quadratic power series,

<summary>The author explains how Weber's Law applies to the ancient system of stellar magnitudes, arguing that astronomers perceive equal steps in brightness because the actual light intensity changes at a constant ratio. He also notes a potential contradiction in the findings of John Herschel and Alexander von Humboldt regarding these light intensities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of the logarithmic relationship between stimulus and perception (Weber’s Law), specifically addressing a potential contradiction found in the astronomical data of John Herschel.
