If it were to be a geometric series <term>Geometric series; a sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number</term>, then every number would have to be derived from the preceding one by multiplication with the same constant factor. To maintain the closest possible connection to the previous series using simple numbers, one would instead have:
->1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 ....<-

At first glance, this contradiction seems all the more significant because the quadratic power series <term>Quadratic power series; here referring to a sequence based on squares, specifically the inverse square law (1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16) where brightness decreases by the square of the distance</term> was preferred over the geometric series by **Herschel** <note>Sir John Herschel (1792–1871), a preeminent English astronomer who conducted extensive surveys of the sky</note> himself. His extremely meticulous revision of stellar magnitudes <term>Stellar magnitude; the measurement of a star's brightness</term> and their comparison with stellar intensities—based on his own photometric determinations <term>Photometry; the science of measuring the strength of light</term>—is one of the most extensive and important foundations upon which one can base any reliable conclusions regarding the question at hand. Meanwhile, in my treatise, I believe I have demonstrated beyond objection that this contradiction is merely apparent and, upon closer inspection, actually dissolves into a complete confirmation of our law. Here are the most essential points:

A significant deviation between the two series above (1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16... and 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16...) only occurs at the 1st magnitude class. In this class, however, the intensity of individual stars varies from a single unit to about 16 times that amount. Consequently, if one arbitrarily chooses the intensity of a single star of this class as the representative for the entire class's intensity, one can bring it into agreement with either series at will. Indeed, such an arbitrary choice took place with **Herschel**. He had a preference for the quadratic power series of intensities because, assuming this series, the ratios of the numbers indicating magnitude would simultaneously represent the ratios of the distances at which the stars stand from us. Accordingly, he selected as the representative of 1st-magnitude stars the one that best fit this assumption—which, however, is by no means the star of average intensity, but rather one of the very brightest: the third in order among the stars of the 1st magnitude, **α Centauri** <note>Alpha Centauri; the closest star system to the Solar System</note>. Meanwhile, **Herschel** himself explicitly designates another star in several places, **α Orionis** (Betelgeuse) <note>original: "Beteugeuze"</note>, as one that occupies a middle position...

According to this data, among the other 14 stars of the 1st magnitude that he determined photometrically <term>Photometry; the science of measuring the intensity of light</term> and ranked using fractional magnitudes, 8 have a smaller intensity and 6 a greater intensity, while 6 have a smaller magnitude number and 8 a greater magnitude number than **$\alpha$ Orionis** <note>$\alpha$ Orionis is the star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion</note>.

From this it is clear that if one seeks a middle or typical value for stars of the 1st magnitude without arbitrary adjustment to any preconceived assumption, one must choose **$\alpha$ Orionis** instead of **$\alpha$ Centauri** <note>$\alpha$ Centauri is the brightest star in the southern constellation of Centaurus</note> for that purpose. If we therefore substitute 0.484 for 1 in the quadratic power series <term>Quadratic power series; a sequence based on the inverse square law (1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16), where brightness decreases by the square of the distance</term>, it transforms into:

->0.484; 1/4; 1/9; 1/16 ...<-

However, 0.484 differs so little from 0.5 (or 1/2), and 1/9 differs so little from 1/8, that—considering the difficulty of precise determination of magnitude and intensity emphasized by **Herschel** himself, and further considering that he himself declared the quadratic power series to be not exactly consistent with observations—one can regard the difference as small enough to find the geometric series <term>Geometric series; a sequence where each value is found by multiplying the previous one by a constant (e.g., 1/2, 1/4, 1/8)</term>:

->1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 ...<-

substitutable for the quadratic series. In higher magnitude classes, the two series would certainly diverge further, but **Herschel’s** photometric determinations do not go beyond the 4th magnitude class, and therefore no grounds for further comparison are offered here.

A more thorough calculation, regarding which I must refer to my treatise, has further demonstrated that the geometric series of stellar intensities is not only compatible with **Herschel’s** observational data, but—when appropriately related and with a suitably determined exponent for the series—represents them even better than the quadratic power series. After everything stated above, one must notice an incidental contradiction found in **J. Herschel’s** statements against our law. Herschel notes, when describing his **astrometer** <term>Astrometer; an instrument designed by John Herschel to measure the brightness of stars by comparing them to a reduced image of the Moon or another light source</term> (*Results from the Cape*, p. 357) in a footnote, that it is useful to use an equilateral prism to help, using its reflective effect to make the line connecting two stars being compared parallel to the horizon, and adds:

> "Occasionally, too, it may be used to enfeeble the light of nearly equal bright stars, by external reflexion in an equal ratio (by bringing the line joining their reflected images parallel to that joining their direct). In this enfeebled state, shades of inequality become apparent, which would otherwise escape detection. By increasing or diminishing (equally) the angles of incidence, the reflected images may be more or less enfeebled. A plain metallic mirror may be used for the same purpose." (A parallel passage is found in *Outlines*, p. 522.) <note>Fechner is citing John Herschel’s 1849 work, "Outlines of Astronomy."</note>

Regardless of how one views this contradiction, it seems impossible to me, based on all the above, to see in the deviation noted by Herschel anything more than a small-order deviation that occurs under certain observation conditions. It seems he observed this deviation only "occasionally," without conducting specific experiments for that purpose; and since he himself speaks elsewhere of "countless" causes that "influence our judgment in a barely credible way during such experiments," one should not consider occasional observations sufficient to establish a contradiction against the specific experiments presented above. The upper limit of the law, where the eye feels blinded, is undoubtedly related to the fact that the eye is adversely affected. In a certain sense, an upper limit of this kind is self-evident. Indisputably, the internal movements upon which **sensation** <term>Sensation (Empfindung); the internal physiological response to a physical stimulus</term> depends cannot be increased beyond a certain limit without destroying the organ and canceling the possibility of any further increase. Even two unequal **stimuli** <term>Stimuli (Reize); physical inputs, such as light, that trigger a sensory response</term> that reach and exceed this limit of excitation will only be able to produce this same maximum of sensation, and thus will no longer be able to yield any detectable difference in sensation. However, in any case, even the approach to this limit brings with it a deviation from the law.

It is natural to attribute the upper deviation from the law simply to the fact that the eye, through **dulling** <term>Dulling (Abstumpfung); the physiological process where a sensory organ becomes less sensitive to a stimulus after prolonged or intense exposure</term> against the light stimulus, simultaneously becomes more insensitive to light differences. If **dulling** <term>Dulling (Abstumpfung); the process by which a sensory organ becomes less sensitive after exposure to a stimulus</term> were the reason that one cannot clearly recognize differences in very bright light, then one would have to distinguish most clearly in the first moment of entering from darkness into the light, and gradually distinguish worse and worse. One might therefore be inclined to attribute the inability to distinguish objects immediately upon entering from the light into the dark to a **persistence of the light impression**, rather than a dulling against the impression; and to attribute the corresponding inability when entering from the dark into the light to the **gradualness** with which impressions assert themselves. And if, in the reverse transition, the stronger impression asserted itself in a slower proportion than the weaker one, then differences between strong light could also not be perceived at first. In fact, I tentatively proposed this explanation in my treatise on "A Psychophysical Basic Law" (p. 487). Yet, upon closer consideration, both sides of the explanation no longer seem tenable to me. For according to all previous experience, the phenomenon of persistence fades too quickly, not to mention other difficulties; and the assumption that a strong light impression asserts itself relatively more slowly than a weak one is contradicted by positive experiments by **Swan** *).

Abnormally, in all sensory domains, sensations can arise through internal causes (**internal stimuli** <term>Internal stimuli (innere Reize); physiological triggers within the nervous system, such as blood flow or neural activity, that create a sensation without external light or sound</term>) independent of external stimuli; these are famously known by the name **hallucinations**. In this respect, it cannot be surprising if such a capacity also expresses itself constantly and normally in a given domain. The sense of sight provides us with a factual example of this, where we must recognize what one might call a "normal hallucination."

The black background of the eye can also increase and decrease in depth. The proof for this is easily demonstrated. ...lady, in whom, under constant light, a complete darkness often suddenly poured over the eyes, from which visible objects appeared only now and then like phantoms and immediately disappeared again as soon as the patient strove to fixate upon them."

Should not only the retina, but also the central parts of the sense of sight be completely paralyzed, one would expect that not only the visual field darkens, but the black of the visual field itself vanishes (just as it vanishes at the boundaries of the visual field in the closed eye) and that one sees with the eyes no more than with a finger or a dead nerve strand. Probably the central conditions for visual sensation in the brain are too essentially connected with the conditions of life for a total and permanent cessation of the one to occur without the other.

Assuming the unlimited validity of the **law at its lower limit** <note>Referring to Weber's Law, which relates the physical intensity of a stimulus to the perceived intensity</note>, even the photometric intensity of the **eye-black** <term>Eye-black (Augenschwarz); the subjective sensation of "black" that is actually a very low-level light sensation generated by the visual system itself</term> can be determined through experiments entirely analogous to those previously conducted to prove Weber's Law. To do this, one only needs to move a single light in the dark of night so far away from a shadow-casting body until the shadow—which is filled only by the eye-black—is just no longer distinguishable from the background, which is illuminated by both the eye-black and the external light simultaneously. If one applies the fractional value of ¹⁄₁₀₀ found by Volkmann <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist who specialized in the study of vision and a close collaborator of the author</note>, then at this distance, the illumination that the light adds to the eye-black amounts to ¹⁄₁₀₀ of the intensity of the eye-black.

Perhaps one might find such a brightness value for the eye-blackness striking and much too large, insofar as it is supposed to be equivalent to the illumination of a surface by an ordinary candle at a distance of nearly 9 feet. But one must not overlook the fact that it is the illumination of a black surface for which this equivalence is claimed, because it is proven by the experiment. However, an absolutely black surface would not be illuminated ***at all*** even by the closest and most intense flame, since it would swallow all the light; and it is only the circumstance that no absolutely black body exists that allows us to speak of a low degree of illumination of a black background at all. Therefore, the black background still reflected some light—though very little—into the area surrounding the shadow, with which the brightness of the eye-blackness could very well be commensurable in the manner shown by the experiment.

This proves that either the brightness of their eye-blackness or their sensitivity was different. Volkmann intends to give these experiments even more precision, further execution, and follow-up. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "eye-blackness" or internal light. The previous page ended midsentence, explaining how an "absolutely black surface" would not be illuminated by a flame, but since no such body exists, the black background still reflects a tiny, but measurable, amount of light.</meta>

measurable, nor immeasurably small; and this is what matters most here.

Insofar as, according to all the preceding points, the blackness of the visual field—even when external light is completely excluded—must still be viewed as an actual **sensation of light**, it must not be neglected when testing **Weber’s Law** <note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the "just-noticeable difference" between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</note>. Suppose we observe two similar **cloud nuances** or shadows with the naked eye; in this case, the brightness of the **eye-blackness** <term>eye-blackness: Also called "Eigenlicht" or "internal light," this is the gray sensation perceived by the nerves of the eye even in total darkness.</term> is added to both cloud nuances or shadows. If we now dim the light of both cloud nuances or shadows by holding a gray glass in front of them in a given ratio, the brightness of the **eye-blackness** remains undimmed. It still adds itself with its constant intensity to the two nuances or shadows, which consequently do not truly maintain the same ratio and thus not the same relative difference as before, but rather a smaller one. This, according to the law, must lead to a reduction in the sensation of the difference. Indeed, if we continue to increase the darkness of the glasses, eventually only the **eye-blackness** remains instead of both nuances, and all difference disappears. In this experiment, the blackness in the eye actually acts—however strange this may seem—exactly like the bright illumination of the sky in which the stars disappear. Therefore, **Weber’s Law**, when referring only to the external **light stimulus**, can only be confirmed insofar and so long as the internal light of the eye is vanishingly small compared to the external light. This is why **Masson** <note>Antoine-Philibert Masson (1806–1860), a French physicist who researched the thresholds of visual perception.</note> only claims the validity of the law from the point where one can read ordinary printed text; whereas, if one descends to great darkness with the experiments, the difference between the nuances must become less distinct. The same applies to all the mentioned modifications of the experiment and is confirmed everywhere by experience.

An excellent illustration of the above is provided by the fact that a glimmer of light, which differs only very slightly from the **eye-blackness**, can be made to disappear by a seemingly opposite means, yet according to the same principle.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the visibility of light against a dark background. The previous page established that the "eye-blackness" (the internal light sensation of the eye) acts as a baseline intensity. It concluded by suggesting that just as stars disappear against the bright sky, they also disappear when the eye's internal "blackness" is relatively too bright, ending with: "...as refering onl..."</meta>

...y can be distinguished from the black background of the sky, one can make it disappear just as well by placing a darkening glass before the eyes as by bringing a lamp close to the eye from the side. A corresponding experience could be seen very beautifully in the magnificent comet of the year 1858 <note>Donati's Comet, one of the brightest and most spectacular comets of the 19th century.</note> at the beginning of October. Through both gray and colored glasses, as well as by bringing a bright lamp near from the side, the tail [of the comet] shortened exceptionally; and a dark red glass, through which I could recognize the finest nuances of clouds in daylight, even caused the entire comet to disappear. The first phenomenon is explained by the fact that the glasses significantly weaken the light of the star or comet, but not the "blackness" within the eye; the second is explained by the fact that the light illuminates not only the spot on the retina where its image falls, but to a certain degree the entire fundus of the eye <note>The interior back surface of the eye.</note>. Several causes contribute to this, which have been highlighted by various observers.

Firstly, the light shines through the <term>sclera <note>original: Sclerotica; the tough, white outer layer of the eyeball.</note></term> and <term>choroid <note>original: Chorioidea; the vascular layer of the eye providing oxygen and nourishment to the outer layers of the retina.</note></term> with a reddish color. From this depend several remarkable phenomena of objective and subjective coloring of images, which **Brücke** <note>Ernst Wilhelm von Brücke (1819–1892), a pioneering German physiologist.</note> studied particularly carefully in *Poggendorff’s Annals*, Vol. 84, p. 418. *Secondly*, a direct scattering reflection occurs from the image onto the other parts of the retina, as well as backward toward the <term>cornea <note>original: Hornhaut; the transparent front part of the eye that covers the iris and pupil.</note></term>, from which the light is partly reflected back again to the retina. **Helmholtz** <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a massive figure in 19th-century science who invented the ophthalmoscope.</note> highlighted these points—while also considering the following one—in *Poggendorff’s Annals*, Vol. 86, p. 501 ff. Thirdly, due to the microscopic composition of the ocular media—made of cells, fibers, and membranes—an irregular scattering of light occurs, apparently according to the principle of diffraction. From this depend the colored halos visible around flames, which **Meyer** made the subject of a special study in *Poggendorff’s Annals*, Vol. 96, p. 235. By virtue of the last cause, as well as by the direct scattering reflection from the image of the light source onto the rest of the retina, the illumination of the retina is strongest in the vicinity of the image, but actually extends with decreasing intensity over the entire fundus of the eye.

Through the combined effect of these causes, the very weak light of a star or a comet's tail is more easily overwhelmed—much like starlight is by daylight—the closer it falls to the image of the light source in the eye, since the illumination of the fundus is strongest in that vicinity.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how internal ocular conditions, specifically the "internal eye-blackness" or intrinsic light of the retina, affect our perception of external light sources. Hence also the statement by Brewster\*):

> "When the light of a candle flame held close to the right eye acts on one part of the <term>retina <note>original: Netzhaut; the light-sensitive inner surface of the eye.</note></term>, it makes all other parts of the retina insensitive to all other light impressions to a greater or lesser degree. This insensitivity reaches its maximum close to the illuminated spot and decreases with the distance from it. Moderately illuminated objects actually disappear in the vicinity of the strongly excited areas, and bodies of vivid colors are not only robbed of all their brilliance but are also changed in their color."

It is for this same reason that, using Helmholtz’s method\*\*), one can see the so-called <term>ultraviolet rays <note>original: ultravioletten Stralen; light beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum.</note></term> of the solar spectrum—which are not seen by the usual method—even without the use of fluorescent substances, if one arranges it so that they can be perceived noticeably isolated from the rest of the spectrum, which otherwise overwhelms them with scattered light.

A general conclusion from the above is further that, although the amount of reflected light on black and white surfaces increases in the same proportion with increased illumination, the difference between white and black appears greater with increasing illumination. This is because the brightness of the <term>eye-blackness <note>original: Augenschwarz; the "intrinsic light" or baseline sensation of the retina even in total darkness.</note></term> always remains the main component of the brightness of the "black." This is, for example, the simple reason that one can read better in the light than in the dark.

Apart from the limits of the law <note>Referring to Weber’s Law, which relates the intensity of a stimulus to the perceived change.</note>, which are related to the degree of light intensity, one must not forget that a confirmation of it through observation is only to be expected insofar as, besides the intensity ratios, the other circumstances remain equal which can exert an influence on the perception of the difference in light. Now, the investigation into the circumstances that can be of significant influence in this regard is still highly incomplete; however, some points shall be mentioned which, according to experience so far, deserve preferential attention.

In Arago's experiments regarding this matter, the components did not consist of two shadows. Instead, they were obtained by using a telescope that contained a <term>Rochon prism <note>original: Rochon’sches Prisma; an optical device that splits a beam of light into two separate images.</note></term> (which produces a double image) and had a <term>Nicol prism <note>original: Nicol’sches Prisma; a device used to polarize light or adjust its brightness.</note></term> attached in front of its objective lens. The observer aimed the device at an opening in black cardboard projected against an overcast sky. From the relative positions of the main sections of the Nicol and Rochon prisms, the relative intensity of the two images produced by the latter could be determined. By moving the Rochon prism linearly within the telescope from the eyepiece toward the objective, the weaker image was set in motion, so that it moved in a measured time from a position where its edge passed through the center of the stronger image to a position where its edge just touched the other's edge.

In three series of experiments conducted in this manner with the assistance of several observers, the disappearance of the weaker image superimposed on the stronger one occurred at a movement speed of 12 <term>arcminutes <note>original: Winkelminuten; a unit of angular measurement equal to 1/60th of a degree.</note></term> per second when the intensity of the weaker image reached the following fractional value of the stronger one:

| **I.** | 1/39 | 1/58 |
| **II.** | 1/51 | 1/87 |
| **III.** | 1/71 | 1/131 |

The room was so dark that the numbers appeared to us only as black spots. If I fixed my gaze on one of these, it did not take long—under a certain very weak illumination—before both the fixed digit and all others completely disappeared into the gray of the paper sheet, which became darker and darker. Once this moment occurred, further fixation became impossible; an unpleasant sensation arose in the <term>orbit <note>The bony socket of the eye.</note></term>, the eyes made a small movement, and immediately the entire sheet with the spots of numbers was visible again. The movement was either perceived as such, or it was made voluntarily, or finally, it was inferred from the fact that a differently positioned number now stood at the <term>point of fixation <note>The specific point in the visual field that the eye is focused on.</note></term>."

Furthermore, it is possible that it is the multiplied perception of the difference through a majority of points, rather than the freshness of these points, which causes the greater noticeability of the difference during movement—insofar as a summation of the impression of the points struck successively in time might occur within certain limits. Finally, the following relationship—which, admittedly, is also not yet explained, but whose generality serves to some extent as an explanatory basis—could be at play. Weber** <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878), a German physician considered a founder of experimental psychology, known for "Weber's Law" regarding sensory perception.</note> highlighted and supported through experiments, and as was already asserted on page 88. Thus, we recognize a small difference between two weights more easily through successive weighing with the same hand than through simultaneous weighing with different hands. Through the movement of the components in our light experiments, however, the simultaneous difference for various <term>retinal points <note>Specific points on the light-sensitive inner lining of the back of the eye.</note></term> is converted into a successive difference for those same points. Onto the same points where stronger light fell just a moment ago, weaker light soon falls, and vice versa; and the faster the movement occurs, the more points enter into this <term>succession <note>A sequence where one thing follows another in time.</note></term> within a given time. However, this explanation is also only conjectural for now.

Furthermore, among the circumstances that influence the recognizability of a difference is the extent of the components, though the law regarding intensity is not changed thereby, provided the extent remains comparable each time; this is immediately evident from the fact that it has proven valid for stars just as well as for broad shadows. ### 2) Sound.

In the field of sound, it is necessary to distinguish between mere noises, which have no definite pitch and where only intensity is considered as something measurable, and tones. For tones, both the intensity—which depends on the <term>vibration amplitude <note>The maximum extent of a vibration; physically, this determines the loudness of a sound.</note></term> and is proportional to its square—and the pitch—which depends on the <term>vibration frequency <note>The number of vibrations per second; physically, this determines how "high" or "low" a sound is.</note></term> and is measured by it—must be specifically taken into account. One will be able to investigate the ratios of intensity in both, but the ratios of pitch only in the latter. Let us first consider intensity.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Weber’s Law, shifting the focus from light to sound intensity. It describes an early, somewhat crude experiment designed to determine if the ability to distinguish between two sounds depends on their absolute volume or the ratio between them.</meta>

be weaker. Since the apparatus, in its raw construction, had no circular scale for determining the specific <term>elevation <note>The height or angle to which the hammer is raised before being released.</note></term> of the hammer, a <term>quadrant <note>An instrument used to measure angles, typically shaped like a quarter-circle.</note></term> with several markings at different heights was placed at the side of the apparatus as a substitute, and the elevation of the hammer was determined this way. The hammer was made of wood and struck against a square glass bottle. 

Two elevations of the hammer were then sought which produced sufficiently distinct sounds so that an observer standing directly by the apparatus would not be mistaken if he guessed, without knowing the elevations, which sound was the louder; yet the sounds were chosen to be similar enough that, if the difference were reduced by about half, the judgment became uncertain and resulted in a mix of correct and false cases. 

Thereupon, the observer moved away successively to 6, 12, and 18 paces, so that his initial distance from the apparatus was increased at least twelvefold. At each of these distances, the same experiment was repeated several times with those two elevations which had offered the observer in close proximity a difference that was still definitely recognizable, yet very weak. Since at a 12-fold distance of the observer, the physical intensity of the sound has dropped to 1/144 of its original strength \*), the difference—which was not much more than just noticeable in close proximity—should have disappeared entirely if it depended at all on the absolute intensity of the sound. However, at all three distances of the observer, his judgment remained just as certain and correct as it had been at the closest proximity.

As crude as the apparatus and experiment were in a certain respect, the essentials seemed sufficiently considered, and the result was so decisive that it was foreseeable that a more precise execution with a more carefully constructed apparatus would lead to no different results. Indeed, this was demonstrated—on a very large experimental scale with sound intensities ranging from a baseline to several hundredfold—in later experiments by <term>Volkmann <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a German physiologist and physicist who collaborated closely with Fechner to prove that the "just noticeable difference" is relative to the stimulus size.</note></term>. These were conducted not with a falling pendulum, but with steel balls falling freely onto a steel plate under the necessary controlled conditions.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sound intensity experiments, specifically focusing on the more refined methodology using falling spheres to test Weber’s Law, as documented in Volkmann’s research journals.</meta>

...have been performed, and in some of which I participated. In these experiments, the height of fall, the weight of the falling spheres, and the distance of the observer were varied across a wide range; however, the heights of fall and their differences were precisely determined using a vertical scale along which the fall occurred. Otherwise, the manner of arrangement and the success of the experiments were consistent with the previous ones. Namely, at the most varied absolute levels of <term>sound intensity <note>The objective physical strength of the sound, as opposed to how loud it is perceived to be.</note></term>, the ratio of the heights of fall of 3 : 4—which, according to the derivation provided below, corresponds to an equal ratio of sound intensities—appeared just sufficient to bring about a certain discrimination for two observers with a good <term>power of discrimination <note>The ability to detect a difference between two stimuli.</note></term>; this agrees well with the results obtained by Renz and Wolf.

Here follows the more detailed description of the experiments, extracted from Volkmann’s observation journal.

> “A prismatic rod is graduated and set up vertically on a board, which can be kept horizontal by means of three screws. Two sliders are attached to this rod, from which two arms, α and β, extend horizontally. A sphere is dropped onto the board from the height indicated by the two arms. The sphere was held between the thumb and index finger; the tip of the index finger touched arm α or β, and then the fingers were carefully moved away from each other to let the sphere fall. I had two spheres of equal weight; I held one with the left hand and the other with the right, so as not to have to pick up or even search for the sphere for the second trial only after the first falling trial.”

> “The greatest proximity of the listening observer to the falling instrument was 1 meter, the greatest distance 6 meters.”

> “The absolute heights of fall that were compared differed as 3 : 4.0.”

> “The weights of the falling spheres differed as 1.35 grams : 14.85 grams...”

> “Numerous trials within the range of these sound differences showed that Heidenhain and I are capable of distinguishing with certainty sound intensities that relate to each other as 3 : 4. If the difference is reduced to a ratio of 6 : 7, individual errors and, even more often, indecision in judgment already occur.”

Fechner, on the other hand, erred very frequently even at the ratio of 3 : 4. However, practice clearly had an influence on the increase of his power of discrimination, for at the end of a very long series of observations, he distinguished sound intensities in a ratio of 3 : 4 correctly every time, whereas at the beginning he erred more often than he heard correctly, and after longer trials still made 1/3 false reports compared to 2/3 correct ones.

The previous experiments are based on the principle of the method of **just noticeable differences** <note>A core concept in psychophysics referring to the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected by an observer.</note>; and since, for reasons stated earlier, this method cannot achieve the same level of precision as the <term>method of right and wrong cases <note>A statistical approach where a subject compares two stimuli and the percentage of correct identifications is measured.</note></term> and the <term>average error <note>A method where the subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard to measure accuracy.</note></term>, experiments using these latter methods undoubtedly remain desirable. However, given the exceptionally large variation in absolute <term>sound intensities <note>The objective physical strength of the sound, as opposed to how loud it is perceived to be.</note></term> that occurred in the trials conducted, they are sufficiently decisive for the general validity of the law <note>Referring to Weber’s Law, which suggests that the ratio between a stimulus and the "just noticeable" increase remains constant.</note> in general. At most, there might still be a minor deviation from it within the limits of the trials conducted, though these results do not establish any probability of such a deviation.

It may be useful to add a few points regarding the apparatus to be used in experiments of this kind and their theory.

Schafhäutl*) <margin>Karl Emil von Schafhäutl (1803–1890) was a German polymath, musician, and geologist who studied acoustics.</margin> has previously described an instrument with falling spheres to measure sensitivity to sound intensity, though he used it merely to measure absolute sensitivity.

The <term>sound pendulum <note>A device used to produce consistent, reproducible sounds by striking an object with a weight swinging from a fixed point.</note></term> has likewise been put to use for this purpose before. Itard**) <note>Jean Marc Gaspard Itard (1774–1838) was a French physician famous for his work with the deaf and his educational efforts with the "Wild Boy of Aveyron."</note> employed such a device for investigating hearing sensitivity in cases of ear disease under the name <term>acoumeter <note>From the Greek 'akouein' (to hear) and 'metron' (measure); an early instrument for testing the sharpness of hearing.</note></term>. This device consists of a hammered copper ring hanging freely by a small rod from a machine mounted on a pillar atop a pedestal; the pendulum strikes against this ring, and its elevation is measured on a graduated arc.

I myself have had a double sound pendulum with a graduated arc manufactured, where two identically constructed pendulums strike against a thick <term>slate plate <note>A flat piece of fine-grained rock used here as a sounding board because it produces a more consistent tone than wood.</note></term>***) from two sides; however, I have not yet found the time to conduct experiments with it.

Regarding the theory of the instruments:

One easily finds that when a body falls onto another body—whether by free fall or as a pendulum—the intensity of the sound produced is, in the composite

<note>*) *Schafhäutl* <note>Karl Emil von Schafhäutl (1803–1890) was a German polymath and pioneer in acoustics.</note> sets the sound intensity proportional to the square root of the drop height of the sound-producing body (*Munich Transactions* VII. p. 517), which I cannot find to be correct based on the derivation following above.</note>

is in a relationship with the drop height and the weight of the falling body *), provided that the influence of air resistance and any other disturbing influences on the falling speed can be neglected.

In fact: the <term>intensity of the sound <note>In physics, intensity refers to the power carried by sound waves, which is perceived as loudness.</note></term> is proportional to the square of the <term>oscillation amplitude <note>The maximum distance a vibrating particle moves from its rest position.</note></term> of the sounding body; the oscillation amplitude of the sounding body is (according to known formulas) proportional to the velocity with which the particles pass through their position of equilibrium—that is, the same velocity with which they are removed from it. This velocity stands in a compound ratio to the speed with which the falling body strikes and its weight. The speed with which the body strikes (that is, the final velocity of its fall) is, according to the laws of falling bodies, proportional to the square root of the drop height. Therefore, the square of this final velocity is proportional to the drop height; consequently, the square of the velocity with which the particles move from their position of rest, and so forth, is also proportional to this drop height. Since it is well known that it makes no difference to the final velocity whether a body falls through a free fall or along a curved path through a certain height, one can apply the previous observation just as well to the hammer of the <term>sound pendulum <note>A device used to create a standardized sound by dropping a weighted arm from a specific height.</note></term> (assuming the friction at the axis is negligible) as to a free-falling body. In both cases, one must only be careful not to impart an initial velocity to the falling body if the specified dependence of sound intensity on the drop height is to remain valid. The air resistance should be negligible given the low drop heights and velocities with which one will generally operate, all the more so if one uses lead as the falling body.

From the foregoing it is clear that the intensity of the sound in the sound pendulum is not in proportion to the <term>angle of elevation <note>The angle $\phi$ to which the pendulum is raised before being released.</note></term> $\phi$ of the pendulum, but rather to the vertical height by which the hammer is raised above its lowest point—that is, in the ratio of $1 - \cos \phi = 2 \sin^2 \phi/2$, according to which the instrument should be graduated...

Since, for example, the cosine of 45° equals the square root of 1/2 = 0.707 and the cosine of 90° equals zero, according to this the ratio of sound intensities at these two elevations is that of 1 − 0.707 = 0.293 to 1, or approximately 3 to 10. The elevation angles of 60°, 90°, and 180° correspond to a ratio of sound intensities of 1/2 : 1 : 2. As long as the elevation does not exceed 60°, one can set the sound intensity as approximately proportional to the square of the elevation, so that a double elevation corresponds roughly to four times the sound intensity, and a triple elevation to nine times the intensity *).

At 180°, the intensity is then twice as great as at 90°, and all intensities at elevations between 90° and 180° fall in between; however, one will not easily use a pendulum at elevations above 90°.

Meanwhile, no special experiments are required to confirm the law in this regard, as it is the simple and, so to speak, notorious testimony of the musical ear that equal ratios of vibration frequencies correspond to a tonal difference perceived as being of equal size in different octaves. Thus, one can consider the law proven here more directly than anywhere else, even for large differences. *Euler*, *Herbart*, and *Drobisch* <note>Leonhard Euler (mathematician), Johann Friedrich Herbart (philosopher), and Moritz Wilhelm Drobisch (mathematician) were key figures who sought to apply mathematical precision to music and psychology.</note> also relied on this in their mathematical consideration of tonal relationships.

I asked several persons with good musical hearing, during occasional experiments with a wooden <term>sound pendulum <note>An apparatus used to create controlled sound intensities by dropping a weight from a specific angle.</note></term> that struck wood, whether they could draw a comparison between the ratio of sound intensities at 45° and 90° and a ratio of pitches. Many declared themselves incapable of this; remarkably, however, most of those who engaged in a comparison agreed (independently of one another and without knowing the judgment of others) to compare this ratio with that of a <term>fourth <note>A musical interval, such as the distance between the notes C and F.</note></term>. However, I am reluctant to place much weight on these experiments given their crude and incidental setup so far, especially since that agreement was not without exception. I even consider it very questionable whether a direct comparison between ratios of intensity and pitch can be drawn by feeling at all. In any case, the result of these experiments aligns confirmingly with those obtained by *Renz* and *Wolf*, as well as by *Volkmann*, according to which one is not inclined to rate fairly significant differences in sound intensities (a ratio of 3 : 10) as very high.

In this same regard, it was interesting for me to hear the statement from a musician (the violin virtuoso *v. Wasilewski* <note>Joseph Wilhelm von Wasilewski, a prominent 19th-century violinist and conductor.</note>) that experience at the Rhenish Singers' Festivals had shown that a choir of 400 male voices did not make a significantly stronger impression than one of 200.

The reasons why our law is required in the field of weight experiments have already been cited on page 138. *Weber’s* experiments have the particular merit that, in a portion of them, the <term>pressure sensation <note>The sense of touch on the skin's surface, distinct from the internal feeling of effort in the muscles.</note></term> of the skin is separated from the <term>muscle feeling <note>The internal sensation of tension or effort within the muscles when lifting or moving a weight; often called kinesthesia.</note></term>, and the results obtained in this way have been compared with those obtained when both sensations are called upon together. In contrast, the experiments I conducted myself according to the <term>method of right and wrong cases <note>A fundamental psychophysical technique (now often called the method of constant stimuli) where a participant compares two objects, and the researcher records the frequency of correct versus incorrect judgments to determine the threshold of perception.</note></term>—which will be discussed in more detail below—refer to the natural connection of both sensations that occurs during the lifting of compared weights. A precise separation of the two was not easily feasible according to the modality of my procedure; however, a common verification of the law for both appeared useful, considering the accuracy that the method promised. Furthermore, these experiments were intended no less for the study of the method itself than for the testing of the law.

For an understanding of what follows, frequent reference will be necessary to what was said in the chapter starting on page 93 regarding the execution of the method, though I do not consider it necessary to return to it in detail here. On the other hand, many proofs and illustrative examples for what was said there will be found in the following sections.

There are two of my main experimental series regarding the subject in question: a two-handed one and a one-handed one (carried out separately with the right and left hands). These, being comparable to one another, were carried out through a series of six <term>main weights <note>The standard weights used as the basis for comparison: 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 3000 grams.</note></term>, namely 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 3000 grams, and have led to very consistent results. The one-handed series was conducted in October and November 1856, and the two-handed series in December 1856 and January 1857. The circumstances of the experiments in both series were generally the "normal circumstances" stated on page 97. Specifically, the following should be noted:

Each of the two series comprises 32 experimental days at 12 divisions at 64 lifts, totaling 32 . 12 . 64 = 24,576 individual lifts or cases. For each main weight *P*, two specific proportional parts were applied (alternating periodically) as an <term>additional weight <note>The small weight added to the main weight to see if the subject can perceive a difference; also called an increment.</note></term> *D*, namely 0.04 *P* and 0.08 *P*. The latter additional weight may appear large, but it nevertheless gives, as one...

...as one can see from the following **experimental tables**, there are still enough false cases. This is related to the setup of the procedure described on page 94 f., which bases every comparison (counted as 2 cases) on a simple **double lift**, instead of repeated back-and-forth weighing; in the latter case, a weight difference of <term>*D* = 0.08 *P* <note>D represents the difference in weight, while P represents the primary or standard weight. Thus, 0.08 P means a weight difference equal to 8% of the total weight.</note></term> would hardly yield any false cases at all. On each experimental day consisting of 12 × 64 = 768 **lifts**, all 6 **primary weights** were tested, each in 2 sections of 64 lifts, all with the same proportional *D*; this was changed only after days or weeks, as indicated below. Furthermore, the order of the primary weights was changed daily, alternating between ascending (↑) and descending (↓) sequences. Thus, in each of the two series of experiments, a total of 32 × 128 = 4096 lifts or "cases" were performed for each of the six primary weights: 2048 with *D* = 0.04 *P* and just as many with *D* = 0.08 *P*; of these, 1024 were in ascending order and 1024 in descending order.

In the **two-handed series**, the 128 lifts of each day were performed <note>original: "in continuo"</note> continuously with each primary weight. In the **one-handed series**, they were performed sequentially: 64 with the left hand and 64 with the right, with the starting hand alternating each day. In the two-handed series, the difference was switched between *D* = 0.04 *P* and *D* = 0.08 *P* every two days, while in the one-handed series, the switch occurred only every 8 days. This resulted in a distinction: in the two-handed series, the **sensitivity values** for both weight differences (*D*) are fully comparable. Therefore, this series can serve to confirm the law according to which the ratio of correct cases to the total number of cases $\frac{r}{n}$ depends on the magnitude of *D* when the sensitivity *h* <note>In early psychophysics, 'h' represents the 'measure of precision' or sensitivity—essentially how consistent and sharp a person's senses are.</note> remains constant <margin>*) According to the discussions in Chapter 7, this law is expressed by the relationship of the values $\frac{r}{n}$ to *t = hD* in our **Fundamental Table** on page 108, whereby a doubled *D* gives a doubled *t*, provided that the influences of *p* and *q* <note>These represent constant errors, such as 'time error' (p) or 'space error' (q), which occur based on which weight is lifted first or in which hand it is held.</note> are eliminated.</margin>. However, this is not the case with the one-handed series, where the weeks using 0.08 *P* yield proportionally smaller sensitivity values than those using 0.04 *P*, a point which relates to the remark on page 83. But regarding the influence of the size of the primary weight on the **measurement values**—which is the only point of importance here—the one-handed series is just as comparable within itself as the two-handed one.

To begin with the simplest, if not the most precise, method of utilizing these series of observations, I will provide the total number of correct cases *r* for the various <term>primary weights *P*<note>The baseline weight used as the standard for comparison in each trial.</note></term>, categorized according to several main circumstances. This will be done without separating the four main cases or reverting to the precise <term>measure-numbers<note>Specific statistical values used to calculate sensitivity; here, Fechner is referring to the mathematical relationship between the weight difference and the probability of a correct response.</note></term>—that is, the values *t=hD*—that can be calculated from them. Even without such calculations, the primary results under consideration can be drawn from the ratios of the correct numbers *r* grouped for all main cases; a more rigorous treatment of these series would yield nothing more than making these same results appear even more clearly.

The unit of weight used in the following text is everywhere the gram.

To leave no doubt about the meaning of the numbers in the following tables, I shall explicitly state it for the first number of the first table. The number 612 for *P* = 300, *D* = 0.04 *P*, *n* = 1024, ↑ indicates that with a primary weight of 300 grams and an <term>added weight *D*<note>The "Difference" weight added to one of the primary weights to see if the subject can perceive the change.</note></term> equal to 0.04 of the primary weight (which is 12 grams), the number of correct cases across all days where the primary weights were used in ascending order (↑) was 612. Meanwhile, the total number of cases—correct and incorrect combined—under these same circumstances was 1024; the number of incorrect cases was therefore 1024 – 612 = 412. Following this, the meaning of the remaining numbers will be self-explanatory. 

Naturally, for the numbers *r* in the vertical total-sum column, the value of *n* is four times that of the special columns—that is, 4096, as noted parenthetically—since the *r* values of the four vertical special columns are added together in the vertical total-sum column. On the other hand, the numbers *r* in the horizontal total-sum column correspond to six times the *n* of the special values—that is, 6144—since the *r* values belonging to the six *P* values in the same vertical column are added together in the horizontal total-sum column.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the data tables from the previous page, specifically addressing why the counts of correct identifications (r) vary slightly across different weight levels despite the constant ratio of the difference weight to the main weight. It establishes a parallel between the perception of weight and the perception of light.</meta>

...which, in both tables for an *n* = 4096, provide the correct counts for the individual main weights.

If the law <note>Referring to the principle later known as the Weber-Fechner Law, which states that the ratio of the increment of a stimulus to the background stimulus is constant.</note> were to be directly and precisely proven by these experiments, then—considering that the same ratio of additional weight to main weight exists throughout—all the values for *r* <note>The number of correct identifications.</note> across the various main weights would have to be not just approximately, but exactly equal. This is not the case. However, the deviation that remains between the experiment and the law in this manner is no more to be regarded as a true deviation than the deviation we found at the lower limit <note>The "lower limit" refers to the threshold of perception where stimuli are very weak.</note> in the field of light sensation <term>Lichtempfindung: The psychological perception of light stimuli.</term>; rather, it should be viewed from a completely analogous perspective as a requirement of the law. 

Just as in the case of light sensation we must take into account the internal light excitation <note>The inherent "noise" or visual activity of the eye even in total darkness.</note> present even without the arrival of external light, so here we must consider the weight of the arm and any covering clothing (in my experiments, merely a light shirt sleeve \*) that is present even without the external weight *P* and is lifted along with it. And just as the law can only be directly confirmed in the former field (vision) to the extent that the internal "eye-light" can be neglected relative to external light, so too in the latter field (weight) can it be confirmed only to the degree that the weight-moment of the lifting and simultaneously lifted arm can be neglected compared to the weight being lifted.

In fact, however, with our highest main weights we see only a very insignificant deviation from the law's requirement, and the general trend of the deviation follows what would be expected based on the previous view—that is, the correct numbers *r* increase slightly as *P* <note>The primary weight.</note> increases. For if we imagine the same absolute addition *A*—due to the weight of the arm—added to the increasingly larger main weights *P*, while the difference *D* increases only proportionally with *P* (as was the case in our experiments), then the ratio *D* / (*P* + *A*)—on which the correct number *r* depends—naturally turns out larger the more *A* vanishes in comparison to *P* in the divisor.

---

\*) Furthermore, it remains questionable to what extent the pressure of the air on the skin must be taken into account with a certain value; however, this seems, so to speak, to be already factored into the organism itself.

<summary>Fechner explains that the slight deviations in his data are not failures of the law, but are caused by the constant weight of the subject's arm, which acts like "internal light" in visual perception. As the experimental weights increase, the arm's weight becomes less significant, and the data more closely matches the theoretical law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of why experimental data deviates from a perfect mathematical law of perception. Specifically, it explores how the weight of the human arm acts as a "constant" background weight (A) added to the external test weight (P), similar to how internal "noise" or light in the eye affects the perception of physical light.</meta>

i.e., the larger P itself is, and it becomes noticeably constant from the point where P has become large enough that A <note>A represents the "internal" weight, such as the weight of the limb or clothing, added to the external weight P.</note> can no longer be seen as a consideration against it; exactly as the experiment shows.

Given the not insignificant weight of the arm, it might initially seem surprising that the increase the main weights from 300 to 3000 grams receive from it does not result in an even stronger increase in the correct identification numbers as P rises; and particularly, that this is not more noticeable at the transition between the two smallest main weights, 300 and 500 grams, where in the two-handed series a small decrease is actually shown instead. But setting aside this latter anomaly for now, which I will return to later; firstly, it is by no means to be taken as settled that the load on the arm from its own weight is to be calculated in the same way as an added external weight; secondly, it must be considered that the lifted weight P acts at the end of the lever arm formed by the lifting arm, whereas the weight of the arm acting at its center of gravity acts on a shorter lever, which relatively reduces its torque <note>original: "Moment"</note>; thirdly, that the addition of this torque to the torque of P only matters for the muscular sensation <term>Muskelgefühl: The internal sensation of effort or tension in the muscles when lifting.</term>, but not for the sensation of pressure <term>Druckgefühl: The tactile sensation of the weight pressing against the skin of the hand.</term>, since only the weight P, and not the weight of the arm, acts pressingly upon the skin; finally, fourthly, that the numbers of correct cases in the previous tables do not yet provide an exact measure for sensitivity, but can only indicate the general trend of sensitivity as it ascends with the main weights. 

Indeed, what was explained on page 117 and following applies here completely; and particularly the circumstance mentioned on page 115 and following comes into consideration: that the influence of the chronological order <note>The "time-order error" where the sequence in which two weights are lifted affects which one feels heavier.</note> of the lift *p* increases with a strong increase in the main weight, and thereby—according to the remark on page 116—makes the sum of correct cases slightly smaller than would be the case without this disruptive influence. Thus, without this disruption, the correct numbers for the highest main weights would have actually been somewhat larger and thus more distinct from the lower ones. This is particularly relevant for the smaller additional weight of 0.04 P, whereas against the larger 0.08 P, the influence of *p* relatively more dis... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "disappears" (verschwindet) or "diminishes" (verringert).</note>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of weight-perception experiments, specifically focusing on the relationship between sensitivity (h) and the magnitude of weights (P). It follows a discussion of the raw data derived from multiple observation series.</meta>

What matters here is that we observe the extent to which the sum values 4 *hD* and 8 *hD*—which were produced by adding *t*<sub>1</sub>, *t*<sub>2</sub>, *t*<sub>3</sub>, and *t*<sub>4</sub> <note>These "t" values likely refer to specific experimental variables or time-intervals in the lifting sequence.</note>—remain constant across the various values of *P*. They should be constant, just like the sums of the numbers *r* from which they are derived, if our law <note>The author refers to Weber's Law, which suggests that the ratio of the "just noticeable difference" to the background stimulus is constant.</note> holds true and if the <term>weight of the arm</term> <note>original: "Armgewicht"; the physiological weight of the subject's arm, which Fechner believed added a constant baseline to the experimental weights.</note> did not contribute to *P*.

The numbers in the columns 4 *hD*, 4 *hD*, and 8 *hD* represent the actual measures of interest here. The first two columns represent each of the two relative <term>additional weights</term> <note>original: "Zusatzgewichte"; the small weight added to one of the main weights to test if a difference can be perceived.</note> specifically, while the latter is the sum of both. These values are what would have been obtained without the combined influences of the temporal and spatial positions of the vessels *p* and *q*. In other words, they are the products of the measure of <term>sensitivity to differences</term> <note>original: "Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit"; a technical term in psychophysics representing the precision of perception, often denoted as "h".</note> *h* and the 4-fold or 8-fold additional weight *D*. From these, the measure of difference *h* itself could be found for the various <term>main weights</term> <note>original: "Hauptgewichte"; the base weights being compared.</note> by dividing by 4 or 8 *D* \*. According to our law, if the weight of the arm did not interfere, this *h* should be found to be inversely proportional to the weights *P* (and thus inversely proportional to the additional weights *D* which are proportional to *P*). Consequently, the products 4 *hD* or 8 *hD* should be found to be equal across the various main weights. Since deviations from equality are easier to judge than deviations from proportionality, we have remained with the products 4 *hD* and 8 *hD* without reverting to *h* itself.

For a easier overview, we now compile the values of the three main columns in the following table, reduced to the simple value *hD* by dividing by 4 or 8 respectively. The designations *v* = 4 and *v* = 8 above the columns indicate, according to the notation given on p. 94, that each number in the columns is derived from 4 or 8 times *n* observations, respectively; where *n* is = 512.

To translate the abstract meaning of the numbers *hD*—with which we are dealing here only to confirm our law—into a meaning for the actual experiment, it is this: if, for each of the <term>main weights</term> <note>original: "Hauptgewichte"; the base weights being compared in the lifting experiment.</note> used, instead of using the same relative additional weight as was done, one had divided this weight by the number *hD* (or a given multiple or fraction of *hD*), then an equal number of $^r/_n$ <note>This ratio represents the proportion of correct judgments (*r*) out of the total number of trials (*n*).</note> would have been obtained everywhere. For example, in the two-handed series, according to the experimental results, one would have to divide the <term>additional weights</term> <note>original: "Zusatzgewichte"; the small weight added to the main weight to create a detectable difference.</note> belonging to the main weights of 2000 and 3000 grams—which are in the same proportion as these main weights—by numbers proportional to 4500 and 4909 respectively, so that they are perceived as equally strong in sensation.

Although these calculation results are not yet the definitive ones, which I will only arrive at in the following sections, I have nonetheless provided them here with diligence because they do not deviate significantly from the definitive ones. Thus, one can certainly rely on them, especially as all the underlying data could be provided without too much verbosity, from which one can reproduce them oneself according to the rules given in Chapter 8. In this process, all <term>correct cases</term> <note>original: "richtigen Zahlen"; literally "correct numbers," referring to the trials where the subject correctly identified which weight was heavier.</note> obtained for the same main case, the same *P* and *D* during the entire month of observation, were taken together and used without <term>fractioning</term> <note>original: "Fractionirung"; Fechner's practice of breaking large data sets into smaller groups, usually of 64 trials, to check for consistency.</note> to derive the *t*-values from the <term>fundamental table</term> <note>original: "Fundamentaltabelle"; a mathematical table used to convert the probability of a correct answer into a measure of the intensity of the sensation.</note>. A detailed discussion of the observation series reveals that the variables *p* and *q* <note>In Fechner's formulas, *p* and *q* typically represent constant errors or probabilities related to the direction of judgment (e.g., overestimating the first weight).</note> did not remain entirely constant during the month-long observation series, but rather varied irregularly. By dividing the series into such small <term>fractions</term> <note>Subsets of the total data set.</note> that the variation within each can be neglected, one removes the disadvantage that would otherwise arise for the <term>elimination</term> <note>The mathematical process of neutralizing or accounting for constant errors.</note> of *p* and *q*. For this reason, the values obtained in Table VI are preferable to those in Table V. In the meantime, however, there is no essential difference in the progression of values between the two tables, so that one could well have stayed with the first, which is derivable much more quickly. In any case, a comparison of these tables can provide a guide as to how the absolute measured values can change approximately depending on the degree of fractionation.

If one compares the definitive <term>mean values</term> <note>Averages.</note> obtained with the one-handed and two-handed series, one finds:

| 3000 | 1.254 |

whereby the ratio of both values decreases slowly as the <term>primary weight</term> <note>original: "Hauptgewicht"; the base weight (*P*) to which a comparison weight is added.</note> increases, but appears to approach a point of constancy.

A look at the progression of the *hD* values <note>A mathematical product used to measure the precision of a subject's discrimination between two weights.</note> in the previous Tables VI and VII now teaches us that it leads essentially to the same result as the progression of the numbers *r* <note>The number of "right" or correct cases.</note> in the first tables, except that the growth of the *hD* values alongside *P* is, for the reasons stated, somewhat more noticeable at the highest *P*-values than that of the numbers *r*. Nevertheless, the increasing approximation toward equality as *P* grows still emerges clearly enough.

Thus, for the three highest *P*-values = 1500, 2000, 3000 grams, the average *hD* values in the two-handed series are 4342, 4500, and 4908; in the one-handed series, they are 5682, 5639, and 6152. While *P* rises from 1500 to 3000—that is, from its single value to double—*hD* rises only a little in proportion, namely from the single value to 1.13 times or 1.08 times respectively.

It seemed to me to be of interest to once again specifically confirm this approximate equality of *hD* at higher weights—which is most important for the validation of the law—for the two highest primary weights of 2000 and 3000; and I took the opportunity to do so during a series of trials that was simultaneously intended...

This provides further evidence for what was stated on p. 183: that one cannot rely on the comparability of <term>measurement values</term> <note>original: "Masswerthe"</note> obtained in different epochs, even if the external circumstances were identical. However, this does not affect the internal comparability of each series regarding the ratios under discussion here.

The fact that in our current series—where the change between the two *D* values took place on the same day—the values of *hD* calculated from *r* <note>The number of correct (recht) identifications of the heavier weight.</note> show themselves to be noticeably proportional to the given *D* values, serves as a validation of our <term>calculation rule</term>.

According to the definitive result, *hD* increased from *P* = 2000 to *P* = 3000 only in the ratio of 31186 to 32938. The deviation of these two numbers from equality represents the deviation from the direct requirement of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>Weber's Law suggests that the ratio of the increment threshold to the background intensity is constant; here, the values should remain equal if the law held perfectly across all weights.</note>, which we explain by the additional <term>arm weight</term> <note>Fechner argued that the sensation of weight includes the weight of the person's own arm, which acts as a constant "base" weight added to the experimental weights.</note>. However, the number 9464 in the table above is indisputably too large due to random chance when compared with all other numbers; consequently, the deviation has turned out slightly smaller than it would have otherwise been. Otherwise, the essential result of this series is the complete confirmation of the results of the earlier ones.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical analysis of his weight-lifting experiments, specifically investigating how the physical weight of the arm (the "arm-moment") interacts with the external weights (P) to influence the subject's sensitivity.</meta>

Since the proportional part by which the <term>moment</term> <note>In physics, a 'moment' (or torque) is the turning effect of a force. Fechner is considering the arm as a lever; the "moment of the arm" is the internal force required just to lift one's own limb.</note> of the raised arm must be added to that of the raised weight cannot well be determined beforehand—partly because the moment in a living subject may not be determinable by exact measurement, and partly because it is not known exactly in what proportion the effect of the <term>muscle sense</term> <note>original: "Muskelgefühl"; refers to the internal sensation of muscular effort or tension, distinct from the sense of skin pressure.</note> contributes to the total effect—one might think of determining the value to be added to *P* from our *hD* values by assuming the validity of our law itself; yet, some reflection shows that these values are likely insufficient for that purpose.

If we base our reasoning on the principles of the <term>probability of errors</term> <note>The mathematical framework for calculating how different independent sources of error or sensory input combine to affect overall precision.</note> regarding the interaction of independent conditions of precision, then if the muscle sense alone had produced the value *t' = h'D* and the <term>pressure sense</term> <note>original: "Druckgefühl"; the tactile sensation of the weight pressing against the skin.</note> alone had produced the value *t'' = h''D* at a certain added weight *D*, the interaction of the two would lead us to expect a value *t =*

->$\sqrt{t'^2 + t''^2} = \sqrt{h'^2 + h''^2} D$<-

and a calculation might be attempted on this basis. Now, according to our law, *t'* is in inverse proportion to *P + A* (if *A* is understood as the arm's weight as described above), and *t''* is simply in inverse proportion to *P*; consequently, one has

->$t^2 = (hD)^2 = \frac{c'}{(P + A)^2} + \frac{c''}{P^2}$<-

where *c'* and *c''* are constants. The three unknowns—*c', c'', and A*—would then have to be determined from the <term>hD</term> <note>As noted previously, *hD* represents the measure of precision multiplied by the weight difference, used here as a proxy for the threshold of sensation.</note> values obtained for the various weights *P*. However, even if the difficulty of this calculation could be overcome, the anomaly at small values of *P*, which shall be discussed shortly, would stand in the way of an exact calculation.

The fact that in the transition from *P* = 300 to *P* = 500 grams, *t* actually decreases slightly instead of increasing, is an anomaly that cannot be explained by what has been stated so far. I find it unlikely that this rests on chance due to a still-insufficient number of observations, though the possibility is not absolutely excluded, as the difference is indeed small and *very large* numbers of trials are required to firmly establish small differences. However, quite apart from the agreement of both experimental series in this regard (each of which counts a great many trials), the increase of *t* with the growth of *P* should be relatively strongest precisely at the smallest values of *P*, since the addition to the moment of *P* caused by the moment of the arm is proportionally greatest here. And if no special...

Although I cannot currently provide a definitive explanation for this anomaly—the certain confirmation of which through new experiments would be highly desirable—the following seems to offer some probability, should it actually exist in nature.

One might imagine that an increasing pressure—quite apart from the decrease in <term>sensitivity</term> <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"; in Fechner’s terms, this is the ability to distinguish between two different intensities of a stimulus.</note> which, according to our law, exists proportionally with the increase of the stimulus—exerts a diminishing influence on sensitivity through the mechanical compression of the nerve endings or the auxiliary tissues involved in the <term>apperception</term> <note>Fechner uses "apperception" to describe the process where a physical sensation is consciously recognized by the mind.</note> of pressure. This influence would vanish at larger weights when compared to the influence following our law (which must have a more general and fundamental cause), but could exert a dominant influence at smaller weights. This would explain the decrease of *t* <note>The variable *t* represents the measure of precision or the subject's sensitivity in Fechner’s formulas.</note> at the initial growth of *P* <note>The variable *P* stands for the initial weight or stimulus being applied.</note>. However, I readily admit that these are merely thoughts that require further testing and may perhaps provide the impetus for it.

It is very probable that, just as the field of weight experiments shares the <term>lower limit</term> <note>The point below which a stimulus is too weak to be perceived or where the proportional relationship of the law breaks down.</note> of the law with the field of light experiments, this will also be the case regarding the upper limit. The only difference is that the experiments were not continued by me to such a limit where the load begins to have a detrimental effect. Looking back at the preceding discussion, the investigation into the validity and limits of our law <note>This refers to Weber's Law, which states that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note> in the field of weight experiments is still far from complete. My own attempts to solve the problem, following those of Weber, are only a second step after his first, and many more with new modifications of the method must follow. Based on what has been achieved so far, one can only say that the observations generally agree so well with the law that its approximate or exact validity within certain limits cannot be doubted. However, the anomaly at the lower limit, the question regarding the upper limit, the more precise confirmation and determination of the influence of the arm's weight, and the complete and exact separation of the <term>sense of pressure</term> <note>original: "Druckgefühl"; the sensation of a weight resting on the skin.</note> and the <term>muscle sense</term> <note>original: "Muskelgefühl"; the internal sensation of effort or tension in the muscles when lifting an object.</note> are still points awaiting resolution through future experiments. Weber's experiments first proved the law in general, though his method was not suited to reliably confirm deviations from it; my experiments have allowed such deviations to be recognized, without being sufficient to eliminate them by precisely accounting for the circumstances on which they depend.

While there can be no doubt that the isolation of the sense of pressure is achieved by one of Weber's experimental methods—where the weight is placed on the last joints of the fingers while the hand rests on the table—it seems to me that the isolation of the muscle sense is not quite so reliably achieved by the other method he described in his <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878) was a founder of experimental psychology.</note> *Treatise on the Sense of Touch and Common Feeling* <note>original: "Abhandlung über Tastsinn und Gemeingefühl"</note>, p. 546. In that method, the observer grasps the gathered corners of a cloth in which a weight hangs; however, the weight must necessarily tend to pull the corners through the hand more forcefully the heavier it is, unless this is countered by a stronger grip—and therefore a stronger pressure. Even if the pressure could be kept constant, a constant pressure would nonetheless factor into the experiments as a complication.

No method for precisely isolating the muscle sense in these experiments occurs to me at all.
