...comparison of the results thus obtained with those provided by the lifting of weights will be of no small interest.

Regardless of the question of our law <note>Weber's Law, which suggests that the ratio between a stimulus and the "just noticeable difference" remains constant.</note>, the direct result of the experiments reported in the preceding section can be stated as follows.

If one lifts a given weight in comparison with another, to which a certain <term>additional weight</term> <note>original: "Mehrgewicht"; the incremental weight added to the standard to test if a difference is felt.</note> has been added relative to the first, then the additional weight—taken in absolute terms—must be greater as the <term>primary weight</term> <note>original: "Hauptgewicht"; the constant base weight used for comparison.</note> increases, in order for the difference between the two weights to be perceived as equally noticeable in one’s sensation.

If the additional weight is allowed to increase proportionally with the primary weight—so that its absolute size does not remain the same, but its relative size in relation to the primary weight always remains constant—then the noticeability of this relative additional weight increases somewhat as one ascends to higher primary weights. However, it tends more and more toward equality, such that the difference in noticeability of equal relative additional weights at primary weights of 1500 and 3000 grams is only slight, corresponding approximately to the ratio of 10 : 11. That is to say, the relative additional weights at 1500 and 3000 grams of primary weight would have to stand in a ratio of approximately 11 : 10, instead of being equal, in order to appear equally noticeable—that is, to provide the same ratio of correct to incorrect cases <note>This refers to the "method of right and wrong cases," a psychophysical method where the subject must judge which of two stimuli is greater; a consistent ratio of correct guesses indicates a consistent level of sensory discrimination.</note> in the corresponding method.

However, this ascending progression of the noticeability of equal relative additional weights along with the size of the primary weights undergoes an exception at very low primary weights, in that the noticeability rather decreases somewhat than increases when ascending from 300 to 500 grams; whereas above 500 grams, the ascending progression is continuously maintained.

The reason for this exceptional progression at low primary weights is virtually unknown, and only on page 198 was a passing conjecture made regarding it; the reason for the deviation from equal noticeability for relatively equal additional weights when ascending to higher primary weights can probably be sought in the fact that the <term>weight-moment</term> <note>original: "Gewichtsmoment"; refers to the effective force or torque generated by the mass of the arm itself during the lifting process.</note> of the lifting arm—which is lifted along with the weight—comes into account as an increase in the primary weight, which

This increased noticeability results in an increased ratio of correct to incorrect cases, as well as to the total number of cases, if one employs the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>A foundational psychophysical method where a subject is presented with two stimuli and must judge which is greater; the ratio of correct answers is used to determine sensitivity.</note> to compare the weights. These results were found through experiments with primary weights of 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 3000 grams, and additional weights equal to 0.04 and 0.08 of the primary weight. These results were consistent whether lifting the weights with only one hand or with both hands, once <term>constant errors</term> <note>systematic biases in an experiment, such as a person always perceiving the second object lifted as heavier simply because it was second in time.</note> were excluded, which depend on the timing and spatial position of the lifted weights.

### 4) Temperature.

<margin>*) *The Sense of Touch and Common Feeling* <note>original: "Der Tasts. und das Gemeing."; referring to Ernst Heinrich Weber's 1846 work *Der Tastsinn und das Gemeingefühl*.</note>, p. 549.</margin>
The question of the extent to which our law <note>Weber's Law, which states that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note> may be applied to the sensation of temperature still involves some obscurities. E. H. Weber*) is inclined to assume,

> “that we are instead better able to perceive the act of the temperature of our skin rising and falling than the specific degree to which the temperature has risen or fallen. We do not perceive, for example, whether our forehead or our hand is warmer until we place the hand against the forehead, where we then often perceive a great difference between the two, sometimes finding the hand warmer, and at other times the forehead,”

to which other experiences asserted by Weber, which point in the same direction, can be added. In the meantime, it seems nonetheless that we are capable of perceiving sustained heat as heat, and sustained cold as cold, if they deviate sufficiently from the usual or mean temperature.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of weights on page 201 to an investigation of whether Weber’s Law applies to the sense of temperature, moving from mechanical pressure to thermal sensation.</meta>

Be that as it may, if one wishes to consider the question of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</note> regarding temperature differences, the stimulus in this case can by no means be considered as the temperature measured from an absolute zero point. Instead, it must simply be the difference from a temperature at which we feel neither heat nor cold, since the magnitude of the sensation of heat and cold depends solely on this. This difference can increase and decrease, and the question for Weber’s Law will be whether an equally large relative increase—not of the absolute temperature, but of this temperature difference—causes an equally noticeable or, more generally, an equally large increase in temperature sensation.

According to some experiments I have conducted on this question—which are by no means sufficient—this seems to be the case within certain limits of moderate temperatures, while it is decidedly no longer the case for very cold and very hot temperatures.

My experiments on this were conducted over 6 days (in Dec. 1855) according to the <term>method of just noticeable differences</term>, using Weber’s procedure of alternately immersing two fingers of the same hand to the same depth into two vessels of water of unequal warmth. For observation, I used a pair of very precise and carefully compared <term>Greiner thermometers</term> <note>Precision instruments made by the Greiner family, famous German glassblowers and instrument makers.</note> divided into half-degrees, using the <term>Réaumur scale</term> <note>An older temperature scale where water freezes at 0° and boils at 80°; 10–20° Réaumur is roughly 12.5–25° Celsius (55–77° Fahrenheit).</note> from the Leipzig Physics Cabinet. On these, tenths of a half-degree—and thus twentieths of a full degree—can still be quite well estimated. Since one of these stood higher than the other by 0.05° or 2/10 of a degree <note>original: "2/10 Grad"; the author likely means two-tenths of the half-degree markings mentioned previously.</note>, according to the information from <term>Hankel</term> <note>Wilhelm Gottlieb Hankel (1814–1894), a German physicist who managed the apparatus at Leipzig.</note>, who had the kindness to lend them to me for the experiments, as well as by my own confirmation, every observation has been corrected accordingly. Regarding the other conditions of the series of experiments, I will cite what is necessary following the results.

Within temperatures from about 10° to 20° R., I found the sensitivity to temperature differences to be so great that the just noticeable differences did not allow for a precise determination. A maximum of sensitivity, where vanishing or almost vanishing differences are <term>apperceived</term> <note>Consciously perceived or mentally processed.</note>, certainly lies within these limits, without a precise...

...found that among a very large number of experiments, I only once made a mistake in the vicinity of the <term>mean temperature</term> <note>The author's neutral baseline of 14.77° Réaumur (approx. 18.5° Celsius or 65° Fahrenheit).</note>, where the just noticeable differences become almost vanishingly small. In that instance, during subsequent verification, the difference I had assumed to be "just noticeable" was actually found in the opposite vessel from where I had suspected it to be. On the other hand, there were very frequent cases where I could find no difference at all between the two water samples; in these cases, I subsequently always found either no difference on the thermometers or a difference that fell below the threshold of noticeability for that specific temperature range. This serves as a kind of mutual control, proving that both the thermometer readings and the subjective reports of sensation were generally reliable.

While the progression of these just noticeable differences above the <term>mean temperature</term>—as far as it can be judged given how tiny the differences are—corresponds sufficiently to <term>Weber's Law</term> <note>A psychological law suggesting that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, there was no such symmetry found below that temperature. Down to about 10° below the mean, the just noticeable differences were still too small to allow for a reliable assessment of their ratios. Further down, however, they increased incomparably faster as the cold intensified than would be compatible with either the progression seen at higher temperatures or with Weber's Law. These results were represented empirically quite well by assuming they were proportional to the third power of *T* — *t*. In this calculation, *T* = 14.77°, *t* is the temperature at which the just noticeable difference was observed, and 0.002734 is the value by which one must multiply (*T* — *t*)³ to obtain the just noticeable difference on the thermometer. This undoubtedly stems from a significant decrease in <term>sensitivity</term> <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"</note> as the cold increases. 

One would likely find a similar deviation if one were to move beyond <term>blood heat</term> <note>Body temperature, approximately 37°C or 29.6° Réaumur.</note> and approach the temperature where the sensation of burning begins. However, it remains striking that while the deviation above the mean temperature only starts at much higher degrees, it begins immediately as one moves below the mean temperature.

<meta>This page continues the researcher’s evaluation of experimental data. The previous page ended while discussing how closely the observations matched a calculated formula, though the author remains cautious about its absolute proof.</meta>

...ly as such, and I consider <term>Weber's Law<note>Named after Ernst Heinrich Weber, this law states that the smallest noticeable change in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.</note></term> to be made quite probable within the stated limits, but by no means proven. It was my intention to further complete or renew the experiments according to these relationships. However, I was interrupted in this and have not found the time since then to return to it.

Regarding the methodology of the experiments, I add the following: The two vessels, in which the water of different temperatures was contained, were large clay pots, in order to slow down temperature changes as much as possible. They were filled with water to such an extent that when the index and middle fingers of the right hand were immersed to the bottom, the water reached exactly the joint between the 1st and 2nd phalanx of the index finger (counting from the <term>palm<note>Original: "Palma," the Latin term for the palm of the hand.</note></term>). In this way, the same amount of contact surface with the water was always established. 

The thermometers, fastened in suitable stands, were immersed with their bulbs into the center of the water, which was well stirred before each observation. The temperature of the water was altered partly by stirring with ice, and partly with metal or clay vessels that stood on the hot stove. The two fingers performing the experiment were first left immersed to the bottom in one of the two vessels until they had reached a constant temperature, then immersed alternately into one and the other vessel until a judgment had been formed. 

If the sensation of temperature was above that which I designated as "just noticeable," the temperature was altered by stirring in the opposite direction, so that I did not know whether the excess temperature had passed to the other vessel or not, and the observation was repeated until—usually only after several repetitions of this modification—a just noticeable difference was found; a procedure which is, admittedly, quite tedious. The temperature was read immediately after the judgment was reached.

Although I have taken only the sensation value "just noticeable" as the decisive standard, I have nevertheless recorded in my observation register the following sensation values, kept as constant as possible, according to the ascending order of their magnitude:

**Imperceptible, barely noticeable, just noticeable, noticeable, distinct, decided, strong, very strong.**

Of course, one cannot count on a sharp separation between these values. The "barely noticeable" values were those where I was not entirely sure I was not deceiving myself; and although this could be verified after the observation, a coincidental agreement was still possible. Therefore, I have used such values only insofar as—when "barely noticeable" closely coincided with "noticeable" or "distinct" on the same or different observation days—I factored in the average of these determinations as "just noticeable," which happened a few times.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion of experimental methodology in psychophysics. While the previous page described his own experiments with water temperature and finger immersion, he now moves on to evaluate the work of other researchers, specifically Lindemann and Volkmann, who used a different statistical method.</meta>

The <term>method of just noticeable differences<note>A procedure where a stimulus is slowly increased or decreased until the subject first perceives a change.</note></term> is added here. Volkmann prompted Mr. Lindemann, a <term>medical student<note>Original: "stud. med.," an abbreviation for "studiosus medicinae."</note></term>, to conduct experiments according to the <term>method of average error<note>Also known as the "method of adjustment," where the subject themselves adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard.</note></term> and to write his <term>doctoral dissertation<note>Original: "Doctordissertation."</note></term> on the subject, which he defended under the title: *On the Sense of Heat. Halle 1857*<note>Original Latin title: "De sensu caloris. Halis 1857."</note>. However, not much can be concluded from these experiments because the temperature scale—ranging respectively from 7° and 14.6° up to 45.55° C—was traversed twice in an ascending order and twice in a descending order, but in such a way that only a few trials were conducted for each temperature interval. This does not permit an application according to the principle of the <term>method of average error</term>. In these trials, the right hand was immersed up to the wrist; in the ascending series, it was always first dipped into the water that was initially warmer, and in the descending series, always first into the water that was initially colder. This was then made to feel equal to the other by adding either colder or warmer water respectively.

In the two ascending series—that is, where Lindemann brought about the equalization of temperatures between both masses of water for the sensation successively at higher and higher temperatures—a positive error was always committed; in the two descending series, conversely, a negative error was always committed. One may ask whether this resulted from the fact that the temperature scale was traversed in opposite directions in the ascending and descending series, or whether in each individual experiment, the transition occurred in opposite directions between the initially warmer and colder water. From the circumstance, however, that the very first trials of each of the four series show the specified relationship, the latter is to be concluded. Furthermore, there is a lack here, as in many respects, of more precise information regarding the circumstances under which the observations were made.

We have results here, then, that are essentially affected by <term>constant errors<note>Systematic errors that consistently skew results in one direction, often due to the experimental setup or the observer's habits.</note></term>. Based on the regularity with which the individual errors in each series change during the ascent or descent through the temperature scale, the entire errors seem to be almost purely constant, since <term>variable errors<note>Random fluctuations in measurement that lack a consistent pattern.</note></term> would necessarily show great irregularities in individual instances. At the same time, the insignificance of these errors is striking.

Between 26.4° and 38.8° C. *) (both inclusive), 23 trials of the first ascending series consistently yielded +0.05 as the error, with the exception of only 5 trials. At higher and lower temperatures, the error grew, though only slightly and somewhat irregularly toward the upper end, such that in the interval from 39.4 to 45.5, errors of only 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8 occur; the growth was more pronounced toward the lower end (+0.5 at 14.6°, where the ascending series began; +0.4 at 16° and 18.2°, etc.). In the second ascending series, from 31.35° to 42.9°, an error of +0.05 was found without exception in 14 ascending trials; this rose higher up to 0.1 at 44.8° and 45.1°, and lower down to +0.25 at 7.9° and 8.4°. In the first descending series, an error of –0.05 was observed from 41.5° to 19.5° in 22 descending trials with the exception of three; it rose to –0.1 at 44.7° and to 0.29 at 7°. In the second descending series, the error of –0.05 was observed without exception in 21 descending trials from 41.65° to 19.35°, and rose to –0.1 at 44.9° and –0.25 at 7.55.

These experiments agree with mine in that, starting from an interval where the errors almost disappear, the errors increase more rapidly or in a greater proportion toward the <term>cold side<note>Original: "Frostseite," literally the frost-side, referring to the colder end of the experimental temperature range.</note></term> than toward the <term>warm side<note>Original: "Wärmeseite."</note></term>. They yield much smaller errors here than the <term>just noticeable differences<note>The smallest change in a physical stimulus that can be detected by the human senses.</note></term> found by me and earlier by **Weber**; however, this is no contradiction, as noted on page 129, since errors must everywhere be smaller on average than the just noticeable differences. This may also partly be due to the fact that I only immersed two segments of two fingers, whereas **Lindemann** immersed the whole hand. A more significant discrepancy lies in the fact that **Lindemann** finds the interval of smallest errors to be around <term>blood heat<note>The internal temperature of the human body, roughly 37°C.</note></term>, whereas in my case, the interval of the smallest noticeable differences lies around a medium temperature. In the meantime, since his errors are evidently constant for the most part, it cannot be judged whether a real contradiction exists here; and new experiments on this subject are certainly necessary in any case. From the experiments conducted thus far, it is already clear that the smallness of the differences that can still be recognized, as well as the errors committed on average, poses great difficulties for precise measurement.

### 5) Extensive Magnitudes.

->(Visual estimation and tactile measurement.)<-

<margin>*) Vierordt's Archive XI. p. 844. 853.</margin>
Aside from the general statement by Weber (p. 137), F. Hegelmayer*), a medical student in Tübingen, has provided an approximate confirmation of <term>Weber's Law<note>The fundamental psychophysical principle stating that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus.</note></term> for visual estimation using the method of right and wrong cases. However, these leave too much to be desired to be considered very authoritative, both regarding the far too small number of trials and the lack of comparability between several trials from which averages were drawn. Essentially, the experiments consisted of comparing lines of a given length—some horizontal, some vertical—with other previously seen lines that differed by certain larger or smaller fractions. This was done while varying the time interval, as investigating the influence of time was the observer's primary intention. He counted how often the estimate of whether a line was larger or smaller was correct, incorrect, or remained <term>in suspenso<note>original: "in suspenso" (Latin); meaning "in suspense" or "undecided."</note></term>. As far as his observations allow one to conclude, the ratio of right and wrong cases appeared not to depend significantly on the absolute size, but only on the relative size of the fractions—a result that Hegelmayer himself draws. Nevertheless, the results are generally very irregular, and I will therefore skip a more specific report of them.

My own and Volkmann's experiments according to the <term>method of average errors<note>A psychophysical method where the subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard; the "average error" is the mean difference between the setting and the standard.</note></term>, in which distances between small points—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of experiments on the visual estimation of space, specifically comparing results from different researchers to test the validity of Weber's Law at various scales.</meta>

...or parallel threads were observed, provide a very decisive confirmation of the law for all significantly large distances—that is, from 10 to 240 millimeters at a viewing distance <note>The distance between the subject's eyes and the object being measured.</note> of 1 foot to 800 millimeters—in that the <term>pure sums of errors<note>In Fechner's statistics, this refers to the sum of the absolute differences between individual observations and their average, after systematic biases have been removed.</note></term> or mean errors obtained here are as exactly proportional to the distances as one could ever expect. In contrast, Volkmann's experiments, as well as those he commissioned from Appel (a student with particularly sharp eyes) using micrometric distances of 0.2 to 3.6 mm at viewing distances around the usual range, do not find this proportionality. However, the pure sums of errors or mean errors obtained (after separating out the constant error) can be broken down into two components: one, which I call the <term>Volkmann Constant<note>Named after Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist and friend of Fechner. This constant represents a fixed baseline of sensory noise or error that does not change with the size of the stimulus.</note></term>\*), remains constant across the various standard distances; the other, which I call the <term>Weber Variable<note>The portion of the error that increases in direct proportion to the stimulus size, adhering to Weber's Law.</note></term>, is proportional to the distances in accordance with Weber's Law. Likely, the former is also at play in experiments with larger distances, but it is so small that it noticeably vanishes compared to the latter component (which is proportional to the distance) and is lost in the uncertainty of its measurement; meanwhile, at very small distances, it constitutes the greater part of the variable sum of errors. For the very smallest distances of 0.2 and 0.3 millimeters, the error for Volkmann's eye also appeared to be abnormally increased by <term>irradiation<note>A visual effect where light spreads from a bright area into a dark one on the retina, making bright objects appear larger or blurred at the edges.</note></term>.

We see, therefore, that here too we are dealing with a lower limit of the law for experimentation; and likely very large distances would also reveal an upper limit.

The main results are contained in the following. They all refer to the pure variable error Δ <note>The Greek letter Delta, used here to represent the difference or error in measurement.</note> in the sense previously indicated (p. 121), and provide everywhere the pure sum of errors ΣΔ, and mostly also (where I have determined them) the pure sum of squared errors Σ(Δ²), derived for each distance specifically from—

\*) This should not be confused with a "constant error" in the sense described on page 121; rather, it arises from variable errors just as much as the other component. $\mu$ represents the number of subsets (fractions) created from each time period, consisting of $m$ observations each\*), so that the total number of errors contributing to each <term>partial sum<note>A sub-total of errors calculated for a specific group of observations.</note></term> is $\mu m$. The values for $\mu$ and $m$ are specified individually for each series of observations. For the horizontal sum columns, a value of $2\mu$ applies, provided that the sums therein are always combined from two partial sums—specifically for Left (L.) and Right (R.), or Top (T.) and Bottom (B.) <note>original: "O. und U." for *Oben* (Top) and *Unten* (Bottom)</note>. Specifically, an equal number of observations were always made with the <term>standard distance<note>The fixed reference length the observer is trying to match or judge.</note></term> in the left and right positions (L. and R.) when the distances were horizontal, or in the top and bottom positions (T. and B.) when they were vertical, for which the results are specified.

Only the micrometric series V was conducted with vertical distances (that is, between horizontal threads); all others were conducted with horizontal distances (that is, between vertical threads, where threads were used).

The proportionality with the distances can be proven directly from the simple sums of errors $\Sigma \Delta$, without first having to derive the <term>mean error<note>The average magnitude of error, calculated as the sum of absolute errors divided by the number of observations.</note></term> $\varepsilon = \frac{\Sigma \Delta}{\mu m}$ from them. If one wishes, the sums of the squares of the errors can serve to derive the <term>quadratic mean error<note>Also known as the root mean square error, a standard statistical measure of the dispersion of values.</note></term> $\varepsilon_q = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(\Delta^2)}{\mu m}}$, which allows one to verify the constancy and the existence of the <term>normal ratio<note>This ratio ($\approx 1.25$) indicates whether the errors follow a "Normal" or Gaussian distribution, which is a cornerstone of classical error theory.</note></term>

->$\frac{\varepsilon_q}{\varepsilon} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}$<-

## Series I. Fechner (Dec. 9, 1856 to Jan. 17, 1857).

5 horizontal distances, determined by the slightly protruding tips (sewing needles) of two otherwise covered <term>compasses<note>In this context, dividers used for measuring distances rather than drawing circles.</note></term> lying side by side on the table before me, and viewed from the clearest viewing distance of approximately 1 <term>Parisian foot<note>A historical unit of length; 1 Parisian foot is approximately 32.5 centimeters or 12.8 inches.</note></term>. The compasses were covered to exclude the influence of the angle on the estimation. However, it seems this defect exerted a significant influence more on the constant errors than on the pure <term>variable error<note>The random fluctuations in measurement that occur by chance; Fechner is looking for the "pure" psychological threshold of perception.</note></term>, which, as the following table shows, remained very precisely proportional to the distances.

At the distance $D = 10$, which according to the above amounted to 10 half Parisian decimal lines ($= 3.6$ duodecimal lines), a pure sum of errors $\Sigma \Delta = 20.27$ was obtained when the <term>standard distance<note>The fixed reference length the observer is trying to match or judge.</note></term> was positioned on the left (L.); that is, if one adds together the absolute values of all the positive and negative pure errors (which are equal in total sum) obtained for (L.) at $D = 10$, the sum of 20.27 half Parisian decimal lines is produced. To obtain the **average error** committed for a unit of distance during an observation—or the fraction of the distance that the error forms on average in one observation—one can divide the mean of the previous values for each series by the number of observations that contributed to a value. For this, one must double the product of *m* and $\mu$ from the observation tables, since $\mu$ applies there specifically to L. <note>Left</note> and R. <note>Right</note> separately, while here both are combined. Since, however, the larger error sums at greater distances promise more accurate values than at smaller ones, one will proceed more precisely \*) if one adds all the error sums—an addition that is already performed in the vertical final sum columns—divides their sum by the sum of all distances (thereby obtaining the error sum for the unit of distance), and divides this by 2 $\mu m$. Thus one obtains:

-> 576.28 / (150 . 240) = 0.016008 = 1 / 62.5 <-

-> 942.9 / (870 . 96) = 0.011287 = 1 / 88.6 <-

-> 902.69 / (870 . 96) = 0.010808 = 1 / 92.5 <-

-> 781.5 / (840 . 96) = 0.0096913 = 1 / 103.1 <-

According to this, I myself estimate a distance incorrectly by approximately 1/60 on average; Volkmann in his earlier experiments (II) by approximately 1/90, and in his later ones (III) by approximately 1/100; and this ratio remains the same for the most varied distances. If one wishes, one can derive the **probable error** from this average error through simple multiplication by 0.845347—that is, the error which is exceeded just as often as it is not reached. This is smaller than the average error because small errors are made more frequently than large ones, but it maintains the stated standard ratio to it, regarding which more details can be found in my <term>Methods of Measurement<note>original: "Massmethoden"; likely referring to Fechner’s seminal work "Elemente der Psychophysik" (1860) or related papers where he established the mathematical foundations of psychophysics.</note></term>.

...Volkmann <note>Referring to the physiologist Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann</note> was considerably greater than mine. This may have been because the distances between three parallel threads might be easier to compare than those between the tips of two compasses placed side by side; or it may be due to a truly greater sharpness of <term>visual judgment</term> <note>original: *Augenmass*; the innate ability to judge distances or sizes by sight</note> compared to mine, which indeed seems to be the case; or perhaps both together. Deciding this would have required further comparative experiments.

Undoubtedly, a more extensive investigation into the extremes and average values of sharpness for a larger number of individuals and for various observation circumstances would be of significant interest. This would include whether one shifts the side thread (as was done in Volkmann's experiments) or the middle thread; whether one uses only one or both eyes; and whether one subjects vertical, horizontal, or angular distances between points, between lines, or circular and square perimeters and surfaces of various sizes to the test. In all such cases, the magnitude and nature of <term>constant errors</term> <note>Systematic errors that consistently skew results in one direction rather than being random</note> must be carefully taken into account. Here, however, the goal was merely to pursue the subject in relation to the law that currently occupies us <note>Referring to Weber's Law, which relates the size of a stimulus to the perceived intensity</note>.

If Volkmann's second series of observations yielded a significantly smaller <term>average error</term>, and thus greater precision than the first, the difference can be attributed to the effect of practice; for between the first and second series, many series of visual judgment experiments took place—including all the micrometric <note>Extremely small-scale measurements</note> ones to be cited hereafter—even though such progress did not show itself in the fractional treatment of the first series alone, as the separate examination of those sections reveals.

Perhaps it may be found of interest that Volkmann's average error for the **extensive side** of visual sensation <note>The "extensive" side refers to spatial perception, such as length or volume</note> matches noticeably with his **just noticeable difference** for the **intensive side** <note>The "intensive" side refers to the strength of a sensation, such as brightness or weight</note>; however, one cannot see anything universally valid in such a correspondence.

<meta>This page transitions from the experimental data of the previous series to a theoretical explanation of the mathematical formulas used to calculate visual errors. It introduces the "Weberian variable" to explain why errors are not simply added together but must be calculated using the sum of their squares.</meta>

...should be designated, while the other is proportional to the distances. This latter component shall be designated as $W$, the <term>Weberian variable</term> <note>The "Weber'sche Variable," named after Ernst Heinrich Weber, refers to the constant ratio between a stimulus and the "just noticeable difference" a person can perceive.</note> for the unit of distance. Consequently, $W$ must be multiplied by the distance $D$ to provide the value $WD$, which is proportional to that distance for every distance measured.

The composition of the <term>pure sum of errors</term> <note>original: *reine Fehlersumme*; the total of all deviations from the correct measurement.</note> $\Sigma \Delta$ for any given distance from both components $V$ <note>Likely representing a constant "variable" or base error inherent to the observer.</note> and $WD$ is, however, according to the theory of how the effects of sources of error combine, not to be represented by a simple addition of both components; that is, one cannot simply state:

->$\Sigma \Delta = V + WD$<-

But rather, the sum of the squares of both components is to be set equal to the square of $\Sigma \Delta$, so that one has:

->$(\Sigma \Delta)^2 = V^2 + (WD)^2$<-

consequently:

->$\Sigma \Delta = \sqrt{V^2 + W^2 D^2}$.<-

Since the square of a sum of errors—that is, $(\Sigma \Delta)^2$—has an *a priori* <note>Latin: "from the beginning" or "beforehand." In this context, it refers to a relationship that can be determined through mathematical theory rather than just observation.</note> determinable relationship to the <term>sum of the squared errors</term> <note>original: *Summe der Fehlerquadrate*; a statistical method used to give more weight to larger errors.</note> $\Sigma (\Delta^2)$ according to the <term>theory of errors</term> <note>original: *Fehlertheorie*; the branch of mathematics dealing with the distribution and impact of measurement mistakes.</note>, one can substitute the sums of squared errors for the squares of the sums of errors in the previous equations. The physiological interest, which I shall address below, likely relates more to the former form, which I have therefore used as the basis for what follows.

Indeed, it can easily be demonstrated theoretically and confirmed through experience that if two independent sources of error are given—one of which would produce a sum of errors $A$ on its own, and the other a sum of errors $B$—their combination cannot result in a sum of errors $A + B$. Instead, it results in a smaller sum of errors, because on average, errors of opposite signs (positive and negative) meet just as often as errors of the same sign from both sources. Only the latter produce a <term>resulting error</term> <note>original: *resultirender Fehler*</note> equal to their sum, while the former produce an error equal to their difference. The theory of errors shows, however, that the sum of the squared errors of the components is normally (that is, strictly speaking, for an infinite number of errors obtained under comparable circumstances) equal to the sum of the resulting squared errors. Similarly, the sum of the squares of the simple sums of errors is normally equal to the square of the resulting sum of errors. A confirmation of this theoretical result through experience can...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mathematical relationship between different sources of error in visual perception. One can easily find this if one composes the errors of two independent <term>error series</term> <note>original: *Fehlerreihen*; sequences of data points representing the deviation of observations from a true value.</note>—obtained in whatever manner—as components through <term>algebraic addition</term> <note>original: *algebraische Addition*; a method of adding numbers that takes their positive or negative signs into account.</note> into resulting errors; in doing so, one obtains an equivalent for the coincidence of the outcome of independent sources of error. Indeed, I have convinced myself of the confirmation of the theoretical result regarding both the <term>sum of squared errors</term> <note>original: *Fehlerquadratsumme*; the sum of each individual error raised to the second power, used to measure total variance.</note> as well as the <term>square of the sum of errors</term> <note>original: *Quadrat der Fehlersumme*; the total sum of errors, which is then squared.</note> through multiple tests, and I will provide the evidence for this elsewhere.

Insofar as there should exist for the eye one source of error independent of the distances and one source dependent on the distances in the sense stated, the preceding logic must also apply to the components dependent thereon, and the above equations will thereby be justified. However, whether the assumption of such sources of error is valid will have to be determined from the observations themselves, provided that, in the case of validity, such values *V* and *W* must be calculable from them such that the observed values can be represented again backwards by the above formulas.

For such a calculation of *V* and *W*, observations at two different distances are sufficient in themselves. If we take the <term>sums of errors</term> <note>original: *Fehlersummen*; the total amount of error recorded across all trials.</note> in Series IV for *D* = 800 and *D* = 1400—which are 1541.5 and 2275.7 respectively—by combining the left (*L.*) and right (*R.*) sides, we must set it up as follows:

-> *$V^2 + 800^2 W^2 = 1541.5^2$* <-
-> *$V^2 + 1400^2 W^2 = 2275.7^2$* <-

From this, *$V^2$* and *$W^2$* are easily found as two unknowns determined by two equations, after which an <term>extraction of the root</term> <note>original: *Wurzelausziehung*; the mathematical process of finding the square root of a number.</note> yields *V* and *W* themselves.

Insofar as trials at more than two distances are available for the determination, one can calculate *V* and *W* from several such combinations; in that case, the <term>admissibility</term> <note>original: *Statthaftigkeit*; the logical or mathematical validity of a premise.</note> of the assumption must also be justified, even before calculating backwards to find the sums of errors according to *V* and *W*. This is done by ensuring that the values of *V* and *W* obtained from the different combinations match closely enough to attribute any remaining deviations to uncompensated accidental occurrences in observation. By <term>taking the average</term> <note>original: *Mittelziehung*; calculating the mean value from multiple results to improve accuracy.</note> from several...

...the number of observations <note>German: *Fehlerzahl*. In this context, it refers to the total count of trials or observations used to calculate the average error.</note> for each distance, which is given by the product *um* <note>Likely variables representing the number of series and observations per series from a previous table.</note> in that same table, the values of the various series must be divided by their respective number of observations—120, 192, 192, and 132—in order to make them comparable with one another. Furthermore, it must be taken into account that since a different *m* <note>The number of observations per distance.</note> was used during the observations, a correction must be applied by multiplying by <gloss>$\frac{3m+1}{3m}$</gloss> due to the finiteness of *m*; this correction, however, is very slight. Finally, it must be considered that the viewing distance from which the distances were perceived was not the same everywhere. While this can have no influence on the value *W*—provided that distances appearing smaller at a greater range still yield the same proportional error *W*—it must certainly affect the error *V*. This *V* is an absolute error magnitude that remains the same for all distances; therefore, to make results obtained from different viewing distances comparable, they must be reduced to the same viewing distance according to the reciprocal ratio of the actual viewing distance used. In doing so, however, 7 mm must be added to every eye-distance measured from the cornea, as this is the distance from the cornea to the intersection point of the lines of sight <note>The nodal point of the eye, where light rays cross before hitting the retina.</note>. For example, for the viewing distance of 333 mm in Series IV, 340 mm must be used for the reduction, and so on.

To conclude the previous discussion on Volkmann’s constant, mention should be made of the calculation used to reduce the magnitude observed in the experiments to the value it represents on the retina itself. According to the table on page 228, Volkmann’s constant—at a visual distance of 340 millimeters, calculated relative to the intersection point of the lines of direction—amounted to 8.210, which is 0.008210 millimeters, given that the unit in which all results of the micrometric <term>micrometric: referring to measurements on a microscopic scale, often millionths of a meter</term> experiments are expressed is 0.001 millimeters. If one now assumes the distance from the intersection point of the lines of direction <term>intersection point of the lines of direction: the "nodal point" where light rays cross as they enter the eye</term> to the retina to be 15 millimeters in round numbers, then the magnitude that *V* represents on the retina relates to the observed *V* as 15 : 340. That is, the constant *V* in the specified series represents a magnitude on the retina equal to 0.0003621 millimeters. This is based on the assumption that the linear size occupied by the image of a perceived distance on the retina is determined by the span on the retina captured between the rays drawn from the boundaries of the external distance through the intersection point of the lines of direction. This is the standard calculation.

It is questionable, however—a remark I owe to E. H. Weber <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878): a German physician considered one of the founders of experimental psychology</note>—whether the intersection point of the lines of direction is the determining factor here. In general, we measure distances with the help of eye movement, by guiding the axis of the eye from one boundary point to another. Accordingly, the center of rotation of the eye <term>center of rotation: the fixed point around which the eyeball turns in its socket</term>, rather than the nodal point, should perhaps be assumed as the point through which the rays from the boundaries of the external distance must be drawn to determine the distance that its image occupies on the retina. This point, however, lies\*) 5.6 lines = 14.224 millimeters behind the foremost point of the cornea, which would be 7.778 millimeters in front of the retina. One might consider whether Volkmann’s constant depends on an error made while estimating the divisions of the scale, which naturally would not depend on the magnitude of the observed distance, and would therefore produce a mean error that remains constant across all distances. However, our *V* is much too large for this; while the direct reading on the micrometer screw gave 0.01 or 10 thousandths of a millimeter, *V* amounted on average to approximately 8 thousandths of a millimeter. One cannot err by nearly that much through mere estimation. Indisputably, however, Volkmann’s constant has received a small increase from this source.

Should it truly have a fixed organic basis in the eye, we would see here, in the realm of extensive light sensation <note>extensive light sensation: the perception of the spatial extent or size of a light source, rather than its brightness</note>, a remarkable analogy to what we found in the realm of intensive sensation <note>intensive sensation: the perception of the strength or brightness of a stimulus</note>. In both cases, Weber’s Law <term>Weber’s Law: a psychological principle stating that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be perceived is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus</term> is only confirmed if we take into account a constant magnitude added to the external, variable influence due to internal organic reasons.

### 6) *Physical and Moral Wealth* <note>original French: "Fortune physique et morale"</note>.

We can trace *Weber’s Law* even further into a more general domain. The physical goods we possess (*physical wealth*) have no intrinsic value or meaning to us as mere inanimate matter. They only matter as external means to produce a sum of valuable feelings within us—our *moral wealth* <note>the term "moral" here refers to mental or psychological state, specifically subjective happiness or utility</note>. In this context, physical goods take the place of a sensory stimulus. Consider a thaler <term>thaler: a large silver coin used throughout Europe for centuries; a standard unit of currency in Fechner's time</term>. In this sense, it holds far less value for a rich person than for a poor one. While a single coin might make a beggar happy for an entire day, the same amount added to the fortune of a millionaire would not be noticed by him at all. This phenomenon can be understood through *Weber’s Law*. To achieve an equal increase in what *Laplace* <note>Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827), a French mathematician who explored the idea that the subjective value of money decreases as one's wealth increases</note> calls moral...

## X. The Fact of the Threshold.

In general, a sensation or a difference in sensation grows with the magnitude of the stimulus or stimulus difference that causes it. At first glance, it seems natural to assume that the point where the sensation—or the difference in sensation—begins to become noticeable coincides with the zero point of the stimulus or stimulus difference. But the facts contradict this assumption; rather, it appears that every stimulus, as well as every stimulus difference, must already have reached a certain finite size before its noticeability even begins—that is, before it produces a sensation that noticeably affects our consciousness or establishes a noticeable difference in sensation. Conversely, the noticeability of the stimulus or stimulus difference vanishes even before it has dropped to a zero value. The zero point of the sensation, or of the sensation difference, lies in this respect above that of the causing stimulus or stimulus difference—a fact that will be demonstrated more closely in what follows.

The point where the noticeability <term>noticeability: the "merklichkeit," or the point at which a stimulus is strong enough to be consciously perceived</term> of a stimulus or a stimulus difference begins and vanishes, we wish to call, for short, the **threshold** <term>threshold: (German: "Schwelle") the boundary between being unaware of a stimulus and consciously perceiving it</term>. This expression applies equally to the sensation and the sensation difference at the limits of noticeability, as well as to the stimulus or stimulus difference, or the stimulus ratio, which the sensation or sensation difference...

### 1) The Intensive Threshold.
#### a) Stimulus Threshold.

In the field of intensive <term>light sensation</term> <note>Lichtempfindung: The subjective experience of seeing light, as opposed to the objective physical light itself.</note>, it is not possible to provide direct proof that a certain strength of light stimulus is first required to awaken sensation—that is, that a <term>stimulus threshold</term> <note>Reizschwelle: The minimum level of physical energy required for a person to detect a stimulus.</note> for light sensation exists at a specific finite value of the light stimulus. This is because the eye, as has been discussed multiple times, is always above the threshold due to an internal excitation <note>Fechner refers here to the "intrinsic light" of the eye; even in total darkness, the nervous system provides a baseline level of activity so that we never experience "absolute" zero sensation.</note>, to which every external light stimulus merely provides an addition. Consequently, the facts which teach us that this addition requires a certain strength to be noticed belong instead to the section on the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>Unterschiedsschwelle: The smallest change or difference in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note>.

Regarding the modification that we call color, however, one can establish the following conditions for visibility: 1) that the refractivity, and thus the oscillation frequency, exceeds a certain limit; 2) that the intensity or amplitude of the oscillations exceeds a certain limit; 3) that the color acts across a sufficient extent, which must be larger the further toward the peripheral parts of the retina the color falls; 4) that it is not mixed with too much white.

As for the first condition, it is well known that beyond the red boundary of the <term>spectrum</term> <note>spectrum: the range of colors produced when light is dispersed, as by a prism.</note>, no more colors are seen or can be made visible in any way; nevertheless, heat phenomena prove the existence of rays beyond this boundary. Now, the red rays have the slowest oscillations, and the inability to perceive <term>infrared rays</term> <note>original: "ultrarothe Stralen"</note> seems to be attributable to nothing other than the fact that their oscillations are too slow. On the other hand, the so-called <term>ultraviolet rays</term>, which cannot be made visible using ordinary prisms under ordinary measures and whose existence was previously inferred only from their chemical effects, have recently been made visible through appropriate measures; to achieve this, it is only necessary to bring them to perception with sufficient strength, which simultaneously provides evidence for the second condition.

In fact, the ultraviolet part of the prismatic spectrum, when using <term>rock crystal prisms</term> <note>Bergkrystallprismen: Prisms made of clear quartz, which, unlike glass, allow ultraviolet light to pass through.</note>, which...

One does not hear a single caterpillar eating in the forest, but when there is a general infestation of caterpillars in the forest, one hears it quite clearly; yet the noise made by many caterpillars is only the sum of the noises of the individual caterpillars. At all times of the day, a certain noise fills the air, but if it does not exceed a certain strength, we believe we hear nothing.

A single <term>galvanic plate pair</term> <note>original: "galvanisches Plattenpaar"; the basic unit of an early battery or "Voltaic pile," consisting of two different metal plates.</note> produces no noticeable sensation, while a column consisting of individual plate pairs produces a shock.

Any pressure on our body merely needs to be sufficiently distributed to become unnoticeable, without it being the case that it is nothing at all.

However, the existence of the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>original: "Unterschiedsschwelle"; the point at which a difference between two stimuli becomes detectable to the senses.</note> cannot be established more beautifully, simply, or strikingly than in the realm of <term>light sensation</term> <note>original: "Lichtempfindung".</note> through the <term>shadow experiment</term> <note>original: "Schattenversuch".</note>, which we cited to prove <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>The law stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>. One places two lamps next to each other and a shadow-casting object in front of them. Each of the two lamps produces a shadow that is illuminated only by the other lamp, while the surrounding background is illuminated by both lamps. Now, if one turns the wick of one lamp lower and lower, or moves it further and further from the shadow-casting object, one sees the shadow it casts become weaker and weaker, as the illumination of the surrounding space differs less and less from it, until finally this shadow disappears—absorbed, as it were, by the general illumination of the background—even though both light sources are still present. I was quite astonished when I first became aware of seeing two lights cast only one shadow. Both lamps are clearly burning, yet only one shadow is there. In a word: when the difference between the illumination of one shadow and the surrounding space falls below a certain limit, the difference disappears totally for the sensation and can no longer be perceived at all.

This experiment is particularly striking because one has the <term>components</term> <note>original: "Componenten"; referring here to the two different light sources/intensities.</note> in view at the same time, and can fix the eye sharply, calmly, and steadily on their <term>boundary line</term> <note>original: "Gränzlinie".</note> while causing their difference to disappear. Thus, there can be no talk of forgetting a previous impression or overlooking the difference—factors one might be inclined to blame for the imperceptibility or disappearance of a difference in other experimental methods.

The experiment allows for many variations. Generally: if one of the shadows is just noticeable, one only needs to turn its lamp slightly lower or the other slightly higher, and it becomes unnoticeable; and if it is unnoticeable, one only needs to turn its lamp as high as necessary, or the other correspondingly

Just as universal as the fact of the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>original: "Unterschiedsschwelle"; the minimum required change in a stimulus for a person to detect that a change has occurred.</note> is the fact of its increase alongside the magnitude of the stimuli. However, even if both factually amount to the same thing, from a formal point of view, it can sometimes be more convenient or appropriate to adhere to one mode of expression rather than the other.

Accordingly, in the future, we shall generally designate the absolute stimulus difference as the **absolute difference threshold**, coinciding with the **just noticeable difference**; the relative stimulus difference as the **relative difference threshold** or **difference constant**; and the ratio of stimuli at which a difference in sensation reaches the threshold as the **ratio threshold** or **ratio constant**, using the letters $\alpha, \omega, v$ respectively. Thus, based on the experiments of **Volkmann** <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist and colleague of Fechner who performed extensive tests on vision and touch.</note>, the difference constant $\omega$ for <term>light intensity</term> is $\frac{1}{100}$, and the ratio constant $v = \frac{101}{100}$.

### 2) Extensive Threshold.

When a white circle on a black background (or vice versa) is too small or viewed from too great a distance, it is no longer recognized. When two points or parallel threads are too close to one another or viewed from too great a distance, they blur together for the eye and the distance between them becomes imperceptible. The boundary where the former occurs can be designated as the **threshold of recognizable size**, and where the latter occurs, the **threshold of recognizable distance**.

On the skin, as is well known, two compass points placed too close together blur into a single common impression; thus, here too, there exists a threshold of recognizable distance. <note>This refers to the famous "two-point discrimination" test developed by Ernst Heinrich Weber.</note>

No less do two impressions blur into an indistinguishable impression if they occur too rapidly after one another. There is, therefore, also an <term>extensive threshold</term> <note>original: "extensive Schwelle"; while "intensive" refers to the strength of a sensation, "extensive" refers to its spread across space or time.</note> in relation to **temporal distance**.

When an object, such as the hour hand of a clock or a star in the sky, moves too slowly, the movement is not recognized; with sufficient acceleration, it is recognized. There is, therefore, also a **threshold of recognizable speed**.

Here, time and space are considered simultaneously. It is probable that speed begins to become recognizable at the point where the **temporal threshold** coincides with the **spatial threshold**; that is, when—within the shortest duration of time that does not blur into a single moment for the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "Seele"; in 19th-century psychophysics, this refers to the internal mind or the seat of conscious perception.</note>—a space is traversed that does not blur into a single point for the eye.

### 3) General Considerations regarding the Threshold.

The existence of a <term>threshold</term> <note>original: "Schwelle"; the boundary point at which a stimulus is just strong enough to be perceived.</note> presents an inherent paradox from the very outset. A stimulus or <term>stimulus difference</term> <note>original: "Reizunterschied".</note> can be increased up to certain limits without being perceived; only from a certain boundary onward is it felt, and its growth perceived. How can that which produces no effect in consciousness when it is weak, begin to produce something through reinforcement? It seems as if the summation of zero-effects could produce a positive effect. However, while this relationship may pose a difficulty for a metaphysician, it presents no difficulty from a mathematical perspective; this suggests that the mathematical viewpoint—according to which the magnitude of <term>sensation</term> <note>original: "Empfindung".</note> can be regarded as a <term>function</term> of the magnitude of the stimulus (or rather, of the internal movements triggered by it)—is also the correct metaphysical one. Indeed, if *y* is a function of *x*, *y* can vanish at certain values of *x*, or pass into negative or <term>imaginary</term> <note>In mathematics, "imaginary" refers to numbers involving the square root of a negative value; Fechner uses this to illustrate states that exist theoretically but not as observable sensations.</note> values, while it is sufficient to increase *x* beyond this value to see *y* regain positive values.

The following fact is naturally connected to the existence of the threshold. The further the magnitude of the stimulus or stimulus difference sinks below the threshold, the less that stimulus or stimulus difference can be felt, and the greater the subsequent increases required before a sensation of it occurs. So long as the stimulus or stimulus difference remains below the threshold, the sensation of it remains, as they say, <term>unconscious</term> <note>original: "unbewusst".</note>; this unconsciousness deepens more and more in proportion to how far the magnitude of the stimulus or stimulus difference falls below the threshold. Thus, distant sounds or the scent stimuli in the atmosphere remain below the threshold, and consequently the sensation awakened by them remains in the unconscious, until the intensity of those stimuli exceeds a certain magnitude—the <term>threshold value</term> <note>original: "Schwellenwerth".</note>. It naturally suggests itself here that if we take the threshold value of sensation as the zero-point and conscious sensation values as positive values, we may represent unconscious sensations as negative values. However, we will only go into this conception more precisely in the future.

Connected to the imperceptibility of small differences is...

<summary>Fechner explores the "paradox" of the threshold, arguing that mathematics resolves the problem of how "zero" sensation can become "something" by treating sensation as a function of stimulus. He introduces the influential idea that unconscious states can be mathematically represented as negative values below the threshold.</summary>

...even a subtle and not unimportant question for the measurement procedure of <term>sensitivity</term> <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"; in this context, it refers to the physiological or psychological capacity to detect small differences in stimuli.</note> according to the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>original: "Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle"; a foundational psychophysical experiment where a subject compares two stimuli and must decide which is greater. Even if they feel they are guessing, the frequency of correct answers is analyzed statistically.</note>.

Suppose the difference between the weights—or more generally, the <term>stimuli</term> <note>original: "Reize".</note>—included in the experiment is so small that it falls below that boundary where it can be consciously recognized; the question then arises whether it can exert any influence at all on the number of right and wrong cases. Would the ratio of the two not be exactly the same as if no difference were present at all, until the difference has exceeded the boundary where it becomes noticeable as such? And should the influence, from that point onward, be judged not by the absolute magnitude of the difference, but by the difference between it and the value where it actually begins to become noticeable?

This seems self-evident at first, for how can a difference that does not affect our consciousness determine our judgment? Nevertheless, one cannot accept this without simultaneously declaring the principles of the measurement procedure in question—as well as the principles by which one calculates the <term>probability of errors</term> <note>original: "Wahrscheinlichkeit der Fehler"; Fechner is referring to the mathematical laws of error (like the Bell Curve) which assume that even tiny factors contribute to a final outcome.</note> relative to their magnitude, upon which that measurement procedure is entirely based—to be invalid. Furthermore, a more detailed consideration leads to a result entirely opposite to what seems self-evident. Despite the fact that a difference is imperceptible on its own, given a sufficient number of comparisons, it will still manifest as a preponderance of right cases in favor of the heavier weight, or more generally, the larger stimulus.

It must be taken into account that, simultaneously with the difference to be grasped, accidental influences are at work; with equal weights, these would determine the judgment in favor of one or the other just as often on average. However, the difference now adds itself to those influences that determine the judgment in favor of one side. It partly causes such influences, which would otherwise have been imperceptible, to become noticeable in favor of this side, and partly strengthens the already noticeable influences on this side, making it easier for them to outweigh the opposing influences. This does not prevent the influence of the extra weight, together with the disturbances currently present, from being un-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "method of right and wrong cases" in psychophysics. ...remains below the noticeable, in which case the judgment remains ambiguous—cases that occur very often in this type of experiment, but can fundamentally be reduced to the other cases by counting them half as correct and half as incorrect cases. <note>In psychophysical experiments, when a participant cannot tell the difference between two stimuli, they are often instructed to guess. Fechner argues that these "undecided" cases should be split equally between the "right" and "wrong" categories for statistical analysis.</note>

In this way, one understands how a difference that is in itself unnoticeable can indeed produce noticeable effects by summing itself with other influences; and the probability—that is, the proportional number of correct and incorrect cases in a very large number of trials—depends on the magnitude of the difference in a manner that allows one to derive a measure of <term>sensitivity</term> <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"; here referring to the capacity to detect small differences.</note> from it, as shown earlier.

The <term>threshold value</term> <note>original: "Schwellenwerth"; the point at which a stimulus or a difference between stimuli becomes detectable.</note> of both the <term>stimuli</term> <note>original: "Reize".</note> and the differences in stimuli is capable of the greatest and most diverse variations due to conditions of fatigue, habituation, practice, internal causes of excitement or paralysis, medications, the periodicity of life, individual constitution, and so on; it is therefore to be regarded as constant only insofar as these conditions produce no change in it. The investigation of these dependency relationships belongs to the most important tasks of <term>psychophysics</term> <note>The scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.</note> and coincides with the general investigation of the dependency relationships of absolute and differential sensitivity—or <term>irritability</term> and <term>excitability</term> <note>original: "Reizbarkeit und Erregbarkeit".</note>—since absolute sensitivity is the <term>reciprocal</term> <note>In mathematical terms, sensitivity = 1 / threshold. As the threshold (the amount of stimulus needed to feel something) goes up, sensitivity goes down.</note> of the <term>stimulus threshold</term>, and differential sensitivity is the reciprocal of the <term>difference threshold</term>.

Should the fact of the <term>threshold</term> <note>original: "Schwelle".</note> be transferable from the stimulus to the <term>psychophysical movement</term> <note>The internal physical or neural activity triggered by an external stimulus.</note> triggered by it—which will be attempted to be proven later—then, according to our general assumption that a firm relationship exists between bodily and psychological changes within us, the threshold value of the psychophysical activity corresponding to the onset of a certain sensation must also be regarded as unchangeable, so that the sensation certainly begins when the activity to which it is tied has reached the threshold height. However, since a stimulus may find it easier or harder to trigger the psychophysical activity at this intensity depending on the changing state of the organism, the threshold value of the stimulus, which is tied to this point...

### 4) **Consequences of the existence of the threshold.**

Many interesting and important consequences follow from the existence of a <term>stimulus threshold</term> and a <term>difference threshold</term>.

If every tiny amount of stimulus were detected, we would be forced to feel an infinite mixture and an unending change of faint sensations of all kinds, since minimal stimuli of every sort are constantly playing around us; this, however, is not the case. The fact that every stimulus must first exceed a certain limit before it awakens sensation ensures that humans remain in a state undisturbed by external stimuli up to certain limits. One does not need to reduce stimuli to zero—which one is not capable of doing—in order to remain undisturbed by them; rather, one simply needs to withdraw to a sufficient distance from those weakened by distance, or more generally, reduce them below a certain limit.

Just as the way every stimulus becomes unnoticeable when falling below a certain limit ensures a state undisturbed by extraneous <term>perceptions</term> <note>original: "Perceptionen"; here referring to the conscious awareness of sensory input.</note>, the way every difference in stimuli becomes unnoticeable when falling below a certain limit ensures a uniform state of perception.

Due to internal and external causes, stimuli will never act with perfect uniformity through time and space; yet this does not prevent us from seeing uniformly bright and colored surfaces, hearing uniformly sustained tones, and so on.

The well-known <term>experiment of the rotating disk</term> <note>This refers to a color wheel or Maxwell disk. When spun rapidly, the eye cannot distinguish the individual black and white segments, and they "fuse" into a solid gray.</note> with white and black sectors provides a simple proof of this. When rotated sufficiently fast, it appears uniformly gray. Now, the intensity of the impression at both edges of a sector 

<summary>Fechner explains that the sensory threshold acts as a vital filter, protecting consciousness from being overwhelmed by a constant "infinite mixture" of tiny environmental stimuli and allowing us to perceive the world as stable and uniform.</summary>

...cannot actually be of equal size, because as a black sector passes, the impression is progressively lost, and as a white one passes, it is regained. However, as soon as the difference at both edges becomes smaller than the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The minimum amount of change in a stimulus required for a person to detect that a change has occurred.</note>, the phenomenon of uniform gray occurs. Indeed, this uniformity appears perfect with sufficiently rapid rotation, so that even with the sharpest attention, it is impossible to discover any alternation.

A similar case occurs when one holds a finger to the edge of a rapidly spinning gear wheel (spur gear). While one can still distinguish the individual teeth during slow rotation, this is no longer the case when it is rapid. Valentin*) <note>Gabriel Gustav Valentin (1810–1883), a German-Swiss physiologist known for his work on the senses.</note> has conducted detailed experiments on this. Among other things, he notes that if the widths of the teeth show only insignificant deviations, this causes no essential disturbance; whereas if, in a wheel of 160 teeth, 3 or 5 located immediately next to each other are 3 or 4 times as narrow as the rest, uniformity can no longer be completely achieved even at high speed.

Just as a disc with white and black sectors appears uniformly gray during rotation with sufficient speed, a surface with regularly alternating white and black squares appears uniformly gray from a sufficient distance. This can have a twofold cause: either that distances under too small a <term>visual angle</term> <note>The angle formed at the eye by the objects in the field of vision, which determines how large an image is on the retina.</note> can no longer be specifically perceived—in which case the phenomenon would depend on the <term>extensive threshold</term> <note>A spatial limit; the point where two points in space are so close they are perceived as one.</note>; or that the <term>irradiation</term> <note>A visual phenomenon where a bright object appears larger than a dark one of the same size because light "bleeds" over the edges in the eye's perception.</note> of the white squares at a very small visual angle causes them to flow into one another—in which case the phenomenon would depend on the <term>intensive difference threshold</term> <note>The threshold relating to the strength or brightness of the stimulus rather than its physical size.</note>. It is possible that both causes work together; nothing seems decided on this matter through the observations made thus far.

Let us cast a brief glance from these facts of <term>outer psychophysics</term> <note>The study of the relationship between external physical stimuli and sensory experience.</note> back to the significance they may gain for <term>inner psychophysics</term> <note>The study of the relationship between internal physiological (neural) activity and mental experience.</note>. If the stimulus is translatable into psychophysical movement, then the soul will also, despite the presence and play of psychophysical movement in an em-

...can remain in a state free of sensation and uniform, provided certain limits are not exceeded. The frequently observed circumstance—that the eye, regarding the intensity of light sensation, is always naturally above the <term>threshold</term> due to a weak internal excitation—gives rise to a particular <term>teleological</term> <note>Teleology refers to the idea that parts of a living being are designed for a specific purpose or function.</note> observation.

Should it first require a certain strength of external light stimulus to raise the internal movements (to which our sensation of light is linked) up to the threshold, then dimly lit and black objects would not be seen at all. Here, an effect similar to the "blind spot" of the retina would arise, which would undoubtedly be very disruptive. If, on the other hand, the eye were raised far above the threshold by internal excitation, then according to ***Weber’s Law*** <note>A principle stating that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note>, slight increases in light would no longer be clearly recognized. The "black" in our externally unstimulated eye, insofar as it represents a very weak degree of light, is therefore undoubtedly the most advantageous arrangement that could exist in the design of our sense of sight.

## XI. Detailed Information on the Magnitude and Dependency Relationships of Threshold Values in the Various Sensory Domains.

Absolutely fixed and universally valid determinations of the magnitude of the <term>stimulus threshold</term> <note>The minimum intensity of a physical stimulus (like light or sound) required for a person to perceive it.</note> and <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note> are not possible in any sensory domain, insofar as the <term>threshold value</term> <note>The point at which a stimulus or change becomes perceptible.</note> depends heavily on the external method of applying the stimuli and the state of the organs' sensitivity, which are highly variable factors. To this is added the difficulty of precisely determining the value at which a sensation or a difference in sensation begins. In the meantime, what was said on page 53 regarding the general measurement of sensitivity applies here as well. The determination of average values for common conditions on the one hand, and extreme values on the other—even if only approximate—remains of constant interest and often cannot be dispensed with. Furthermore, the dependency on circumstances is itself to be regarded as a subject of investigation.

The lower the threshold value, the greater the sensitivity under otherwise equal circumstances. Indisputably, given the design of the human organism, there is a limit that cannot be exceeded in this regard; whereas many circumstances—including abnormalities of constitution or organs, and all kinds of chance occurrences—can push the threshold higher. Therefore, all actually obtained threshold values are to be regarded only as upper limits, below which lies the "ideal" threshold, so to speak, which would be found under absolutely optimal conditions. The smallest threshold values, provided they are based on sound observation, therefore hold the greatest interest,

Most of these figures, however, will only be able to refer to the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The smallest detectable difference between two stimuli, also known as the "just noticeable difference."</note>, as little information is currently available regarding the <term>absolute stimulus threshold</term> <note>The minimum amount of energy required for a stimulus to be detected at all.</note>.

## 1) Intensive Threshold.

### a) Light and Color.

The fact that a stimulus threshold regarding <term>sensations of brightness</term> <note>How our eyes perceive the intensity of light.</note> cannot be captured in an experiment was discussed earlier on page 240. Regarding the difference threshold, the information collected to date was shared in the 9th chapter, and the following is the summary.

**Bouguer** found, through experiments with shadows—though it is questionable whether these involved movement or not—that the difference threshold was equal to 1/64 of the light's intensity; **Arago**, without using movement, found values between 1/131 to 1/151 across various individuals, and 1/48 to 1/131 with movement (cf. p. 172); **Volkmann**, through shadow experiments with various individuals during movement, found approximately 1/100 (cf. p. 149); **Masson**, through experiments with the <term>rotated disc</term> <note>A "Masson’s disk" is a white circle with a black segment that, when spun, creates a grey ring used to test the eye's ability to detect subtle changes in shade.</note> in various individuals, found 1/50 to 1/120 and beyond (cf. p. 152).

According to **Masson**, the value remains the same for different colors, but varies according to the eyes of different individuals.

In the experiments by which the above determinations were obtained, light or shadow surfaces of a certain extent and direct vision were used throughout. It is certain, however, that the difference threshold depends—at least up to certain limits—on the extent of the visible sizes, and behaves differently on the peripheral parts of the <term>retina</term> <note>The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.</note> than on the central parts.

In general, a small black area on a white background, or vice versa, disappears into the background more easily,
