### b) Sound Intensity and Pitch.

**Schafhäutl** <note>Karl Emil von Schafhäutl (1803–1890), a German polymath and acoustic researcher.</note> \*\*) conducted experiments on the limit of audibility of sound using suitable measuring devices. This sound was generated by the falling of a small pellet \*\*\*) from a measured height onto a rectangular plate made of ordinary mirror glass, which was held fixed at its nodal points by screws, while the ear was held firmly in a fixed position relative to the sounding plate. The horizontal distance from the center of the sounding plate where the pellet struck to the center of the opening of the ear intended to perceive the sound was 55 mm; the vertical distance was 74 mm; and the straight-line distance was 94 mm. "Experience has taught me," says the author, "that this is the best distance at which the ear reliably perceives the faintest sound that is still capable of affecting it." The essential result of these experiments (which were not described in detail) is stated by the author as follows:

> "In my attempts to determine the quantity of sound that is still audible to my ear, I have found that the sound produced by a cork pellet weighing 1 milligram falling from a height of 1 millimeter is, for my ear at..."

"Therefore, I do not hesitate to adopt the sound magnitude produced by the fall of a cork pellet weighing 1 milligram from a height of 1 millimeter as the <term>acoustic dynamis</term> <note>A term coined by Schafhäutl to represent a fundamental unit of sound energy or a "standard unit" for the threshold of hearing.</note>, which marks the average limit of sound magnitudes still audible to the healthy human ear under the influences of our civilization."

Undisputably, experiments with more significant sound magnitudes at a greater distance from the ear would be desirable, as naturally small disturbing influences and measurement errors lose their impact in such cases. It should also be considered that, according to the circumstances of the previous experiments, hearing could only occur perceptibly with one ear, whereas we generally use both ears for hearing.

Regarding differences in sound intensity, according to the experiments by **Renz** and **Wolf**, as well as **Volkmann** <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a German physiologist who collaborated closely with Fechner on psychophysics.</note>, mentioned on page 175, there appears to exist a much lower sensitivity than for differences in light intensities; sound intensities that are in a ratio of about 3 to 4 can still be reliably distinguished, though they become more uncertain as they come closer to one another from that point.

As for the pitch, there is a generally accepted lower limit for the absolute audibility of tones, which is usually assumed to be 30 vibrations (**Chladni** <note>Ernst Chladni (1756–1827), a pioneer in acoustics known for 'Chladni figures.'</note>) or 32 vibrations (**Biot** <note>Jean-Baptiste Biot (1774–1862), a French physicist who studied the speed of sound in solids.</note>) per second. Meanwhile, according to more recent experiments by **Savart** <note>Félix Savart (1791–1841), a French physicist known for his research on the limits of human hearing.</note> \*) using the rod-siren, a tone corresponding to 14 to 16 vibrations per second would still be audible, and he is inclined to believe that it—

it only depends on sufficiently lengthening the individual impressions to make even deeper tones audible, so that there is no actual limit in this regard. However, Despretz\*), who carefully repeated Savart’s experiments, contradicts his assertions with certainty and draws the following result: 

> » that it is currently not proven that the human ear can perceive and determine tones of fewer than 32 simple vibrations. « <note>In 19th-century acoustics, a "simple vibration" (*einfache Schwingung*) referred to a single back-and-forth movement, or a half-cycle. Therefore, 32 simple vibrations correspond to 16 modern Hertz (Hz), which is still widely considered the lower limit of human pitch perception.</note>

Savart was probably misled by the great intensity of his apparatus's tone, which indeed produced very strong tones, but ones that were no longer musical or determinable by their pitch; these would, accordingly, have the character of noise instead.

Indeed, if Despretz is correct, it was the noise produced by each individual strike of the rod siren on its own, heard *in continuo* <note>Latin: "continuously" or "without interruption."</note> due to the successive duration of the strikes, which gave the illusion of a tone.

Regardless of how the difference between Savart and Despretz is resolved, it would be absurd to assume no lower limit of tones for a human ear. A tone generated by vibrations lasting an hour could, of course, no longer be perceived by humans as a tone. Perhaps by beings organized differently; but certainly not by humans.

The audibility of tones seems to have not only a lower but also an upper limit.

Sauveur in the *Memoirs of the Academy, Year 1700* sets the upper limit at 12,400 vibrations per second. Wollaston believes that the voice of the bat and the field cricket forms the limit of the highest perceivable tones. From the lowest tones of the organ to the highest of the insects, the vibrations are said to be 600 to 700 times faster, which would bring the upper limit to 19,000 to 22,000 simple vibrations. Biot assumes only 8,192, Chladni 12,000, Olivier\*\*) 16,000, and Young 18,000 to 20,000 as the upper limit.

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the absolute limits of high-frequency hearing to the precision with which the human ear can distinguish between different musical pitches. It introduces 19th-century experimental data from physicists Wilhelm Weber and Charles Delezenne.</meta>

Previous findings regarding the sensitivity of the ear to pitch differences were not nearly as impressive. W. Weber <note>original: "Pogg. XIV. S. 398." This refers to *Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik*, Volume 14, page 398.</note> notes occasionally that under favorable circumstances, the ear can determine tones so accurately by ear alone—that is, without the aid of <term>beats</term> <note>A pulsing sound heard when two tones of nearly the same frequency interfere with each other.</note> and without taking averages—that the error never exceeds 1/4 of a <term>vibration</term> <note>In 19th-century physics, this usually refers to a "simple vibration" or half-cycle; 200 simple vibrations equal 100 Hz.</note> out of 200.

Delezenne <note>original: "Recueil des travaux de la soc. de Lille. 1827. p. 4." This refers to the *Collection of the Works of the Society of Lille*, 1827, page 4.</note> determined more than just the <term>just noticeable difference</term> <note>The smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note> from a pure <term>unison</term> <note>original: "Einklang"</note>, which had been the focus of previous studies; he also examined other <term>musical intervals</term>, such as the octave, the fifth, the major third, and the major sixth. It should be noted that this involves determining not just the difference between one tone and another, but the deviation of one pitch interval or ratio from another. Each pure interval between two tones played in succession represents a specific ratio; an "impure" interval represents a ratio that deviates slightly from it. However, the case where one determines the just-noticeable deviation from a pure unison can be seen as a special instance of the general case—namely, the instance where one determines the deviation from a "zero-difference" between two tones.

The experiments were conducted as follows. A string was stretched over two bridges on a <term>monochord</term> <note>original: "sonomètre"; a scientific instrument used to study the mathematical relationships of vibrating strings.</note>. The length of the string between the bridges was exactly 1147 millimeters, and it produced 120 vibrations per second. The string was divided at a certain point by a movable bridge placed underneath it, so that the two parts of the string produced tones forming one of the musical intervals mentioned above. The movable bridge was tapered to a sharp edge: it was positioned under the string in a way that did not increase its tension and was held in place by another sharp edge pressed against it. Delezenne first ensured the interval was perfectly pure. Then, the movable bridge was shifted slightly—by up to 4 or a few millimeters to the right or left—and the observer judged when a deviation from the purity of the interval became noticeable. At other times, without the observer being able to see, the bridge was adjusted until the interval seemed pure again, and the researcher then checked the extent of the error.

Although these experiments appear to have been conducted with great diligence and care, they unfortunately lack a truly exact methodology. Consequently, one cannot place too much confidence in the comparability of the figures obtained. It should therefore be highly desirable that these for the musi—

The following is the result of Delezenne's experiments.

When a <term>bridge</term> <note>A small wooden support (Steg) used to divide a string and change its pitch.</note> placed in the middle of a string 1147 millimeters long (which produced 120 <term>vibrations</term> <note>original: "Schwingungen"; in this period, a "vibration" often referred to a single swing of a pendulum, or half a cycle in modern hertz.</note> per second) was moved slightly, the <term>unison</term> <note>Two tones sounding at the exact same pitch.</note> of the two parts of the string was disturbed. It required very fine ears to perceive a difference between the two tones heard in succession when the bridge was moved only 1 mm from the center. In this case, one part of the string measured **1147 / 2 + 1** and the other **1147 / 2 — 1** mm; therefore, the ratio of their lengths and simultaneously of their vibration numbers was **1149 / 1147**. At a ratio of **1151 / 1143**, the difference was recognized even by completely unpracticed ears.

> "If the movable bridge is shifted by two millimeters to the right or left, the difference becomes noticeable to the least practiced ears, as I have confirmed with several people. If the displacement of the bridge is only one millimeter, one must have a sufficiently delicate ear to notice it immediately. The person subjected to this test closes their eyes, either to avoid being distracted by surrounding objects, or to remain unaware of the feigned or real movements of the bridge and thus avoid being biased toward the change they would see performed. A very delicate ear is therefore sensitive to this slight difference. Let us assume this to be the extreme limit of the sensitivity of the human ear, and let us calculate the ratios between these two sounds which differ so little. We shall see <note>original: "Si l'on déplace le chevalet mobile..."</note>

-> ( (1147 / 2) + 1 ) / ( (1147 / 2) — 1 ) = 1149 / 1145 = ( 81 / 80 )^0.2807 <-

> the best-organized ear is therefore sensitive to a difference of 4 vibrations out of 1149!! <note>original: "l'oreille la mieux organisée..."</note>"
> "To compare this interval to that represented by the <term>comma</term> <note>Specifically the syntonic comma (81/80), a very small interval used in music theory to describe the difference between certain tuned notes.</note> **81 / 80**, which we shall take as our unit throughout, we can say that the ear is barely sensitive to a quarter of a comma on the unison."
> "We have seen that a displacement of 2 mm was noticeable to persons who had never tried to compare sounds. — For the sounds compared in this way, we find the interval <note>original: "Nous avons vu..."</note>

### d) Temperature.

Regarding the magnitude of the <term>just noticeable differences</term> <note>The smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected by a person.</note> in temperature, E. H. Weber*) has shared some data. According to this, using the method of alternately dipping the hands into two vessels containing water of unequal warmth, one can—with great attention—still discover a difference between two temperatures with the whole hand that amounts to only 1/8 to 1/6 <term>degrees Réaumur</term> <note>The Réaumur scale is a temperature scale where water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 80 degrees. 1 degree Réaumur is equal to 1.25 degrees Celsius.</note>; however, he did not precisely determine the temperatures at which these differences are noticeable. I have found that in moderate temperatures, even smaller differences can be recognized, and that they vary greatly according to the baseline temperature. On this point, one should compare what was shared in Chapter 9, page 202 ff.

Regarding the degrees of heat and cold that are capable of inducing pain, the experiments and discussions by E. H. Weber can be read in the same treatise, page 571 ff.

### a) Sense of Sight.

...to produce a perceptible extension for sensation, a question that is certainly to be distinguished from: what fraction of the existing number <note>Fechner is referring here to the number of nerve fibers or sensory receptors.</note> is required to perceive one part of the general <term>visual field</term> <note>original: "Gesichtsfeld"; the entire area that can be seen when the eyes are fixed in one position.</note> as distinct from the rest, when it is stimulated differently from the rest. However, there is currently no way to decide that former question, and so I will set it aside here—even though it is actually the fundamental question regarding an <term>extensive threshold</term> <note>original: "extensive Schwelle"; the minimum spatial requirement for a sensation to be perceived as having size or width, rather than just being a single dimensionless point.</note>—only to return to it from a theoretical perspective in a later chapter, and instead turn my attention to the investigation of the extensive threshold in the following sense.

->*What are the smallest still-just-recognizable sizes, distances, and differences in size and distance?*<-

The task of determining the smallest recognizable distance essentially coincides with determining the smallest recognizable size, insofar as one can consider the diameter of any just-perceivable size as a just-perceivable distance between its <term>boundary points</term> <note>original: "Gränzpuncten"; the points defining the outer edges of an object.</note>; conversely, the just-perceivable distance can be seen as a just-perceivable size. However, experiments are divided into those where a point, a line, a thread, or a small surface was observed against an extensive uniform background, noting at what viewing distance—and therefore at what <term>visual angle</term> <note>original: "Gesichtswinkel"; the angle formed at the eye by the rays coming from the extremities of an object, which determines the size of the image on the retina.</note>—this small size was still recognizable or vanished; and those where two or more distant points, lines, threads, or small surfaces were observed against a given background, noting at what visual angle of their mutual distance a uniform merging occurred. The former experiments may be specifically designated here as those concerning the smallest recognizable sizes, and the latter as those concerning the smallest recognizable distances. The experimental conditions differ in that, in the former, <term>irradiation</term> <note>original: "Irradiation"; an optical effect where a bright object appears larger than its actual size against a dark background due to light spreading on the retina.</note>—which plays a very significant role in the outcome of the experiments—is considered from only two boundaries, whereas in the latter, it involves four boundaries.

Any size that is to be recognized by sight will always appear against a certain background, and thus be recognized only according to the degree of its difference from that background—

He notes that the phenomenon of irradiation affects these two types of measurements differently.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "extensive threshold" in visual perception, specifically how our ability to distinguish the size or separation of objects is linked to the brightness and contrast of those objects. It transitions into a specific critique of experiments conducted by the researcher Twining regarding the mathematical relationship between light intensity and perceived magnitude.</meta>

...whereby the question of the <term>extensive threshold</term> <note>The minimum physical size or spatial separation required for an object to be perceived.</note> for sight is connected to the question of the <term>intensive difference threshold</term> <note>The smallest change in the intensity of a stimulus—like brightness—that can be detected by the senses.</note>, a topic that was already addressed on page 256. A visible size is more easily distinguished at the same degree of extension the greater the relative difference in light is; on the other hand (at least up to certain limits), it is more easily distinguished at the same relative difference the larger the size is. Whether the background is black and the surface to be distinguished is white, or vice versa, this principle remains valid.

**Twining**\*) intentionally directed experiments toward determining a mathematical law in this regard. He determined at what distances an illuminating lamp caused black, round, regularly arranged spots on a white background—which received its light only from this lamp—to cease appearing as separate when the eye was placed at various distances from them. This led him to the law that, while the distances of the eye decrease in <term>geometric progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16).</note>, the corresponding lamp distances increase in <term>arithmetic progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers such that the difference between consecutive terms is constant (e.g., 2, 4, 6, 8).</note>\*\*).

If one now sets the illumination intensity $J$ as <term>reciprocal</term> <note>Inversely related; as one value increases, the other decreases.</note> to the squares of the lamp distances $L$, and the apparent diameters $D$ of the black spots as reciprocal to the eye distances $A$, one can substitute $\sqrt{\frac{1}{J}}$ for $L$ and $\frac{1}{D}$ for $A$. According to this, the expression of the law translates to the idea that equal ratios $\frac{D'}{D}$ correspond to equal differences $\sqrt{\frac{1}{J}} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{J'}}$. Such a law is not inherently probable, and the results from—

---

\*) **Twining**, *Enquiries concerning Stellar Occultations by the Moon and the Planets, — experiments upon Light and Magnitude in relation to Vision*, in American Journal of Science, July 1858. Vol. XXVI. [2]. p. 15.

\*\*) The author himself expresses the result of these experiments (p. 23) as follows: <note>original: Twining wrote the following summary in English.</note>
> "That while the distances of the eye diminish in a geometrical ratio, the corresponding distances of the light increase in a arithmetical ratio. In other words, the distance of the light is a logarithm of the linear magnifying effect."

> "One remarkable result of this law is that a small fractional change of a faint light possesses as great efficacy to balance a given magnifying effect as a large fractional change of a much brighter light."

Twining’s assumption that *A* is reciprocal to *D* is undeniably inadmissible because of the influence of <term>irradiation</term> <note>A visual phenomenon where a bright object appears larger than it is, "bleeding" into its darker surroundings, which complicates measurements of size and distance.</note>, which—as will be discussed shortly—cannot possibly be neglected under the conditions of these experiments. Therefore, despite the fact that the author's experiments (as shown below) align very well with the stated law, it is likely merely an empirical expression—whose general validity under different experimental circumstances remains doubtful—rather than a true law of nature. Nevertheless, these experiments are not without interest, insofar as they demonstrate that the <term>illumination intensities</term> <note>The amount of light falling on a surface.</note> at which the clear recognition of spots begins or ends increase in a very high ratio when a large <term>viewing distance</term> <note>The distance between the observer's eye and the object. The German text uses "Augenabstand."</note> is increased by a given proportion. Conversely, intensities increase in a much smaller ratio when a small viewing distance is increased by that same proportion. For instance, for the two largest viewing distances used by the author—107.29 and 134.11 English inches, a ratio of 4:5—the corresponding lamp distances were 29.5 and 15.5 English inches. This represents an intensity ratio of 1:3.62. In contrast, for the two smallest viewing distances he used—28.12 and 35.16 inches (also a ratio of 4:5)—the lamp distances were 131.6 and 110.5, which is an intensity ratio of only 1:1.119. In this observation, one will always be able to find a general point of reference.

The essential components of the apparatus used by the author consist of a box, blackened both inside and out and otherwise completely sealed, but which has a square opening on its front side. Light enters through this opening from one side while the observer looks in from the other; the illuminating lamp and the eye are positioned far enough to the side (on opposite sides of the opening) so as not to obstruct one another during illumination and viewing. On the back wall inside the box is a piece of paper with small, round, black spots, regularly arranged and equidistant from one another *), which receives the light and is the object being viewed. While the eye is placed at different distances from the back wall of the box in various experiments, the—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of visual perception from the previous page, moving from Twining’s specific experiments with lamp distances to a broader scientific analysis of irradiation and its impact on how we perceive small objects. ...visibility of small visible objects against a background is highly dependent on the effects of **irradiation** <term>irradiation: an optical effect where a bright object appears larger than it actually is because light spreads across the retina</term>. This influence must now be considered more closely. Here, we define irradiation as the physical spreading of light from the impression on the **retina** <term>retina: the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that functions like a camera's sensor</term>, which is dependent on optical aberrations and **diffraction** <term>diffraction: the slight bending of light as it passes around the edge of an object, such as the pupil of the eye</term>.

In all experiments concerning the smallest recognizable size or distance, one either decreases the size or distance to such a degree, or moves so far away from it, that—leaving irradiation aside—the image on the retina shrinks to a point or a line of entirely negligible diameter. Generally, until Volkmann’s recent treatise on irradiation \*), researchers have calculated the diameter of the smallest recognizable image or the smallest recognizable distance without regard for irradiation. However, Volkmann’s delicate experiments, the results of which follow below, have established beyond doubt that even in the best and most perfectly **accommodated** <term>accommodation: the eye’s ability to change its focus to see objects clearly at various distances</term> eyes, a noticeable and measurable spreading of the light impression occurs through irradiation. If one compares his data on the size of the **irradiation circle** <term>irradiation circle: the blurred area created by light spreading out from a single point of focus on the retina</term> during the clearest possible vision—be it with his own observations or those of others regarding the smallest recognizable sizes—one finds that the diameter of the irradiation circle not only takes on a very significant ratio to the diameter of the images calculated without regard for irradiation (or to the smallest recognizable distances), but generally exceeds them by a great deal. Consequently, the light impression must be considerably more extensive, but at the same time weaker due to this scattering, than the calculation for the smallest recognizable sizes would suggest.

Indeed, according to Volkmann’s measurements provided below, the edge of a silver thread appearing in **specular light** <term>specular light: a bright, mirror-like reflection of light from a surface</term> against a black background widens toward the black side by 0.0012 to 0.0032 \*\*) mm = 0.000532 to 0.001418 **lines** <note>original: "Lin."; a historical unit of measurement approximately equal to 1/12 of an inch</note> in the minimum and maximum among six persons with the best possible accommodation of the eye; and, if the thread is black against a bright...

Since, according to the remark made on page 252, the extent of **irradiation** <term>irradiation: an optical effect where light spreads from a bright area into a dark area on the retina, making the bright object appear larger</term> caused by physical circumstances cannot grow with the intensity of the light, the light of an intense point and a faint point is spread across the same spatial area; however, the light of the faint point can thereby be weakened until it is imperceptible against the background, while the light of the bright point remains noticeable.

If a point of light is not intense enough to still be distinguishable from the background by the **difference threshold** <term>difference threshold: the minimum difference in intensity required for the brain to perceive two things as different</term> at the center of the irradiation circle, it can no longer be recognized. If one uses a black point on a white background instead of the reverse, analogous considerations apply; the surrounding points of light spread out through irradiation and "overflow" the black point with light. This creates a spreading of the black point through irradiation while weakening its blackness, just as white points spread on a black background, as Volkmann discussed in more detail (in the previously cited work, p. 120 <note>original: "a. a. O." (am angeführten Orte)</note>) and supported with experiments.

Bergmann <margin>Henle and Pfeufer's Journal, 3rd Series, Vol. II, p. 93.</margin> observes that the points or lines used in experiments regarding the smallest recognizable sizes appear very pale at the greatest distance, such that the straining eye could easily confuse them with some light shadow. He also notes that whenever one gradually approaches a grid drawing of millimeter-wide black and white stripes from the distance where they were first recognized, the white gains in purity and the black in depth. These are circumstances easily explained by the fact that at distances greater than the distance of clear vision, the spreading of light increases due to optical aberrations.

The preceding, taken together, shows that the previous experiments on the smallest still-recognizable sizes and distances on the **retina** <term>retina: the light-sensitive inner surface of the eye</term> cannot be used to draw certain conclusions about the finesse of the spatial sense or the degree of **extensive sensitivity** <note>This refers to the sensitivity of the spatial aspect of perception, such as size and distance.</note>, as long as the question of how much irradiation contributes has not been clarified and this portion eliminated; and that the calculation of the size of the smallest images on the retina based on the size and distance of objects, as well as the judgment of the relationship in which these stand to the final elements of the retina, is illusory and erroneous insofar as irradiation is not taken into account. If the light source falls below this number, the objects must be significantly larger.

It can be calculated that the image of a 2 cm wide strip, at the stated distance from the eye, measures 0.9 mm on the **retina** <term>retina (Netzhaut): the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eyeball where images are formed</term>, which far exceeds the value of **irradiation** <term>irradiation: an optical phenomenon where a bright object appears larger than its actual size because light scatters within the eye</term> in accommodated eyes according to the above data (p. 272). If even larger objects become visible under weaker illumination, then the influence of size cannot depend on irradiation alone. However, more extensive experiments specifically directed at this subject, varying both size and absolute brightness, are still to be desired.

With all the foregoing, it is only claimed that previous determinations of the smallest recognizable sizes and distances, made without regard for irradiation, are not valid; it is not claimed, however, that there is no threshold of **extension** <term>extension (Extension): in this context, the spatial size or physical area covered by a stimulus</term> for the eye independent of irradiation. It may indeed be that the extension of an impression on the retina or skin could be reduced arbitrarily and still produce a sensation, provided a living nerve ending is struck and the impression exceeds the **intensive threshold value** <term>threshold value (Schwellenwerth): the minimum amount of energy or size required for a stimulus to be detected by the senses</term>; but this does not mean that this impression is truly perceived as something extended—that is, felt in such a way that a plurality of points are distinguishable within it—if the extension of the impression falls below a certain limit. Similarly, and essentially related to this, it does not mean that a distance can be arbitrarily small on the retina and still be perceived as a distance, since such a perception presupposes the distinction of two boundaries and thus also a plurality of points.

It is indeed an assumption now generally regarded as valid in the **physiology** of the **nervous system** that impressions are only distinguishable insofar as they are made upon different **sensory circles** <term>sensory circles (Empfindungskreise): a concept pioneered by Ernst Heinrich Weber, suggesting that the skin and retina are divided into discrete functional areas; to perceive two separate points, two different "circles" must be stimulated</term>, where "sensory circle" is understood to mean the end—or, in the case of branching, the collective ends—of a **primary nerve fiber** <term>primary nerve fiber (Primitivnervenfaser): an 19th-century term for an individual axon or nerve cell unit</term>. A sensory circle, whether belonging to an unbranched or a branched fiber, necessarily has a certain diameter,

<meta>This page continues the mathematical and experimental breakdown of Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann’s research on irradiation. Fechner is explaining how the size of the "irradiation circle"—the blur of light that expands the perceived size of an object—is calculated from the physical distance between micrometer threads and their appearance on the retina.</meta>

...mutual distance, one can calculate not only the diameter $2r$ of the **retinal image** <note>The image formed on the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.</note> of each micrometer thread, but also the distance $\epsilon$ of the axis of one wire from that of the other in the retinal image, setting aside the scattering caused by **irradiation** <note>The optical phenomenon where a bright object appears larger than a dark one of the same size because light "bleeds" into the surrounding dark areas.</note>; accordingly, through a simple observation for the case realized in the experiment—where the distance $\delta$ between the widened wire-images appears equal to the diameter $2\rho$ of a widened wire-image—the diameter of an irradiation circle is found to be $\frac{\epsilon}{2} - 2r$; namely, since $\epsilon = \delta + 2\rho$ and $2\rho = \delta = \frac{\epsilon}{2}$. Now, Volkmann found, in an average of 39 trials, a light distance = 0.207 mm, which appeared equal to a dark thread of 0.0445 mm width at a distance from the eye = 333 mm, according to which $\frac{\epsilon}{2} = 2\rho = 0.0085$ mm; $2r = 0.00499$ mm, and consequently $\frac{\epsilon}{2} - 2r = 0.0035$ mm. As a control, Volkmann conducted another 10 trials in such a way that he sought to make the distance between the threads appear twice as large as the diameter of the threads. According to the results of the previous trials, it can be calculated (p. 144) that this distance should amount to 0.328 mm, with which the mean result of 0.337 mm emerging from the 10 trials agreed noticeably; this proves that this experimental method deserves confidence.

The following points also deserve attention: Irradiation behaves differently in vertical and horizontal directions. When Volkmann viewed the wires in a horizontal position from the same distance as in the previous trials in a perpendicular <note>vertical</note> position, the image was indistinct to the highest degree, so that he had to use a weak **convex lens** <note>A magnifying lens used to correct farsightedness or assist in focusing on close objects.</note> to maintain the same **visual distance** of 333 mm, where, against a light background, an average of 10 observations yielded a diameter of the irradiation circle = 0.0047 mm, whereas (without glasses) in the perpendicular position it was only 0.0035 mm.

The specification of the 5 trial days for method *a* <note>Method *a* refers to observing dark threads against a light background.</note> regarding brightness yielded the following distances *D* for Volkmann between the micrometer threads at which apparent equality with the wire diameter occurs (the number attached below *D* signifies the number of trials):

1. Trial day (no details given) . . . D$_9$ = 0.1897
2. Day, cloudy weather . . . . . . D$_{10}$ = 0.2271
3. Day, bright sky . . . . . . . . . D$_{10}$ = 0.2153
4. Day, very bright sky . . . . . . D$_{10}$ = 0.2074

Heidenhain's trials according to method *b* <note>Method *b* refers to observing light threads against a dark background.</note> yielded on the:
1. Day (no details given) . . . . . D$_{20}$ = 0.111
2. Day, very bright light . . . . . D$_{20}$ = 0.153

A definite influence of the degree of illumination does not result from this.

# Specific Findings on the Smallest Discernible Magnitudes.

Even if, based on the preceding discussion, the current findings on the smallest discernible magnitudes and distances do not seem suited to yield pure results of any kind, they are nonetheless important, partly because they define a limit beyond which the eye's performance certainly does not reach, and partly because they hold practical interest; therefore, a compilation of these findings should not be unwelcome.

Unfortunately, this compilation reveals only a slight agreement between the results obtained by different observers. And since the precarious value that can be assigned to them would vanish entirely if the circumstances of the observation were not precisely specified, I am providing them as much as possible in the observers' own words.

Insofar as it is necessary to translate the **visual angle** <term>the angle formed at the eye by the light rays coming from the edges of an object; it determines how large an object appears on the retina</term> into magnitudes on the **retina** <term>the light-sensitive inner surface of the eye</term>, or vice versa, the following is assumed based on **Listing’s** <note>Johann Benedict Listing (1808–1882), a mathematician and pioneer in physiological optics.</note> findings: the distance from the intersection point of the primary rays <note>The "nodal point" where light rays cross before hitting the back of the eye.</note> to the retina is 15.1774 mm (6.735 **Parisian lines** <term>an archaic French unit of length; one line is approximately 2.25 mm</term>), and the distance from the **cornea** <term>the clear front window of the eye</term> is 7.4696 mm (3.315 Parisian lines); accordingly, for 1 second of the visual angle, a value of 0.00007357 mm or 0.00003265 Parisian lines is substituted.

The following statement from **Smith’s** *Optics* is found used most frequently, which I share here according to the French translation of his work (Vol. I, p. 40) available to me:

> "Dr. Hook <note>original: 'Le Dr. Hook nous assure...' — Referring to Robert Hooke (1635–1703), the English polymath who first proposed this limit for the human eye.</note> assures us that the most acute eye cannot clearly distinguish a distance in the sky, such as a spot on the body of the moon, or the distance between two stars, which subtends at the eye an angle smaller than half a minute <note>30 arcseconds.</note> (See his remarks on Hevelius's celestial machine, p. 8). If the angle is not larger, the stars will appear to the naked eye as a single star. I assisted at an experiment where one of my friends, who had the best eyes in the company, could barely distinguish a white circle on a black background, or a black circle on a white background or against the light of day, when it subtended at his eye an angle of less than two-thirds of a minute; or what amounts to the same thing, when its distance from the eye..."

Tobias Mayer*) <note>Tobias Mayer (1723–1762), a German astronomer known for his studies of the moon and visual acuity.</note> gives the result of several experiments as follows:

> The first experiments were conducted in a shaded location, with windows open but facing away from the midday sun; the objects were painted with India ink (called *Tusche* [in German]) on flat and very white paper. <note>original: "Prima experimenta facta sunt in loco umbroso, apertis fenestris a sole tum meridiano aversis; objectis atramento sinico, Tusche vocant, in charta plana et albissima pictis."</note> 1) A black, round point with a diameter of 1/4 **Parisian line** <term>an archaic French unit of length; one line is approximately 2.25 mm</term>, viewed by a myopic [near-sighted] eye but equipped with a suitable lens, could still be distinguished fairly well when the eye was 10 Parisian feet away. At a distance of 12 feet, it was seen unclearly, but at a distance of 13 feet, it had already completely vanished. — 2) A similar point, but with a diameter of 0.44 lines, was still visible when the eye was 14 3/4 feet away; however, at a distance of 17 feet, barely a trace of it appeared, just as it completely vanished when the eye was moved back to a distance of 18 feet. — 3) Another point with a diameter of 0.66 lines was still perceived at a distance of 24 1/2 feet, but with great difficulty and uncertainty at a distance of 26 feet, and when the eye was moved slightly further, nothing of it could be seen.

After recounting several more experiments with grid patterns, which will be discussed below, he adds:

> The points and figures used in the above experiments, even when illuminated by the summer midday sun—and thus very strongly lit—began to appear blurred at nearly the same distances as mentioned above; any discrepancy, if there was one, seemed to suggest sometimes greater distances and sometimes smaller ones when the experiment was repeated several times. <note>original: "Puncta et figurae, quae in superioribus adhibitae sunt... incipiebant confusa apparere..."</note>

This result—that the level of illumination has no influence on the recognition of the points—stands, of course, in decisive contradiction to the results of **Plateau's** <note>Joseph Plateau (1801–1883), a Belgian physicist who conducted extensive research on physiological optics.</note> experiments that follow below.

**Plateau** <note>Joseph Plateau (1801–1883), a Belgian physicist known for his research on visual perception and the physics of soap films.</note> \*) considered both color and the degree of illumination in his experiments. **Hueck** <note>Alexander Friedrich von Hueck (1802–1842), a professor of anatomy who studied the physiology of the eye.</note> \*\*) conducted experiments in the following manner: a clearly seen point is sharply fixed by a normally formed eye; the observer gradually moves away from the object until it disappears and the board on which the point or line is located appears completely blank.

> "From several hundred observations made by various individuals, it resulted that a white, non-glossy point on a black field disappears at a 10-second visual angle," which corresponds to 0.00033 **Parisian lines** <term>an archaic unit of length; approximately 0.00075 mm</term> or 0.00074 mm on the **retina** <term>the light-sensitive inner surface of the eye</term>. According to him, a white line on a black field is still seen at a visual angle of less than 2 seconds; on the other hand, the visual angle at which black points on a white field disappear was found to be 20 seconds. The former corresponds to 0.0000652 Parisian lines or 0.0001470 mm, the latter to 10 times this amount on the retina. Further details about the number of experiments and the degree of agreement obtained for the latter statement were not provided. Nothing was said about the lighting conditions during the experiments either.

<meta>This page continues Ehrenberg's account (quoted by Fechner) regarding experiments on the limits of visual perception, moving from general observations of groups to specific conclusions about the standard capacity of the human eye and the exact physical dimensions of the smallest visible objects.</meta>

observation continued attentively at the most varied viewing distances made it likely to me that there is a fairly fixed general limit for the **visual capacity** of the clear and healthy human eye, which must allow for a conclusion regarding the maximum power of **microscopes**. Following this, I conducted many observations to determine to what extent the differences between nearsighted <term>myopic</term> and farsighted <term>presbyopic</term> eyes influence the general expression of that power; I have frequently convinced myself that the common opinion—that nearsighted persons see more or more sharply than others—is unfounded. The result of my experience is twofold:

1) There appears to be a **standard capacity** for the human eye regarding the vision of the smallest parts, and deviations from this appear to be much rarer than is commonly believed.

We can only speak of those who are capable of seeing clearly at any distance at all. Among more than 100 persons whom I observed, those with the sharpest vision under ordinary conditions were not able to distinguish more than I saw myself; and those who considered themselves weak-sighted or farsighted were usually able to see the same things I saw. They merely required more specific instructions and, especially when seeing with the naked eye, usually a slightly closer or further distance of the object from their eye than I did.

2) The smallest square size <note>The original uses the symbol ☐ to denote a square area.</note> usually reachable for the natural human eye is **1/36 of a Paris line** <note>The "Paris line" was a standard unit of length before the metric system, roughly 2.25 millimeters. Therefore, 1/36 of a line is approximately 0.06 mm.</note> in diameter, both for white color on a black background and for black color on a white or light background. It is still possible, through the greatest light condensation and intense attention, to recognize sizes between 1/36 and 1/48 of a line, but only without sharpness and with doubt. *)

This is the limit of the power of the natural human eye for colored bodies, which anyone can easily test, as I have—

<meta>This page continues Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg’s experimental observations (as quoted by Fechner) regarding the limits of human vision, specifically detailing how to verify these limits and how factors like distance and motion affect perception.</meta>

I have observed, can be verified by placing very fine black dust—for example, from dry ink, India ink, and the like—onto very white paper. One then picks up the smallest of these particles with a very fine point and places them on a glass micrometer <note>A glass slide etched with a very fine scale used for measuring microscopic objects.</note>, which directly indicates at least ¼ of a line <note>A "line" (Linie) was a traditional unit of length, roughly 1/12 of an inch or 2.25 mm. Thus, 1/4 of a line is approximately 0.56 mm.</note>. Sunlight and lamp light also easily allow one, with or without a mirror, to view these black particles on the glass micrometer against a bright background. Bodies that are smaller than those specified cannot, despite all effort, be recognized individually, but can still be seen by the naked eye when arranged in a simple straight line. Furthermore, if several of these are situated in close proximity and in multiple rows, they create a collective impression on our eye and deceive us into thinking we see a single, larger body or surface *). The usual distance that good eyes observe when they wish to recognize these smallest bodies, I found through measurement to be 4–5 inches <note>The "Zoll" or inch used here is likely the Prussian inch, roughly 26.1 mm.</note>, sometimes 6 inches, which the latter is the usual distance for the very sharp-sighted. Nearsighted <term>myopic</term> persons rarely bring these same objects closer than 4 inches, even more rarely 3 inches, etc., and at that point usually become equal to the others. Someone whose sharpest visual range is 4 inches cannot increase their **visual capacity** by bringing the eye closer to the object, but instead feels pain and sees unclearly. Once one has fixed <note>To "fix" an object here means to successfully focus the gaze upon it.</note> the object, one can move it significantly further away without losing sight of it. I myself cannot see ¼ of a line at a distance of 12 inches, black on white; but if I have sought it out at a distance of 4–5 inches, I can move it away up to 12 inches and still see it clearly. This phenomenon is based on the well-known power of the eye to **accommodate** <note>The biological process by which the eye changes optical power to maintain a clear image or focus on an object as its distance varies.</note> itself somewhat to distance. Often one also recognizes small objects at a greater distance as soon as one's attention is drawn to their location, or if they move. Similar phenomena are provided by a hot air balloon in a clear sky and a ship on the horizon; one sees them easily as soon as one is attentive

*) "I am accustomed to recognizing the very fine eyelashes <note>original: 'Wimpern'; in this context, Ehrenberg refers to **cilia**, the hair-like structures used by microscopic organisms for movement.</note> of infusoria <note>A historical term for a wide range of microscopic organisms found in water.</note> in this way. As soon as they are moved, they form a small apparent surface which is visible; but as soon as they are at rest, their fineness is often so great that the **visual capacity** cannot reach them even with the **microscope**."

made, but the ability for rapid orientation <note>Original: "Orientirung." In this context, it refers to the ability to quickly locate and distinguish a specific object within one's field of view.</note> depends on habit and mental acuity, without allowing for a conclusion about visual power in general. If someone is more vividly stimulated by visual impressions than another, they orient themselves more quickly, but they do not, for that reason, see more than someone else who, because they receive these impressions less vividly, orients themselves more slowly. I often employ the method of first searching for very small objects with a magnifying glass when I want to recognize them with the naked eye, perhaps to change their position with a fine point. This phenomenon is also only relevant for orientation regarding the location of the objects, and it only facilitates the speed of this orientation. Nearsighted <term>myopic</term> eyes always orient themselves more easily because they are less distracted, as their field of vision is smaller.

Finally, a higher power of the absolute visual capacity of the human eye must likely be added: the recognition of luminous particles. It is well known that small bodies shining in the dark always appear much larger than they are; these—whether they are self-luminous or reflecting light—can easily affect the human eye at sizes much smaller than ¼ line <note>A "line" (Linie) was a traditional unit of length, roughly 1/12 of an inch or 2.25 mm. Thus, 1/4 of a line is approximately 0.56 mm.</note>, depending on the intensity of the light. I have never had the opportunity to observe self-luminous sizes that were of such a truly small diameter that I could identify a limit in this regard. .... Metallic luster, which is a very powerful reflection of light, can—according to my observations made on gold dust—be recognized with the naked eye in ordinary daylight down to ¹⁄₁₀₀ of a line <note>Approximately 0.02 mm.</note>, which is twice as far as colors.

«—» The situation is different with lines. Opaque threads of ³⁄₁₀₀ line in thickness can be recognized against the light with the naked eye. Spider silk measures ⁸⁄₁₀₀₀ to ¹⁄₁₀₀ lines; silkworm threads measure ²⁄₁₀₀. The latter are doubled in the cocoon. «»

When one converts the size of ³⁄₁₀ lines at a 4–6 inch <note>The "Zoll" or inch used here is likely the Prussian inch, roughly 26.1 mm.</note> eye distance—which Ehrenberg gives as the limit of visual power for non-linear particles—into lines on the retina <note>The light-sensitive inner surface of the eye.</note>, one finds 0.0039 to 0.0025 lines. This is strikingly larger (10 times as large) than Hueck's 0.00033 lines, despite both results being derived from a large number of experiments, and it also exceeds Mayer's result by more than double. Likewise

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the limits of human vision, specifically focusing on the "visual angle"—the minimum size an object must occupy in our field of vision to be seen. It transitions from Ehrenberg’s general observations to a comparison of experimental data from various researchers regarding how contrast and shape influence these thresholds.</meta>

Hueck and Ehrenberg differ in that, according to Hueck, black dots on a white background require a larger visual angle <note>The angle formed at the eye by the object being viewed; it determines the size of the image projected onto the retina.</note> than the reverse, whereas according to Ehrenberg, both are equivalent.

A difference in circumstances may lie in the fact that Ehrenberg's experiments were conducted by observing tiny particles from a very close distance, while those of Mayer and Hueck used dots of significant dimensions from a greater distance; both of the latter allowed the observer to gradually move away from the point of clearest vision until the dot disappeared. Now, while according to Mayer's experiments the distance makes no significant difference, since his distances amounted to 12 feet and more, a much greater proximity—such as occurred in Ehrenberg's experiments—could indeed make a difference; this remains to be investigated more closely.

In cases where it is necessary not merely to recognize the existence of a visible size, but also to determine its shape, a larger visual angle is required. According to Hueck *), a square of 1.2 lines <note>Original: 1.2''. In this context, the double prime likely refers to "lines" (Linien), a historical unit roughly 1/12 of an inch, rather than inches.</note> in diameter was still recognized as a square at a distance of 11 feet—that is, at a visual angle of 2' 35''. Likewise, a slanted line of 1.5 lines <note>Original: 1.5'''. The triple prime explicitly denotes "lines" (1/12 inch).</note> in length was still recognized as slanted at 13 feet, under an angle of 2' 45''. Hueck was able to read printed text (Double Medium <note>A traditional size of printing type, approximately 28 points.</note>) with a letter width of 1.5 lines and spaces within the letters of 0.5 lines at a distance of 13 feet, using spectacles suitable for his eyes.

Bergmann **) found "that short lines were seen less far than longer lines of equal width."

E. H. Weber ***) remarks: "According to my experiments, a white line on a black background can be seen from more than three times as great a distance as an equilateral square of the same width as the line; the brightness of the illumination of the line and a highly contrasting background can increase this distance even further."

## Specific Findings Regarding the Smallest Recognizable Distances.

The experiments on this subject have been conducted in various forms, and the results vary accordingly.

-> α) Two distant points or squares. <-

The report by **Smith** regarding two stars has already been shared on page 280.
**Volkmann** \*) allowed the flame-images of two lights to fall upon a small thermometer bulb with a diameter of 0.15 inches <note>Original: Zoll. At the time of writing, a German "Zoll" was roughly equivalent to a British inch.</note>; the lights were 4 inches apart from each other and 8 inches away from the bulb.... Using eyeglasses, he recognized the complete separation of the small images in the glass up to a distance of 20 1/2 inches; at 26 inches, the images appeared to be touching in the middle but were still clearly double.... One of his friends repeated the experiment and recognized the images up to a distance of 37 inches. To fully recognize the doubleness <note>The quality of seeing two distinct objects; "Duplicität" in the original.</note> without glasses, Volkmann had to approach within 12 inches of the glasses.

According to **Hueck** \*\*) two black dots on a white background, which were 0.45 lines <note>Original: 0.45'''. A "line" (Linie) is a historical unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch.</note> apart, merged with one another at a distance of 10 feet <note>Original: Fuss.</note> from the observer, which gives a visual angle <note>The angle formed at the eye by the distance between the two points; it determines how far apart the images fall on the retina.</note> of 1' 4'' for their distance. Lines that were just as far apart gave the same result.

**E. H. Weber** \*\*\*) adds to his determination of ratios (shared on page 287) regarding the distance at which white lines and squares on a black background vanish from sight:

> "On the other hand, two white, equilateral squares on a black background, separated by a black gap as wide as the squares themselves, are still distinguished as two from a distance nearly equal to that from which two white lines on a black background—being just as wide as those squares and separated by an equally wide black line-shaped space—are still distinguished as two."

### $\beta$) Two Distant Threads.

Volkmann*) stretched two spider web threads in a parallel direction and at a distance of 0.0052 lines <term>line: a historical unit of measurement, often the "Paris line," roughly 2.25mm</term> next to each other, and found that he recognized them as double at a distance of 7 inches, but not further. The most keen-sighted among his friends recognized this duality <note>original: "Duplicität"</note> at a distance of 13 inches. Two black parallel lines on a white background at a mutual distance of 0.016 lines were recognized by Volkmann with the help of glasses at a distance of 27 inches.

Valentin**) was still able to distinguish two lines when their images on the retina <note>The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.</note> were separated from each other by only 0.0009 lines.

Hueck found the same result for lines as he did for points (cf. p. 282).

### $\gamma$) Striped and Checkered Figures.

Tobias Mayer***) describes experiments in diffused daylight as follows:

> 1. A striped figure <note>original: "Figura striata"</note>, whose black strokes, equal to the white ones placed between them, were 0.36 Paris lines wide, when viewed directly at a distance of 11 feet <note>original: "pedd. 11"</note>, already appeared somewhat blurred, so that it was barely possible to distinguish the white intervals from the black ones. At a distance of 12 feet, all distinction between the stripes was gone. Certainly, it was felt only with the greatest difficulty. When the eye was moved a little further away, the entire figure simulated the same color, appearing almost grayish <note>original: "cineritium"</note>.
> 2. A figure likewise striped, but whose black stripes were twice as thick as the white ones—for the width of the latter was 0.2 lines and the former 0.4 lines—began to appear blurred when the eye was at a distance of 9 or 10 feet.
> 3. At the same distance, another striped figure, whose white lines were twice as wide as the black ones—namely, in the reverse order of the preceding—ceased to be seen distinctly; the width of the white stripes was 0.4 lines, and the black lines were 0.2.

### Behavior of the Peripheral Parts of the Retina in the
### Recognition of Smallest Sizes and Distances.

In the information provided so far, the perception of visible sizes and distances was assumed to be via the most clearly seeing, central part of the <term>retina: the layer at the back of the eyeball that triggers nerve impulses</term>. Toward the periphery, the recognizability of both sizes and distances decreases, but by no means in the same proportion in all directions. Observations on this matter have been provided by *Hueck*, *Volkmann* with *Hüttenheim*, some by *Bergmann*, and the most detailed by *Aubert* with *Förster*, in which, among other things, it is specifically demonstrated that the impossibility of distinguishing two points at some distance from the <term>visual axis: the line of sight passing through the center of the pupil to the fovea</term> <note>original: "Augenaxe"</note> can by no means be blamed on optical aberrations of the eye; and that different

### **Distance Differences (Visual Judgment).**

Regarding the precision of visual judgment (the ability to estimate sizes by eye), E. H. Weber*) provides the following data:

> "I cut a sheet of common writing paper of the most usual size into eight equal parts and drew a straight and uniform line on each part, ensuring at the same time that all lines were of equal thickness and darkness, but of different lengths. The shortest line was 100 millimeters; another longer line was 100 1/2<sup>mm</sup>, and another longer one was 101<sup>mm</sup>. ## b) Sense of Touch.

Regarding the magnitude of the just noticeable distance between <term>compass points<note>A common tool in these experiments was a mathematical compass; the experimenter would touch the skin with one or two points to see if the subject could tell the difference.</note></term> on the skin, E. H. Weber, as is well known, first conducted investigations and found that this distance varies exceptionally across different parts of the skin. He found the sensitivity to be greatest at the tip of the tongue, where at a distance of only ½ <term>Parisian line<note>An obsolete unit of length, approximately 2.25 millimeters.</note></term> the compass points were still recognized as double; followed by the <term>volar side<note>The palm side of the hand or the sole of the foot.</note></term> of the final segment of the finger (1 Parisian line), the red part of the lips (2 lines), the volar side of the second segment of the finger (2 lines), etc.; and the lowest sensitivity at the upper part of the spine and on the middle of the upper arm and lower leg (30 Parisian lines). His table of observations is given most extensively in his *Collection of Programs* (*Progr. coll.*) p. 50 ff., condensed more briefly in the articles <term>Sense of Touch</term> and <term>Common Sensation<note>German: "Gemeingefühl." A term used at the time to describe general bodily awareness, including temperature, pain, and internal sensations.</note></term> in Wagner's Dictionary p. 539, and reproduced in his *Treatise* (*Abhandl.*) in the reports of the Leipzig Society 1853, p. 85 ff. \*) at which latter location he provides various supplements regarding the general conception of the <term>spatial sense<note>The ability to perceive the spatial characteristics of a stimulus, such as size or distance between two points on the skin.</note></term> and the methods for determining its fineness. Weber's observations were first confirmed by Allen Thomson (in *Edinb. Med. and Surg. Journ.* no. 116), later by Valentin (*Textbook of Physiology* 1844, Vol. II, p. 565), and finally by Czermak (*Physiological Studies* or *Reports of the Vienna Academy* XV, p. 425; XVII, p. 563; Moleschott, *Researches*, p. 183), and were expanded in several respects by the latter.

Lichtenfels has published very interesting findings in the academy reports, showing that the use of chloroform and anesthesia greatly increases the just noticeable compass-point distances on the skin.

## Perception of Time and Movement.

When two impressions are made too quickly after one another, they blend into a single uniform sensation, and one can ask how large the interval between two impressions must be in order to still be able to perceive them as distinct. 

A pure experimental answer to this, for a reason analogous to that regarding the extensive <term>spatial threshold<note>The minimum physical distance between two stimuli required for them to be perceived as separate (e.g., two points on the skin).</note></term>, cannot be given. For, just as every impression has a <term>circle of irradiation<note>The area around a point of stimulus where the sensation "spreads" or is felt, even if not directly touched.</note></term> around it, every impression leaves behind an <term>after-echo<note>Also known as "persistence of sensation"; the phenomenon where a sensation lingers after the physical stimulus has ceased.</note></term>. If the after-echo left by the first impression is still strong enough when the second occurs so that the difference from the second does not reach the intensive <term>difference threshold<note>The minimum amount by which a stimulus must change in order for the difference to be detectable.</note></term>, then one impression must blend uniformly with the other. 

One can ask whether the impossibility of perceiving two impressions occurring too quickly after one another as distinct depends solely on this circumstance. On this point, nothing has been decided by experience, and it is difficult to decide with certainty. However, by analogy to spatial relationships, it is probable...

The question at hand is relevant, among other things, to experiments involving a rotating disk with white and black sectors. While a white sector passes by, the impression increases; while a black sector passes, it decreases. Is the appearance of uniformity merely linked to the fact that the difference between the minimum and maximum does not reach the intensive <term>difference threshold<note>The "just noticeable difference," or the smallest change in stimulus intensity that a person can detect.</note> that exists for calmly observed light impressions? Or is the appearance of uniformity promoted by the fact that the minimum and maximum of the impression occur so quickly after one another that we cannot keep the two apart in time? Consequently, could the difference be larger than in a calmly observed impression without endangering the appearance of uniformity?

It seems to me that there is some possibility of deciding the first question based on an experiment, provided that a few other data points have been determined beforehand.

### XII. Parallel Law to Weber's Law.

It is a fundamental question, to which we have been led during the substantiation of <term>Weber's Law<note>A historical psychological law stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, and which will have to be considered more closely here: whether and to what extent the sensitivity to differences runs parallel to the sensitivity to absolute stimulus magnitudes; specifically, whether the modification of sensitivity to stimuli, which arises through the influence of the stimuli themselves, also involves the sensitivity to differences between them.

A white disc on black paper becomes covered, upon sustained observation, with a gray veil that grows ever darker up to certain limits—a proof that the sensitivity to light is blunted <note>German: *abgestumpft*. In modern terms, this refers to sensory adaptation or "fatigue."</note> by its own influence, to which enough other proofs can be added. After fatigue from carrying or lifting loads, on the other hand, a load is felt to be much heavier, according to which the sensitivity...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on sensory perception and sensitivity, specifically how the body reacts to stimuli like light and weight when in a state of fatigue or previous exertion. The text picks up mid-word from the previous page's discussion on sensitivity.</meta>

...sensitivity for weights is shown to be increased through the prior effect of those weights. In that case, a larger light stimulus is required, while here, a smaller load is needed to be perceived as equally strong.

The question arises: will the just-noticeable—or generally equally-noticeable—difference in light or weight appear increased or decreased along with this change? Or will the fatigued organ still sense the same difference in physical impact as strongly as it did without the fatigue?

At first glance, it might seem quite natural that if each of the two stimuli is perceived as weaker or stronger on its own, their difference would also be perceived as weaker or stronger. However, since <term>Weber's Law</term><note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> has taught us that when two stimuli are truly weaker or stronger, the difference is still perceived just as strongly as before—provided that the difference has weakened or grown in the same proportion as the stimuli themselves—the altered impression of stimuli caused by internal factors could possibly have the same result as a real, objective change in the stimuli. Consequently, the difference would still be perceived just as strongly.

Indeed, what does it mean <term>psychophysically</term><note>Psychophysics is the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations and perceptions they evoke.</note> to say that the sensitivity to a stimulus is altered? If a fixed relationship exists between psychophysical activity and sensation, it can mean nothing other than this: a different magnitude of stimulus is required to evoke the same impression—that is, the same psychophysical activity. 

If <term>Weber's Law</term> is understood fundamentally—applying not merely to the relationship of sensation to the external stimulus, but rather to the relationship of sensation to the internally triggered <term>stimulus-effect</term>, then the result must be the same whether the externally acting stimulus is weakened or its internal effect is weakened. This is because even the weakening of an external stimulus is only relevant by virtue of the weakening of the internal effect. In short, the dulling of the stimulus-effect internally and the weakening of it externally must have the same result: they leave the difference for sensation unchanged, provided they affect the components in the same proportion.

To be sure, if <term>Weber's Law</term> were not [transferred] from the external stimulus to the internal effect—that is, the [psychological]... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the page breaks.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether changes in absolute sensitivity (due to factors like fatigue) affect the ability to distinguish between two stimuli, specifically focusing on the transition from "outer" psychophysics (stimulus to sensation) to "inner" psychophysics (neural activity to sensation).</meta>

...psychophysical activity were not transferable, the <term>difference in sensation</term><note>The subjective perception of the gap or distinction between two different stimuli.</note> would not remain constant when the relative difference or the ratio of the somehow-measured internal effects remains constant, but would instead change according to some function of their absolute difference. In that case, this conclusion of the law could not be transferred from the external to the internal. Thus, one sees that the question at hand here indeed gains a fundamental significance for our doctrine. It is the question of one of the bridges between <term>external and internal psychophysics</term><note>External psychophysics studies the relationship between physical stimuli and sensation; internal psychophysics studies the relationship between the physiological/neural processes and sensation.</note>.

Even apart from this, the question of the extent to which a dependency exists between absolute sensitivity and <term>differential sensitivity</term><note>The capacity to perceive differences between stimuli; also known as "difference sensitivity."</note>—and whether this is essential or not—is of important concern. The decision on this matter is very well suited to allow us to take a step forward in clarity within the hitherto still-obscure doctrine of <term>irritability and excitability</term><note>In 19th-century physiology, these terms referred to the capacity of tissues (like nerves or muscles) to respond to stimuli.</note>.

I wish to call the law—which is the main subject of this question, insofar as it is to be regarded as a transfer of Weber’s Law from the external to the internal—the **parallel law** of Weber’s, or simply the **parallel law**. It may be expressed as follows:

> When the sensitivity for two stimuli changes in the same proportion, the sensation of their difference nevertheless remains the same.

Equivalent to this is the following statement:

> When two stimuli are both perceived as weaker or stronger than before, their difference still appears just as great to the sensation as it did previously; provided that one would have to modify both stimuli in the same proportion to maintain the former absolute strength of sensation for both.

Connected naturally to the question of whether a temporal change in the <term>absolute sensitivity</term><note>The minimum intensity of a stimulus required for it to be detected at all.</note> of one and the same sensing organ essentially carries with it—or has dependent upon it—a change in its differential sensitivity, is the question of whether a spatial difference in absolute sensitivity (that is, a difference in absolute sensitivity between different body parts) essentially carries with it a difference in their differential sensitivity—

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s investigation into the relationship between absolute and differential sensitivity, specifically moving from how sensitivity changes over time (temporally) to how it varies across different locations on the body or sensory organs (spatially).</meta>

...leads to [the law] having it dependent on itself; and thus the question of our law transfers from the temporal to the spatial. The various parts of the <term>retina</term><note>The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eyeball; original: "Netzhaut."</note> demonstrably possess a different <term>absolute sensitivity</term><note>The minimum amount of stimulus energy needed for a person to detect its presence.</note> and a different <term>differential sensitivity</term><note>The ability to detect a change in or a difference between two stimuli; original: "Unterschieds-Empfindlichkeit."</note> to light. Do they proceed essentially in parallel in this regard? The same loads are perceived as having different weights on different parts of the body; do we also recognize given <term>weight differences</term><note>The threshold at which one can tell that two objects have different masses.</note> more easily with those parts of the body that perceive the same weights as heavier?

It does not seem to me that such questions have been clearly posed at all, much less that they have been answered clearly and decisively; yet they are fundamental questions.

Indisputably, if <term>differential sensitivity</term> can remain the same despite a temporal difference in absolute sensitivity, it will also be able to hold true for spatial differences, and vice versa. Thus, validations of the law on the temporal side also speak in favor of its existence on the spatial side and vice-versa—though one cannot evade the task of proving it specifically on both sides.

In general, the validity of the law under certain circumstances cannot yet be safely inferred for its validity under other circumstances. Even if absolute and differential sensitivity do not depend on each other essentially—that is, everywhere, necessarily, or by the fundamental laws of their nature—there may still be circumstances that act to increase or decrease both at once. Therefore, to prove that both are not essentially dependent on each other, it is not so much a matter of showing that one **always** remains constant when the other changes, but rather that they can change just as well without and against each other as they can with each other in the same sense. In other words, the <term>parallel law</term><note>Fechner’s "Parallelgesetz," which suggests that changes in absolute sensitivity (due to fatigue or location) do not necessarily disrupt the proportional relationship required to perceive a difference between two stimuli.</note> exists under certain conditions, even if it does not exist everywhere.

It is important not to overlook the condition of the law: that the sensitivity for both <term>stimuli</term><note>Plural of stimulus; any energy or event that evokes a sensory response; original: "Reize."</note> must actually change in the same proportion if the constancy of the sensation difference is to be expected. Suppose, for example, an identical stimulus hits two spots on the retina that were initially equal—

This difference must grow as the gap in absolute sensitivity increases, just as if the sensitivity of both remained constant while the <term>stimulus</term><note>Any physical energy, such as light or weight, that evokes a sensory response; original: "Reiz."</note> striking one area increased while remaining constant for the other.

All questions and relationships discussed here regarding <term>intensive sensations</term><note>Sensations that vary in magnitude or strength, such as brightness or loudness.</note> apply equally to <term>extensive sensations</term><note>Sensations that involve spatial dimensions, such as the perceived length of a line or the size of an area on the skin.</note>. Here too, one can ask: are given <term>differences in extension</term><note>The ability to distinguish between two different lengths or sizes; original: "Ausdehnungsunterschiede."</note> felt most easily when and where the extensions themselves appear largest? And does the <term>just noticeable difference</term><note>The smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect; original: "eben merkliche... Unterschied."</note> in extension thus run parallel to the perceived extension itself?

All of this shall be dealt with in the following, insofar as there are experiences available. To be sure, these do not yet offer the desired consistency and completeness required to state a general, simple, and elegant result. However, one can say in general that an essential dependence between absolute and differential sensitivity is directly negated by the following verification of the parallel law in the field of <term>weight experiments</term><note>Studies where subjects lift different weights to determine the thresholds of their perception.</note>.

Furthermore, the validation of <term>Weber’s Law</term><note>The rule that the change in a stimulus needed to produce a noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> itself seems impossible without the inclusion of the parallel law; it is, so to speak, inextricably linked with its validation. This is because <term>irritability</term><note>The physiological capacity of a sense organ to respond to a stimulus; original: "Reizbarkeit."</note> or absolute sensitivity must necessarily change during experiments due to the continuous or repeated and varied influence of stimuli. It does not seem that a validation of Weber’s Law through a scale of various stimulus intensities could succeed unless its applicability to the internal effect—its parallel law—also held true.

I consider this indirect argument to be quite compelling. In the meantime, it does not exclude the requirement for more direct proofs, of which I shall list below what is available to me.

<summary>Fechner argues that the Parallel Law is essential to Weber's Law, as it explains how we can still perceive consistent stimulus ratios even when our baseline sensitivity (irritability) fluctuates during an experiment.</summary>
<keywords>absolute sensitivity, differential sensitivity, Parallel Law, Weber's Law, intensive sensations, extensive sensations, irritability, psychophysics</keywords>
