### 1) Weight Experiments.

A 32-day, one-handed series of experiments (June and July 1858) involving 32 . 8 . 64 = 16,384 lifts was carried out using one and the same <term>main weight</term><note>The baseline weight used for comparison; original: "Hauptgewicht."</note> *P* = 1000 grams and two <term>additional weights</term><note>The small increments added to the main weight to test if the subject can detect a difference; original: "Zusatzgewichten."</note> *D* = 40 and 80 grams, which were alternated from one day to the next. These were performed under the standard conditions specified on page 97, except for the varied duration during which a weight was held aloft. Specifically, the following four <term>lifting durations</term><note>The amount of time the weight is held in the air during a trial; original: "Hebungszeiten."</note> of 1/2, 1, 2, and 4 seconds were employed. On each of the 32 experimental days, 64 lifts were performed with the left hand followed by the same number with the right hand for each of these four lifting durations; thus, each day consisted of 8 . 64 = 512 lifts.

In every instance involving the 4-second lifting duration, a strong sensation of <term>fatigue</term><note>Physical exhaustion or muscle tiredness; original: "Ermüdung."</note> in the hand occurred, because the main weight of 1 kilogram had to be held suspended for so long. I perceived no such fatigue with the shorter lifting durations, even at two seconds (to which I directed my attention specifically). Now, if this fatigue had an influence on <term>differential sensitivity</term><note>The ability to detect a difference between two stimuli; original: "Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit."</note>, it would have to become noticeable in the <term>correct cases</term><note>The number of times the subject correctly identified the heavier weight; original: "richtigen Zahlen."</note> *r* and the <term>hD-values</term><note>A statistical measure used by Fechner where *h* represents the precision of observation and *D* is the difference between stimuli; these values serve as a mathematical proxy for sensitivity.</note> derived from them (according to page 112 ff.), which provide the measure of this sensitivity when *D* is held constant. 

Indeed, one might expect the duration of the lift to exert an influence on differential sensitivity in general; for even when fatigue is not clearly felt, a longer lifting time must surely demand more strength and consequently cause more strain than a shorter one. However, no such influence is evident from my experiments. For the four main cases, I obtained the following summed correct cases *r* (for *n* = 2048 in the specific figures) and the following values for 32 *hD* in total for both *D*’s (and 64 *hD* in total for the left and right hands), which are proportional to the differential sensitivity at the various lifting durations. It should also be noted that each of the four lifting durations served as the start and the end of an experimental day an equal number of times*).

The previous result was obtained incidentally during a series of experiments conducted for other purposes. To further increase the influence of fatigue caused by the duration of lifting even more than in the previous series, I recently (in January and February 1859) conducted another series under normal conditions (aside from the lifting duration) specifically directed toward this purpose, using two heavier <term>main weights</term><note>The standard weights used for comparison, denoted as P.</note>. Unfortunately, for reasons stated below, this series remained a fragment; however, the result of this fragment deserves mention as it reinforces results obtained elsewhere.

In total, this fragment comprises only 16 × 64 = 1024 lifts, distributed over 8 days, each consisting of 2 sections of 64 lifts. These were performed consecutively each day using only the left hand, whereas I usually alternate between the left and right hands. Two <term>main weights</term> (*P*) were used = 1500 and 3000 grams, alternating every two days; the <term>difference</term> (*D*) was in both cases 0.06 *P* <note>Meaning the difference between the weights was 6% of the total mass.</note>. For every two consecutive days, the same *P* and *D* were maintained, but from one day to the next, the experimental conditions were switched between the following:

a) Duration of each individual lift: 1 second; interval between each pair of lifts: 5 seconds (these being the usual standard times).

b) Duration of each individual lift: 4 seconds; interval between each pair of lifts: 3 seconds.

Thus, in condition (b), the time the weight had to be held suspended was four times as long, and the rest period between pairs of lifts was shorter by a ratio of 3 to 5 compared to condition (a).

The swinging of the weights <note>Fechner used a specific exercise of swinging heavy lead weights to induce "violent fatigue" in his muscles before testing his ability to perceive weight differences.</note> does not only fatigue the muscles, but simultaneously excites the entire organism. This was evidenced by a tremendously increased pulse, which was always so fast and faint immediately after completing the swinging that I was usually unable to count it; however, a few times I found it to be at 150 beats per minute or even higher. On the other hand, the lifting trials with the vessels of 1 kilogram weight under normal circumstances—during the approximately one hour before the violent fatigue procedure or without subsequent fatigue—by no means had the same increasing influence on the pulse. On the contrary, among 29 experimental days in the current and an adjacent series where I determined the pulse immediately before and immediately after the trials (in the same body position and with the same arm posture), the pulse was more frequent before the trials than after them 21 times; the average was 87.8 before and 85.2 after. This decrease may perhaps depend on the slow, uniform rhythm of the procedure, and a faster rhythm might have yielded a different result.

The following experiences support the suspicion that an excitement, indicated by an increased pulse rate, exerts an enhancing influence on the sensitivity to differences <term>Unterschieds-Empfindlichkeit: The capacity to distinguish between two nearly identical stimuli; the higher the sensitivity, the smaller the difference a person can detect.</term>: During the previous experimental series, my pulse was very variable from day to day. Given the very uniform lifestyle I lead, this could likely only result from the fact that the daily repeated violent fatigue procedure extended its influence across the entire duration of the experimental series, albeit in a variable manner. Unfortunately, as the consideration of the pulse only occurred to me later, I neglected to determine and record it in the earlier parts of the series; however, this was done in the final 14 days of the series. ...was higher than in the previous series; also, the **fatigue operation** was applied not only to both arms together, as in the previous series, but also unilaterally to each arm individually, and the results were compared. The entire experimental setup was as follows.

On each experimental day in the morning, after an initial **pulse count** for 1 minute, the session began with 4 two-handed sets of 64 lifts each; then the pulse was counted again for 1 minute; then one arm alone was fatigued; and then 2 two-handed sets of 64 lifts were performed, in exactly the same manner as those before fatigue; then the other arm was fatigued in the same way; then again 2 two-handed sets were conducted; then both arms were fatigued together, and once more two such sets were conducted. After each set, the pulse was always counted again, but each time only for ½ minute, and the tallying of the cases <note>The "cases" refers to the recording of correct and incorrect weight identifications (*r* and *f*).</note> was only performed before the new fatigue operation, so that the two related sets after each fatigue are interrupted only by the ½ minute pulse count.

In total, therefore, 4 sets of 64 were conducted daily without fatigue, and 6 after fatigue. The 4 sets before fatigue made up the beginning, and the 2 sets after two-handed fatigue made up the conclusion of each experimental day; between these two occurred the 4 sets after unilateral fatigue. Here, the arms were alternated in such a way that, if the left arm was fatigued first on one day, this would occur with the right arm on the following experimental day.

The interval between the fatigue and the start of the lifting of the vessels <note>The "vessels" (*Gefässe*) were the standardized containers Fechner used to hold the weights during discrimination trials.</note> always amounted to only the half-minute of the pulse count, plus a few extra seconds for putting away the lead weight or weights and transitioning to the vessels. The fatigue itself was carried out as follows.

In the case of unilateral fatigue, a <term>lead weight</term> <note>original: "Bleigewicht"</note> of 9½ pounds customs-weight <note>A "Zollpfund" (customs pound) was standardized at 500 grams, slightly heavier than the traditional English pound.</note> was lifted slowly according to the counter for 4 seconds from a fully lowered position to the horizontal of the shoulder height and lowered again for 4 seconds. The arm was stretched out in front of me, not to the side. This was repeated until the lift could no longer be completed; then there was a ½ minute pause, and fatigue was resumed until it could no longer be completed; this was done 5 times in a row, each time with a ½ minute interval. ...fatigues <note>original: "müdungen", the conclusion of the word "Ermüdungen" from the previous page</note> (fractions), I count as a single **fatigue operation**. The slowness of the lifting served the purpose of increasing the **pulse rate** less, while the repetition aimed to accumulate the fatigue. The number of possible **lifts** decreased during these 5 **fatigue fractions** of the same fatigue operation due to the accumulating fatigue—sharply from the first to the second, but only slightly during the following fractions. The left hand could perform considerably fewer lifts than the right, especially from the beginning of the **experimental series**, but gradually approached the same level over the course of the series; practice <note>Fechner uses "Uebung" to describe the "practice effect," where a subject's performance improves simply through repetition of the task.</note> also made itself felt in other ways. The simultaneous fatiguing of both arms occurred in exactly the same way as that of one arm, except that two weights of 9 1/4 lbs. each were lifted at the same time. Since the left hand was weaker than the right, the limit for lifting with both arms was always set by the predominant fatigue of the left, as immediate sensation revealed.

   It might be of some interest to specify the conditions observed during these fatigues, which were carried out quite methodically and in a comparable manner on all days; I also have cause for some remarks in this regard below. One can see that the results before and after fatigue do not differ in any significant way, which means that the **parallel law** <note>The parallel law in psychophysics suggests that sensitivity to differences remains relatively constant even when the overall threshold of sensation changes due to factors like fatigue or adaptation.</note> is well-confirmed.

On the other hand, the values 8 *hp* and 8 *hq* <note>In Fechner’s formulas, *p* and *q* represent constant errors related to the spatial position (p) and the temporal sequence (q) of the weights being compared.</note> underwent highly significant changes due to fatigue (*hp*, as usual, in a negative direction), the details of which I must omit here, as the report and discussion could not be presented without great complexity.

I believe I must mention only the following point as unexpected. Since, generally speaking, one perceives a load to be heavier than usual after fatigue, it was to be expected that after one-sided fatigue, this would also manifest one-sidedly. Consequently, in the sections following one-sided fatigue of the left hand, *hq* would show a change in a positive sense, and after one-sided fatigue of the right, in a negative sense, compared to the sections without fatigue. Indeed, this change was expected to be strongest on the days when the fatigue of the respective hand occurred before that of the other—so that a previous fatigue of the other hand had not yet left a counter-effect—and furthermore, strongest in the first portion (half) of the section following the fatigue (after a 1/2 minute interval). However, the investigation of this portion yields the result that *hq* changed in a positive sense in both cases, both after one-sided fatigue of the right and the left, though incomparably more so after fatigue of the left than after fatigue of the right. Even after the bilateral fatigue that formed the conclusion, the *hq* of the first portion shows a change in a positive direction compared to the non-fatigued state, though less so than after one-sided fatigue of the left, and more than after one-sided fatigue of the right. This, in my opinion, is to be interpreted as follows: Fatigue generally had a universal influence of such a kind that *hq* increased in a positive direction; this was intensified by the one-sided fatigue of the left and diminished by that of the right. What that general influence is based upon is unknown; however, the sense of that increase and this decrease actually corresponds to what was to be expected from the outset.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on sensitivity, specifically comparing experimental data from E. H. Weber regarding the distinction between the ability to perceive differences and the absolute magnitude of sensation across various parts of the body.</meta>

To consider whether areas with greater absolute sensitivity also possess greater difference sensitivity <note>Difference sensitivity (Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit) refers to the ability to detect a small change between two stimuli, whereas absolute sensitivity (absolute Empfindlichkeit) here refers to how "heavy" or "intense" a single stimulus feels on a specific part of the body.</note>, one can examine the experiments of E. H. Weber. This involves comparing the results he obtained at specific body parts using the method of just noticeable differences <note>original: "Methode der eben merklichen Unterschiede"</note> *) with those he obtained at the same parts using the method of equivalents <note>original: "Methode der Aequivalente"</note> **); the former method relates to difference sensitivity, while the latter relates to absolute sensitivity.

When a stack of 6 silver taler coins <note>original: "Speciesthalern." These were large silver coins used by Weber as convenient standardized weights for his tactile experiments.</note> was placed on the following parts on both sides of the body, the weight difference was perceived when the following number of coins was removed from one side, thus representing the just noticeable difference:

| | |
|---|---|
| Palmar surface of the fingers | 1 |

One can see that there is not the slightest correspondence between the two scales. The just noticeable difference on the fingers and the sole of the foot is the same, yet the weights perceived as equal on both parts relate to each other as 4 to 10.4. Conversely, the weights perceived as equal on the fingers and the back of the head are almost the same, while the just noticeable difference relates as 1 : 4.

### **2) Observations in the field of light sensation.**

In the field of light sensation <note>Lichtempfindung: The psychological experience of perceiving light and color.</note>, we still completely lack direct experiments regarding the extent to which the parallel law <term>Parallel Law: The hypothesis that a person's absolute sensitivity (the lowest intensity they can detect) and their difference sensitivity (their ability to distinguish between two slightly different intensities) increase or decrease at the same rate.</term> is valid. However, there are many facts available that relate to this question, which shall be discussed here. The questions are: whether and how these facts align with the law, to what extent they serve to confirm it, and what explanations they receive through it.

First, one might be inclined to use a well-known fact against the parallel law—a fact already touched upon in the chapter on Weber’s Law, but whose further discussion was postponed until now. By staying in the dark for a long time, one gains the ability to see in the dark; by staying in the light for a long time, one loses this ability. But what does it mean "to see in the dark"? It means to distinguish a light that differs only slightly in its physical intensity from the darkness of the night. For in fact, this is not merely a matter of an absolute impression, but of a difference; since even the "darkness of night" has its own photometric <note>Photometry is the science of measuring light as it is perceived by the human eye.</note> value. It would seem, then, that the fatigue of the eye caused by light stimuli also blunts the sensitivity to differences.

Although the fact itself is notorious and requires no detailed proof, I will compile a few instances here as an insertion, showing how this phenomenon appears in particularly striking or interesting forms.

> "Buffon relates that an officer in a prison, where light could only rarely enter from above, was able to see mice after only a few months, as long as food was being handed down to him. When he was set free after several months, he had to get used to the light very slowly. A man who had been imprisoned for 33 years could see the smallest objects at night, but nothing during the day. (Ruete, *Ophthalmology*, after Larrey, *Memoirs of Military Surgery* <note>original French: "Mém. de Chir. méd."</note> Vol. I. p. 6)."

V. I myself, and older people in general, remember quite well that in the past, one used to be satisfied with a <term>Tallow light: A candle made from rendered animal fat, which produced a dimmer and flickering light compared to later oil lamps or gaslight.</term> for evening illumination at the family or writing table. Now, after brighter lamp lighting has become common, this is considered a "ruiner of the eyes"; one is no longer able to see by it without exertion.

I have been told the following about a factory that was set up so that part of the work was performed by the workers at home. The previous, poorer lighting in the factory was replaced by a brighter one. It was not long before the workers demanded a return to the previous poorer lighting, because they were no longer able to get by with the ordinary weak lighting they could provide for themselves at home.

Aubert, in his *Contributions to the Knowledge of Indirect Vision* <note>Original: "Beitr. z. Kenntniss des indirecten Sehens." Hermann Aubert (1826–1892) was a physiologist known for his work on vision and adaptation.</note> *), remarks the following:

> "If one is in a heavily darkened room for days, one estimates it to be just as bright as a room perhaps ten times brighter was previously estimated. I myself have experienced a striking example of this. When, in my 14th year, I had to stay in a room so darkened because of the measles for over 8 days that those entering fumbled around in it as if in the pitch dark, it seemed very bright to me after a few days; and as boredom plagued me greatly, I reached for a fairly small map with fine script; I could see the colors quite well here and read the fine script everywhere as well as I usually could under ordinary daylight illumination. I also brought books to my bed, but was never caught with them, for those entering did not see the book at all, even if they were just a few..."

All these experiences seem to speak directly against the validity of the <term>parallel law: Fechner’s proposition that the sensitivity to differences between stimuli remains proportional to the overall sensitivity of the organ.</term> in the field of light sensation; in that, through the dulling <note>original: "Abstumpfung." This refers to the sensory adaptation where the eye becomes less sensitive after exposure to a stimulus.</note> to the light stimulus, the sensitivity to light differences is simultaneously shown to be weakened. For as noted, the recognition of faint glows or low-light objects in the dark is nothing other than a distinction of these from the dark background; and this no longer occurs with a dulled eye.

But one easily sees that this deviation from the parallel law occurs under quite analogous conditions as the deviation from <term>Weber's Law: The principle that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</term> at its lower limit. Just as one or both components approach black, both Weber’s Law and the parallel law cease to be valid. However, we do not claim the validity of the parallel law within wider limits than those of Weber's Law.

The only questions will be: 1) whether a reason can be found for the lower limit of the parallel law corresponding to that of Weber's Law; 2) whether the deviation for higher degrees of light disappears just as it does with Weber's Law.

Both can, in my opinion, be answered in the affirmative. As far as the first is concerned, I view the subject from the following perspective.

The external light stimulus dulls the effect of the external light stimulus; but the <term>internal black: original "Augenschwarz." Fechner’s term for the "intrinsic light" or "dark light" of the retina—the sensation of a gray background that exists even in total darkness.</term> of the eye increases relatively little in darkness; thus, the relative difference in the effect of an external light compared to it becomes smaller. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s analysis of visual sensitivity. He is arguing that the "parallel law"—which suggests our ability to distinguish differences stays constant relative to our sensitivity—remains valid even when our eyes are "dulled" by bright light or disease. He introduces the concept of "eye-darkness" (idioretinal light) to explain why we struggle to see in the dark after being exposed to brightness.</meta>

The darkness of the eye can only deepen to certain limits—as is indeed the case in the afterimages of bright objects—but it can never be extinguished. Even in cases of "black cataract" <note>original: "schwarzen Staar." A historical medical term for amaurosis, a condition where the eye appears healthy but the patient is blind, often due to nerve damage or brain issues.</note>, where the strongest external light no longer makes an impression, darkness is still perceived; indeed, under certain circumstances, it seems that colors can still be seen. It stands to reason that the retina, the nerves, and other parts that conduct the stimulus to the brain can become paralyzed or impenetrable due to many causes, so that the external stimulus causes little or no internal excitation, without the central parts—upon whose excitation the sensation of the eye-darkness <note>original: "Augenschwarz." This refers to the subjective sensation of darkness, which is not a "nothingness" but a positive sensory state of the visual system even in total absence of light.</note> depends—suffering significantly as a result.

If the internal "eye-light" is not significantly weakened by this dulling <term>Abstumpfung: A reduction in sensory sensitivity or responsiveness, similar to modern concepts of sensory adaptation or a raised threshold.</term>, or at least weakened to a much lesser degree than the external impression, then this must act as a relative brightening of the eye-darkness while the light impression remains the same. In the case of "black cataract," which can be viewed as the highest degree of dulling, even the strongest impression can no longer be distinguished from the eye-darkness because no impression is being made anymore, while the internal eye-darkness still persists; just as through very dark glasses, the difference between lights disappears for our perception at the same time as the lights themselves.

If this explanation is to be valid, one must demand confirmation in the following conclusion: those same people who, due to dulled irritability <note>original: "Reizbarkeit." In 19th-century physiology, this referred to the capacity of an organ or tissue to respond to a stimulus.</note>, see poorly in the dark or in twilight—that is, they distinguish poorly—must be able to distinguish just as well as those with normal sensitivity if the light impression of the components is strong enough that the brightness of the eye-darkness can be considered negligible by comparison. That this is indeed the case can be supported by positive facts, which appear all the more proving as they were published without reference to or knowledge of the present theory.

> "Only in a few cases, where the disease had a long duration or was of great intensity, did a weakness of vision also emerge during the day. <meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of visual pathology and spatial perception into a new chapter regarding the laws of sensory "mixtures." Fechner moves from discussing simple changes in intensity to more complex changes in the quality of a stimulus.</meta>

case. <note>This sentence completes a thought from the previous page regarding specific instances of sensory change.</note> It was always a matter of to what extent the **sensation** increases or decreases, begins or vanishes, when a **stimulus magnitude** <term>stimulus magnitude (Reizgrösse): the physical measurement of a stimulus, such as the intensity of light or the weight of an object.</term> undergoes an increase or a reduction, under the assumption that what is added or taken away is of the same quality as the stimulus magnitude being increased or decreased; thus, the stimulus undergoes no change in its nature through the addition or reduction. However, among all conceivable cases where a stimulus undergoes an increase or a reduction—or any change at all—the case where the added or subtracted part is of the same nature as that to which it is added or from which it is withdrawn is merely the simplest one. But, for example, the stimulus of a white light can change not only by increasing or weakening the intensity of all **color rays** <note>original: "Farbestralen." In 19th-century physics, light was often described as composed of individual rays of specific colors that combined to form white.</note> in the same proportion, but also by adding colored light to the white, or by withdrawing this or that color ray—or a mixture of color rays that is not white—from the white color mixture. And as is easy to see, the same can be applied to color mixtures other than white, to mixtures of tones or sounds, to smells, and to substances that excite the sensation of taste. For the sake of brevity, we will generally designate the phenomena depending on such changes as *mixture phenomena* <note>original: "Mischungsphänomene"</note> in contrast to the earlier ones, which we call *homogeneous* <note>Homogeneous here refers to "same-kind" changes, where only the quantity of the stimulus changes, not its type or color.</note>, and in discussing them we will primarily stick to the example of colors.

It is easy to see that, since mixture phenomena no longer concern purely **quantitative** but also **qualitative** changes of the stimulus, one should expect not merely quantitative but also qualitative changes in sensation, as experience indeed shows to be the case. Our task will be to bring these under **viewpoints** of measurability that are connected to those that have found application for quantitative changes.

In general, we find the following:

When two simple or even compound stimuli *A, B*, each of which is capable of awakening a simple sensation of a particular kind, *a, b* respectively—for example, two colors—are in such a mixture or general combination...

<summary>Fechner introduces "mixture phenomena," distinguishing between changes in stimulus quantity (intensity) and changes in quality (such as mixing different colors or tones). He proposes that these qualitative changes can be measured using the same psychophysical principles applied to quantitative ones.</summary>
<keywords>stimulus magnitude, sensation, mixture phenomena, homogeneous phenomena, qualitative change, color rays, psychophysics, measurement</keywords>

--- Page 345 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of simple sensory intensity to the "mixture phenomena" introduced on the previous page. Here, Fechner defines the "mixture threshold" and explains how it relates to his earlier work on stimulus and difference thresholds.</meta>

presented to perception in such a way that a simple impression of them arises once again, this resulting impression—this resulting **sensation**—generally corresponds neither with the impression *a* that *A* would have produced on its own, nor with *b*, which *B* would have produced; however, depending on whether *A* or *B* predominates in effect, or if the effects of both remain in balance, the resulting impression can approach impression *a* or *b* more closely. It may also be the case that neither impression appears to predominate over the other, as is the case, for example, with complementary colors <note>original: "Complementärfarben." These are pairs of colors that, when combined, cancel each other out by producing a grayscale color like white or black.</note> that complete each other to form white, or with yellow and red flowing together to form orange. If we begin by allowing *A* to act alone, the admixture of *B* must first reach or exceed a certain magnitude before the deviation from pure *a* becomes noticeable; and vice versa regarding *b*, if we add *A* to *B*. And if we begin by letting *A* and *B* act together in such a proportion that neither *a* nor *b* appears predominant, then *A* or *B* must first be increased in a certain proportion so that the resulting impression appears to approach the character of *a* more than that of *b*.

In general, regardless of the simple stimulus or the composition of stimuli—and thus the resulting impression—from which we may start, if we either add more of another simple or composite stimulus or take away something from one of the stimuli, the added or withdrawn portion must exceed a certain magnitude so that the simple or resulting impression appears qualitatively changed compared to before.

These are relationships that, in the context of mixture phenomena, lead us back to the concept of the **threshold** <term>threshold (Schwelle): the boundary at which a physical stimulus becomes strong enough to be perceived by the mind.</term>, which we can briefly contrast here as the **mixture threshold** in opposition to the **homogeneous threshold** <note>The "homogeneous threshold" refers to the point where a stimulus of the same kind is increased in intensity, whereas the "mixture threshold" involves a change in the quality or composition of the stimulus.</note> considered earlier in the case of homogeneous phenomena.

Looked at more closely, the homogeneous stimulus threshold and the difference threshold in our earlier conception are only the simplest special cases of the more general case of the mixture threshold. Indeed, if a stimulus *B* is added to a stimulus or a stimulus mixture *A*, and one asks: at what value of *B* does the addition begin to [be perceived] as such—

<summary>Fechner introduces the "mixture threshold," explaining that a certain amount of a new stimulus must be added to an existing one before a qualitative change in sensation is perceived. He argues that his previous concepts of stimulus and difference thresholds are merely specific, simplified versions of this broader mixture threshold.</summary>

to be recognized or to allow a difference against the mere effect of *A* to become perceptible, then among all possible magnitude values that *A* can have in this regard, we can also imagine the case where *A* is zero; then we have the case of the ordinary homogeneous **stimulus threshold** <term>stimulus threshold (Reizschwelle): the minimum intensity at which a stimulus becomes perceptible</term>; no less can we imagine, among all possible qualities that *A* can have, those which are identical to *B*; then we have the case of the ordinary homogeneous **difference threshold** <term>difference threshold (Unterschiedsschwelle): the smallest detectable difference between two similar stimuli</term>.

Now let us assume the case where the addition of a stimulus *B* to stimulus *A* produces a just noticeable change—or a change noticeable to a certain degree—in the impression *a* corresponding to the mere *A*; the question then arises whether, if *A* is increased or decreased in a given proportion, *B* must also be increased or decreased in the same proportion to produce an equally noticeable change in *a*. If this should be the case for any arbitrary quality of *A* and *B*, we would have here, in addition to the previously mentioned generalization of the fact of the threshold, also a generalization of **Weber’s Law**, which represents only that case of the general law where the difference between *A* and *B* is vanishingly small.

Investigations into this matter are still lacking; however, I have conducted some experiments myself <gloss>*)</gloss>, from which I conclude that, at least for small additions of color ($= B$) to white ($= A$), the law is valid within similar limits, but also with analogous restrictions, as Weber’s Law.

One can easily produce just noticeable **glimmers of color** <term>glimmers of color (Farbenscheine): faint tints of color perceived on a neutral white background</term> on white, either by means of colored pigments or by positioning a piece of colored glass at an angle against a window onto a sheet of white paper. always possible to increase the darkening of the eyes through [tinted] glasses to the point where a colored shadow, visible to the naked eye, disappears; and on the other hand, I myself previously found <note>original: "*)" referring to *Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik*, Vol. 50, p. 465.</note>, and the same was found again in newer experiments by Helmholtz, that the impression of every color, whether homogeneous or mixed, approaches white at high intensity.

The deviation from the law at the lower limit could, however, be just as much an illusion, based on a reason analogous to the corresponding deviation from **Weber's Law** in homogeneous phenomena. If I view a colored shadow on white with the naked eye and then place a glass so dark before my eyes that the white of the background approaches the blackness of the closed eye, I have indeed weakened the color and the external light entering the eye in the same proportion; but the blackness of the eye—which, being colorless, represents a low degree of white light <note>Fechner refers here to "intrinsic light" or the "Eigenlicht" of the retina, the sensation of light or grayness one perceives even in total darkness.</note>—has not been weakened along with it; thus, the excess color now has a smaller ratio to the white than before and must therefore become less noticeable.

The reason for the law's upper limit is unknown.

In reality, strictly speaking, we will rarely deal with entirely homogeneous phenomena, and thus not with a completely pure <term>stimulus threshold (Reizschwelle)</term> <note>The minimum intensity at which a stimulus is first perceived.</note> or <term>difference threshold (Unterschiedsschwelle)</term> <note>The smallest detectable difference between two stimuli.</note>, the very simple <term>Weber's Law</term>, but rather in general with the more general case of the <term>mixture threshold (Mischungsschwelle)</term> or the **law of mixtures**; yet homogeneous phenomena can be approximately produced; the consideration of the simplest cases, even if only approximately producible, is for now the most important and will therefore remain our primary focus later on, especially since few investigations yet exist regarding the lawful relationships of mixture phenomena.

Even if one allows the simplest <term>spectral color (Spectrumfarbe)</term> <note>A pure color found in the light spectrum, like those in a rainbow.</note> to fall into an otherwise darkened eye and asks what intensity it must have to be recognized, one is dealing not with a pure <term>stimulus threshold</term>, but with a <term>mixture threshold</term>, because one

one is actually asking here what intensity the spectral color must

that in the first case, one is dealing with a very low intensity, 
and in the latter case—where one speaks simply of white—with 
a high intensity of the white or the color-indifferent mixture 
to which the color is added. Indeed, one finds that in the first 
case, the black appears just as black (only nuanced by a trace of 
color) as the white appears white (only nuanced by a trace of color) 
in the latter case, when the added color just becomes noticeable.

Therefore, **ultraviolet** would undoubtedly be perceived more 
easily—that is, at a lower intensity—than is currently the case, 
if it did not have to appear as an addition to the weak white 
already present in the eye.

The question of whether and how a phenomenon of mixture 
changes when all <term>stimulus components (Reizcomponenten)</term> 
which contribute to the <term>mixed sensation (Misch-Empfindung)</term> 
increase or decrease in the same proportion is, of course, itself 
only a specific question subordinated to the general question: 
how does the mixed sensation turn out and change in general 
when the stimulus components stand in any arbitrary ratio and 
change?

To bring this question into a clear perspective, three main 
cases seem to hold as points of reference: 1) when stimulus *B* 
becomes large enough that, when added to *A*, it just 
noticeably changes the quality of the mixed impression compared 
to sensation *a* alone; 2) when *B* becomes large enough that the 
influence of *A* just disappears, and the impression is no 
longer noticeably different from pure sensation *b*; and 
3) when *A* and *B* balance each other so that the impression 
is found to be no closer to *a* than to *b*. Between these 
three <term>threshold cases (Schwellenfälle)</term> necessarily fall 
all variations that can arise through the mixing of *A* and *B*. 
The goal would now be to find laws that represent these 
<term>threshold values (Schwellenwerthe)</term> and the variations 
of sensation falling between them as a function of the mixing 
ratio of the stimuli; but so far, nothing is available on this

...of homogeneous <term>threshold values (Schwellenwerthe)</term> <note>The "threshold" is the point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to be consciously perceived.</note> can only ever remain an approximation through experimentation; this seems to apply even more so to the **mixture thresholds**.

An important distinction must be made among the **mixture phenomena**, depending on whether the <term>stimuli (Reize)</term> that produce the mixed impression strike the sensory organ already mixed themselves—as is the case when compound colors strike the eye, or mixtures of noises or tones strike the ear, just as happens in ordinary seeing or hearing—or whether the stimuli strike the sensory organ separately, and their effects combine into a mixed impression only through the mediation of the sensory organs themselves. This latter case occurs when different colors fall on <term>corresponding spots</term> <note>Points on the two retinas that, when stimulated, produce the sensation of a single location in space.</note> of both eyes, or different tones fall separately into both ears. We shall briefly distinguish these two as **conjunctive** and **disjunctive** mixed impressions.

Indeed, experience teaches us that with two eyes or two ears, one can obtain mixed impressions from separately acting stimuli that correspond to those obtained when the stimuli arrive already mixed in the same eye or ear, even though the anatomical and physiological mechanisms upon which this relies are unknown. However, the nature of disjunctive impressions depends on more complicated relationships and can be co-determined by secondary conditions in more varied ways than conjunctive ones. Specifically, the **conjunction** of two light impressions *A* and *B*, differing in intensity or color, on the same spot of the retina can only ever occur in one way; but the **disjunction** of these stimuli on corresponding spots can happen in infinitely different ways. For example, zero might act on one eye and *A + B* on the other; or *A* on one and *B* on the other; or half of *A* on one and *B* plus half of *A* on the other, and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of disjunction, various ratios of the stimuli on both retinas can lead to interactions with neighboring impressions that cannot occur in the case of conjunction on the same retina. Experience has taught that differences in the resulting mixed impression can depend on these variations between conjunctive and disjunctive mixed impressions, according to which the distri- <note>The text cuts off here at "Verthei-", likely "Vertheilung" (distribution).</note>

<summary>Fechner defines the difference between "conjunctive" mixtures (stimuli arriving already mixed at a single sensory organ) and "disjunctive" mixtures (stimuli arriving at separate but corresponding organs, like the two eyes). He notes that disjunctive mixtures are far more complex because the stimuli can be distributed between the two organs in infinite proportions.</summary>

<margin>/</margin> *The Little Book of Life After Death* <note>original: *Das Büchlein vom Leben nach dem Tode*; this refers to Fechner's popular 1836 work which explored his philosophical views on the immortality of the soul, contrasting with his more rigorous scientific writing here.</note>

<summary>This page is the modern library catalog and digital title entry for the first volume of Fechner’s seminal work, "Elements of Psychophysics," originally published in 1860.</summary>
